n: Susurluk crash exposed Grey Wolves gunman working with police and an MP
rank: deputy chief of Istanbul police; member of parliament
d: Abdullah Catli, a leader of the Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist militant group, was working alongside Turkish police and a member of parliament while on Interpol's wanted list for murder and drug trafficking. This came to light when their Mercedes crashed near Susurluk, Balikesir province, on 3 November 1996. In the car with Catli were Huseyin Kocadag, deputy chief of the Istanbul police, and Sedat Bucak, a True Path Party MP and village-guard clan leader. Parliament set up an inquiry on 12 November 1996. Its chairman Mehmet Elkatmis issued a 350-page report in April 1997 concluding that state bodies had used the Grey Wolves. In February 2001 a court sentenced Ibrahim Sahin and Korkut Eken to six years each.
cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk inquiry commission (Elkatmis), report April 1997; Istanbul court verdict 12 February 2001

n: Interior minister Mehmet Agar signed papers for Grey Wolves fugitive
d: Turkey's interior minister, Mehmet Agar, who ran the police, signed a gun licence for Abdullah Catli, a Grey Wolves leader wanted by Interpol for murder and drug trafficking. The Grey Wolves are a Turkish ultranationalist militant group. Investigators found the licence, and a false passport Catli carried, after the Susurluk car crash of November 1996, in which Catli died beside a senior Istanbul police officer and an MP. Agar had met the group shortly before the crash. He resigned on 8 November 1996, and parliament voted on 11 December 1996 to lift his immunity from prosecution and that of MP Sedat Bucak. Agar was not punished and was later re-elected to parliament.
cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk inquiry commission, report April 1997

n: US-funded Counter-Guerrilla unit hidden inside Turkey's army
rank: Special Warfare Department of the General Staff
d: NATO's 'stay-behind' programme placed a secret US-funded unit, the Counter-Guerrilla, inside the Turkish army's Special Warfare Department. Stay-behind networks were cells set up during the Cold War to resist a Soviet invasion, funded and guided from outside the national government. Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit said he learned of the unit only when General Kemal Yamak asked him for money after US financing ended around 1973-74. The department had been renamed from STK in 1967 and later became Special Forces Command. Ecevit suspected the unit was involved in the 1977 Taksim Square shooting, whose gunmen were never caught. A December 1990 Prime Ministry statement denied that the Special Warfare Department was a counter-guerrilla force.
cite: Statements of PM Bulent Ecevit; Prime Ministry press release December 1990; academic histories of NATO stay-behind networks

n: Grey Wolves' leader Alparslan Turkes served as deputy prime minister
d: Alparslan Turkes led the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), whose youth wing is the Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist militant group. He served as deputy prime minister in Suleyman Demirel's Nationalist Front coalition governments of 1975-77 and 1977-78, putting the movement's leader at the top of the government. During those same years the Grey Wolves were active in the street violence of the late 1970s, so the head of a movement whose members were fighting in the streets sat in the cabinet that ran the police and security services.
cite: Turkish government records of the First and Second Nationalist Front cabinets; academic histories of the MHP

n: Ergenekon convictions overturned; government blames Gulenists in courts
rank: Court of Cassation ruling on officers, MPs, journalists
d: Turkey's government says followers of the Gulen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gulen, placed themselves in the police and courts and used those posts to bring the Ergenekon case. That case accused 275 officers, politicians, lawyers, academics and journalists of a plot to overthrow the government. On 21 April 2016 the Court of Cassation in Ankara, Turkey's top appeals court, overturned their convictions. It found no evidence that an 'Ergenekon terror organisation' existed, and said the 2013 verdict relied on illegal wiretaps, anonymous witnesses and unlawful searches. At a retrial in 2019 an Istanbul court acquitted 235 defendants. The claim that Gulen-linked staff drove the prosecution is the government's attribution, not a court finding in this record.
cite: Court of Cassation ruling, 21 April 2016; Istanbul retrial verdict, July 2019

n: 2013 graft probe: Turkey says Gulenist police and prosecutors drove it
d: Turkey's government says members of the Gulen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gulen, had placed themselves inside the police and judiciary and used those posts against it. The claim arose in December 2013, when Istanbul prosecutors and police opened a corruption investigation reaching Prime Minister Erdogan's inner circle; four ministers left office in the fallout. The government called the probe a plot by this 'parallel structure'. On 30 December 2014 the judicial council HSYK, which appoints and disciplines judges and prosecutors, dismissed the four prosecutors who led it: Zekeriya Oz, Celal Kara, Muammer Akkas and Mehmet Yuzgec. The corruption case itself was dropped for lack of evidence.
cite: Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK) decision, 30 December 2014

n: Turkey moves police it says were Gulen 'parallel structure'
d: Turkey's government said in early 2014 that members of the Gulen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gulen, formed a hidden 'parallel structure' inside the national police. It made the claim after a December 2013 corruption investigation by police and prosecutors reached Prime Minister Erdogan's inner circle. In the weeks that followed, the government removed or reassigned police officers across Turkey, including around 1,000 officers that officials described as a 'routine' rotation. The removals were ordered by the government, not by a court, and the record does not show individual findings against the officers. They were an early step towards the much larger purges after the 2016 coup attempt.
cite: Turkish government statements reported by Ahram Online and Hurriyet Daily News, January 2014

n: 2,745 judges removed in one day over alleged Gulen membership
d: Turkey's government says the Gulen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gulen, placed its followers as judges and prosecutors over many years. On 16 July 2016, the day after a failed military coup that Turkey blames on the movement, the judicial council HSYK, which appoints and disciplines judges, removed 2,745 judges, about 36% of those then serving, and ordered their detention for alleged Gulen links. By 19 July 755 judges and prosecutors had been arrested. Over 1,000 more members of the judiciary were dismissed by emergency decree in July 2018. Turkey designates the movement a terrorist organisation under the name 'FETO'.
cite: Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK) decision, 16 July 2016; emergency decrees 2016-2018

n: About 23,000 police dismissed over alleged Gulen membership
d: Turkey's government says the Gulen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gulen, placed its followers throughout the national police. After the failed military coup of July 2016, which Turkey blames on the movement, officers accused of Gulen links were dismissed. Turkey's top police chief said in December 2017 that 22,987 police officers had been dismissed since the coup attempt. President Erdogan gave a figure of 31,000 police removed in April 2019. Across the public sector, about 150,000 people were dismissed from government jobs by emergency decree, a power that let the government act without a court ruling on each person.
cite: Statement of the Director General of Security, December 2017; emergency decrees 2016-2018

n: Turkey removes 15,000 soldiers over alleged Gulenist officers
d: Turkey's government says the Gulen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gulen, placed followers as officers in the armed forces and used them in the coup attempt of 15 July 2016. The next day Prime Minister Binali Yildirim announced 2,839 soldiers arrested, including at least 34 generals or admirals; by 18 July 103 generals and admirals were detained. A July 2018 emergency decree dismissed over 6,000 more military members. President Erdogan said in April 2019 that 15,000 military personnel had been removed in total.
cite: Turkish government announcements and emergency decrees 2016-2018

n: Ex-air force commander jailed for life as coup leader tied to Gulen
rank: former commander of the Turkish Air Force
d: An Ankara court found that the Gulen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gulen, had followers in the armed forces who carried out the coup attempt of 15 July 2016. In June 2019, in the main trial over the coup, the court sentenced Akin Ozturk, a former commander of Turkey's air force, to multiple aggravated life terms as the military leader of the attempt. 'Aggravated life' is Turkey's harshest sentence, with no parole. Ozturk denied the charges.
cite: Ankara High Criminal Court, General Staff coup trial verdict, 20 June 2019

n: Akinci air base trial: 337 life sentences over Gulen-linked coup
d: Turkish prosecutors said the Gulen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gulen, ran the 15 July 2016 coup attempt through officers at Akinci air base near Ankara, the coup's command centre. On 26 November 2020 a court sitting in Sincan, Ankara, ruled on 475 defendants tied to the base: 291 received aggravated life sentences, Turkey's harshest with no parole, 46 received life, and 70 were acquitted. Prosecutors described a civilian, Adil Oksuz, as the movement's link to the plotting officers. He was arrested in 2016, released, and remains missing.
cite: Ankara High Criminal Court, Akinci trial verdict, 26 November 2020

n: Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi elected Egypt's president
d: Mohamed Morsi, a senior figure in the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 that works to bring its members into power, won Egypt's presidential election in June 2012. He stood as the candidate of the Brotherhood's own political party, the Freedom and Justice Party, so a member of the movement held the country's highest office. The army removed him on 3 July 2013. Most of the Brotherhood's leadership was jailed in the following months, and the government later declared the group a terrorist organisation.
cite: Egyptian Presidential Election Commission results, June 2012

n: Ex-Saudi spy chief fronted BCCI's secret takeover of a US bank
rank: former head of Saudi General Intelligence
d: BCCI, a Pakistani-founded international bank, secretly and illegally took control of First American, a bank in Washington, by using shareholders who appeared to own it on their own account. US prosecutors said Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence until 1979 and a major BCCI shareholder, played a key role in that takeover. US regulators did not know BCCI was the real owner. Adham was prosecuted in the US federal and New York cases that followed BCCI's collapse. Under a plea agreement in 1992-93 he paid a $105 million fine in exchange for a reduced sentence and was barred from the finance sector.
cite: US federal and New York County prosecutions in the BCCI case, plea agreement 1992-93

arch.t: Bank of Credit and Commerce International — Abedi and Iqbal: BCCI Was the Largest Bank Fraud in History; CIA Used It for Covert Operations; 62 Countries Affected

n: 'UAE 94' trial: Islah accused of infiltrating state institutions
rank: ministries, schools and universities (per the Attorney General)
d: The UAE's attorney general, Salem Saeed Kubaish, accused members of Islah, an Emirati Islamist group, of trying to infiltrate state institutions including schools, universities and ministries as part of a plot to overthrow the government. The prosecution says Islah is linked to the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt; Islah denies organisational ties. 94 Emiratis were tried. On 2 July 2013 the Federal Supreme Court jailed 56 for 3 to 10 years, sentenced 8 in their absence to 15 years and acquitted 26. Those convicted included Sheikh Sultan bin Kayed Al-Qassimi of the Ras al-Khaimah ruling family and lawyer Mohammed al-Roken.
cite: UAE Federal Supreme Court verdict, 2 July 2013

n: Muslim Brotherhood's party largest in Jordan's parliament; then banned
rank: largest party in parliament (Islamic Action Front)
d: The Islamic Action Front, the political arm of Jordan's Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement that works to bring its members into power, won 31 of 138 seats in the September 2024 election, making it the largest party in parliament. On 23 April 2025 Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya banned all activities of the Brotherhood and said its assets would be seized. The ban followed the arrest of 16 people, including Brotherhood members, over an alleged plot involving weapons; the group denied knowledge.
cite: Jordanian Interior Ministry announcement, 23 April 2025

n: Islamist NIF used army officers to seize Sudan in 1989 coup
d: Sudan's National Islamic Front (NIF), Hassan al-Turabi's movement derived from the Muslim Brotherhood, took power through its supporters inside the army. On 30 June 1989 Brigadier Omar al-Bashir seized power in a coup organised with the NIF. Bashir ruled for 30 years until his fall in 2019. In 2020 he and other military and Islamist figures were put on trial in Khartoum for the 1989 coup, and during the trial Bashir admitted his role.
cite: Khartoum criminal court, 1989 coup trial opened 2020
org_note: NIF/National Congress Party is the Sudanese branch of the Brotherhood tradition.

n: Sudan purges judges placed under the Islamist regime
d: Under the regime that the National Islamic Front, an Islamist movement derived from the Muslim Brotherhood, set up after the 30 June 1989 coup, its supporters were placed in state jobs, including the courts. In November 2019, after the regime fell, Sudan's transitional government set up the Empowerment Removal Committee to dismantle that regime and remove people placed under it. The committee dismissed judges, prosecutors and judicial staff. On 7 October 2021 the High Court's appeals department overturned the dismissals and on 12 October ordered 15 judicial staff back to work. The committee rejected the ruling.
cite: Empowerment Removal Committee decisions 2019-2021; Sudan High Court ruling, 7 and 12 October 2021

n: Kuwait's Muslim Brotherhood party Hadas in parliament and cabinet
rank: members of parliament; occasional cabinet ministers
d: The Kuwaiti Muslim Brotherhood, part of the Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt that works to bring its members into power, placed members in Kuwait's parliament and cabinet through its own party. After the 1990 Iraqi invasion it broke with the international Brotherhood and founded the Islamic Constitutional Movement, known as Hadas. Hadas regularly won several seats in parliament in the 1990s and 2000s and occasionally sent members to the cabinet. A coalition including Hadas was out of parliament after it boycotted the 2013 elections.
cite: Foreign Policy / Carnegie analysis, 20 November 2013

n: Hojjatieh Society purged from Iranian state bodies
org_note: Hojjatieh (Anjoman-e Imam-e Zaman), Shi'a society founded 1953 by Sheikh Mahmoud Halabi
rank: officials in government, judiciary and education bodies
d: The Hojjatieh Society, a Shia religious association in Iran founded by Mahmoud Halabi, had affiliates in decision-making, academic and educational bodies after the 1979 revolution. In a speech on 12 July 1983 Ayatollah Khomeini, Iran's supreme leader, attacked the society. Halabi announced its suspension the same day, and its affiliates were then purged from those bodies. Former members are reported to have later held posts in the judiciary, the security system and government staffing offices. Claims that senior figures were members, and that the society had influence under President Ahmadinejad, are contested.
cite: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah (1999); RFE/RL reporting 2006

n: Iran's Grand Master Sharif-Emami twice served as prime minister
d: Jafar Sharif-Emami was Grand Master, the head, of the Grand Lodge of Iran, the country's main Freemason body, for several years. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. He was also the Shah's prime minister, first from 31 August 1960 to 5 May 1961, and again from 27 August to early November 1978, in the last months before the revolution that ended the monarchy. The head of the lodge therefore also ran the government.
cite: Biographical and historical accounts of Iranian Freemasonry

n: D.F. Malan, first apartheid prime minister, was a secret Broederbond member
d: The Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918, placed its members in South Africa's top posts, and the first apartheid prime minister was one of them. D.F. Malan, who led South Africa from 1948 to 1954 and began apartheid, the system of legal racial segregation, was a member, and every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to it. The society had 37 members by 1920. Its membership was kept secret until journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom printed a near-complete list of about 7,500 members in their 1978 book The Super-Afrikaners.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: J.G. Strijdom, prime minister, was a secret Broederbond member
d: J.G. Strijdom, South Africa's prime minister from 1954 to 1958, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918 that placed its members in top state posts. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to it. Members did not declare their membership; it became public when journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom listed about 7,500 members, including Strijdom, in their 1978 book The Super-Afrikaners.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: H.F. Verwoerd, apartheid prime minister, was a secret Broederbond member
d: H.F. Verwoerd, South Africa's prime minister from 1958 until his assassination in 1966, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918 that placed its members in top state posts. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to it. Members did not declare their membership; it became public when journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom listed about 7,500 members in their 1978 book The Super-Afrikaners.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: B.J. Vorster, prime minister and president, was a secret Broederbond member
d: B.J. Vorster, South Africa's prime minister from 1966 to 1978 and state president from 1978 to 1979, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918 that placed its members in top state posts. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to it. Members did not declare their membership; it became public when journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom listed about 7,500 members in their 1978 book The Super-Afrikaners.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: P.W. Botha, defence minister and prime minister, was a Broederbond member
d: P.W. Botha, South Africa's defence minister and then prime minister from 1978 (state president from 1984), was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918 that placed its members in top state posts. He later left the organisation. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to it. Membership became public when journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom listed about 7,500 members in their 1978 book The Super-Afrikaners.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: F.W. de Klerk, last apartheid president, was a Broederbond member
d: F.W. de Klerk, South Africa's state president from 1989 to 1994, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918 that placed its members in top state posts. He was the last in an unbroken line of members to lead the apartheid state: every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to it. Apartheid was South Africa's system of legal racial segregation.
cite: Afrikaner Broederbond membership records as reported in published histories

n: Smuts orders civil servants to quit the secret Broederbond
d: The Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918, recruited members inside the civil service and state schools. In the mid-1940s Prime Minister Jan Smuts denounced it as a fascist organisation and ordered civil servants and state schoolteachers to give up their membership or resign. The order lapsed after Smuts's United Party lost the 1948 election to D.F. Malan's National Party. Malan was himself a Broederbond member, and every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to it.
cite: Order of the Smuts government, mid-1940s

n: All but two South African cabinet ministers were Broederbond (1979)
d: By 1979 members of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918, held almost every seat in South Africa's cabinet. A report in The Spectator that year, drawing on the 1978 exposé by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, put membership at about 12,000 in 800 cells and said all but two ministers were members. The exceptions were Finance Minister Owen Horwood, who was English-speaking, and Marais Steyn, a former United Party member. The report also counted 49 Broeders in key posts at the state broadcaster SABC.
cite: The Spectator, 'South Africa's secret government', 13 January 1979, drawing on the 1978 Wilkins and Strydom exposé

n: Defence Force chief Magnus Malan reported as Broederbond member
rank: chief of the South African Defence Force
d: General Magnus Malan, head of the South African Defence Force and later defence minister, was reported in 1979 to be a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918 that placed its members in top state posts. The report, in The Spectator, also described the Broederbond's close ties to the security police and to BOSS, the Bureau for State Security, apartheid South Africa's intelligence service.
cite: The Spectator, 13 January 1979

n: BOSS spy chief Hendrik van den Bergh was a Broederbond member
rank: head of the Bureau for State Security (BOSS)
d: Hendrik van den Bergh, head of apartheid South Africa's state security apparatus, including the Bureau for State Security (BOSS), its intelligence service, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond. The Broederbond was a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918 that placed its members in top state posts; every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to it. Van den Bergh later left the organisation.
cite: Published histories of the Afrikaner Broederbond

n: Broederbond chairman Gerrit Viljoen moved into government posts
rank: Administrator-General of South West Africa; minister of education
d: Gerrit Viljoen chaired the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society that placed its members in top state posts, from 1974 to 1980. While still chairman he was appointed in 1979 Administrator-General of South West Africa (now Namibia), which South Africa then controlled. He went on to serve as minister of education from 1980 to 1989 and minister of constitutional development from 1989 to 1992, so the head of the secret society moved directly into running government departments.
cite: Official records of South African government appointments; The Spectator, 13 January 1979

n: Gabon's President Omar Bongo founded and led its Masonic lodges
d: Omar Bongo, president of Gabon from 28 November 1967 until his death on 8 June 2009, was also the head of the country's Freemasonry for decades. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. Initiated in 1953, he founded two Masonic bodies: the Grand Rite Equatorial, affiliated with the Grand Orient de France, and the Grand Lodge of Gabon, linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise (GLNF). He held the grand mastership until his death, tying Gabon's ruling elite to French lodges.
cite: Afrik-News, 'Freemason Presidents in Africa: Ali Bongo ordained Grand Master of Gabon', 2009; Nicholas Shaxson, Poisoned Wells (2007)

n: French lodge installs Gabon's Ali Bongo as Grand Master
d: In 2009 Francois Stifani, Grand Master of the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise (GLNF), a French Freemason body, installed Ali Bongo as Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Gabon and the Grand Equatorial Rite, succeeding his father Omar Bongo. Ali Bongo became president of Gabon the same year, so the head of state again also led the country's lodges. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. He kept the grand mastership until after his overthrow in the August 2023 coup.
cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Africa Intelligence, October 2023

n: Gabon's Freemasons keep a state official as Grand Master after 2023 coup
d: Gabon's main Freemason body, the Grand Lodge of Gabon, has kept a serving state official at its head. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. The grand mastership had traditionally gone to the head of state, and President Ali Bongo held it until the coup that removed him. In October 2023 the lodge replaced him with Jacques Denis Tsanga, governor of Haut-Ogooue province and minister of water and forests in 2018-19. Transitional president Brice Oligui Nguema reportedly declined the post. Africa Intelligence reported the change.
cite: Africa Intelligence, 20 October 2023, as reported by Connection Ivoirienne

n: Congo's President Sassou-Nguesso reported as Grand Master
d: Denis Sassou-Nguesso, president of the Republic of Congo, is reported to be Grand Master, the head, of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, which is linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise, a French Freemason body. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. The reports appeared in Afrik-News in 2009 and in a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier on African heads of state in lodges. A 2013 report also said he sponsored the initiation of the Central African Republic's president, Francois Bozize.
cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Jeune Afrique dossier as republished by L'Hebdo Ivoirien, May 2013

n: Niger's President Mamadou Tandja reported as a Freemason
d: Mamadou Tandja, president of Niger from 1999 to 2010, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting by Afrik-News on African heads of state who belong to Masonic lodges. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. Several presidents of former French colonies in West and Central Africa were named in the same reporting. No lodge is named for Tandja, and the record is press reporting, not an official finding.
cite: Afrik-News, 'Freemason Presidents in Africa', 2009

n: CAR's President Bozize initiated under Sassou-Nguesso's sponsorship
d: Francois Bozize, president of the Central African Republic from 2003 to 2013, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting by Afrik-News on African heads of state in Masonic lodges. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. A 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier said he joined under the sponsorship of the Republic of Congo's president Denis Sassou-Nguesso, who is reported to lead the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville. The record is press reporting, not an official finding.
cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Jeune Afrique dossier as republished by L'Hebdo Ivoirien, 29 May 2013

n: Cameroon's Biya paid state oil money to a Templar order
org_note: Ordre Souverain du Temple Initiatique (OSTI) and its charity CIRCES, esoteric Templar order founded by Raymond Bernard, former head of AMORC (Rosicrucians) in France
d: President Paul Biya of Cameroon passed state money to OSTI and CIRCES, esoteric Templar orders led by Frenchman Raymond Bernard, Le Monde reported in December 1999. The paper said Biya gave them tens of millions of francs between 1988 and 1992, including 40 million francs personally, and that 11.2 million francs moved from Cameroon's state oil company SNH to Bernard's personal account. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and would not comment on the payments. Bernard was questioned in the inquiry into the Solar Temple, a separate order whose members died in mass killings and suicides in the 1990s, but was not charged.
cite: Le Monde, 'L'argent africain des Templiers', 24 December 1999; Le Monde, 17 August 2000

n: Liberia: Masonic lodge membership needed to lead the ruling party
d: In Liberia, membership of the Masonic Order, the country's Freemason lodge, was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the ruling True Whig Party, and by the 1970s most high officials were Masons. William Tolbert, vice-president from 1952 to 1971 and president from 1971 to 1980, was the order's Grand Master, its head. Tolbert was killed on 12 April 1980 in Samuel Doe's coup, and much of the Masonic leadership was killed with him.
cite: Histories of the Masonic Order of Liberia

n: Liberia's Samuel Doe banned Freemasonry, then joined it
d: Liberia's Masonic Order, its Freemason body, had long supplied the country's rulers; most high officials were members before 1980. After the April 1980 coup in which President William Tolbert, the order's Grand Master, was killed, the new ruler Samuel Doe banned Freemasonry. He later lifted the ban. The order was formally reinstated in 1988, and Doe himself was initiated in 1989 while head of state, bringing the lodge back into the presidency.
cite: Histories of the Masonic Order of Liberia

n: Unification Church tied to 179 of 379 ruling-party lawmakers
rank: ruling-party members of the National Diet
d: The Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, built ties with lawmakers of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) by supplying money, events and campaign volunteers. On 8 September 2022 LDP secretary-general Toshimitsu Motegi released the party's own survey of its 379 members of the Diet, Japan's parliament: 179 reported ties to the church or affiliated groups. Of these, 96 had attended church or affiliated events, 20 gave speeches, nearly 50 paid money at events, 29 accepted donations and 17 used church followers as campaign volunteers. The survey relied on lawmakers reporting on themselves, and left out former prime minister Shinzo Abe because he had been killed that July.
cite: Liberal Democratic Party internal survey, 8 September 2022 (AP report)

n: Japan's defence minister used Unification Church campaign helpers
d: Unification Church members worked on the election campaigns of Nobuo Kishi, Japan's defence minister and younger brother of former prime minister Shinzo Abe. The Unification Church is a Korean-founded religious movement. Kishi said so himself in July 2022, after Abe's killing put the church's political ties under scrutiny. In the governing Liberal Democratic Party's own survey of 8 September 2022 he was named among the 17 lawmakers who had accepted church followers as campaign volunteers.
cite: Statement by Defense Minister Kishi, July 2022 (The Diplomat); LDP survey 8 September 2022 (AP)

n: Ex-minister Koichi Hagiuda used Unification Church campaign helpers
rank: former economy and industry minister, senior LDP lawmaker
d: Followers of the Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, worked as volunteers on the election campaigns of Koichi Hagiuda, a former Japanese Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry. He was named in the governing Liberal Democratic Party's survey of 8 September 2022 among the 17 lawmakers who had accepted church followers as campaign volunteers. The party ran the survey after the killing of former prime minister Shinzo Abe in July 2022 exposed the church's ties to politicians; it relied on lawmakers reporting on themselves.
cite: Liberal Democratic Party internal survey, 8 September 2022 (AP report)

n: Minister Daishiro Yamagiwa resigns over Unification Church ties
d: The Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, built ties with lawmakers of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party, and one of them, Daishiro Yamagiwa, sat in the cabinet as economic revitalisation minister. Yamagiwa confirmed he appeared in a 2019 group photo with church leader Hak Ja Han and had attended a church-organised event in 2018. He said he regretted that his attendance at several of the group's meetings had given it credit. He resigned on 24 October 2022 and Prime Minister Fumio Kishida accepted the resignation; the week before, Kishida had ordered a government probe into the church.
cite: Resignation accepted by Prime Minister Kishida, 24 October 2022 (AFP via Philstar)

n: Ex-PM Nobusuke Kishi co-founded Unification Church's political arm
d: Former Japanese prime minister Nobusuke Kishi, Shinzo Abe's grandfather, helped the Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, set up its political operation in Japan. In 1968 he founded the International Federation for Victory over Communism (Shokyo Rengo) with Ryoichi Sasakawa and Yoshio Kodama; it handled the church's political work in Japan. A 1975 FBI report named Kishi and Sasakawa as heads of its Japanese branch. The church built its Tokyo headquarters next to Kishi's former residence in Shibuya, and Kishi gave speeches to followers there in 1970, 1971 and 1973. These ties came back into view after Abe's killing in 2022.
cite: The Diplomat, July 2022 (citing 1975 FBI report); Tansa investigative series 'The True Mother Files' (citing Kishi's memoirs and Arita 2024)

n: Nippon Kaigi members held 15 of 19 seats in Abe's 2014 cabinet
rank: cabinet ministers including the prime minister
d: Members of Nippon Kaigi, a Japanese nationalist lobby, held 15 of the 19 seats in Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's cabinet after his September 2014 reshuffle, Abe among them. The lobby campaigns for revision of Japan's post-war constitution and for patriotic education. It works partly through an association of members of the Diet, Japan's parliament, and ministers belonged to it through that association. This meant most of the ministers running Japan's government were members of a group campaigning to change the constitution. The count came to light through press reporting of the association's membership lists, not from an official finding.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily, 'Abe's reshuffle promotes right-wingers', 5 September 2014 (as cited in Wikipedia's Nippon Kaigi article)

n: Shinto lobby's Diet league counted 16 of 19 Abe cabinet members
org_note: New key: Shinto Seiji Renmei (Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership), the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines; works closely with Nippon Kaigi.
d: Shinto Seiji Renmei, the political arm of Japan's Shinto shrine association, had most of Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's cabinet in its league of supporters in the Diet, Japan's parliament. The league is made up of Diet members who back the shrine association's aims. Researcher Ernils Larsson of Uppsala University reported in December 2014 that 296 Diet members were listed supporters of the league, including 16 of the 19 members of Abe's cabinet at the time. He also wrote that a majority of cabinet ministers belonged to Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby. Membership of the league was listed, not secret.
cite: Ernils Larsson, 'Abe's cabinet reshuffle reflects growing influence of the religious right', East Asia Forum, 3 December 2014

n: Soka Gakkai-backed Komeito in Japan's ruling coalition, 1999-2025
d: Soka Gakkai, a lay Buddhist movement with about 8.3 million member households, got its own party, Komeito, into Japan's government. Komeito's electoral support comes largely from the movement's members, and from 1999 it was a formal coalition partner of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which gave the party ministers and a voice in government policy. The arrangement lasted 26 years. On 10 October 2025 Komeito announced it was leaving the coalition, citing the LDP's weak response to its proposal for stricter rules on political donations.
cite: Komeito press conference, 10 October 2025; CSIS analysis 'Japan's 26-Year-Old Ruling Coalition Collapses'

n: Aum Shinrikyo follower inside Tokyo police tied to shooting of police chief
rank: Tokyo Metropolitan Police officer; target was the National Police Agency chief
d: Toshiyuki Kosugi, an officer of the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department, was a follower of Aum Shinrikyo, the doomsday sect that released sarin gas on the Tokyo subway on 20 March 1995. Ten days later, on 30 March 1995, National Police Agency chief Takaji Kunimatsu was shot and wounded. Kosugi confessed to a role, but in June 1997 prosecutors declined to charge him for lack of supporting evidence. Kosugi and three other Aum-linked men were arrested in July 2004; on 17 September 2004 prosecutors again declined to indict, doubting Kosugi's changed confession.
cite: Tokyo District Public Prosecutors Office decisions, June 1997 and 17 September 2004 (The Japan Times)

n: Aum Shinrikyo recruited soldiers and a Mitsubishi insider
d: Aum Shinrikyo, the doomsday sect behind the 1995 Tokyo subway sarin attack, recruited people from the military and from industry. A 1995 US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations staff report named a Mitsubishi employee arrested on suspicion of helping an Aum member, a former Self-Defense Force soldier, steal company secrets. The report listed three former members of Japan's Self-Defense Forces, its armed forces, in the sect: Shinya Asano, Takahisa Shirai and Akira Yamagata. Yamagata, a subordinate in Aum's 'Home Affairs Ministry', was alleged to have used VX nerve agent to kill members who had left.
cite: US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, 'Global Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction: A Case Study on the Aum Shinrikyo', staff report 1995, Appendix A

n: Unification Church gifts to South Korea's first lady: Kim Keon-hee jailed
d: A Unification Church official, Yun Young-ho, sent luxury gifts to Kim Keon-hee, wife of South Korea's then president Yoon Suk Yeol, to gain influence. The Unification Church is a Korean-founded religious movement. On 28 January 2026 the Seoul Central District Court found that in July 2022 she received a Chanel bag worth 12 million won and a Graff diamond necklace worth 62 million won from the church, passed through shaman Jeon Seong-bae on Yun's behalf. It sentenced her to one year and eight months in prison. She was acquitted over an April 2022 bag, the Deutsch Motors stock case and a political-funds charge.
cite: Seoul Central District Court verdict, 28 January 2026 (Korea Times)

n: Unification Church leader Han Hak-ja jailed for bribing politicians
d: The Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, used its money to buy influence with South Korea's governing camp, a Seoul court found. Special counsel Min Joong-ki indicted church leader Han Hak-ja on 10 October 2025 for bribery, political-funds violations, embezzlement and destroying evidence. On 31 August 2026 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced her to two years. It found she arranged a necklace and handbag for first lady Kim Keon-hee in July 2022 to seek favours, and colluded to give 100 million won to lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong in January 2022. Prosecutors had asked for 13 years; the church said it would appeal.
cite: Special counsel indictment, 10 October 2025; Seoul Central District Court verdict, 31 August 2026 (Korea Times)

n: Lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong took Unification Church cash, loses seat
rank: five-term lawmaker, People Power Party floor leader until June 2025
d: Kweon Seong-dong, a South Korean lawmaker of the People Power Party (PPP) and close ally of Yoon Suk Yeol, accepted 100 million won from Unification Church official Yun Young-ho in January 2022, before the March 2022 presidential election that Yoon won. The Unification Church is a Korean-founded religious movement. Kweon was arrested in September 2025 and indicted the next month. On 16 July 2026 the Supreme Court upheld a two-year prison term and forfeiture of the 100 million won, and he lost his seat in the National Assembly, South Korea's parliament.
cite: Supreme Court of Korea ruling, 16 July 2026 (Korea Times)

n: Shincheonji signed up 56,000 members to ruling party; founder indicted
d: Shincheonji, a South Korean religious movement, registered at least 56,472 of its members as members of the People Power Party (PPP) between July 2021 and August 2023, a joint prosecutor-police team found. Party members vote in candidate selection, so mass sign-ups give a group weight inside a party. 6,482 joined in July 2021 alone, before the 2022 presidential election. Founder Lee Man-hee, 94, was arrested on 24 June 2026. On 13 July 2026 the team announced he and seven other leaders were indicted for violating the Political Parties Act, which bars forcing anyone to join a party, and for obstruction of business.
cite: Joint investigation headquarters indictment, June–July 2026 (Asia Economy; Korea JoongAng Daily)

n: Senator Sam Dastyari backed China's line after donor paid his bills
d: Australian Labor senator Sam Dastyari had a company linked to political donor Huang Xiangmo pay his legal bills. Huang chaired the Australian Council for the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China, described as a peak body for groups linked to the United Front, the Chinese Communist Party's network for building influence abroad. At a June 2016 press conference for Chinese media, with Huang present, Dastyari said China's borders were 'a matter for China', against Labor policy. In October 2016 he reportedly warned Huang his phone was probably tapped by Australian agencies. He lost his party posts on 30 November 2017, announced his resignation on 12 December 2017 and lodged it on 25 January 2018.
cite: Australian Senate record; AAP reporting (InDaily, 12 December 2017)

n: Australia expels donor Huang Xiangmo over foreign interference
rank: major donor to both main parties
d: Huang Xiangmo, a property developer, gave about AU$2 million with associates to Australia's Labor Party and over AU$1 million to the Liberal Party, while chairing groups linked to the United Front, the Chinese Communist Party's network for building influence abroad. In February 2019 the Australian government cancelled his permanent residency and rejected his citizenship application. ASIO, Australia's domestic intelligence agency, judged him 'amenable to conducting acts of foreign interference', citing his roles chairing the Australian Council for the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China (2014-17) and the Oceanic Alliance of the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China.
cite: Australian Department of Home Affairs decision on ASIO advice, February 2019 (The Diplomat)

n: Banned donor Huang Xiangmo's $100,000 cash hidden in NSW Labor funds
rank: state parliament member and party head office
d: Huang Xiangmo, a property developer barred from donating in New South Wales, supplied $100,000 in cash delivered to NSW Labor's offices in 2015, disguised as donations from restaurant staff at a Chinese Friends of Labor dinner. The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), the state's anti-corruption body, reported this on 28 February 2022. ICAC found former NSW Labor MP Ernest Wong engaged in corrupt conduct by concealing illegal donations and trying to get a donor to give false testimony. ICAC made no finding about the United Front, the Chinese Communist Party's influence network abroad; the link is through Huang's roles chairing a reunification council linked to it.
cite: NSW ICAC, Operation Aero report, 28 February 2022 (AAP)

n: Melbourne community leader first convicted of foreign interference
rank: acting federal immigration and multicultural affairs minister (target)
d: Di Sanh Duong, a Melbourne community leader, prepared to use his standing to reach Alan Tudge, then Australia's acting immigration minister, on behalf of China, a jury found. The Crown said he used roles in groups such as the Oceania Federation of Chinese Organisations for Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, and hid links to the United Front Work Department (the Chinese Communist Party's influence body), the Ministry of State Security (China's spy agency) and the Chinese consulate. On 19 December 2023 a County Court of Victoria jury found him guilty of preparing a foreign interference offence, the first conviction under Australia's 2018 law. He was sentenced on 29 February 2024 to 2 years 9 months.
cite: Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions case report; County Court of Victoria, verdict 19 December 2023, sentence 29 February 2024

n: Taiwan ex-official Chang Hsien-yao indicted for Beijing election plan
org_note: Prosecutors say Chang met Wang Huning, chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, the top body of China's united front system; the indictment speaks of 'sources of infiltration'. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
rank: former legislator; former deputy head of the Mainland Affairs Council (2013–14)
d: Taiwanese prosecutors allege that Chang Hsien-yao, a former People First Party legislator for Kaohsiung (2005-08) and special deputy head of the Mainland Affairs Council, Taiwan's agency for policy on China, worked on Beijing's instructions in the 2024 presidential election. They say that from June 2023 he took instructions from people linked to the Chinese government to promote Terry Gou's presidential bid, gave Chinese officials a document on the election on 6 September 2023, and met senior Chinese leader Wang Huning in Beijing on 11 September 2023 to confirm the plan. He was indicted on 12 February 2025 under Article 4 of the Anti-Infiltration Act and the presidential election law.
cite: Taiwan prosecutors' indictment, 12 February 2025 (Central News Agency)

n: Taiwan's Gong He Party leader jailed for Beijing-funded campaigns
org_note: Funding came through officials of the Putian Taiwan Affairs Office in Fujian; the court called it 'united front' activity. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
rank: registered political party and its 2022 local-election candidates
d: Money from Fujian, the Chinese province facing Taiwan, funded the Gong He Party's November 2022 election campaigns in Taiwan, prosecutors said, including a Taipei mayoral candidate who got 316 votes. Taiwan's Ministry of Justice indicted party chairman Chou Ke-chi and Taipei Puxian Association board members Pan Jindong and Chu Chun-yuan on 9 August 2023 under the Anti-Infiltration Act, which bars taking money or instructions from China for political activity. In late June 2025 the Taipei District Court sentenced Chou to two years, Pan to 18 months and Chu to one year, finding they took Beijing funds for united front activity, the Chinese Communist Party's work to build influence abroad. The sentences can be appealed.
cite: Taipei District Court verdict, June 2025 (Taipei Times via ANI); indictment 9 August 2023 (UCA News)

n: Beijing-directed money for a New Taipei council candidate
org_note: Prosecutors allege the Federation of Hong Kong Jiangsu Youth took assignments from the United Front Work Department of the CCP Jiangsu Provincial Committee. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
d: Prosecutors allege that 100,000 yuan was sent on Beijing's instructions to fund Labor Party candidate Wang Cheng in the 2022 New Taipei City Council election in Taiwan. On 26 February 2024 New Taipei prosecutors indicted Sun Chih-chuan of the Chinese Youth Development Union and a Chinese woman surnamed Da, director of the Federation of Hong Kong Jiangsu Youth, under the Anti-Infiltration Act and the Political Donations Act. They say the money moved via a US$10,000 transfer from Da's Hong Kong account, and that Wang received NT$435,000. Both defendants deny ties to Beijing.
cite: New Taipei District Prosecutors Office indictment, 26 February 2024 (Central News Agency)

n: Taiwan raids pro-China party founded by Bamboo Union gang leader
org_note: Party founded by Chang An-le ('White Wolf'), former Bamboo Union gang leader. Prosecutors were examining China-sourced funding; no united-front finding by a court is recorded here. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
d: Taiwanese legislators alleged that money from Chinese officials and state-linked firms was moved through the Taolue Group, a company of Chang An-le, to his Chinese Unity Promotion Party, which campaigns for unification with China. Chang is a former leader of the Bamboo Union, a Taiwanese organised crime gang. In August 2018 Taipei prosecutors raided the party's head office and its leaders' homes, citing possible breaches of the National Security Act, the Political Donations Act and the Organized Crime Prevention Act. Chang said the party received money from China but that it came from his company's profits there.
cite: Taipei District Prosecutors Office search operation, August 2018 (Taipei Times)

n: Argentine interim president Raúl Lastiri on secret P2 lodge lists
d: Raúl Alberto Lastiri, interim president of Argentina from 13 July to 12 October 1973, appears on the membership lists of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli that recruited senior officials in Italy and Argentina. The lists were found in Gelli's files at Castiglion Fibocchi in March 1981 and published by the Italian government in May 1981. An Italian parliamentary inquiry, the Anselmi Commission, reported on the lodge in 1984.
cite: P2 membership lists seized at Castiglion Fibocchi, March 1981, published by the Italian government May 1981; Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984

n: Minister José López Rega, Triple A funder, was a P2 member
d: José López Rega, Argentina's minister of social welfare from 25 May 1973 to 11 July 1975 under Cámpora, Lastiri and Juan and Isabel Perón, is listed as a member of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli. Gelli visited him often. López Rega's ministry funded the Argentine Anticommunist Alliance (Triple A), a death squad blamed for about 1,500 deaths. The P2 lists were seized in Italy in March 1981. López Rega was arrested in the US in 1986, extradited, and died in prison in Buenos Aires on 9 June 1989 while awaiting trial.
cite: P2 membership lists seized at Castiglion Fibocchi, March 1981, published by the Italian government May 1981; Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984

n: Junta member Admiral Massera was in P2 and helped its grand master
rank: commander-in-chief of the navy; junta member
d: Admiral Emilio Massera, commander of the Argentine Navy from 1973 to September 1978 and a member of the 1976-78 military junta, was found in 1981 to be a member of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli. Massera promoted Gelli's appointment as an economic adviser and defended the issue of Argentine diplomatic passports to Gelli, saying Gelli had supported the junta 'in the struggle against subversion'. Massera was sentenced to life in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas and pardoned by President Menem on 29 December 1990.
cite: P2 membership lists seized at Castiglion Fibocchi, March 1981, published by the Italian government May 1981; Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984

n: General Suárez Mason, P2 member, reported to divert oil money to P2
rank: commander, First Army Corps; president of state oil company YPF
d: General Carlos Guillermo Suárez Mason commanded Argentina's First Army Corps, which garrisoned Buenos Aires, from 1976 to January 1980, and was named president of the state oil company YPF by Galtieri in December 1981. He is listed as a member of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli, and is reported to have diverted funds to P2 through a front company, Sol Petróleo. Extradited from the US in 1988, he was convicted in Argentina of 43 murders and 23 kidnappings, then pardoned in 1990. An Italian court sentenced him in his absence to life in 2000.
cite: P2 membership lists seized at Castiglion Fibocchi, March 1981, published by the Italian government May 1981; Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984

n: Anti-communist league's Latin American chair led Argentina's military
rank: army general; chairman, Joint Military Chiefs
d: The World Anti-Communist League, an international network of governments, parties and militant groups set up to fight communism, had its Latin American chairman at the head of Argentina's armed forces. Carlos Guillermo Suárez Mason chaired the league's Latin American chapter while serving as a senior Argentine army general. In 1980 he moved from command of the First Army Corps, which garrisoned Buenos Aires, to chairman of the Joint Military Chiefs, the top command over the armed forces. He also financed and relaunched the far-right magazine Cabildo.
cite: Biographical record of Carlos Guillermo Suárez Mason (academic and press histories of the Argentine dictatorship)

n: Foreign minister Alberto Vignes, P2 member, honoured its grand master
d: Alberto Vignes, Argentina's minister of foreign affairs and worship from 1973 to 1975, is on the membership lists of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli. With Juan Perón, Vignes drafted the August 1974 decree that gave Gelli the Gran Cruz de la Orden del Libertador, a state honour, and an honorary economic counsellor post at Argentina's embassy in Italy. The P2 lists were seized in Italy in March 1981 and published by the Italian government in May 1981.
cite: P2 membership lists seized at Castiglion Fibocchi, March 1981, published by the Italian government May 1981; Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984

d: Celestino Rodrigo, Argentina's minister of economy in 1975 and a friend of social welfare minister José López Rega, is named among the Argentine members of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli that recruited senior officials. Its membership lists were seized at Castiglion Fibocchi in March 1981 and published by the Italian government in May 1981; an Italian parliamentary inquiry, the Anselmi Commission, reported in 1984.

d: César Augusto de la Vega, Argentina's secretary of state for minors and the family (1973-74) and then ambassador to UNESCO (1974), France (1974-75) and Denmark (1975-76), is named among the Argentine members of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli that recruited senior officials. n: P2-listed diplomat Federico Barttfeld removed as under-secretary
d: Federico Carlos Barttfeld is named on the membership lists of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli, seized in Italy in March 1981. He went on to serve as Argentina's ambassador to Yugoslavia (1991-95) and China (1998-2001), and later as an under-secretary of state under Néstor Kirchner. He was relieved of his functions in 2003 over alleged involvement in the Dirty War, the military regime's campaign of kidnapping and killing of opponents.
cite: P2 membership lists seized at Castiglion Fibocchi, March 1981, published by the Italian government May 1981; Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984

n: P2 grand master Licio Gelli given Argentine diplomatic post
d: Licio Gelli, grand master of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge whose members included Argentine ministers and generals, was given a place inside Argentina's state. In August 1974 a decree drafted by Juan Perón and foreign minister Alberto Vignes, himself a P2 member, gave Gelli the Gran Cruz de la Orden del Libertador and an honorary economic counsellor post at the Argentine embassy in Italy. Gelli was later named minister plenipotentiary for cultural affairs there, with diplomatic immunity, and held four Argentine diplomatic passports. He became the main economic and financial consultant to Isabel Perón and José López Rega. Gelli also claimed he initiated Perón as a Mason in Madrid in June 1973; this is Gelli's own claim.
cite: Argentine decree of August 1974; biographical histories of Licio Gelli

n: BCCI paid Argentine central bank officials $500,000
d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), a Luxembourg-registered bank later shut down worldwide for fraud and money laundering, paid Argentine Central Bank officials a $500,000 'political' contribution in 1983–84, according to a 1992 US indictment of the bank. The central bank regulates Argentina's banks. In the same period BCCI bought Argentina's Finamerica bank, a sale Fiat authorised in December 1984. The US Senate's 1992 report on BCCI adds that BCCI Argentina's accounts were emptied a week before the central bank moved to revoke its licence.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5; 1992 BCCI indictment

n: Opus Dei member Joaquín Lavín as Chile's education minister
rank: minister of education; minister of social development
d: Joaquín Lavín, a supernumerary member of Opus Dei, served as a Chilean government minister twice under President Sebastián Piñera. Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members that encourages its members to carry their faith into their professional and public lives. A supernumerary is a member who lives an ordinary family life while following the group's rules. Lavín was minister of education from 11 March 2010 to 18 July 2011, in charge of the country's school system, and minister of social development from October 2011 to June 2013.
cite: Biographical record; press reporting

n: BCCI accused of bribing Peru's central bank for reserve deposits
rank: central bank president and general manager
d: A 1991 New York indictment alleged that the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, paid $3 million in bribes so that Peru's Central Reserve Bank would deposit national reserves with BCCI-Panama. The deposits reached $270 million in June 1987, about three-tenths of the government's cash reserves. Peruvian reporting named former central bank president Leonel Figueroa and general manager Héctor Neyra as the officials; both denied it. A Peruvian parliamentary commission led by Fernando Olivera alleged that President Alan García was the real beneficiary. García called this a fabrication.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5; Peruvian congressional commission (Olivera), 1991; Christian Science Monitor, 6 Aug 1991

n: Opus Dei numerary Rafael Rey as Peru's production and defence minister
rank: minister of production; minister of defence
d: Rafael Rey, a numerary member of Opus Dei, held two cabinet posts in Peru under President Alan García. Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members that encourages its members to carry their faith into their professional and public lives. A numerary is a celibate member who commits fully to the organisation, usually living in its centres. Rey was minister of production from 28 July 2006 to 14 October 2008 and minister of defence, in charge of the armed forces, from 11 July 2009 to 14 September 2010.
cite: Biographical record; press reporting

n: BCCI secretly owned a Brazilian bank through Sarney associates
d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, secretly controlled a Brazilian bank by having nominees hold it in their names, the US Senate's 1992 BCCI report found. A nominee is a front person listed as owner on someone else's behalf. One was former ambassador Sergio da Costa, paid $150,000 a year as a front-man. The report says close associates of President José Sarney were among the nominees, and that Sarney presented a BCCI-funded prize in 1987.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

n: BCCI paid off the mortgage of Panama's future president Barletta
d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, paid off the mortgage of Nicolás Ardito Barletta on the instructions of General Manuel Noriega, Panama's military ruler, the US Senate's 1992 BCCI report found. Barletta was Noriega's chosen presidential candidate and became president of Panama in 1984. The payment put BCCI money behind the man Noriega placed at the head of government, while BCCI was also handling Noriega's own accounts.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

n: World Anti-Communist League leader as Guatemala's vice-president
d: Mario Sandoval Alarcón, a leader of the World Anti-Communist League (WACL), was vice-president of Guatemala from 1 July 1974 to 1 July 1978. The WACL was an international network of right-wing parties, governments and militants that pushed anti-communist policy in member countries. Sandoval had founded Guatemala's National Liberation Movement (MLN) in 1960. Historians link the MLN to killings by the Mano Blanca death squad.
cite: Academic histories of WACL and Guatemala

n: Book alleges El Yunque placed members in PAN and Fox cabinet
d: El Yunque, a secret Catholic group founded in Puebla, Mexico, in 1953, is alleged to have placed its members in the leadership of the National Action Party (PAN), then Mexico's governing party, and in President Vicente Fox's cabinet, without their membership being disclosed. The claim was made in 2003 by journalist Álvaro Delgado in his book 'El Yunque: la ultraderecha en el poder' (El Yunque: the far right in power). PAN officials called the claims 'pure fiction'. Former PAN leader Luis H. Álvarez said he believed the group was real but negligible. The claims rest on Delgado's reporting.
cite: Álvaro Delgado, El Yunque (Grijalbo, 2003); Proceso reporting

n: Ex-mayor says El Yunque member led the PAN and ran four states
d: Luis Paredes Moctezuma, former mayor of Puebla, said that Manuel Espino Barrientos, national leader of Mexico's National Action Party (PAN), was a member of El Yunque, a secret Catholic group founded in 1953. He also said El Yunque helped back Vicente Fox's 2000 presidential campaign, and claimed in 2007 that the group controlled four state governments through members in office. The PAN denied the group had anything to do with the party.
cite: Statements of Luis Paredes Moctezuma, 2007, as reported in Mexican press

n: Guanajuato governor Oliva and aides named as El Yunque members
d: Juan Manuel Oliva, governor of the Mexican state of Guanajuato for the National Action Party (PAN) from 2006 to 2012, his chief of staff Gerardo Mosqueda and local politician Alberto Diosdado were named in the 2000s as members of El Yunque, a secret Catholic group founded in Puebla in 1953 that is alleged to place its members in public office without declaring it. All three denied it.
cite: Mexican press reporting, 2000s

n: Scientology planted a clerk inside the IRS to copy its files
d: The Church of Scientology's Guardian's Office, its intelligence and legal arm, placed members in jobs inside the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the US tax agency, in a programme called Operation Snow White. Gerald Bennett Wolfe took a clerk-typist job there around late 1974 and copied files on tax-exempt organisations for the church. He was arrested in June 1976 with a forged federal pass. After the FBI raided Scientology offices in Los Angeles and Washington on 8 July 1977, eleven Scientologists, including Mary Sue Hubbard, were convicted. Wolfe received five years and a $10,000 fine.
cite: United States v. Mary Sue Hubbard et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, guilty pleas and sentencing 1979

arch.t: Scientology — Operation Snow White: Church Infiltrated 136 Government Agencies in 30 Countries; 11 Senior Officials Including Founder's Wife Convicted of Federal Crimes (PROVEN)

n: Scientology took files from the Justice Department and prosecutors
rank: Department of Justice and U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C.
d: Under Operation Snow White, the Church of Scientology's Guardian's Office broke into or copied documents from the US Justice Department and from the office of Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathan Dodell, a federal prosecutor handling Scientology litigation. Documents were also taken from the D.C. Metropolitan Police, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Treasury. The aim was to see what the government knew about the church. Mary Sue Hubbard, wife of founder L. Ron Hubbard and head of the Guardian's Office, was sentenced to five years and a $10,000 fine. Jane Kember and Mo Budlong were convicted at trial in 1980 after fighting extradition from the UK.
cite: United States v. Mary Sue Hubbard et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, 1979; Kember and Budlong convicted 1980

arch.t: Scientology — Operation Snow White: Church Infiltrated 136 Government Agencies in 30 Countries; 11 Senior Officials Including Founder's Wife Convicted of Federal Crimes (PROVEN)

n: Scientology Toronto planted members in Ontario police and law offices
rank: Ontario Provincial Police and Ontario Ministry of the Attorney General offices
d: The Church of Scientology of Toronto placed its members as staff inside the offices of the Ontario Provincial Police and the Ontario Ministry of the Attorney General, which runs prosecutions in the province. Operations against the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), Canada's federal police, were also part of the case. On 25 June 1992 the church was convicted on two counts of breach of the public trust, a crime of abusing a public position. Seven members were convicted in total. The church was fined $250,000 and member Jacqueline Matz $5,000. The Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the church's appeal.
cite: R v Church of Scientology of Toronto, Ontario Court (General Division), 1992; Court of Appeal for Ontario, 1997

n: Moon Organization hid its money in a bid to control a US bank
rank: Federally regulated bank in Washington (Diplomat National Bank)
d: Sun Myung Moon's Unification Church tried to gain control of the Diplomat National Bank in Washington by hiding where the money came from, a US House subcommittee led by Rep. Donald Fraser found in 1978. Shares were bought in the names of individual church members, so the bank and its regulators would not see that one organisation was buying a controlling stake. The subcommittee asked the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which polices share dealing, and other agencies to examine the purchases, and asked congressional tax committees to review the tax filings of Moon-run entities.
cite: Fraser Report, House Subcommittee on International Organizations, 31 Oct 1978

n: South Korean spy agency paid US congressmen; Rep. Hanna convicted
d: South Korean businessman Tongsun Park, acting for the Korean Central Intelligence Agency (KCIA), paid cash to members of the US Congress to keep American support for the Park Chung-hee government. The scandal became known as Koreagate. In 1978, testifying under immunity, Park admitted giving money to 30 members. Former KCIA director Kim Hyong-uk described the scheme to a House committee. Former Rep. Richard Hanna was the only member convicted; he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to prison.
cite: U.S. District Court for D.C., Hanna plea 1978; House hearings on Korean influence, 1977–78
org_note: koreagate = the 1970s Tongsun Park / KCIA influence network in the U.S. Congress

n: Koreagate: House reprimanded three congressmen paid by Tongsun Park
rank: U.S. Representatives (Edward Roybal, Charles H. Wilson, John J. McFall)
d: Tongsun Park, a South Korean businessman acting for his country's intelligence agency (the KCIA), paid US congressmen to keep support for the Seoul government. After a House ethics investigation into the payments, the House reprimanded Representatives Edward Roybal, Charles H. Wilson and John J. McFall in 1978. A reprimand is a formal rebuke voted by the House. Reported payments ranged from $100,000 to $200,000 per person. Rep. Edward Patten was investigated and found not guilty.
cite: U.S. House of Representatives, reprimand votes following the Korean influence investigation, 1978
org_note: koreagate = the 1970s Tongsun Park / KCIA influence network in the U.S. Congress

n: Koreagate: foreign-aid chair Otto Passman tried and acquitted
d: Tongsun Park, a South Korean businessman acting for his country's intelligence agency (the KCIA), paid US congressmen to keep support for the Seoul government. Former Rep. Otto Passman had chaired the House subcommittee that set foreign-aid spending, which decided how much US aid South Korea received. He was indicted on bribery, conspiracy, illegal gratuities and tax evasion charges over money from Park. His trial was moved to Monroe, Louisiana, where a jury acquitted him.
cite: U.S. v. Passman, federal trial in Monroe, Louisiana (acquittal)
org_note: koreagate = the 1970s Tongsun Park / KCIA influence network in the U.S. Congress

n: The Fellowship housed members of Congress at its C Street townhouse
d: The Fellowship, also called the Family, a private Christian network that runs the National Prayer Breakfast in Washington, gave members of Congress subsidised lodging. A group affiliated with it owns a townhouse on C Street where lawmakers lived for about $950 a month including housekeeping. Mother Jones named eight residents: Senators Sam Brownback, Tom Coburn, Jim DeMint and John Ensign, and Representatives Mike Doyle, Heath Shuler, Bart Stupak and Zach Wamp. Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a watchdog group, filed ethics complaints arguing that the lodging was an undeclared gift that broke House and Senate rules, and the Office of Congressional Ethics reviewed it in 2010.
cite: Mother Jones reporting (2010); CREW ethics complaints; Office of Congressional Ethics review reported by Roll Call, June 2010

n: Russian agent Maria Butina worked her way into US political circles
rank: National Prayer Breakfast (event attended by the sitting president)
d: Maria Butina, working under Russian official Alexander Torshin, built back channels for Russia into Republican circles in the United States. She worked through the National Rifle Association (NRA) and helped arrange for Russians to attend the February 2017 National Prayer Breakfast, an event run by the religious network the Fellowship and attended by the president. A planned private meeting between Torshin and President Trump was cancelled after a national security aide flagged him. Butina pleaded guilty on 13 December 2018 to conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government and was sentenced on 26 April 2019 to 18 months. The FBI interviewed Fellowship organiser Doug Burleigh about his ties to her.
cite: United States v. Maria Butina, U.S. District Court for D.C., plea 13 Dec 2018, sentence 26 Apr 2019
org_note: The Fellowship was the host of the event she used, not the agent; the vehicle was a Russian state-directed network.

n: Skull and Bones member George H. W. Bush as CIA director and president
rank: Director of Central Intelligence; later President
d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, has had its members in top US government posts. One of them, George H. W. Bush (Skull and Bones 1948), served as the 11th Director of Central Intelligence, head of the CIA, in 1976–77 and as the 41st President in 1989–93. His father, Prescott Bush (Bones 1917), was a US Senator from Connecticut. Membership comes from published Skull and Bones rosters; no forum has found the society directed his official acts.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official CIA and White House records of office

arch.t: Skull and Bones — Systematic CIA / Government Placement Network

n: Both 2004 US presidential nominees were Skull and Bones members
rank: President (George W. Bush) and Secretary of State (John Kerry)
d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, has had its members fill top US government posts, and in 2004 both major-party presidential nominees came from it: George W. Bush (Bones 1968) and John Kerry (Bones 1966). Bush served as the 43rd President; Kerry later became the 68th Secretary of State (2013–17), the government's chief diplomat. Both confirmed their membership publicly while declining to discuss the society.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: Skull and Bones member Stimson ran the War and State departments
rank: Secretary of War (twice) and Secretary of State
d: Two members of Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, ran the US War Department together during the Second World War. Henry L. Stimson (Bones 1888) was Secretary of War under Roosevelt and Truman from 1940 to 1945, having earlier been Secretary of War under Taft and Secretary of State under Hoover. Robert A. Lovett (Bones 1918) worked under him as Assistant Secretary of War for Air and later became Secretary of Defense. Other members of the society have also gone on to fill top US government posts. The link rests on published membership rosters set against official records of office.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: Skull and Bones members in US national security posts
d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, had its members in top US national-security posts. McGeorge Bundy (Bones 1940) was National Security Adviser, the president's chief aide on defence and foreign policy, to Presidents Kennedy and Johnson from 1961 to 1966. Other Bonesmen in national security posts include CIA officers Charles S. Whitehouse (1947) and William Sloane Coffin (1949), and F. Trubee Davison (1918), the CIA's Director of Personnel, who oversaw hiring. The record comes from published membership rosters and official records of office; it shows members in posts, not decisions taken for the society.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: Skull and Bones member Steven Mnuchin as Treasury Secretary
d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University, had one of its members, Steven Mnuchin (Bones 1985), at the head of the US Treasury, the department in charge of US government finances. Skull and Bones picks 15 students a year, and its members have gone on to fill top US government posts. Mnuchin served as the 77th Secretary of the Treasury from 2017 to 2021. An earlier member, Franklin MacVeagh (Bones 1862), held the same post under President Taft.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: Trilateral Commission members Carter, Mondale and 19 others in office
d: Members of the Trilateral Commission, a private policy network of business, political and academic figures from North America, Western Europe and Japan, took the top posts in Jimmy Carter's administration. Banker David Rockefeller founded the commission in July 1973, with Zbigniew Brzezinski as organiser. Carter and Walter Mondale were members before taking office as President and Vice President in 1977. Brzezinski and Harold Brown also served in the administration, and the Christian Science Monitor reported in 1980 that 17 other former commission members did too.
cite: Christian Science Monitor, 'The trilateral controversy', 17 Apr 1980; Trilateral Commission membership lists

arch.t: Trilateral Commission — 19/20 Carter Senior Appointments Were Members

n: Trilateral members Brzezinski, Vance and Brown in Carter cabinet
rank: National Security Adviser, Secretary of State, Secretary of Defense
d: Three members of the Trilateral Commission, a private policy network founded by David Rockefeller, took the top foreign and defence posts under President Jimmy Carter. Zbigniew Brzezinski, the commission's founding director, became National Security Adviser. Cyrus Vance became Secretary of State, and Harold Brown became Secretary of Defense. The appointments were raised during the 1980 campaign as evidence of the commission's reach.
cite: Christian Science Monitor, 17 Apr 1980; Trilateral Commission membership lists

arch.t: Trilateral Commission — 19/20 Carter Senior Appointments Were Members

n: Council on Foreign Relations secretly drafted State Dept war planning
d: From 1939 to 1945 the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private New York foreign-policy club, ran a confidential programme called the War and Peace Studies that wrote postwar planning papers for the US State Department. It was paid for entirely by the Rockefeller Foundation. Four groups (economic, security, territorial, political) produced 682 memoranda, which the State Department classified and circulated among government departments. Allen Dulles, later CIA director, led the security and armaments group. Council members outside the project were not told it existed.
cite: Council on Foreign Relations institutional history; Shoup and Minter, Imperial Brain Trust (1977)

arch.t: Council on Foreign Relations — Submergence of US Sovereignty (Insider Testimony)

n: BCCI secretly owned First American, Washington's largest bank
rank: Federal Reserve (bank approval) and the U.S. banking system
d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, secretly controlled CCAH, a holding company that took over Financial General Bankshares in 1981 and renamed it First American, a US Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee found. The Federal Reserve, which must approve bank takeovers, did so on assurances that BCCI was neither financing nor directing the deal; the report found those assurances false. The Treasury did not pass on CIA information about BCCI's ownership in 1985–86, and the Fed did not open a formal investigation until 3 January 1991.
cite: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry–Brown report), December 1992

arch.t: Bank of Credit and Commerce International — Abedi and Iqbal: BCCI Was the Largest Bank Fraud in History; CIA Used It for Covert Operations; 62 Countries Affected
