Mariano Navarro Rubio, an Opus Dei member, was Franco's finance minister from 25 February 1957 to 8 July 1965 and helped drive the Stabilisation Plan that opened Spain's economy. He then became governor of the Banco de España, the central bank. He was accused in the 1969 MATESA scandal, over about 10 billion pesetas of state export credits to a textile-machinery firm, and left the central bank. Franco pardoned the accused former ministers before any verdict.
cite: Spanish government records; academic history

n: Opus Dei member Ullastres: trade minister, then envoy to the EEC
d: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests, had one of its members in charge of Spain's trade policy and then its relations with Europe. Alberto Ullastres, one of the Opus Dei ministers known as 'Opusdeístas', was Franco's trade minister from 1957 to 1965 and led the Stabilisation Plan's opening of Spain's trade, ending the policy of self-sufficiency. From 1965 to 1976 he headed Spain's mission to the European Communities, the forerunner of the European Union. He was one of 8 Opus Dei members historians count among Franco's 116 ministers.
cite: Academic history

n: Opus Dei member López Rodó ran Franco's development plans
rank: Minister for Development Planning 1965–73; Foreign Minister 1973–74
d: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests, had one of its members direct Spain's economic planning for nearly two decades. Laureano López Rodó, an Opus Dei member close to Luis Carrero Blanco, Franco's chief aide and later Prime Minister, was technical secretary of the Presidency from 1956 to 1962 and Commissioner of the Development Plan from 1962 to 1965. He was then minister for development planning from 1965 to 1973, and foreign minister from 12 June 1973 to 4 January 1974. He was one of 8 Opus Dei members historians count among Franco's 116 ministers.
cite: Spanish government records; academic history

n: Opus Dei member López-Bravo: Franco's industry and foreign minister
d: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests, had another member among Franco's senior ministers in Gregorio López-Bravo. He served as Franco's minister of industry and then foreign minister until 1973, and was part of the 1969 'monocolor' cabinet, in which eleven members had ties to Opus Dei. Historians count 8 Opus Dei members among Franco's 116 ministers, none before 1957. López-Bravo died in the Mount Oiz air crash in 1985.
cite: Spanish government records; academic history

n: MATESA scandal and the 1969 Opus Dei-dominated cabinet
rank: finance and trade ministers; state industrial bank
d: By 1969 most of Franco's cabinet had ties to Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests. The MATESA scandal broke on 23 July 1969: the textile-machinery firm MATESA owed about 10 billion pesetas in export credits from the state Banco de Crédito Industrial. Former ministers Mariano Navarro Rubio, an Opus Dei member, Juan José Espinosa San Martín (finance) and Faustino García-Moncó (trade) were charged, and Franco pardoned them before any verdict. Instead of reducing the movement's presence, the reshuffle of 29 October 1969 produced a 'monocolor' (single-colour) cabinet in which eleven members had ties to Opus Dei.
cite: Spanish Supreme Court proceedings; Franco pardon 1971

n: IDEA: secret officers' society inside Greek army led 1967 coup
d: IDEA (Holy Bond of Greek Officers) was a secret society inside the Greek army whose members seized power in 1967. It was formed in 1945 by officers who had served in the collaborationist Security Battalions, units that worked with the German occupiers; its 1952 manifesto called dictatorship the only solution for Greece. Several leaders of the 21 April 1967 coup, including Georgios Papadopoulos, were members, and IDEA members took key posts under the military junta that ruled until 1974. In 1975 Papadopoulos and other coup leaders were sentenced to death for high treason, commuted to life imprisonment.
cite: Academic history (Kassimeris)
org_note: IDEA: Ieros Desmos Ellinon Axiomatikon, secret society of Greek army officers

n: Golden Dawn ties inside the Greek police
d: Golden Dawn, a Greek neo-Nazi party later found by a court to be a criminal organisation, had support and ties inside the Greek police. After the May 2012 election, polling stations used by officers of the Attica police directorate showed just over 20% for Golden Dawn against about 6% at civilian stations in the same district. In 2012 an officer was suspended over a raid on migrant stalls in Missolonghi carried out alongside party members. In 2013 the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner, Nils Muižnieks, said he had strong evidence of ties between police and the party. In October 2020 the Athens Court of Appeals convicted the party's leaders of directing a criminal organisation.
cite: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, 2013; election returns 2012
org_note: Golden Dawn: neo-Nazi party ruled a criminal organisation

n: Narendra Modi, a career RSS organiser, became Prime Minister
d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation that places its members in the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and other affiliated groups, had a long-serving organiser of its own become India's Prime Minister. Narendra Modi joined the RSS as a boy and served as a full-time organiser (pracharak) from the early 1970s, before the RSS seconded, or assigned, him to the BJP in 1985. He became Prime Minister in 2014. The RSS does not publish membership rolls; Modi's RSS career is set out in his official biographies and was acknowledged by the organisation.
cite: Official PM biography; RSS statements; widely documented in Indian and international press

n: Hizb ut-Tahrir recruited a brigadier inside Pakistan's army
d: Hizb ut-Tahrir, an international Islamist movement that seeks to set up a caliphate (a single Islamic state) and is banned in Pakistan, recruited serving Pakistani army officers. Brigadier Ali Khan was arrested in May 2011, and in August 2012 a military court convicted him and four majors of links to the group; he was sentenced to five years. The army said Hizb ut-Tahrir had tried to recruit officers to its programme of a coup and a caliphate.
cite: Pakistan Army field general court martial, August 2012; reported by Reuters, BBC, Dawn

n: Hizb ut-Tahrir linked to army officers' coup plot in Bangladesh
d: Hizb ut-Tahrir, an international Islamist movement that seeks a caliphate and has been banned in Bangladesh since 2009, was named among those behind a plot by army officers to seize power. In January 2012 the Bangladesh army announced it had stopped a coup attempt by serving and retired officers it described as religious extremists, and named Hizb ut-Tahrir among those behind it. Two retired officers were arrested and a serving major was named as a fugitive.
cite: Bangladesh Army press briefing, 19 January 2012; reported by BBC, Reuters

n: Iglesia ni Cristo head made a presidential special envoy
rank: Special Envoy of the President for Overseas Filipinos' Concerns (Department of Foreign Affairs)
d: The Iglesia ni Cristo (INC), a Philippine church that tells its members to vote as a bloc for the candidates it chooses, had its leader given a government post after backing the winning presidential candidate. The church backed Rodrigo Duterte in the 2016 election. Duterte then appointed Eduardo Villanueva Manalo, the INC's executive minister (head), as Special Envoy of the President for Overseas Filipinos' Concerns under the Department of Foreign Affairs. The appointment papers were dated 13 February 2018 and set a term from 30 January 2018 to 29 January 2019.
cite: Presidential appointment papers dated 13 February 2018, reported by Philippine Daily Inquirer, 14 February 2018

n: Iglesia ni Cristo rallies for its member-senator Marcoleta
d: The Iglesia ni Cristo (INC), a Philippine church that tells its members to vote as a bloc, helped elect one of its own members to the Senate and then mobilised to defend him. Senator Rodante Marcoleta, an INC member elected in 2025 with the church's support, was set to be charged by Ombudsman Jesus Remulla, the official who investigates public officers, for failing to declare 75 million pesos in unused campaign contributions. On 30 June 2026 the church held a rally along EDSA, Manila's main highway, that police estimated at about 12,000; its spokesman called the case 'selective justice'. Marcoleta was expected to vote against convicting Vice-President Sara Duterte at her Senate impeachment trial.
cite: Malay Mail (AFP), 30 June 2026; Wikipedia 'Iglesia ni Cristo' (2025 Senate support)

n: Moon's church acted as secret envoys for South Korea's government
rank: South Korean defence industry and senior officials (Kim Jong-pil, Pak Chon-kyu)
d: The Unification Church, the religious movement founded by Sun Myung Moon (the 'Moon Organization'), built close ties inside South Korea's government and worked on its behalf. In its 1978 final report the US House Subcommittee on International Organizations (the Fraser committee) named Kim Jong-pil, founder of the Korean Central Intelligence Agency (KCIA), and Pak Chon-kyu as the church's influential allies. It found that a Moon Organization business was an important Korean defence contractor making M-16 rifles, and that in late 1977 Moon representatives tried to renegotiate the Colt–ROK Government M-16 co-production agreement in circumstances suggesting they were secret envoys of the Korean government. It also found that the Moon-founded Korean Cultural and Freedom Foundation advanced the Seoul government's political interests.
cite: US House Subcommittee on International Organizations, 'Investigation of Korean-American Relations', final report 1978 (excerpt on Wikisource)

n: Chinese officials paid for Taiwan village chiefs' trips to sway votes
rank: village and ward chiefs (local elected officials)
d: A Chinese government office, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Taizhou City, paid for trips that Lin Hsueh-feng, a former Kuomintang (KMT) city council candidate, organised for Chiayi village and ward chiefs, who are elected local officials in Taiwan. On the 2023 trips to Zhejiang the Taizhou office covered lodging and local travel, and prosecutors said Chinese officials urged the chiefs to vote for a particular party's candidate. On 28 May 2025 Chiayi District Court sentenced Lin to four years in prison under the Anti-Infiltration Act, a law against campaigning or political donations directed by hostile foreign forces, and the presidential election law. The ruling could be appealed.
cite: Chiayi District Court, judgment of 28 May 2025; Tribune India (citing CNA), 31 May 2025

n: Chinese military intelligence recruited aides in Taiwan's government
rank: Presidential Office consultant; assistant to the foreign minister
d: Chinese military intelligence, working for the Central Military Commission, recruited four former members of Taiwan's governing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) who worked close to the top of government. Huang Chu-jung, ex-assistant to a New Taipei councillor, did the recruiting. Ho Jen-chieh was an assistant to Foreign Minister Joseph Wu, Chiu Shih-yuan was deputy director of the Taiwan Foundation for Democracy, and Wu Shang-yu was a Presidential Office consultant. They passed on President William Lai's travel schedules and records of Joseph Wu's talks with foreign envoys. On 25 September 2025 Taipei District Court convicted all four of spying, jailing Huang for 10 years, Ho for 8 years 2 months, Chiu for 6 years 2 months and Wu for 4 years. The sentences could be appealed.
cite: Taipei District Court, judgment of 25 September 2025; Taipei Times, 26 September 2025

n: Romania's interior minister and police chief named as undeclared Masons
rank: interim interior minister and deputy prime minister; head of the Gendarmerie
d: Newsweek România reported in September 2019, citing anonymous Masonic sources, that two men running Romania's security forces belonged to Masonic lodges without declaring it. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in local groups called lodges. The magazine said Mihai Fifor, then interim interior minister and deputy prime minister, joined in 2008 through Loja Armonia and later Loja Basarab, and that General Constantin Florea, head of the Gendarmerie (the militarised police), belonged to Loja Basarab. Neither had listed membership in his declaration of interests, which the magazine said the law required. Fifor neither confirmed nor denied. Costin Mihalache, head of the Government Chancellery and a former foreign-intelligence (SIE) officer, said he had been a Mason but no longer was. The claim rests on that one outlet.
cite: Newsweek România investigation, republished by Alba24, 22 September 2019 (anonymous Masonic sources; the claim rests on that one outlet)

n: Burkina Faso's President Compaoré reported as former Masonic grand master
d: Freemasonry, a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges, had Burkina Faso's president and then his foreign minister at the head of the country's national lodge, Jeune Afrique reported in 2012. It said Blaise Compaoré, who ruled Burkina Faso from 1987 to 2014, was a former grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina while he was president, and that his foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé, had succeeded him as head of the lodge. A grand lodge is the national body over local lodges, and its elected head is the grand master. The source is a 2012 survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on Jeune Afrique's own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Burkina Faso's foreign minister reported as Masonic grand master
d: Freemasonry had its national leader in Burkina Faso's government: foreign minister Djibrill Bassolé was grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina, having taken over the post from President Blaise Compaoré, Jeune Afrique reported in 2012. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges; a grand lodge is the national body over them, and its elected head is the grand master. The source is a 2012 Jeune Afrique survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on its own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Mali's President Touré reported as overseeing the Grand Lodge
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Amadou Toumani Touré, president of Mali until the military coup of 21 March 2012, oversaw ('chapeaute') the Grande Loge du Mali while in office. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges; a grand lodge is the national body over them, and its elected head is the grand master. The report describes a sitting head of state presiding over a private society whose membership is not made public. The source is a 2012 Jeune Afrique survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on its own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Guinea's President Condé reported as overseeing the Grand Lodge
d: Guinea's sitting president, Alpha Condé, was reported in 2012 to oversee ('chapeauter') the Grande Loge de Guinée, the country's national Masonic body, so the head of state also presided over a private society whose membership is not made public. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges; a grand lodge is the national body over them, and its elected head is the grand master. The report came in a Jeune Afrique survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on its own reporting. It does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Senegal's President Wade reported as an initiated Freemason
d: Abdoulaye Wade, president of Senegal from 2000 to 2012, had been initiated into Freemasonry, the magazine Jeune Afrique reported in 2012. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges; a grand lodge is the national body over them, and its elected head is the grand master. Initiation is the ceremony by which a member joins. The report came from a survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on the magazine's own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge. After Wade lost power, his camp accused his successor Macky Sall of being a member too, which Sall denied.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Côte d'Ivoire's prime minister and interior minister named as Masons
rank: prime minister; minister of the interior
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that two of Côte d'Ivoire's most senior office-holders, Prime Minister Jeannot Ahoussou-Kouadio and Interior Minister Hamed Bakayoko, were Freemasons, and that state prosecutor Simplice Koffi Kouadio had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges; a grand lodge is the national body over them, and its elected head is the grand master. It said President Alassane Ouattara was not officially known to be a member. The source is a 2012 Jeune Afrique survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on its own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Gabon's police chief headed a Grand Lodge; ministers at Bongo's lodge
d: Freemasonry had Gabon's police chief and its president at the head of the country's two grand lodges, Jeune Afrique reported in 2012. A grand lodge is the national body over local lodges, whose members meet privately; its elected head is the grand master. The report said Antoine Embinga, head of Gabon's police until his removal in January 2012, was grand master of the Grande Loge symbolique du Gabon. It said ministers Paul Toungui and Séraphin Moundounga and Léon Paul Ngoulakia, head of the National Security Council, attended the installation of President Ali Bongo as grand master of the Grande Loge du Gabon on 31 October 2009. The source, a survey by Pascal Airault based on Jeune Afrique's own reporting, does not show particular decisions taken for the lodges.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Moon's church bought into a Uruguayan bank that lent to its own firms
rank: de facto president Aparicio Méndez; Uruguayan banking system
d: The Unification Church, the religious movement led by Sun Myung Moon, took part-ownership of one of Uruguay's oldest banks during military rule. In 1981 Moon's group bought 49% of Banco de Crédito and founded the daily Últimas Noticias, whose early editorial declared it 'fully identified' with the military 'process'; that year Moon's aide Bo Hi Pak met de facto president Aparicio Méndez, according to a book by Juan de Montemayor. The group also bought Montevideo's Hotel Victoria Plaza. Banco de Crédito closed in 2002. A parliamentary investigative commission on the financial and banking system found it had taken excessive risk by lending about US$100 million to Moon-linked companies, out of about US$600 million in total loans.
cite: Uruguayan parliamentary investigative commission on the financial and banking system; El Observador, 1 September 2012; Christianity Today, 13 May 1988

n: Moon aide Bo Hi Pak and CAUSA tied to Bolivia's 1980 coup regime
rank: de facto president Luis García Meza
d: Journalist Robert Parry wrote that the Unification Church, Sun Myung Moon's religious movement, and its political arm CAUSA backed General Luis García Meza's government after his July 1980 coup in Bolivia, known as the 'cocaine coup'. Parry wrote that the church published a photo of Moon's aide Bo Hi Pak meeting García Meza, and quoted Pak saying 'I have erected a throne for Father Moon in the world's highest city'. He also wrote, without naming a source, that CAUSA ran joint operations with the junta and that later Bolivian investigations found Moon's group had invested about US$4 million in the coup. He cited Martin Andersen's 'Dossier Secreto' for García Meza attending a congress of the Latin American Anti-Communist Confederation (CAL), the regional branch of the World Anti-Communist League (WACL). This is a single-author account.
cite: Robert Parry, The Consortium, 19 August 1998 (single-author account)

n: Honduran army chief's group took Unification Church front money
rank: commander of the armed forces (Gen. Gustavo Álvarez Martínez)
d: A front group for the Unification Church, Sun Myung Moon's religious movement, gave money to a political group headed by Honduras's top military officer. The Association for the Progress of Honduras (APROH), led by armed forces commander General Gustavo Álvarez Martínez, joined business leaders and officers; the Library of Congress country study says it received a US$50,000 contribution from the church front. The Christian Science Monitor reported in March 1984 that APROH and allied forces had taken control of university, professional, teacher, labour and peasant bodies. Fellow officers removed Álvarez on 31 March 1984, and APROH declined after that.
cite: Library of Congress, 'Honduras: A Country Study' (1995); Christian Science Monitor, 21 March 1984

n: CIA secretly funded and ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom
rank: US Central Intelligence Agency (International Organizations Division)
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly paid for and ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom, an organisation of writers and intellectuals opposed to communism. It was founded in West Berlin in June 1950 and run from Paris by Michael Josselson, a CIA officer. At its height it had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines, including Encounter (London) and Preuves (Paris). The New York Times named the CIA funding in April 1966; Ramparts and the Saturday Evening Post followed in 1967, and Thomas Braden, former head of the CIA's International Organizations Division, admitted in print that the CIA had funded the Congress and Encounter for more than ten years. CIA historians now call it one of the agency's 'more daring and effective Cold War covert operations'. After 1967 it was renamed the International Association for Cultural Freedom and funded by the Ford Foundation until it dissolved in 1979.
cite: New York Times series, April 1966; Thomas Braden, 'I'm Glad the CIA Is Immoral', Saturday Evening Post, May 1967; CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence, 'Origins of the Congress for Cultural Freedom'

n: Asia Foundation set up and secretly funded by the CIA
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) created the Asia Foundation and ran it as a 'proprietary', meaning an organisation it secretly owned and controlled while it appeared independent. A CIA memorandum to the White House 303 Committee, which approved covert operations, dated 22 June 1966, describes the foundation as 'established in 1954 to undertake cultural and educational activities on behalf of the United States Government in ways not open to official U.S. agencies'. It grew out of the Committee for a Free Asia (1951), and CIA support ran under the code name DTPILLAR. After press disclosures of CIA funding of private groups in 1966-67, a review led by Secretary of State Dean Rusk decided the foundation should be kept and funded openly by the US government.
cite: Foreign Relations of the United States 1964-68, vol. X, doc. 132 (CIA memorandum to the 303 Committee, 22 June 1966)

n: CIA secretly paid for the US National Student Association
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly funded the National Student Association (NSA), the federation of US college student governments, from the early 1950s until 1967. The money paid for its international programme and some domestic work, and a few NSA officers worked closely with CIA officials. Former staffer Michael Wood exposed the arrangement in Ramparts magazine in February 1967. President Johnson then set up the Katzenbach Committee to review CIA funding of US private voluntary groups, and in August 1967 the NSA formally cut its ties to the CIA.
cite: Ramparts, February 1967; New York Times, 16 Feb 1967; US Senate Church Committee Final Report, Book I (1976), on the Katzenbach Committee

n: CIA channelled money through the AFL's union committee from 1948
rank: 1948 Italian general election (party and union politics)
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly passed money through the Free Trade Union Committee of the American Federation of Labor (AFL) to influence politics and unions in Europe. The committee, run by Jay Lovestone, was set up in 1944 to back non-communist unions abroad. Historian Anthony Carew found that the CIA channelled money to it for about 20 years, starting with efforts to influence Italy's 1948 elections. The committee also subsidised the French union Force Ouvrière from 1948 through its Paris representative Irving Brown, and French journalist Frédéric Charpier writes that the CIA division under Thomas Braden gave Brown and Lovestone about $1 million a year in 1951-54.
cite: Anthony Carew, 'The American Labor Movement in Fizzland: The Free Trade Union Committee and the CIA', Labor History (Feb 1998); Frédéric Charpier, La CIA en France (Seuil, 2008)

n: CIA-linked IBAD paid for Brazilian opposition campaigns in 1962
rank: Candidates for the National Congress and state governorships, October 1962
d: The Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action (IBAD), linked to the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and backed by multinational companies, paid for the campaigns of many opposition candidates in Brazil's October 1962 elections for Congress and eleven state governments, aiming to change who held office. A Brazilian Parliamentary Inquiry Commission (CPI) investigated the funding, and President João Goulart closed the institute the following year. In 1977 former US ambassador Lincoln Gordon admitted that the United States had funded the opposition in that election.
cite: Brazilian Chamber of Deputies Parliamentary Inquiry Commission (CPI) on IBAD, 1963; Lincoln Gordon statement, 1977

n: Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty secretly run on CIA money
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly created and funded Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, which presented themselves as private stations. Radio Free Europe (1949) was set up by the National Committee for a Free Europe, a CIA front organised by Allen Dulles in New York, and Radio Liberty followed in 1951; both broadcast from Munich into the Soviet bloc. The CIA and State Department set broad policy directives for the stations. In 1971 Senator Clifford Case introduced a bill to take their funding out of the CIA budget. CIA funding ended in 1971-72, and from 1974 a Board for International Broadcasting passed open congressional appropriations to the stations.
cite: US Congress, S.18 (Senator Clifford Case, 1971); Presidential Study Commission on International Radio Broadcasting (1972-73); Board for International Broadcasting Act 1973

n: Church Committee: CIA ran money through foundations and campus ties
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly routed money through private US foundations and kept covert ties to academics and journalists, according to the Senate committee that investigated US intelligence in 1975-76 (the Church Committee). It found that, leaving out Ford, Rockefeller and Carnegie, at least 108 of the 700 grants over $10,000 made by 164 other US foundations in 1963-66 involved partial or complete CIA funding, and that CIA money was in nearly half of these foundations' grants for international activities. CIA labour, student and media projects peaked in 1964-67 and were cut back after the 1967 Ramparts disclosures and the Katzenbach Committee review. The committee also reported that the CIA was then using several hundred American academics at more than 100 colleges and universities, and until February 1976 had covert ties to about 50 US journalists.
cite: US Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, Final Report, Book I, pp. 182-192 (26 April 1976)

n: Ford-funded Berkeley economists took over Suharto's economic ministries
rank: Head of BAPPENAS, finance minister and other economic ministries
d: A group of University of Indonesia economists trained at the University of California, Berkeley on Ford Foundation money, later called the 'Berkeley Mafia', took over Indonesia's economic policy-making under Suharto. In the late 1950s the Ford Foundation paid for economists from dean Sumitro Djojohadikusumo's faculty to take graduate degrees at Berkeley. After Suharto took power in 1966 he made them his economic team: Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency BAPPENAS (1967-83) and was Coordinating Minister for Economics, Finance and Industry (1973-83); Ali Wardhana was Finance Minister (1968-83); Emil Salim and Mohammad Sadli also held ministries. Their 1966 programme cut inflation from 650% to 13% by 1969 and opened the country to foreign investors.
cite: Ford Foundation, 'Celebrating Indonesia'; Hal Hill and Thee Kian Wie, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies (2008)

n: Ford-funded Berkeley graduate Widjojo ran Indonesia's planning agency
rank: Head of National Development Planning Agency (1967-83); Coordinating Minister for Economics, Finance and Industry (1973-83)
d: Widjojo Nitisastro, one of the Ford Foundation-funded University of Indonesia economists trained at Berkeley (the 'Berkeley Mafia'), led that group into the top of Suharto's government. After taking his doctorate at Berkeley under the programme, he led the economists who presented a stabilisation plan to Suharto at the army staff college seminar in August 1966. He then headed BAPPENAS, the national development planning agency, from June 1967 to March 1983 and wrote Indonesia's Five-Year Development Plans, which set the direction of the economy for that period.
cite: Widjojo Nitisastro, The Indonesian Development Experience (ISEAS, 2011)

n: Ford-funded Berkeley graduate Ali Wardhana was Suharto's finance minister
d: Ali Wardhana, one of the University of Indonesia economists trained at Berkeley on Ford Foundation money and counted among the 'Berkeley Mafia', ran Indonesia's finance ministry for 15 years. He studied at the University of Indonesia, earned his doctorate at Berkeley under the Ford-funded programme, and served as Suharto's Minister of Finance from June 1968 to March 1983, one of the longest-serving ministers in Indonesian history. The finance ministry controls the national budget, taxes and borrowing.
cite: Hal Hill and Thee Kian Wie, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies

n: US- and Ford-funded Chicago graduates took Pinochet's economic posts
rank: Ministers of finance, economy, planning; Central Bank presidents
d: Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago under a US-funded exchange, the 'Chile Project', took the top economic posts in General Augusto Pinochet's military government; they became known as the 'Chicago Boys'. The project began in the mid-1950s as a US government Point Four aid scheme linking Chicago's economics department with Santiago's Catholic University. Between 1955 and 1973, 126 Chilean students trained under it, funded through US aid to 1964 and then by the Ford Foundation. Their 189-page plan 'El ladrillo' ('the brick') became the junta's economic programme in 1975. Graduates then held top posts: Sergio de Castro (Economy 1975-76, Finance 1976-82), Pablo Baraona (Economy 1976-79), Miguel Kast (Planning, Labor, Central Bank), Sergio de la Cuadra (Central Bank, Finance 1982) and Rolf Lüders (Economy and Finance 1982-83).
cite: Milton and Rose Friedman, Two Lucky People (1998); University of Chicago-Catholic University exchange records as summarised in the Wikipedia article 'Chicago Boys'

n: Chicago-trained Sergio de Castro ran Pinochet's economy and finance
rank: Minister of Economy (1975-76); Minister of Finance (1976-82)
d: Sergio de Castro, a graduate of the US-funded Chile Project linking the University of Chicago with Chile's Catholic University, carried that group's programme into Pinochet's government. He was a co-author of 'El ladrillo', the 'Chicago Boys' economic plan that the military junta adopted. He was Minister of Economy from April 1975 to December 1976 and Minister of Finance from December 1976 to April 1982, when the 1982 debt crisis ended his term.
cite: Chilean government records; Wikipedia biography citing Chilean sources

n: Chicago-trained Miguel Kast held Pinochet's planning and central bank posts
rank: Minister of Planning (1978-80); Labor Minister (1980-82); Central Bank governor (1982-83)
d: Miguel Kast, one of the Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago and known as the 'Chicago Boys', held a run of senior posts in Pinochet's government. He studied at the Catholic University of Chile and took a master's at Chicago. Under Pinochet he headed the planning office ODEPLAN, then the labour ministry, and in 1982 became governor of the Central Bank of Chile, which sets interest rates and controls the money supply.
cite: Chilean government records; Wikipedia biography citing Chilean sources

n: China's vice-minister of public security sat as Interpol president
rank: Vice-Minister of Public Security (2004-18) while Interpol president (2016-18)
d: China placed one of its senior police officials at the head of Interpol, the international police cooperation body: Meng Hongwei was elected Interpol's first Chinese president on 10 November 2016 while still serving as China's Vice-Minister of Public Security. He disappeared after flying to China on 25 September 2018; on 7 October the Communist Party's discipline commission said he was under investigation for bribery, and Interpol received his resignation. In January 2020 a Tianjin court sentenced him to 13 and a half years for taking more than 14.5 million yuan (about $2.1 million) in bribes. His wife Grace Meng, granted asylum in France, says the case is political.
cite: Tianjin No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, judgment of 21 January 2020; Reuters, 21 Jan 2020

n: UAE interior official elected Interpol president after UAE donations
rank: Inspector General, UAE Ministry of Interior; Interpol president (2021-25)
d: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) put one of its own interior ministry officials at the head of Interpol, the international police cooperation body, after giving it large donations. Major General Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, inspector general of the UAE Interior Ministry, was elected Interpol president in Istanbul on 25 November 2021 with about 69% of the votes in the third round. Before the vote, 19 NGOs opposed him, 35 French parliamentarians wrote to President Macron, and a report by former UK Director of Public Prosecutions David Calvert-Smith called him unsuited and questioned UAE donations to Interpol. Britons Matthew Hedges and Ali Issa Ahmad accuse him of responsibility for their torture in UAE custody; in March 2022 French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry. The UAE denies the accusations.
cite: French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office, preliminary inquiry (March 2022); The Guardian, 24 March 2022

n: UAE donations to Interpol's foundation matched all other members
rank: Interpol funding through the Interpol Foundation for a Safer World
d: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) gave Interpol, the international police cooperation body, donations reported at about $54 million through the Interpol Foundation for a Safer World, set up in 2013. That sum is estimated to equal the statutory contributions, the fixed annual dues, of the other 194 member countries combined. Critics say the money helped the UAE win the right to host Interpol's 2018 General Assembly and helped elect its interior ministry official Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi as Interpol president in 2021. A report by former UK Director of Public Prosecutions David Calvert-Smith raised the same concern in April 2021; Interpol rejected it.
cite: David Calvert-Smith, report on UAE and Interpol (April 2021); The Guardian, 7 April 2021

n: Tobacco companies secretly worked to undermine WHO from inside
rank: WHO decision-making and member-state health delegations
d: Tobacco companies ran a hidden campaign to weaken tobacco control at the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN's health agency, working through consultants, scientists and other UN bodies. At Director-General Gro Harlem Brundtland's request, a committee of experts chaired by Thomas Zeltner, director of the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health, examined company documents released in US lawsuits. Its 246-page report, received by WHO on 28 July 2000, found an 'elaborate, well financed, sophisticated and usually invisible' effort, which also worked through FAO, ECOSOC and the World Bank and through the companies' food subsidiaries, which offered partnerships to UN agencies. It urged member states to investigate tobacco-company influence on their own decisions. The report led into the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003).
cite: Committee of Experts on Tobacco Industry Documents, 'Tobacco Company Strategies to Undermine Tobacco Control Activities at the World Health Organization', WHO, July 2000

n: Brazil's Olympic chief paid an IOC member $2m for Rio 2016 votes
rank: Head of Rio 2016 bid and Brazilian Olympic Committee, working with Rio state governor
d: Carlos Arthur Nuzman, head of the Brazilian Olympic Committee and the Rio 2016 organising committee, was found to have channelled $2 million to Lamine Diack, a member of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), to secure votes when Rio was chosen as host in 2009. The IOC is the body whose members vote on which city hosts the Olympic Games. Police arrested Nuzman in October 2017 in the 'Unfair Play' phase of Operation Car Wash, Brazil's large corruption investigation, and the IOC suspended him that month. On 26 November 2021 federal judge Marcelo Bretas sentenced him to 30 years, 11 months for corruption, organised crime, money laundering and currency evasion; he remained free while appealing.
cite: 7th Federal Criminal Court of Rio de Janeiro, sentence of 26 Nov 2021; Agência Brasil, 26 Nov 2021

n: Rio governor Cabral admits paying an IOC member $2m for Olympic votes
rank: Governor of Rio de Janeiro state (2007-14)
d: Sérgio Cabral, governor of Rio de Janeiro state from 2007 to 2014, testified in July 2019 that he paid $2 million to Lamine Diack, a member of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), to buy votes for Rio's 2009 bid to host the Olympics. The money went through businessman Arthur César de Menezes Soares Filho. Cabral had been arrested in November 2016 in Operation Car Wash, Brazil's large corruption investigation, and later received sentences totalling over 400 years in many cases, some annulled in 2024. He was a co-defendant with Brazilian Olympic Committee head Carlos Nuzman in the federal case.
cite: Testimony before Judge Marcelo Bretas, 7th Federal Criminal Court, Rio, July 2019; BBC, 5 July 2019

n: Durão Barroso — WEF 'Global Leader for Tomorrow' 1993, later PM
rank: Prime Minister of Portugal (2002-04); European Commission president (2004-14)
d: The World Economic Forum (WEF), the Geneva foundation that runs the annual Davos meeting of business and political leaders, picked José Manuel Durão Barroso for its leadership network in 1993, while he was Portugal's foreign minister. He went on to be Prime Minister of Portugal (2002-04) and European Commission president (2004-14). The WEF picks rising figures for this network: Global Leaders for Tomorrow from 1992, renamed the Forum of Young Global Leaders in 2003-04, and lists Barroso among its 1993 Global Leaders for Tomorrow. Membership is a WEF selection, not a finding of influence; no forum has found that the network directed government decisions.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'The World Economic Forum: A Partner in Shaping History 1971-2020' (WEF, 2019/2020), list of 1993 Global Leaders for Tomorrow

n: IEA says 14 of Boris Johnson's cabinet were its 'alumni'
d: The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA), a London free-market think tank and UK partner of the Atlas Network, claimed that 14 members of Boris Johnson's first cabinet had come through its programmes. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. When Johnson formed his cabinet in July 2019, the IEA told supporters that 14 of those around the cabinet table, including Chancellor Sajid Javid, Foreign Secretary Dominic Raab and Home Secretary Priti Patel, were 'alumni of IEA initiatives'. Javid had said in 2015 that the IEA 'deeply influenced' his views. Matthew Elliott, chief executive of the Vote Leave campaign, had founded the TaxPayers' Alliance, another Atlas partner. The claim is the IEA's own; the Guardian reported it.
cite: The Guardian, 'How the right's radical thinktanks reshaped the Conservative party', 29 Nov 2019

n: Atlas-partner IPA's policy director became Human Rights Commissioner
rank: Australian Human Rights Commissioner (2014-16); Assistant Minister for Industry, Energy and Emissions Reduction (2021-22)
d: Tim Wilson moved from the Institute of Public Affairs (IPA), an Australian free-market think tank that is an Atlas Network partner, into a government post and then parliament. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. Wilson was IPA policy director from 2007 to 2013. The Abbott government appointed him Australia's Human Rights Commissioner in 2014; he entered parliament in 2016 and was an assistant minister in 2021-22.
cite: Australian Parliament biography; Atlas Network partner directory

n: Atlas-partner think-tank head became Piñera's chief minister
d: Cristián Larroulet moved from running Libertad y Desarrollo, a Santiago think tank that is an Atlas Network partner, to the centre of Chile's government. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. Libertad y Desarrollo runs a Free Enterprise Training Centre with Atlas. Larroulet, its executive director, had earlier been chief of staff at the Treasury under Hernán Büchi. President Sebastián Piñera made him Minister Secretary-General of the Presidency, the minister who coordinates the government's legislative agenda, from 2010 to 2014, and later head of presidential advisers.
cite: Chilean government records; Atlas Network partner listings

n: Atlas think tank Fundación Pensar merged into Macri's party
rank: PRO party of President Mauricio Macri (2015-19)
d: Fundación Pensar, an Argentine think tank in the Atlas Network, merged with PRO, the party formed by Mauricio Macri, who became President of Argentina in December 2015. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. Atlas leader Alejandro Chafuen told The Intercept in 2017 that Atlas-affiliated people were ministers in the new Argentine government; the article does not name them.
cite: The Intercept, 'Sphere of Influence', 9 Aug 2017

n: Director of NED-funded Atlas think tank signed Venezuela's coup decree
rank: Short-lived coup government of Pedro Carmona (April 2002)
d: The director of Cedice Libertad, the Atlas Network's main think tank in Caracas, which received US government-backed grants, signed the decree of the short-lived government that seized power in Venezuela's April 2002 coup. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. From 1998 Cedice received regular grants from the Center for International Private Enterprise, a core institute of the US-funded National Endowment for Democracy (NED); one grant letter lists NED funds for Cedice to advocate 'a change in government'. The 'Carmona Decree', named after coup leader Pedro Carmona, dissolved the National Assembly and Supreme Court during the coup against Hugo Chávez.
cite: The Intercept, 'Sphere of Influence', 9 Aug 2017, citing NED grant records

n: Milner, named by Quigley as Rhodes's secret-society heir, ran South Africa
rank: High Commissioner for Southern Africa; Governor of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony
d: Alfred Milner, whom Carroll Quigley names as a leader of Cecil Rhodes's secret society, ran British South Africa for eight years. Historian Carroll Quigley argued in The Anglo-American Establishment (1981) that Cecil Rhodes founded a secret society to extend British rule, whose circle, the Milner Group, placed members in government. Milner was High Commissioner for Southern Africa and Governor of the Cape from May 1897, administrator and then Governor of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony from 1901 to April 1905, and a Rhodes Trust trustee from Rhodes's death in March 1902; these offices are on the record. Quigley says Milner was named to the society's 'Junta of Three' in 1891, was Rhodes's chosen successor as its leader, and that the group 'caused the Boer War of 1899–1902'. The membership and the war claim rest on Quigley.
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 3–5, 33; Wikipedia 'Alfred Milner, 1st Viscount Milner' (offices)

n: Milner placed his Oxford recruits in the Transvaal government
rank: Transvaal colonial secretary, treasurer, town clerk of Johannesburg, Intercolonial Council secretary
d: Alfred Milner, Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa, filled the colonial government of the conquered Boer republics with young Oxford graduates he recruited from 1901, a group known as 'Milner's Kindergarten'. Patrick Duncan became Transvaal Treasurer and then Colonial Secretary (1903–07); Richard Feetham and Lionel Curtis served as town clerks of Johannesburg; Robert Brand was secretary of the Intercolonial Council; Geoffrey Robinson (Dawson) was Milner's secretary and then editor of the Johannesburg Star. The appointments are documented. Historian Carroll Quigley calls the group the 'Association of Helpers', the outer circle of Cecil Rhodes's secret society; that classification is his.
cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4

n: Milner's Kindergarten pressed for South African union from inside
rank: National Convention of 1908–09; Transvaal Legislative Council
d: Members of 'Milner's Kindergarten', the young Oxford men Alfred Milner had placed in South Africa's colonial government, worked from official posts and a funded journal to bring about the union of the four colonies. Lionel Curtis founded the monthly The State, funded by mining magnate Abe Bailey, in 1908; Robert Brand served as secretary to the Transvaal delegates at the National Convention and wrote The Union of South Africa (1909); and Richard Feetham sat on the Transvaal Legislative Council (1907–10). The group wanted a federal model, but the Convention chose a unitary state, and the Union came into being in 1910. Historian Carroll Quigley writes that the group 'created the Union of South Africa in 1906–1910'; that is his summary.
cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Brand, 1st Baron Brand', 'Richard Feetham', 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, p. 5

n: Lord Esher, named in Rhodes's secret 'Junta', reshaped the War Office
d: Reginald Brett, Lord Esher, whom Carroll Quigley names as one of three leaders of Cecil Rhodes's secret society, reorganised Britain's army command and advised the king. Historian Carroll Quigley argued in The Anglo-American Establishment (1981) that Cecil Rhodes founded a secret society to extend British rule, whose circle, the Milner Group, placed members in government. Quigley, citing Esher's journals, says Brett was told of Rhodes's plan on 3 February 1890 and named with W. T. Stead and Alfred Milner to the society's 'Junta of Three' in February 1891. Esher chaired the War Office (Reconstitution) Committee with Admiral John Fisher and Colonel George Clarke; its 1904 report created the Army Council and a permanent secretariat for the Committee of Imperial Defence. He declined the War Office and the Viceroyalty of India and advised Edward VII almost daily from 1903.
cite: Wikipedia 'Reginald Brett, 2nd Viscount Esher'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 3, 38–39

n: Rhodes company director and trustee Earl Grey became Canada's Governor General
d: Albert Grey, 4th Earl Grey, a director of Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company and one of the first trustees of the Rhodes Trust, became Governor General of Canada, the Crown's representative there, from 10 December 1904 to 13 October 1911. He had been Administrator of Rhodesia after Jameson resigned in 1896. Historian Carroll Quigley lists Grey in the 'Circle of Initiates' that Rhodes and the journalist W. T. Stead drew up for Rhodes's secret society in 1891; that membership rests on Quigley.
cite: Wikipedia 'Albert Grey, 4th Earl Grey'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 12, 39

n: Milner and his circle in Lloyd George's War Cabinet
rank: Member of the War Cabinet; Secretary of State for War; Colonial Secretary
d: Alfred Milner, whom Carroll Quigley names as the leader of a group descended from Cecil Rhodes's secret society, sat in Britain's five-man War Cabinet and brought an associate into his ministry. Lloyd George asked Milner to join the War Cabinet on 8 December 1916; he sat in it until November 1918, was Secretary of State for War from April 1918 to January 1919 and Colonial Secretary from January 1919 to February 1921. Leo Amery, whom Quigley counts in the group, served under him as personal secretary at the Colonial Office (1919–21). Quigley says Milner held regular 'Ginger Group' meetings with close associates in 1913–1919 to coordinate them as a pressure group; that account is his.
cite: Wikipedia 'Alfred Milner, 1st Viscount Milner' and 'Leo Amery'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope (1966), p. 951

n: Round Table editor Philip Kerr in Lloyd George's Downing Street team
rank: Private secretary to the Prime Minister; Prime Minister's Secretariat
d: Philip Kerr, founding editor of The Round Table, the journal of the Round Table movement that Alfred Milner's associates set up to promote imperial unity, was placed in the Prime Minister's personal staff. In December 1916 Lloyd George set up a secretariat in huts in the garden of 10 Downing Street, the 'Garden Suburb'. Its first members were W. G. S. Adams, David Davies, Joseph Davies, Waldorf Astor and Kerr, who edited The Round Table from 1910 to 1916. Kerr stayed as the Prime Minister's private secretary until March 1921 and wrote the Fontainebleau Memorandum of March 1919. H. W. Massingham attacked the group in The Nation (24 February 1917) as 'illuminati'. Historian John Turner (Historical Journal, 1977) found Milner's influence on its staffing; Carroll Quigley treats it as a Milner Group placement.
cite: J. A. Turner, 'The Formation of Lloyd George's "Garden Suburb": "Fabian-like Milnerite Penetration"?', Historical Journal 20:1 (1977), 165–184; Wikipedia 'Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian'

n: Round Table study group with India Office officials drafted 'dyarchy'
rank: India Office; Government of India constitution (Government of India Act 1919)
d: Lionel Curtis of the Round Table movement, the imperial-unity network built by Alfred Milner's associates, ran a study group with India Office officials that worked out the 'dyarchy' system later written into law. Historian Carroll Quigley writes that Curtis formed the group inside the London Round Table about 1911, joined by three India Office officials (Sir William Duke, Malcolm Seton, Sir Lionel Abrahams), and that it settled on dyarchy, meaning some provincial functions were handed to elected Indian ministers. Lord Chelmsford, Viceroy of India, told the Lords in November 1927 he had been handed a pamphlet with the 'diarchic principle' at the India Office in 1916, thinking it came from an official committee. James Meston, a Kindergarten adviser, sat in the Imperial War Cabinet in 1917. Dyarchy was enacted in the Government of India Act 1919; Curtis described the work in Dyarchy (1920).
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 11, pp. 202–204; Lionel Curtis, Dyarchy (1920); Wikipedia 'Lionel Curtis'

n: Milner Group member chairs the Irish Boundary Commission
d: Historian Carroll Quigley says the Milner Group, a private network of British imperialists formed around Lord Milner's young South African staff (the 'Kindergarten'), placed its member Richard Feetham, a South African judge, in charge of the Irish Boundary Commission of 1924–25. The commission was to fix the border between the Irish Free State and Northern Ireland. Its report was unacceptable to both governments and was buried. Another member, Lionel Curtis, had been involved in the making of the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty. Quigley writes that most of Feetham's posts 'came to him as a member of the Milner Group' and that the group's part in the Irish settlement was 'considerably more' than its journal, The Round Table, admitted; those are his claims.
cite: Wikipedia 'Richard Feetham' and 'Lionel Curtis'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4 and ch. 9

n: Round Table member Geoffrey Dawson edits The Times through appeasement
rank: Editor of The Times (influence on government policy)
d: The Round Table, a private network of British imperialists around Lord Milner, placed its own members as editors of The Times, according to historian Carroll Quigley, who says it 'controlled The Times for more than fifty years' (except 1919–22). One was Geoffrey Dawson, Milner's secretary in South Africa and a lifelong Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford, who edited the paper in 1912–19 and 1923–41. During the policy of appeasing Hitler, Dawson wrote to fellow member Lord Lothian on 23 May 1937: 'I spend my nights in taking out anything which I think will hurt their susceptibilities', meaning German opinion. A Times leader of 7 September 1938 suggested Czechoslovakia might gain from ceding its German-speaking border districts. Quigley places the 'Cliveden set' of appeasers near the group's centre.
cite: Wikipedia 'Geoffrey Dawson'; The Times leader of 7 Sept 1938 as quoted at airminded.org; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 4–5

n: Lord Halifax: Foreign Secretary Quigley counts in the Round Table
rank: Foreign Secretary; Viceroy of India; Ambassador to the United States
d: Historian Carroll Quigley claims Edward Wood, Lord Halifax, was a member of the inner core of the Round Table, a private network of British imperialists, while he held top state posts. Halifax, a Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford, from 1903, was Viceroy of India (1926–31), met Hitler in November 1937, was Foreign Secretary from 21 February 1938 to 22 December 1940 and defended the Munich Agreement, which handed part of Czechoslovakia to Germany, in the Lords on 3 October 1938. He was then ambassador in Washington until 1946. Quigley writes that Halifax was close to the group from 1903 'but did not really become a member until after 1920' and should 'probably be placed in the inner core'. The membership claim is Quigley's.
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 5–6; Wikipedia 'E. F. L. Wood, 1st Earl of Halifax'

n: Milner Group's Patrick Duncan, as Governor-General, installs Smuts
rank: Governor-General of the Union of South Africa
d: Historian Carroll Quigley says the Milner Group, a private network of British imperialists, had a man at the top of South Africa's state in Patrick Duncan, once Milner's Transvaal Colonial Secretary. Duncan became the first South African citizen appointed Governor-General, the Crown's representative, in 1937 and served until his death on 17 July 1943. In 1939, after Prime Minister Hertzog lost a parliamentary vote and resigned, Duncan refused his request for a general election and asked Jan Smuts to form a government instead. Quigley calls Duncan Smuts's 'chief lieutenant', inherited 'directly from Milner', and counts Smuts in the Milner Group, so on his account the decision put the group's own man in power.
cite: Wikipedia 'Patrick Duncan (governor-general)'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 78–79

n: John Buchan: Milner's Kindergarten member as Canada's Governor General
d: John Buchan, the novelist, served on Lord Milner's staff in South Africa until 1903 and is listed as a member of Milner's Kindergarten, the group of young officials who went on to form a private network of British imperialists. He entered Parliament in 1927 and was Governor General of Canada, the Crown's representative there, from 1935 until his death in 1940. Historian Carroll Quigley counts him in the wider Milner Group, which he argues placed its members in high imperial posts; the record does not show any decision Buchan took on the group's behalf.
cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment

n: Lord Lothian: Rhodes Trust chief sent as ambassador to Washington
rank: British Ambassador to the United States
d: Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian, led the Milner Group, a private network of British imperialists, from 1925 to 1940 while also holding British state posts, according to historian Carroll Quigley. Kerr was General Secretary of the Rhodes Trust, which runs the Rhodes Scholarships, from 1925 until 1939, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster (August–November 1931) and Under-Secretary for India (1931–32). He met Hitler in January 1935 and May 1937 and argued for revising the Versailles treaty in Germany's favour until March 1939. He was then British ambassador in Washington from 1 September 1939 until he died there on 12 December 1940. The leadership claim is Quigley's, made in The Anglo-American Establishment.
cite: Wikipedia 'Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, p. 4

n: Round Table's Robert Brand runs Britain's wartime missions in Washington
rank: Head, British Food Mission; UK Treasury representative in Washington
d: The Round Table, a private network of British imperialists, had one of its leaders running Britain's food and Treasury missions in Washington during the Second World War, according to historian Carroll Quigley. Quigley names Robert Brand, a banker, as the network's leader after Lionel Curtis (to 1963) and calls him an 'international financier' of its inner circle. Brand joined the merchant bank Lazard Brothers in 1909 and became a managing director. In 1915 he helped set up the Imperial Munitions Board in Canada. He headed the British Food Mission to the United States (1941–44), was the Treasury's representative in Washington (1944–46) and was made a peer in 1946. The leadership claim is Quigley's; the record shows a member in state posts, not a decision taken for the group.
cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Brand, 1st Baron Brand'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 950–951

n: CFR study group's Greenland memo shapes Roosevelt's policy
d: The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private New York foreign-policy club, wrote policy for the US government from outside through its War and Peace Studies. On 17 March 1940 a confidential memo from Isaiah Bowman's Territorial group argued that Greenland was strategically important and should be placed within the Monroe Doctrine, the US policy of keeping outside powers out of the Americas. CFR's 1947 anniversary book says Roosevelt summoned Bowman to the White House with the memo in hand. After Germany invaded Denmark in April 1940 Roosevelt declared Greenland part of the North American continent, and the Danish government-in-exile later granted US base rights there. The account is CFR's own.
cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 25–27, citing CFR's 1947 anniversary book

n: Allen Dulles carries CFR war plans into the OSS, then runs the CIA
d: The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private New York foreign-policy club, ran War and Peace Studies in 1939–45 to draft plans for the US government. Allen Dulles, who sat on the CFR board in 1928 according to historian Carroll Quigley, led its Security and Armaments group. CFR's own history says the Office of Strategic Services, the wartime US spy agency, recruited him to carry out the group's plans for occupied Germany, so a private club's plans entered government through him. He later became the longest-serving Director of Central Intelligence, head of the CIA (1953–61).
cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 23–25; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, p. 952

n: CFR member John Foster Dulles sets out 'massive retaliation' at the CFR
d: John Foster Dulles, described by the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private foreign-policy club, as 'a long-serving Council member', was Secretary of State under Eisenhower. On 12 January 1954 he used a televised CFR address to set out the administration's policy of meeting Soviet aggression 'instantly, by means and at places of our choosing', known as massive retaliation. CFR's history calls the speech a break with its off-the-record rule. Earlier CFR members in the same office included Frank Kellogg, who spoke at the Council in 1928 months before the Kellogg–Briand Pact outlawing war, and Henry Stimson.
cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 17–19, 41

n: John J. McCloy: War Department, World Bank, Germany, then CFR chair
rank: Assistant Secretary of War; President of the World Bank; US High Commissioner for Germany
d: John J. McCloy moved between top US posts and the leadership of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private foreign-policy club. He was Assistant Secretary of War (April 1941–November 1945), President of the World Bank (1947–49) and US High Commissioner for Germany (1949–52), the official running the American occupation zone. He then chaired the CFR board from 1953 to 1970 while also chairing Chase Manhattan Bank (1953–60) and the Ford Foundation (1958–65), and sat on the Warren Commission, which investigated President Kennedy's assassination, in 1963. CFR's own history names him as board chair.
cite: Wikipedia 'John J. McCloy'; G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021)

n: CFR members held about half of top US foreign-policy posts, 1945–72
rank: Senior US foreign-policy officials (State, Defense, Treasury, CIA)
d: Members of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private foreign-policy club, filled a large share of senior US foreign-policy posts after the Second World War. A study by Laurence Shoup and William Minter (Imperial Brain Trust, 1977) found that more than half of 502 senior US government officials it surveyed between 1945 and 1972 were CFR members. By its count members held about 42% of top foreign-policy posts under Truman, 40% under Eisenhower, 51% under Kennedy and 57% under Johnson. Eisenhower himself was a member. Membership was not secret; the study measures how far one club's members staffed government.
cite: Shoup and Minter, Imperial Brain Trust (Monthly Review Press, 1977), as summarised in Wikipedia 'Council on Foreign Relations'

n: Senate inquiry says Communists used the IPR to steer Far East policy
d: A US Senate subcommittee concluded that Communists had used the Institute of Pacific Relations (IPR), a private research body on Asia, to steer US Far East policy. The Internal Security Subcommittee under Pat McCarran reviewed about 20,000 IPR documents in 1951–52 and reported in 1952 that it 'was a vehicle used by the Communists to orient American far eastern policies toward Communist objectives'. Owen Lattimore, editor of the IPR journal Pacific Affairs, was a central target. The IRS revoked its tax exemption in 1955, but the courts rejected all IRS allegations in 1959; the IPR dissolved in 1960. Historian Carroll Quigley, who says the Milner Group dominated its British branches, argued that Boston banker Jerome Greene, who wrote the IPR constitution in 1926 and channelled Wall Street funds into it, mattered more 'than any Communists or fellow travelers'.
cite: US Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, report on the Institute of Pacific Relations (1952); Wikipedia 'Institute of Pacific Relations'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 946–956; The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10

n: Freemasons inside UK police forces, as exposed in 'The Brotherhood'
rank: Metropolitan Police and provincial police officers
d: Freemasons, members of a fraternal society organised in local lodges whose members swear to help one another, held posts throughout British police forces, according to journalist Stephen Knight's book The Brotherhood (Granada, 1983–84). It had chapters on the police, Birmingham City Police and Operation Countryman, a corruption inquiry. An extract in Police Review (28 October 1983) described City of London Freemasons helping secure a Metropolitan Police Commissioner's post for a candidate. After the book, Met Commissioner Kenneth Newman advised officers to stay away from lodges, and his Principles of Policing manual advised against joining. A lodge for Scotland Yard officers, the Manor of St James, was then formed and included chief officers. Knight died in July 1985.
cite: Stephen Knight, The Brotherhood (1984); Police Review vol. 91 no. 4733 (28 Oct 1983) via Statewatch; The Conversation, 'The Freemasons no longer have significant influence in the British police'; Wikipedia 'Kenneth Newman'

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: Operation Countryman: Met corruption inquiry and Masonic lodge claims
d: Freemasons' lodges inside London's Metropolitan Police were alleged to be tied to corruption among its detectives during Operation Countryman (1978–82), an inquiry run by officers from outside forces. Assistant Chief Constable Leonard Burt returned to Dorset in May 1980, and evidence was handed to the Metropolitan Police's own internal unit. Chief Constable Arthur Hambleton alleged obstruction by Commissioner David McNee and the Director of Public Prosecutions; eight officers were prosecuted and none convicted. MP Dale Campbell-Savours later alleged that police membership of particular Masonic lodges was tied to a criminal conspiracy, and Stephen Knight's The Brotherhood gave the operation a chapter. Parliament's requests for the findings were refused on public-interest immunity, a rule that lets the state withhold documents.
cite: Wikipedia 'Operation Countryman'; Knight, The Brotherhood (1984), ch. 9

n: Detective says Masonic officers took him off an Islington fraud case
rank: Detective Chief Inspector, Metropolitan Police Company Fraud Department
d: Detective Chief Inspector Brian Woollard of the Metropolitan Police said fellow officers who were Freemasons removed him from a corruption inquiry when it pointed to Freemasonry. He had been investigating corruption in Islington council's street-property renovation contracts. In a petition presented by Austin Mitchell MP on 20 December 1985 he said he was taken off the inquiry when it 'began to indicate a connection between corruption and Freemasonry', by officers who were Masons, and moved to uniform in April 1982. On 29 July 1988 Home Office minister Douglas Hogg told Jeremy Corbyn that the Home Secretary would not order an inquiry under section 32 of the Police Act 1964, and that Woollard had been dismissed by a disciplinary board on 25 May 1988 for absence from duty.
cite: HC Deb 20 December 1985 vol 89 cc671–2 (petition); HC written answer 29 July 1988

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: Police lodge members' victims charged; Lancashire pays £170,000
rank: Lancashire Constabulary officers; Chief Constable of Lancashire
d: Members of the Victory Lodge, a Masonic lodge made up mostly of serving Lancashire police officers, were involved in an assault in 1988 for which the victims, not the attackers, were charged. A Leicester shop owner and his son were assaulted at a Blackburn hotel during a lodge ladies' night; the hotel manager was a lodge member and the investigating officer was a Mason. The father and son were acquitted by a jury in February 1989. Their civil action against seven lodge members, the hotel group and the Chief Constable settled for about £170,000, most paid by the Chief Constable. The account comes from journalist Martin Short's 1996 evidence to the Home Affairs Committee, reprinted in his foreword to The Brotherhood.
cite: Martin Short, foreword to Stephen Knight, The Brotherhood (Harper Perennial ed., 2007), quoting his 1996 evidence to the Home Affairs Committee

n: Ku Klux Klan backs member Hugo Black into the US Senate
d: The Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret society, helped its member Hugo Black win Alabama's 1926 Democratic Senate primary. Black joined the Knights of Pythias and the Masons as a young man and around 1920 was an officer of his Masonic lodge; he joined the Klan in September 1923. The Birmingham chapter, Robert E. Lee Klan No. 1, was led from 1921 by James Esdale, later Grand Dragon (state leader). By the mid-1920s the Alabama Klan claimed to speak for the state's elite, 'including Masons, bankers, and ministers', and by 1926 Esdale oversaw 148 klaverns (local chapters) with a reported 94,301 members. Black visited all 148 during the race, and afterwards Esdale had him thank a Klan meeting alongside Governor-elect Bibb Graves. Black later sat on the US Supreme Court from 1937.
cite: Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Ku Klux Klan in Alabama from 1915–1930' (K. Hébert) and 'Hugo L. Black' (S. Suitts); Bhamwiki 'James Esdale'; The Nation, 'Hugo Black: A Personal History'
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (existing key)

arch.t: US Supreme Court Justice Was Documented KKK Member; Alabama KKK-Masonic Network Used as Political Infrastructure to Reach Highest Judicial Office

n: Ku Klux Klan member Bibb Graves wins Alabama's governorship
d: Bibb Graves, a member of the Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret society, won Alabama's 1926 governor's race with the Klan's secret endorsement and served 1927–31 and 1935–39. He was almost certainly the Exalted Cyclops (local leader) of the Montgomery Klan. His membership became public when he resigned in 1928, and in 1937, during the Senate row over Hugo Black's appointment to the Supreme Court, Graves acknowledged his former membership. He and Black received gold Klan 'passports' and were nicknamed 'the Gold Dust Twins'. In 1937 Graves appointed his wife Dixie Bibb Graves to Black's vacated Senate seat.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bibb Graves'; Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Ku Klux Klan in Alabama from 1915–1930'
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (existing key)

arch.t: US Supreme Court Justice Was Documented KKK Member; Alabama KKK-Masonic Network Used as Political Infrastructure to Reach Highest Judicial Office

n: Wagner man Valery Zakharov becomes CAR president's security adviser
rank: national security adviser to the president
d: Russia placed Valery Zakharov, a Russian tied to the Wagner Group, inside the Central African Republic's presidency as national security adviser. Wagner is a private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin that Russia used to place fighters and advisers with African governments. Zakharov served President Faustin-Archange Touadéra from 2018 and publicly told rebels in 2021 to hand over their leaders. Ukraine's SBU security service said in 2018 he headed Wagner's security firm in the country. The US Treasury put him on its sanctions list under its CAR programme with the note 'linked to: Private Military Company Wagner'; the listing shows he also held a Central African passport issued in June 2018.
cite: US Treasury OFAC sanctions list entry (CAR programme); Ukrainian SBU statement Dec 2018, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Prigozhin's strategists pay Madagascar presidential candidates
d: Russian political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Wagner Group, offered money to candidates in Madagascar's 2018 presidential race to shape who would hold office. The Russian investigative outlet Proekt and the BBC reported in 2019 that 15–20 such strategists dealt with as many as eight candidates, including the winner, Andry Rajoelina. Candidate André Mailhol said they gave him €5,000 in cash; ex-prime minister Omer Beriziky said he was promised $2 million. Rajoelina denied being Russia's candidate and the BBC found no evidence he took Russian money. Prigozhin's representatives denied any link.
cite: Proekt investigation (March 2019) and BBC, as reported by Meduza, 8 April 2019

n: Gupta family offers Mcebisi Jonas the finance ministry
d: The Gupta brothers, Indian-born businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma, tried to choose South Africa's ministers by offering cabinet posts to officials who would cooperate. Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas said the Guptas offered him the finance minister's job shortly before Zuma sacked minister Nhlanhla Nene in December 2015; former MP Vytjie Mentor testified she was offered the public enterprises ministry in 2010. The Zondo Commission, a judicial inquiry, found the Gupta network had 'captured' parts of the state, meaning it controlled appointments and contracts for its own gain. The US Treasury later cited a promised payment to a potential finance minister. The Guptas denied it.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo Commission), report parts 1–5, Jan–June 2022

n: Zondo report: ministers and state-firm chiefs acted for the Guptas
rank: public enterprises minister; Transnet and Eskom chief executives
d: A judicial inquiry found that South African ministers and heads of state-owned companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family, businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma. Chief Justice Raymond Zondo chaired the state capture inquiry, which heard over 300 witnesses from 2018 and published its report in five parts between 4 January and 22 June 2022. It named former public enterprises minister Malusi Gigaba and former Transnet (state rail and ports firm) chief Brian Molefe, and found that state advertising placed in the Gupta newspaper The New Age defied 'logic and legal requirements'.
cite: Zondo Commission report, 2022

n: US sanctions the Gupta brothers for buying South African officials
rank: network that offered ministries and paid officials
d: The US Treasury found that the Gupta family, businessmen close to South Africa's President Jacob Zuma, bought influence inside the state. On 10 October 2019 it sanctioned Ajay, Atul and Rajesh Gupta and their associate Salim Essa under the Global Magnitsky programme, which freezes US assets of people accused of corruption or abuses. Treasury said the family offered government members money or posts for cooperation, paid an official to appoint people friendly to its businesses, and took hundreds of millions of dollars through state contracts. The brothers moved to Dubai in 2016; in 2023 the UAE refused to extradite Atul and Rajesh to South Africa.
cite: US Treasury press release SM789, 10 October 2019

n: Bain & Company helped Zuma's allies take over the tax service
d: Bain & Company, a US management consultancy, worked with President Jacob Zuma and tax commissioner Tom Moyane to take over the South African Revenue Service (SARS), the Zondo Commission found, partly to stop SARS investigating corruption. Bain had been paid for a 2015 restructuring that cut the SARS unit producing a third of revenues. Bain denied 'wilfully' facilitating capture. South Africa's National Treasury barred Bain from state contracts for 10 years on 29 September 2022, and Bain closed its South African consulting business in 2025.
cite: Zondo Commission report (2022); Nugent Commission on SARS (2018); National Treasury restriction, 29 Sept 2022

n: McKinsey bribed South African state-firm officials, pays $122m
d: McKinsey & Company, a US consultancy, paid bribes to officials at South Africa's state power utility Eskom and rail firm Transnet to win contracts, working with Trillian, a firm owned by a Gupta associate. In 2024 McKinsey entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department, a deal that suspends charges if the company meets conditions, and paid a $122 million penalty for bribing South African officials between 2012 and 2016; half goes to South Africa. It had earlier repaid about R1 billion to Eskom and R870 million to Transnet. South Africa's prosecutors charged McKinsey SA and former partner Vikas Sagar in 2022.
cite: US Department of Justice deferred prosecution agreement (Dec 2024); Zondo Commission part 4 (April 2022)

n: Iran-aligned Hezbollah holds two ministries in Lebanon's government
d: Hezbollah, a Shia Lebanese party with an armed wing aligned with Iran, places its own nominees in Lebanon's cabinet. In the 24-member government Prime Minister Nawaf Salam formed in February 2025, Hezbollah's picks hold the public health ministry (Rakan Nasreddine) and the labour ministry (Mohammad Haidar); with its ally Amal it controls six portfolios. Hezbollah holds about 14 of 128 seats in parliament and is listed as a terrorist group by at least 28 countries, including the US and UK.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Hezbollah' (section on Lebanese politics)

n: US sanctions Hezbollah MPs and its liaison to Lebanon's security agencies
rank: members of parliament; liaison to state security agencies
d: The US Treasury said two sitting Lebanese MPs, Hezbollah's Amin Sherri and Muhammad Raad, acted inside parliament on behalf of Hezbollah, the Iran-aligned armed party. On 9 July 2019 it sanctioned them, the first time it had sanctioned sitting Lebanese MPs. It also sanctioned Wafiq Safa, head of Hezbollah's Liaison and Coordination Unit, which deals with Lebanon's security agencies. A State Department official urged the Lebanese government to cut ties with them; Hezbollah called it a 'humiliation'. Raad is now Hezbollah's deputy secretary-general.
cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, 9 July 2019, reported by Al Jazeera

n: Iran-backed militias written into Iraq's armed forces by law
rank: Popular Mobilization Forces, a branch of the armed forces
d: Militias backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards became a branch of Iraq's armed forces, paid by the Iraqi state. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in June 2014 to fight Islamic State and are made up of about 67 mostly Shia factions, almost all backed by the Guards. A law passed in November 2016 and signed by President Fuad Masum on 19 December 2016 placed them under the prime minister and on the state budget.
