In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said publicly that it took orders from Iran's supreme leader. A 2025 reform bill to tighten state control was tabled under US pressure.
cite: Law of the Popular Mobilization Commission (2016); Washington Institute and Carnegie analyses, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Falih al-Fayyadh: head of Iran-backed PMF sanctioned by the US
rank: chairman of the Popular Mobilization Commission; former national security adviser
d: Iran's Revolutionary Guards have allied militias inside Iraq's state through the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), militias almost all backed by the Guards and run by an Iraqi state body, the Popular Mobilization Commission. Falih al-Fayyadh, the commission's chairman, was at the same time Iraq's national security adviser, the government's senior adviser on security. On 8 January 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned him over the killing of protesters in 2019, and on 13 January it sanctioned PMF chief of staff Abu Fadak al-Mohammadawi. Iraq's foreign ministry said it was 'surprised'. Fayyadh remains PMF chairman, so the Iran-backed forces still sit under a state body he heads.
cite: US Treasury press release SM1231, 8 January 2021

n: Kata'ib Hezbollah, Iran's proxy, staffs three Iraqi state brigades
d: Kata'ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi Shia armed group that operates under Iran's Revolutionary Guards, staffs the 45th, 46th and 47th Brigades of Iraq's state-funded Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF). The US listed it as a terrorist organisation in 2009. It is a founding member of the PMF, and its commander Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis led the PMF in the field until a US strike killed him in January 2020. The US linked the group to the January 2024 Tower 22 drone attack in Jordan that killed three US soldiers.
cite: US State Department FTO listing (2009); US Treasury designations; Washington Institute analyses, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Ali Karti: Islamic Movement chief and ex-minister sanctioned
rank: former foreign minister; secretary-general of the Sudanese Islamic Movement
d: The Sudanese Islamic Movement, rooted in the Muslim Brotherhood, placed its members in power during Omar al-Bashir's 1989–2019 rule. Ali Karti was Bashir's foreign minister (2010–2015) and became the movement's secretary-general in June 2021. In September 2023 the US sanctioned him for undermining the transition to civilian rule and obstructing a ceasefire between the army and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group; Canada (April 2024) and the EU (June 2024) followed.
cite: US Treasury designation, Sept 2023; EU Council decision, 24 June 2024, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Sudan's Islamist finance minister and IRGC-trained brigade sanctioned
rank: finance minister; Islamist militia fighting beside the army
d: The US Treasury said Islamists tied to Iran hold posts inside Sudan's wartime government. On 12 September 2025 it sanctioned Gebreil Ibrahim, Sudan's finance minister and leader of the Justice and Equality Movement, which it tied to Islamist leader Hassan al-Turabi, saying he built ties with Tehran. It also sanctioned the al-Baraa bin Malik Brigade, an Islamist militia that grew from Bashir's Popular Defense Forces and has supplied up to 20,000 fighters against the Rapid Support Forces; Treasury said the brigade got training and weapons from Iran's Revolutionary Guards. Treasury used the word 'Islamist', not 'Muslim Brotherhood'.
cite: US Treasury press release, 12 Sept 2025

n: Muslim Brotherhood party member heads Libya's High Council of State
rank: chairman of the High Council of State
d: The Libyan Muslim Brotherhood placed one of its party's members at the head of a top state body. Libya's Justice and Construction Party was founded in March 2012 as the Brotherhood's political arm; it won 17 party-list seats in the 2012 congress and had five ministers until 2014. Its member Khalid al-Mishri chaired the High Council of State, the upper consultative body of the Tripoli-based government, from 8 April 2018 to 6 August 2023, and represented it at talks in Palermo, Doha, Moscow and Istanbul. The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Khalid al-Mishri' and 'Justice and Construction Party', citing Libya Observer and Reuters

n: UAE-backed southern council's chief becomes Yemen's vice-president
rank: vice-president of the Presidential Leadership Council
d: The United Arab Emirates got its client, the Southern Transitional Council (STC), into Yemen's top leadership. The STC was formed in May 2017 with UAE help to seek a separate southern state. In April 2022 it joined Yemen's eight-member Presidential Leadership Council and its leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi became a vice-president. After an STC offensive in December 2025 and a Saudi-backed counter-offensive, al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council. A delegation in Riyadh announced the STC's dissolution, which its UAE-based spokesman rejected.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Southern Transitional Council', citing Al Jazeera (7 Jan 2026)

n: Grand Orient de France chief meets Gabon's coup leader, a Freemason
rank: president of the transition (now elected president)
d: The Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body (a society of lodges whose members pledge mutual help), reached out to Gabon's new ruler, described as one of its own. Gabonreview, citing the newsletter Africa Intelligence, reported that in November 2023 Grand Master Guillaume Trichard met coup leader Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema in Libreville in secret and offered support to his transitional council. It described Oligui as a non-practising Freemason. Trichard also met the council of the Grande Loge symbolique du Gabon, the country's own lodge. Oligui was elected president in April 2025.
cite: Gabonreview, 22 Nov 2023, citing Africa Intelligence

n: Egypt bribed Senator Bob Menendez, who was convicted as its agent
rank: US senator, chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee
d: Egypt's government, through businessmen, paid US Senator Bob Menendez in cash, gold bars and other gifts while he chaired the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which shapes US arms sales and aid, including to Egypt. Prosecutors said he passed sensitive US information to aid the Egyptian government and spoke up for Qatar to help a New Jersey developer get Qatari royal funding. A halal-meat monopoly granted by Egypt to businessman Wael Hana's company was used to channel bribes. A Manhattan federal jury found Menendez guilty on all counts on 16 July 2024, including bribery, extortion, acting as a foreign agent and conspiracy. He resigned on 20 August 2024, was sentenced to 11 years on 29 January 2025 and is in prison; his wife Nadine was convicted on 21 April 2025 and sentenced to 4½ years.
cite: US v. Menendez et al., Southern District of New York: jury verdict 16 July 2024, sentence 29 January 2025; Wikipedia 'Bob Menendez'
org_note: Government of Egypt (with Qatari royal-linked funding) — foreign-state influence

n: Tom Barrack: acquitted of acting for the UAE inside Trump's circle
rank: chair of Trump's 2017 inaugural committee; US ambassador to Turkey and Syria envoy from 2025
d: US prosecutors charged that the United Arab Emirates used Tom Barrack, chair of Trump's 2017 inaugural committee, as its agent while he advised the Trump campaign and administration. The charges of 20 July 2021 were acting as an unregistered agent of the UAE, obstruction and false statements; the May 2022 indictment added that he sought hundreds of millions of dollars in UAE investment while lobbying for the UAE. A Brooklyn jury acquitted him and his aide Matthew Grimes on 4 November 2022. The Senate confirmed him as ambassador to Turkey on 29 April 2025 (60–36), and he was named special envoy for Syria in May 2025.
cite: US v. Barrack, Eastern District of New York, acquittal 4 November 2022; Senate confirmation vote 29 April 2025; Wikipedia 'Tom Barrack'
org_note: Government of the United Arab Emirates

n: Michael Flynn was paid for Turkish-interest work before becoming NSA
d: Michael Flynn's consulting firm was paid $530,000 for lobbying work that may have benefited Turkey's government, shortly before he became National Security Adviser, the official who runs the White House's foreign-policy staff. The money came in autumn 2016 from Inovo BV, a company owned by Turkish businessman Ekim Alptekin. Flynn served as National Security Adviser from 22 January to 13 February 2017, and on 8 March 2017 filed a retroactive foreign-agent registration acknowledging the work may have benefited Turkey. His business partner Bijan Kian was convicted of acting as an unregistered agent of Turkey in 2019, but the judge threw out the verdict for insufficient evidence.
cite: Flynn Intel Group FARA registration, US Justice Department, 8 March 2017; US v. Rafiekian (E.D. Va. 2019); Wikipedia 'Michael Flynn'
org_note: Turkish government interests via Inovo BV

n: Henry Cuellar charged with taking Azerbaijan bribes; later pardoned
rank: US representative (Texas), senior member of the House Appropriations Committee
d: US prosecutors charged that the government of Azerbaijan and a Mexican bank paid Representative Henry Cuellar of Texas, a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee (which sets federal spending), to act in their interests in Congress. In May 2024 Cuellar and his wife Imelda were indicted on bribery, money-laundering and honest-services fraud counts over about $600,000 from a company controlled by Azerbaijan's government and from a bank based in Mexico City. A judge refused to dismiss the case in September 2025. On 3 December 2025, before any trial, President Trump announced a full and unconditional pardon for both.
cite: US v. Cuellar, Southern District of Texas, indictment May 2024; presidential pardon announced 3 December 2025 (Roll Call)
org_note: Government of Azerbaijan (state-controlled company) and a Mexican bank

n: Cuban intelligence placed Victor Manuel Rocha in the US diplomatic service
rank: US ambassador to Bolivia; White House National Security Council staff; adviser to US Southern Command
d: Cuba's General Directorate of Intelligence (DGI) had an agent inside the US foreign service for decades, prosecutors said. Victor Manuel Rocha joined the foreign service in 1981, served at the White House National Security Council and the US Interests Section in Havana, was ambassador to Bolivia and later advised the commander of US Southern Command, the military command for Latin America. Prosecutors said he had acted for the DGI since at least 1981; in recorded conversations with an undercover agent he boasted of more than 40 years of service. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced in April 2024 to 15 years in prison and a $500,000 fine.
cite: US v. Rocha, Southern District of Florida, guilty plea and sentence April 2024 (AP via Britannica News)
org_note: Cuba's General Directorate of Intelligence (DGI)

n: Eric Adams charged over Turkish favours; case dismissed
d: Prosecutors charged that Turkish officials and businessmen bought favours from Eric Adams, the Mayor of New York City. In September 2024 a federal grand jury charged him with bribery, wire fraud, conspiracy and soliciting foreign campaign contributions. Prosecutors said he accepted luxury travel, took straw donations (money given in others' names) that drew city matching funds, and pressed the fire commissioner to let a Manhattan tower housing Turkey's consulate open in time for a visit by President Erdoğan. After the Justice Department asked to drop the case, Judge Dale Ho dismissed it with prejudice on 2 April 2025, so it cannot be brought again; Adams was never tried.
cite: US v. Adams, Southern District of New York, indictment September 2024, dismissal with prejudice 2 April 2025
org_note: Turkish government officials and businessmen

n: NYPD officer charged as Chinese consulate agent; charges dropped
rank: New York police officer and Army reservist
d: US prosecutors charged in 2020 that officials at China's consulate in New York directed Baimadajie Angwang, a New York police officer and Army reservist, to report on Tibetans in the United States. He was held for about six months. His lawyers said his contacts with the consulate were to get a visa to visit family. On 19 January 2023 a federal judge in Brooklyn granted the government's request to dismiss the case, prosecutors citing new, classified information. The NYPD later fired him.
cite: US v. Angwang, Eastern District of New York, dismissal 19 January 2023 (ABC7 New York)

n: Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 authors staff Trump's second term
rank: OMB director, FCC chair, CIA director, 'border czar', SEC chair and other senior posts
d: The Heritage Foundation, a Washington think tank, organised Project 2025, a governing plan for a conservative administration, and people who wrote or advised on it took senior posts under Trump from 2025. Axios listed Russ Vought (OMB director, the budget office; wrote the chapter on the Executive Office of the President), Brendan Carr (FCC chair; wrote the FCC chapter), Tom Homan (border czar), John Ratcliffe (CIA director; consulted on the intelligence chapter), Paul Atkins (SEC chair), Pete Hoekstra (ambassador to Canada) and Elbridge Colby (Pentagon policy). A CNN review found six cabinet secretaries had authored or contributed to the plan. On 20 January 2025 Trump revived the 'Schedule F' order it recommended, which lets officials reclassify and dismiss career civil servants. In July 2024 Trump had said he knew nothing about Project 2025.
cite: Axios, 26 November 2024; CNN review cited in Wikipedia 'Project 2025'; Executive order of 20 January 2025; Trump statement on Truth Social, 5 July 2024, reported by Spokesman-Review/AP (https://spokesman.com/stories/2024/jul/05/trump-tries-to-distance-himself-from-conservative-)

n: Center for American Progress alumni staff the Biden White House
rank: White House chief of staff, staff secretary, senior advisers, Veterans Affairs secretary
d: The Center for American Progress (CAP), a Washington think tank founded by John Podesta in 2003 as a Democratic counterpart to the Heritage Foundation, supplied many senior Biden-administration officials. They included chief of staff Ron Klain, economic advisers Brian Deese and Gene Sperling, Veterans Affairs Secretary Denis McDonough, Pentagon chief of staff Kelly Magsamen, Neera Tanden (CAP president 2011–21, then White House staff secretary and senior adviser) and John Podesta himself (senior clean-energy adviser). Business Insider counted nearly 70 CAP employees who had left for administration posts by mid-2021. The record shows the staffing route, not specific decisions taken for CAP.
cite: Fox News, 15 September 2022, citing Business Insider (2021); Wikipedia 'Center for American Progress'

n: Federalist Society members fill 43 of Trump's 51 appeals-court picks
rank: federal appeals-court judges and Supreme Court justices
d: The Federalist Society, a network of conservative and libertarian lawyers founded in 1982 with about 70,000 members, has placed its members on the federal bench. It helped assemble the list of 21 names Trump said he would choose from for the Supreme Court in 2016. The New York Times found that 43 of Trump's 51 appeals-court nominees by March 2020 were current or former members. At least five sitting Supreme Court justices — Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett — are or were members.
cite: New York Times, 16 March 2020; Wikipedia 'Federalist Society'

n: Trump says the Federalist Society was his 'recommending source' on judges
rank: federal judges and Supreme Court justices
d: President Trump said in May 2025 that he had used the Federalist Society, a network of conservative lawyers, to pick federal judges. On 29 May 2025, a day after a trade court with a Trump-appointed judge ruled against his tariffs, he wrote that 'it was suggested that I use The Federalist Society as a recommending source on Judges' and that he did so 'openly and freely'. He called its former leader Leonard Leo a 'sleazebag' who 'brags how he controls Judges, and even Justices of the United States Supreme Court', and blamed the society for 'bad advice' on nominations. The post is the President's own account of the society's role.
cite: Donald Trump, Truth Social posts, 29 May 2025 (American Presidency Project)

n: ALEC: corporations and state lawmakers draft 32 new model bills
d: The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) lets corporate members write laws with state lawmakers: the two sides draft 'model policies' that legislators then file as bills in their own states. At its December 2024 States and Nation Policy Summit in Washington, legislators introduced 32 new model policies, and ALEC handed out an 'Essential Policy Solutions' playbook for 2025 covering taxes, energy plant closures, public-sector unions, school vouchers and bans on ranked-choice voting. More than 400 state lawmakers signed an ALEC letter backing a permanent extension of the 2017 federal tax cuts.
cite: ALEC 2024 Annual Report; Center for Media and Democracy analysis published by Truthout, February 2025

n: Hogue inquiry: India's proxies may fund Canadian politicians
d: India's government, through proxy agents, may have given, and may still give, illicit money to Canadian politicians to get pro-India candidates elected, Canada's Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference found from intelligence it reviewed. The inquiry, led by Justice Marie-Josée Hogue, reported on 28 January 2025 with 51 recommendations and named India as the second most active state interfering in Canada. It found no evidence of 'traitors' in Parliament but noted 'some concerning conduct by parliamentarians'. India rejected the findings.
cite: Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference in Federal Electoral Processes and Democratic Institutions, Final Report, 28 January 2025 (CBC; Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada)
org_note: Government of India

n: Universal Church bishop Marcelo Crivella: senator, minister, Rio mayor
rank: Mayor of Rio de Janeiro; earlier senator and federal minister of fisheries
d: The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD), a Brazilian Pentecostal church founded in 1977 by Edir Macedo, has put its bishops into public office. Marcelo Crivella, an IURD bishop and Macedo's nephew, was a senator (2003–2016), Minister of Fishing and Aquaculture under Dilma Rousseff (2012–2014) and mayor of Rio de Janeiro (2017–2020). Police arrested him at home on 22 December 2020, nine days before his term ended, in an investigation into a kickback scheme in his administration, and he was suspended from office. He has sat in the federal Chamber of Deputies since February 2023.
cite: Rio de Janeiro state prosecutors and courts, arrest of 22 December 2020; Wikipedia 'Marcelo Crivella'

n: Universal Church bishop Marcos Pereira: minister and party chief
rank: Minister of Industry, Foreign Trade and Services; president of the Republicanos party; vice-president of the Chamber of Deputies
d: Pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD), a Brazilian Pentecostal church, founded the Republicanos party in 2005, and commentators describe it as a base from which the church's bishops run for office. Marcos Pereira, an IURD bishop, was Minister of Industry, Foreign Trade and Services under Michel Temer (2016–2018), has led the party since 2018 and has been a federal deputy and vice-president of the Chamber since 2019. The party holds about 40 of 513 Chamber seats and 4 of 81 Senate seats, and São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas is a member.
cite: Wikipedia 'Republicanos' (party history and officeholders)

n: Evangelical Parliamentary Front signs up 132 deputies and 14 senators
d: Brazil's evangelical churches have built a voting bloc inside Congress, the Frente Parlamentar Evangélica, a registered cross-party caucus that votes together on issues its churches care about. Agência Pública counted 93 federal deputies tied to evangelical churches in the 2023–2027 Chamber, led by the Assemblies of God (25) and Baptists (15), with the Universal Church among the three largest groups. The front's vice-president, Cezinha de Madureira, said in February 2023 that it brought together 132 deputies and 14 senators; signatories need not be evangelical themselves.
cite: Agência Pública, 'As igrejas que dominam a nova ala evangélica na Câmara', February 2023

n: Atlas Network-trained MBL leader Kim Kataguiri enters Congress
d: The Atlas Network, a US-based network that funds and trains free-market think tanks worldwide, trained activists in Brazil who went on to hold office. In April 2015 Atlas described Kim Kataguiri, head of the Movimento Brasil Livre (MBL), which led street protests against President Dilma Rousseff, as working with its Brazilian partner Estudantes Pela Liberdade, and said 'many members' of the MBL had passed through its training programme. Kataguiri was elected to the federal Chamber of Deputies in 2018 and re-elected in 2022.
cite: Atlas Network, 'Students For Liberty Plays Strong Role in Free Brazil Movement', 1 April 2015

n: MIRA — Colombian church's party holds Senate and council seats
d: The Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ International, a Pentecostal church founded in Colombia with branches in many countries, has its own political party, which puts church members into Colombia's Congress and local councils. The party, MIRA (Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation), was founded in 2000 by Carlos Alberto Baena and Alexandra Moreno Piraquive and lists the church as its religion. It currently holds 3 seats in the Senate, 1 seat in the House of Representatives and 47 local council seats.
cite: Wikipedia 'Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation'

n: Javier Milei — Atlas Network says its partners shaped his reforms
d: The Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks, says its Argentine partner groups helped shape the policies of President Javier Milei, who came up through its circles. Before entering politics Milei won the Liberty Prize of Fundación Atlas in 2018, sat on the advisory board of Fundación Libre and spoke at events of Atlas partners Fundación Libertad y Progreso and Federalismo y Libertad; his adviser Alberto Benegas Lynch is a Mont Pelerin Society director active in several Atlas groups (DeSmog, August 2023). Milei took office in December 2023. In August 2025 the Atlas Network credited Libertad y Progreso, Fundación Libertad and the Asociación Argentina de Contribuyentes with helping push his deregulation, tax and labour reforms; these are the network's own claims.
cite: DeSmog, 22 August 2023; Atlas Network, 'Sharpening Milei's Chainsaw', 29 August 2025

n: Horacio Cartes — US says Hizballah-linked bribes reached Paraguay's leaders
rank: former President of Paraguay; serving Vice-President Hugo Velázquez
d: The US Treasury says people tied to Hizballah, a Lebanese armed movement and party that the US designates as a terrorist organisation, paid bribes to Paraguay's former president Horacio Cartes and sitting vice-president Hugo Velázquez. Hizballah has long-standing finance networks in South America's Tri-Border Area. On 26 January 2023 the Treasury sanctioned both men for corruption, stating that both 'have ties to members of Hizballah', that Hizballah 'regularly held private events in Paraguay', and that representatives of both men collected bribes at those meetings. Sanctions freeze a person's US assets and bar Americans from dealing with them. The US removed the sanctions on Cartes and several of his companies in 2025.
cite: US Treasury, press release JY1221, 26 January 2023 (E.O. 13818); OFAC delisting reported by WorldECR, October 2025

n: Rafael López Aliaga — Opus Dei member as mayor of Lima
d: Rafael López Aliaga, a member of the Catholic organisation Opus Dei, governed Peru's capital as mayor of Lima. Opus Dei's lay members seek holiness in ordinary work, and it has long had members in Latin American governments. López Aliaga, leader of the Renovación Popular party, describes himself as an Opus Dei member who keeps celibacy. He was mayor from 1 January 2023 until he resigned on 13 October 2025 to run for president; he came third in the April 2026 first round with 11.91% and was elected to the national Senate, taking office in July 2026.
cite: Wikipedia 'Rafael López Aliaga' (Opus Dei membership and offices)

n: Eduardo Arana — Peru PM's ministry hired a reputed lodge member
rank: President of the Council of Ministers (prime minister); earlier Minister of Justice
d: Peruvian television reported that a Masonic lodge member was hired into Peru's Justice Ministry while a reputed senior Freemason ran it. Freemasonry is a network of private fraternal clubs called lodges; the Scottish Rite is one of its branches, and the 33rd degree is its highest rank. In July 2025 the programme Cuarto Poder reported that Prime Minister Eduardo Arana reportedly holds that degree, and that while he was Justice Minister a lodge member, Elías Falla Villegas, was hired as a consultant in November 2023 at S/15,600 a month. Another reputed lodge member's foundation received an official certification at a July 2024 ceremony Arana attended. Arana said membership of a private association was no grounds to assume favours and that the hire met the job's requirements. No lodge was named.
cite: Canal N, 7 July 2025, citing Cuarto Poder (América TV)

n: Sanae Takaichi — Nippon Kaigi Diet league member becomes PM
d: Sanae Takaichi, a member of the parliamentary league of the nationalist lobby Nippon Kaigi, became Japan's prime minister in October 2025. Nippon Kaigi (Japan Conference) is Japan's largest nationalist lobby group, founded in 1997, with about 38,000–40,000 members; it works on politicians through a cross-party league of members of the Diet, Japan's parliament. Takaichi has served in that league, as The Japan Times reported in 2021. She won the Liberal Democratic Party leadership in October 2025 and was elected prime minister by the Diet on 21 October 2025, at the head of an LDP–Japan Innovation Party coalition. She still holds the office.
cite: The Japan Times, 5 September 2021; Wikipedia summary of Nippon Kaigi and of Takaichi's election

n: Takaichi cabinet — 10 of 19 ministers in Nippon Kaigi's Diet league
d: Ten of the 19 ministers in Sanae Takaichi's first cabinet belonged to the parliamentary league of Nippon Kaigi, Japan's largest nationalist lobby group, which works on politicians through that league. On 23 October 2025 Japan Press Weekly, the English service of the Communist Party paper Akahata, listed the affiliations of the cabinet appointed on 21 October. It named Hiraguchi Hiroshi, Motegi Toshimitsu, Katayama Satsuki, Matsumoto Yohei, Ueno Kenichiro, Kaneko Yasushi, Ishihara Hirotaka, Kihara Minoru, Akama Jiro and Kiuchi Minoru. In Abe's 2014 cabinet the count reported was 15 of 19. Takaichi reshuffled the cabinet in September 2026; the count for the reshuffled cabinet was not checked.
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Takaichi cabinet — 12 ministers in the Shinto Political League
d: Twelve ministers in Sanae Takaichi's first cabinet belonged to the parliamentary league of the Shinto Political League (Shinto Seiji Renmei), the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines. The league gathers members of the Diet, Japan's parliament, who back its aims, such as constitutional revision and official honours for Yasukuni Shrine, where Japan's war dead, including convicted war criminals, are enshrined. Japan Press Weekly (Akahata) reported the count on 23 October 2025; the members include Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, Finance Minister Katayama Satsuki and Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru. Seven of them were also listed as Nippon Kaigi league members.
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Takaichi cabinet — five ministers with Unification Church ties
d: Five ministers in Sanae Takaichi's first cabinet had ties to the Unification Church (Family Federation for World Peace and Unification), a Korean-founded church whose links to lawmakers of the governing Liberal Democratic Party came to light after Shinzo Abe's killing in 2022; Tokyo courts ordered its Japanese branch dissolved in 2025. Japan Press Weekly (Akahata) reported on 23 October 2025 that Matsumoto Yohei's party branch paid dues to the church-linked Women's Federation for World Peace (revealed in 2019); Ueno Kenichiro paid fees to affiliated bodies in 2018–19 and attended an affiliated lawmakers' meeting in 2021; Akazawa Ryosei and Ishihara Hirotaka spoke at affiliated meetings; and Kiuchi Minoru sent a congratulatory telegram to an affiliated company's event in 2018.
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Soka Gakkai's party Komeito sat in Japan's government for 26 years
d: Soka Gakkai, a Buddhist lay movement, put its own party into Japan's government for most of 1999 to 2025. Komeito was founded in 1964 by Soka Gakkai's leader, and the movement's members supply its votes. As junior partner to the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) it held government posts from 1999 to 2009 and from 2012 to 2025. On 10 October 2025 Komeito leader Tetsuo Saito announced the party was leaving the coalition, citing disagreements with Sanae Takaichi's leadership and the LDP's handling of its slush-fund scandal. Takaichi then formed a coalition with the Japan Innovation Party, and Komeito is now in opposition.
cite: Komeito announcement, 10 October 2025 (NHK, CNBC); Wikipedia: Komeito

n: Unification Church papers say it backed 290 LDP lawmakers in 2021
d: Documents of the Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, say it backed 290 members of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) in the October 2021 lower-house election. The documents were seized in South Korean investigations, and in January 2026 South Korean media reported that Eiji Tokuno, then head of the church's Japan branch, gave that figure to church leader Han Hak-ja in a report. The LDP's own 2022 survey had found 179–180 of its lawmakers with ties to the church. The same documents are reported to describe Abe as pleased with church support at a meeting before the 2019 upper-house election. Akahata separately reported that an August 2021 'TM Special Report' to Han said Takaichi becoming LDP president would be 'Heaven's greatest wish fulfilled'.
cite: Jiji Press, 2 January 2026, citing South Korean media; Akahata/Japan Press Weekly, January 2026

n: Chun Jae-soo — Korean oceans minister quits over Unification Church cash
d: South Korea's Unification Church is accused of paying Chun Jae-soo, a Democratic Party lawmaker, to help a project it wanted. Yun Young-ho, former head of the church's world headquarters, told the special counsel investigating ex-first lady Kim Keon-hee that the church gave Chun 30 million won in cash and two luxury watches in 2018–2020 to seek his help with a Korea–Japan undersea tunnel project. Chun was by then serving as President Lee Jae-myung's oceans minister, and he resigned on 11 December 2025. The special counsel passed the matter to police, who booked Chun as a bribery suspect and barred him from travel. Chun denies the allegations.
cite: Reuters/The Star, 11 December 2025; Korea JoongAng Daily, 15 December 2025

n: Hu Peng-nien — retired Taiwan cabinet official jailed for China recruiting
d: A retired official of Taiwan's cabinet, the Executive Yuan, was jailed for trying to recruit insiders for China's Communist Party. China's united front system works to win over or recruit people abroad, including in Taiwan. In September 2026 Taiwan's High Court sentenced businessman Cheng Ming-chia to 10 years and six months for building a network for united front officials, arranging meetings in China from 2021 to 2025. It sentenced the retired official, Hu Peng-nien, to five years. Prosecutors said Hu tried to recruit military personnel and others for information on the military and on government and legislative work, and carried a Chinese-supplied communications device into Taiwan. Both rulings can be appealed.
cite: Taiwan High Court ruling (Taipei Times, 11 September 2026)

n: Solomon Islands MPs say Beijing and Taipei offered cash for their votes
d: Members of the Solomon Islands parliament said both China and Taiwan offered them money to sway a decision on which of the two governments their country would recognise. In September 2019 Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare ended 36 years of diplomatic ties with Taiwan and recognised the People's Republic of China. The Guardian and the Solomon Star reported that MPs said both Beijing and Taipei had offered them hundreds of thousands of dollars to sway the vote. Riots over the switch followed, and anger over it was a factor in the violent unrest in Honiara, the capital, in November 2021.
cite: The Guardian and Solomon Star reporting, 2019; Wikipedia: China–Solomon Islands relations

n: China-funded Solomon Islands PM's fund paid 39 of 50 MPs
d: Money from China, paid into a fund controlled by the Solomon Islands prime minister's office, went to 39 of the country's 50 MPs weeks before a vote on removing him. China agreed in 2019 to fund this discretionary fund, as Taiwan had done before. At a livestreamed parliamentary budget committee hearing in August 2022, the prime minister's secretary Jimmy Rodgers said China had provided SBD20.9 million (about US$2.49 million) spent in 2021, and that the MPs received payments in two tranches, on 22 November and 13 December 2021. Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote in December 2021; opposition leader Matthew Wale accused him of using the money to stay in power, which Sogavare's office denied.
cite: Parliamentary budget committee hearing, August 2022 (Reuters via VOA, 25 August 2022)

n: Jian Yang and Raymond Huo — NZ MPs leave over China concerns
d: Jian Yang sat in New Zealand's Parliament for the National Party from 2011 to 2020. He had been a Communist Party member and taught at People's Liberation Army institutions that trained intelligence linguists before moving to New Zealand, as New Zealand media reported in 2017. Several outlets reported in 2021 that his retirement at the 2020 election came after New Zealand's intelligence agencies raised concerns about his relationship with the Chinese government. The same reports said Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and opposition leader Todd Muller agreed that Labour MP Raymond Huo would also leave Parliament for the same reason.
cite: New Zealand media reports, 2017 and 2021; Wikipedia: Jian Yang

n: Huang Jing — Singapore expels professor as foreign agent of influence
rank: foreign-policy academic (target: Singapore foreign policy and opinion)
d: Singapore's government says a foreign intelligence service used a professor at its state university's public-policy school to influence Singapore's foreign policy. On 4 August 2017 the Ministry of Home Affairs cancelled the permanent residence of Huang Jing, a US-citizen professor at the National University of Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, and of his wife, and banned both from re-entering. The ministry called him 'an agent of influence of a foreign country' who worked with that country's intelligence agents to influence Singapore's foreign policy and public opinion. It did not name the country. Huang denied the charge.
cite: Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs statement, 4 August 2017
org_note: prc_state is used because the case is widely read as China, but Singapore's ministry did not name the country

n: Alice Guo — Chinese citizen elected mayor where POGO hub ran
d: Chinese-run gambling hubs in the Philippines had a mayor in office who was later ruled to be a Chinese citizen. Alice Guo was elected mayor of Bamban in 2022; a court later ruled she is Guo Hua Ping, born in Fujian. POGOs were Chinese-run online gambling firms licensed from 2016; 2024 Senate hearings tied many to fraud and trafficking, and senators linked Guo to the Zun Yuan Technology hub raided in her town. The Ombudsman removed her on 13 August 2024. In June 2025 a Manila court voided her election, and on 20 November 2025 she was convicted of qualified human trafficking and sentenced to life. Self-confessed Chinese spy She Zhijiang told Al Jazeera she was a Chinese intelligence asset; she denies it, and the claim is untested in court.
cite: Ombudsman decision, 13 August 2024; Manila RTC Branch 34, June 2025; trafficking verdict, 20 November 2025

n: Chen Zhi — alleged scam-empire boss served as Hun Sen's adviser
rank: adviser to Hun Sen and other leaders
d: Chen Zhi, whom US prosecutors call the head of a cyber-fraud empire run from scam compounds, served as an official adviser to Cambodia's top leaders. Born in Fujian, China, he took Cambodian citizenship in 2014 and built the Prince Group, one of Cambodia's largest conglomerates. He held the honorary title Neak Oknha, and advised Hun Sen, interior minister Sar Kheng and National Assembly president Heng Samrin. On 14 October 2025 the US Justice Department indicted him for fraud and money laundering and seized about 127,271 bitcoin (about US$14 billion), while the US and UK sanctioned 146 people and firms linked to the group. In January 2026 Cambodia said it had arrested him, revoked his citizenship and sent him to China to face charges.
cite: US Department of Justice indictment and OFAC/UK sanctions, 14 October 2025; Cambodian government statement, January 2026

n: RSS roots — 38 of 53 BJP ministers in Modi's second government
d: Most ministers of India's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) come from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation founded in 1925 from whose political wing the BJP grew. ThePrint counted in January 2020 that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers in Narendra Modi's second government (71%) had RSS roots, up from 41 of 66 (62%) in 2014. All eight members it listed on the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, including Rajnath Singh, Amit Shah and Nitin Gadkari, had RSS links; Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar did not. It also counted 146 of 303 BJP members of the Lok Sabha, the lower house, with RSS links.
cite: ThePrint, 27 January 2020

n: C. P. Radhakrishnan — RSS member since 16, now Vice President
d: C. P. Radhakrishnan, a member of the Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) since the age of 16, became Vice President of India in 2025. He was also active in the RSS's earlier political wing, the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, and later served as a BJP MP for Coimbatore and as governor of several states. He was elected the 15th Vice President and took office on 12 September 2025. The vice president also chairs the upper house of Parliament, the Rajya Sabha.
cite: Wikipedia: C. P. Radhakrishnan (citing Indian press)

n: Gnanasara — anti-Muslim monk named to draft Sri Lanka's 'one law'
d: Sri Lanka's president gave the leader of an anti-Muslim monks' group charge of drafting proposals for the country's legal code, work that normally belongs to Parliament and the Justice Ministry. Bodu Bala Sena (BBS, 'Buddhist Power Force') is a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist monks' group founded in 2012, accused of stirring anti-Muslim violence. On 26 October 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed its general secretary, Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, to chair a presidential task force on 'One Country, One Law' to draft proposals on a single legal code. Justice Minister Ali Sabry said he had not been consulted, and the Bar Association, the lawyers' professional body, said the task force would take over the work of Parliament and the Justice Ministry.
cite: Presidential gazette, 26 October 2021 (Daily FT)

n: Ma Ba Tha's drafts became Myanmar's race and religion laws
d: A Buddhist nationalist monks' group wrote the texts that Myanmar's government turned into four national laws. Ma Ba Tha (Association for the Protection of Race and Religion) was formed in 2014. In 2013–14 Myanmar's Ministry of Religious Affairs drafted four Race and Religion Protection Laws, covering religious conversion, marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men, monogamy and birth spacing, based on texts proposed by its members. Parliament passed them in 2015, the first being signed in May 2015.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 29 May 2014; Wikipedia: Ma Ba Tha

n: Eva Kaili — European Parliament vice-president charged in Qatargate
d: Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid cash to people inside the European Parliament to favour them, a case known as Qatargate. On 9 December 2022 Belgian police arrested Greek MEP Eva Kaili, then one of the Parliament's 14 vice-presidents; bags of cash were found at her home and a suitcase of cash with her father. Parliament removed her as vice-president on 13 December 2022 by 625 votes to 1. She is charged with corruption, money laundering and membership of a criminal organisation, and denies the charges. In February 2026 the Brussels Court of Appeal ruled the investigation had been lawful, so the case continues.
cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office (investigating judge Michel Claise); European Parliament vote of 13 December 2022; Brussels Court of Appeal ruling, February 2026

n: Fight Impunity — NGO used as channel for Qatar and Morocco cash
rank: former MEP and chair of the EP human rights subcommittee
d: Belgian prosecutors say Morocco's foreign intelligence agency (DGED) paid a former member of the European Parliament to lobby for Morocco there, and that a Brussels charity was used to route foreign payments. Fight Impunity was a human-rights NGO founded by former Italian MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri, who had chaired the Parliament's human rights subcommittee. Police found about €600,000 in cash at his home in December 2022. Prosecutors say the DGED agreed in 2019 to pay Panzeri and his former assistant Francesco Giorgi €50,000 a year each. Giorgi told investigators that payments from Qatar and Mauritania were routed through the NGO. Panzeri signed a plea deal with Belgian prosecutors in January 2023 to tell what he knew.
cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office; Panzeri plea agreement, January 2023; Financial Times and Der Spiegel reporting on the case file

n: Marc Tarabella and Andrea Cozzolino — immunity lifted in Qatargate
d: Two MEPs who led the European Parliament's delegations for the Gulf and North Africa were arrested in the Qatargate case, in which Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid people inside the Parliament. Immunity protects MEPs from prosecution unless the Parliament lifts it; in February 2023 it lifted the immunity of Belgian MEP Marc Tarabella and Italian MEP Andrea Cozzolino at Belgium's request. Tarabella, vice-chair of the delegation for relations with the Arabian Peninsula, was arrested and charged with corruption and money laundering; he denies wrongdoing. Cozzolino, long-time chair of the delegation to the Maghreb countries, was arrested in Naples on a Belgian warrant on 10 February 2023. Neither stood again in 2024; Tarabella was re-elected mayor of Anthisnes in October 2024.
cite: European Parliament immunity votes, February 2023; Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office

n: Huawei bribery probe — European Parliament offices searched
d: Belgian prosecutors suspect that Huawei, a Chinese telecoms company with a large lobbying office in Brussels, was favoured by people in the European Parliament in exchange for gifts. In March 2025 they arrested several people and searched offices inside the Parliament on suspicion that, since 2021, gifts, travel and football tickets were given in exchange for political positions favouring Huawei. On 18 March 2025 four people were charged with active corruption and membership of a criminal organisation and a fifth with money laundering; the number charged later rose to eight. Parliament banned Huawei lobbyists from its buildings and the European Commission stopped meeting groups that speak for Huawei.
cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office statements, 13 and 18 March 2025; European Parliament and European Commission decisions, 2025

n: Huawei suspected of buying MEPs' favours with gifts
d: Huawei, the Chinese telecoms company, is suspected by Belgian prosecutors of buying favours inside the European Parliament with gifts to its members (MEPs). In May 2025 Parliament President Roberta Metsola passed on the prosecutors' requests to lift the immunity from prosecution of three sitting MEPs: Fulvio Martusciello (Italy, Forza Italia), Nikola Minchev (Bulgaria) and Daniel Attard (Malta). One of Martusciello's staff had been arrested in Naples in March 2025 on a European arrest warrant. Prosecutors later said the Daniel Attard who received gifts was a namesake, the mayor of Għasri, and in June 2026 Parliament voted not to lift the MEP's immunity.
cite: European Parliament plenary announcements, May 2025; Parliament vote on Attard immunity, June 2026

n: Petr Bystroň — MEP suspected of taking Voice of Europe money
rank: AfD member of the Bundestag, then MEP
d: German prosecutors suspect AfD politician Petr Bystroň of taking money from a Russian-funded network in return for speaking and voting in Russia's interest. Voice of Europe was a Prague-based news site that Czech intelligence exposed in March 2024 as a Russian-funded influence network run for Viktor Medvedchuk, a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician, paying European politicians. Prosecutors in Munich suspect Bystroň took cash or crypto from it. The Bundestag lifted his immunity in 2024 and police searched his offices; after he became an MEP, the European Parliament lifted his immunity again on 6 May 2025 by a large show of hands. Bystroň denies the allegations.
cite: Munich Public Prosecutor's Office; Bundestag immunity decision 2024; European Parliament plenary vote, 6 May 2025

n: Nathan Gill — ex-MEP jailed for taking pro-Russian bribes
rank: Member of the European Parliament (UKIP/Brexit Party), later Reform UK leader in Wales
d: Nathan Gill, who sat in the European Parliament for Wales from 2014 to 2020, was paid to make pro-Russian statements there. In September 2025 he pleaded guilty to eight counts of bribery between December 2018 and July 2019: Ukrainian MP Oleg Voloshyn paid him to make the statements in the Parliament and on Ukrainian TV channels, passing on requests from 'V', said in court to be Viktor Medvedchuk, a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician. On 21 November 2025 the Old Bailey, England's main criminal court, sentenced him to 10 years and 6 months in prison.
cite: Central Criminal Court (Old Bailey), sentence of 21 November 2025; Metropolitan Police Counter Terrorism Command investigation

n: Tatjana Ždanoka — MEP reported to Russia's FSB for 20 years
d: Leaked emails show Tatjana Ždanoka, a Latvian member of the European Parliament from 2004 to 2024, reporting to officers of Russia's FSB, its main security and intelligence service, from at least 2004. She was co-chair of the Latvian Russian Union party. The emails were published in January 2024 by The Insider and partners. Latvia's State Security Service opened a criminal case on 22 February 2024 for possible cooperation with Russian intelligence and searched her property in July 2024; the European Parliament imposed a penalty on her in April 2024 for breaking its code of conduct.
cite: Latvian State Security Service (VDD) criminal case, opened 22 February 2024; European Parliament President's penalty decision, April 2024
org_note: Russian intelligence acting directly; org kept generic

n: Béla Kovács — Jobbik MEP convicted of spying for Russia
d: Béla Kovács, a member of the European Parliament for the Hungarian nationalist party Jobbik, was convicted of spying on EU institutions for Russia from inside the Parliament. Hungarian prosecutors brought the accusation, and the European Parliament lifted his immunity from prosecution on 14 October 2015. In September 2022 Hungary's top court, the Curia, sentenced him in absentia to five years in prison for espionage. He lives in Russia.
cite: Curia of Hungary, judgment of September 2022; European Parliament immunity vote, 14 October 2015
org_note: Russian intelligence acting directly

n: Salvini associate negotiated secret Russian oil money for the Lega
rank: party (Lega) – aide to deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini
d: A close associate of Matteo Salvini, leader of Italy's Lega party, negotiated with Russians over an oil deal meant to channel Russian money illegally into the party. At an October 2018 meeting at the Metropol hotel in Moscow, Gianluca Savoini, president of the Lombardy–Russia cultural association, discussed the deal; a recording of the meeting was published in 2019. Milan prosecutors investigated Savoini and others for international corruption. In April 2023 a Milan judge closed the case: the judge found the actions were 'unequivocally aimed' at illegally financing the party, but the deal never reached the point where it could achieve that.
cite: Milan Public Prosecutor's Office investigation; dismissal order of the Milan preliminary-investigations judge, April 2023

n: Evghenia Guțul — Gagauzia governor jailed over Russian party money
rank: Governor (başkan) of the autonomous region of Gagauzia
d: A Moldovan court found that Evghenia Guțul, governor of Gagauzia, an autonomous region of Moldova, used undeclared Russian money to finance the party that put her in office. The Șor Party, led by businessman Ilan Shor, was declared unconstitutional by Moldova's Constitutional Court on 19 June 2023 for serving a foreign state's interests. Guțul won the governorship as its candidate in 2023 and met Vladimir Putin in March 2024. In August 2025 a court sentenced her to seven years in prison for the financing; the party's former secretary was sentenced at the same hearing for handing out 9.8 million lei to pay protesters.
cite: Constitutional Court of Moldova, decision of 19 June 2023; Chișinău court sentences, 5 August 2025

n: Jian Guo — AfD MEP's aide jailed for spying for China
d: China's Ministry of State Security, its main spy agency, had an agent working inside the European Parliament as an assistant to AfD MEP Maximilian Krah. The agent, Jian Guo, a German citizen of Chinese origin, was arrested in April 2024. On 30 September 2025 the Dresden Higher Regional Court sentenced him to 4 years and 9 months for working for the ministry, including passing on information about European Parliament business. The Bundestag lifted Krah's own immunity on 11 September 2025 and police searched his homes and offices in Berlin, Dresden and Brussels.
cite: Dresden Higher Regional Court judgment, 30 September 2025; Bundestag immunity vote, 11 September 2025

n: Frank Creyelman — Flemish ex-senator paid by China's spy agency
rank: former Belgian senator and Flemish MP (Vlaams Belang)
d: An officer of China's Ministry of State Security, its main spy agency, paid Frank Creyelman, a Belgian politician, to influence debate in Europe for three years. Creyelman had sat in the Belgian Senate (1999–2007) and the Flemish Parliament (2007–2014) for Vlaams Belang. A joint investigation by the Financial Times, Der Spiegel and Le Monde reported the payments on 15 December 2023. Vlaams Belang expelled him; Belgian police investigated but reported that a gap in Belgian criminal law prevented prosecution.
cite: Financial Times / Der Spiegel / Le Monde joint investigation, 15 December 2023; Vlaams Belang expulsion

n: Christopher Cash — parliamentary researcher's China spy case dropped
rank: parliamentary researcher; director of the MPs' China Research Group
d: Christopher Cash, a researcher inside the UK Parliament, was charged with passing information about Westminster that investigators suspected reached senior Chinese Communist Party official Cai Qi. Cash worked for Conservative MP Alicia Kearns and directed the China Research Group of Conservative MPs. He and Christopher Berry were charged under the Official Secrets Act 1911, the UK's old spying law. In October 2025 the Director of Public Prosecutions, who heads the state prosecution service, dropped the charges, a decision that became a political row in Westminster.
cite: Crown Prosecution Service charges, 2024, and decision to discontinue, 2025

n: Ye Jianming — Chinese 'friendship' body veteran advised Czech president
rank: economic adviser to President Miloš Zeman
d: Czech President Miloš Zeman made Ye Jianming, a former officer of a Beijing 'friendship' body, his economic adviser. The China Association for International Friendly Contact (CAIFC) is a body that builds contacts with foreigners on China's behalf. Ye was its deputy secretary-general from 2003 to 2005 and chairman of the oil conglomerate CEFC China Energy. Zeman made him an economic adviser (from 2015 per some sources, January 2017 per others) while CEFC bought Czech assets. Ye was detained in China in March 2018 and Shanghai state investors took over CEFC.
cite: Czech Presidential Office statements; Reuters and Fortune reporting on CEFC

n: PACE inquiry finds Azerbaijan money reached Assembly members
rank: members and a former president of the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly
d: An inquiry found that Azerbaijan's government used money to win support among members of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), which brings together MPs from 46 national parliaments and monitors elections and human rights. The Independent Investigation Body, chaired by a former president of the European Court of Human Rights, reported in April 2018 'strong suspicions' of corruptive activity involving former PACE president Pedro Agramunt, and found that Luca Volontè and Azerbaijani member Elkhan Suleymanov had seriously breached the code of conduct. It found former German MP Eduard Lintner received €799,500 into personal accounts from Azerbaijan-linked companies and named breaches by members from Belgium, Germany, Poland, Romania, the UK and others. PACE then stripped several current and former members of rights and access.
cite: Report of the Independent Investigation Body on the allegations of corruption within the Parliamentary Assembly, 15 April 2018

n: Luca Volontè — ex-PACE group leader jailed for Azerbaijani bribes
rank: former Italian MP and leader of the EPP group in PACE
d: Azerbaijani officials paid Luca Volontè, leader of the centre-right EPP group in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), a human-rights body of national MPs, for support in the Assembly. Milan prosecutors charged him in 2016 with taking €2.39 million, routed through companies. The 2018 PACE investigation body found he played 'an important role in undermining' the Strässer report on political prisoners in Azerbaijan. In January 2021 the Court of Milan sentenced him to four years in prison for corruption.
cite: Court of Milan, judgment of January 2021

n: Bundestag lifts immunity of two CDU MPs over Azerbaijan money
rank: members of the Bundestag (CDU) sitting in PACE
d: German prosecutors investigated two sitting CDU members of the Bundestag, Germany's parliament, for taking money from Azerbaijan to lobby for it in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE). In January 2021 the Bundestag lifted the immunity of Karin Strenz, accused of taking at least €22,000; she had already been fined in 2019 for not declaring Azerbaijani income. On 4 March 2021 it lifted the immunity of Axel Fischer, under federal police (BKA) investigation for taking money from Azerbaijan. Former CSU MP and junior interior minister Eduard Lintner was investigated in the same case.
cite: German Bundestag immunity decisions, January and 4 March 2021; Munich prosecutors and BKA investigation

n: Azerbaijani Laundromat — $2.9bn scheme paid European politicians
rank: bank supervision; payments reaching sitting European politicians
d: Leaked bank records show that money from Azerbaijan's ruling circle, moved through shell companies, paid European politicians, including people who defended Azerbaijan in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE). In September 2017 the OCCRP, a journalists' network, and partner newspapers published 16,000 leaked transactions showing about $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 through four UK shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch. Almost half came from an account at the International Bank of Azerbaijan linked to the Aliyev family, which rules Azerbaijan. Recipients included Bundestag member Karin Strenz and Slovenian MP Zmago Jelinčič.
cite: OCCRP 'The Azerbaijani Laundromat' investigation, September 2017

n: Kosovo's intelligence service secretly handed six Turks to Ankara
rank: director of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency; interior minister
d: Kosovo's police and intelligence service carried out an operation for Turkey's government without the knowledge of Kosovo's own prime minister. Turkey calls the movement of preacher Fethullah Gülen a terrorist group and has sought its members abroad since the 2016 coup attempt. On 29 March 2018 Kosovo police and intelligence seized five teachers and a doctor accused by Ankara of Gülen links and flew them to Turkey on a private plane. Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj, who said he had not been told, sacked the interior minister and the intelligence chief. In 2023 the Basic Court in Pristina sentenced former intelligence chief Driton Gashi to four years and eight months for abuse of office over the deportations.
cite: Basic Court of Pristina judgment, 2023; Kosovo government dismissals, 30 March 2018
c_note: Kosovo is not in the canonical country list

n: French state report alleges Muslim Brotherhood entry into local politics
d: A French government report says the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928, works its way into French local politics. In May 2025 the report, by two senior civil servants and commissioned by the government, was examined by President Macron's Defence Council. It called the Brotherhood a 'threat to national cohesion', said 'political Islamism' was spreading 'from the bottom up' at municipal level, and named the federation Musulmans de France (formerly UOIF) as the Brotherhood's national branch. The authors also wrote that no recent document showed a wish by Muslims in France to set up an Islamic state. Musulmans de France rejected the findings.
cite: French government report on the Muslim Brotherhood and political Islamism, Defence and National Security Council, 21 May 2025

n: Moroccan spies ran Brussels Great Mosque and Belgium's Muslim body
d: Belgian intelligence reported that Morocco had placed its own people in charge of the Great Mosque in Brussels, and that three staff, including a director, were members of Moroccan intelligence. The mosque in Cinquantenaire park was run under a Saudi lease until 2018. In December 2020 Justice Minister Vincent Van Quickenborne refused it state recognition, unless its management changed. The Muslim Executive, the body the Belgian state recognises to speak for Muslims, was ordered to remove representatives of the Moroccan government.
cite: Belgian Federal Justice Ministry decision, December 2020
org_note: Moroccan state intelligence (DGED) using a religious institution

n: Castelvetrano secret association steered a Sicilian town council
rank: former Sicilian regional MP; former president of the Sicilian Regional Assembly
d: Trapani prosecutors say a secret association steered the Castelvetrano town council in Sicily through its mayor and deputy mayor in 2012–2017. Forming a secret association has been a crime in Italy since the P2 scandal, when a hidden Masonic lodge was found to include politicians, generals and officials. On 21 March 2019 prosecutors and Carabinieri had 27 people arrested in the case. Former regional MP Giovanni Lo Sciuto was alleged to have exchanged favours with an official of the INPS pensions office for disability pensions that delivered votes; former Sicilian Assembly president Francesco Cascio was placed under house arrest.
cite: Trapani Public Prosecutor's Office; arrest order of the Trapani preliminary-investigations judge, March 2019

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

n: Jorge Fernández Díaz — Opus Dei member as Spain's interior minister
d: Jorge Fernández Díaz, reported to be a member of the Catholic institution Opus Dei, ran Spain's police and Guardia Civil as interior minister from 2011 to 2016. Opus Dei's lay 'supernumerary' members follow its spiritual programme while working in ordinary jobs. Fernández Díaz, a Partido Popular politician, served in Mariano Rajoy's government and is reported to be a supernumerary.
cite: Spanish press reporting compiled in Wikipedia biography

n: Paola Binetti — Opus Dei numerary in Italy's parliament
rank: Senator and member of the Chamber of Deputies (from 2006)
d: Paola Binetti, a celibate 'numerary' member of the Catholic institution Opus Dei, sat in Italy's parliament from 2006. Numeraries live in Opus Dei's centres. Binetti, a psychiatrist and professor at the Opus Dei-founded Campus Bio-Medico University in Rome, was latterly a senator elected in 2018, for The Daisy, the Democratic Party and then the Union of the Centre. She has said publicly that she is a numerary and wears a cilice, a spiked band worn as penance.
cite: Italian Senate member record; Binetti's own public statements

n: PwC partner leaked Australian Treasury tax plans to PwC colleagues
d: PwC, one of the 'Big Four' accounting firms that advise both governments and large companies, had a partner inside the Australian Treasury's work on new tax laws, and he passed confidential plans back to the firm. In 2013 the Treasury engaged PwC partner Peter Collins to advise on laws against multinational tax avoidance; he shared confidential Treasury information with at least 53 PwC partners. The Tax Practitioners Board suspended his licence for two years in December 2022, and a Senate committee concluded PwC had followed a deliberate strategy over many years to cover up the breach. CEO Tom Seymour stepped down in May 2023, PwC removed eight partners, and in June 2023 sold its government consulting arm for $1 (now Scyne Advisory). Treasury referred the case to the Australian Federal Police in May 2023; police raided PwC's Sydney office in October 2024 and no charges have been reported.
cite: Senate Finance and Public Administration References Committee inquiry (2023); Tax Practitioners Board decision Dec 2022; AFP referral 24 May 2023

n: McKinsey Africa bribed officials at South Africa's state firms
rank: state power and rail company officials
d: McKinsey Africa, part of the US management-consulting firm McKinsey & Company, paid bribes to officials at Eskom and Transnet to get inside information that helped it win consulting contracts. Eskom (electricity) and Transnet (ports and freight rail) are South Africa's largest state-owned companies. On 5 December 2024 McKinsey Africa admitted the bribery conspiracy in a three-year deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department, a deal in which charges are dropped later if the company meets set conditions. It agreed to pay $122.85 million, part of it in South Africa; the Justice Department put McKinsey's profit from the scheme at about $85 million. Former senior partner Vikas Sagar pleaded guilty separately.
cite: US Department of Justice, deferred prosecution agreement, 5 Dec 2024 (Reuters via Daily Maverick)

n: Bain & Company helped take over South Africa's tax service
d: The US consulting firm Bain & Company worked with President Jacob Zuma and tax commissioner Tom Moyane to take control of the South African Revenue Service (SARS), the national tax agency, according to the Zondo Commission into state capture ('state capture' means private interests steering state bodies for their own ends). SARS's units investigating organised crime were seen as a threat. An earlier commission under Judge Robert Nugent concluded that one Bain contract was aimed at disabling SARS. The Zondo Commission published this finding in Part 1 of its report on 4 January 2022. Bain says the allegations against it are unproven.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo Commission), Report Part 1, 4 Jan 2022; Nugent Commission of Inquiry into SARS, 2018

n: Gupta family steered South African ministers and state firms
d: The Gupta brothers, who ran a business group in computers, media and mining, used their closeness to President Jacob Zuma to influence who held cabinet posts and how state companies were run. Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas said the Guptas offered him the finance minister's job shortly before Zuma sacked Finance Minister Nhlanhla Nene on 9 December 2015; Jonas refused, and the Guptas deny it. The Zondo Commission found that ministers, senior ANC members and heads of state companies acted corruptly to help the Guptas, named minister Malusi Gigaba, and said Nene's firing showed Zuma acted for the Gupta brothers. The US sanctioned the family in October 2019; the UAE later rejected South Africa's extradition request on a technicality.
cite: Public Protector, 'State of Capture' report, 2 Nov 2016; Zondo Commission reports 2022; US Treasury sanctions Oct 2019

n: Big Four accountants seconded to the Treasury to help write tax law
d: The Big Four accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC), which sell tax advice to large companies, lent their own staff to the UK Treasury to help draft tax legislation. On 26 April 2013 the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee reported that these seconded staff could return to their firms and use what they had learned to advise clients on loopholes in the same laws. Committee chair Margaret Hodge called it 'a ridiculous conflict of interest'. The committee recommended banning the practice and noted that the four firms employ almost 9,000 tax advisers.
cite: House of Commons Public Accounts Committee, 'Tax avoidance: the role of large accountancy firms', 26 Apr 2013 (Public Finance)

n: Uber Files: Macron as minister secretly helped Uber in France
d: Emmanuel Macron, as France's economy minister (2014–16), worked behind the scenes for the US ride-hailing company Uber, according to the Uber Files. These are 124,000 internal Uber documents from 2013–2017, leaked by Uber's former Europe lobbying chief Mark MacGann and published by The Guardian and partners on 10 July 2022. Texts with Uber chief executive Travis Kalanick suggest Macron brokered a secret deal with Uber's opponents in the cabinet. When police in Marseille banned an Uber service, Macron's office was contacted and the ban was lifted two days later. Macron said he was proud of supporting the company.
cite: The Guardian / ICIJ, 'The Uber Files', 10 July 2022

n: Ex-EU commissioner Kroes lobbied Dutch leaders for Uber
d: Neelie Kroes, the EU's digital commissioner until 2014, helped the US ride-hailing company Uber lobby Dutch politicians, including Prime Minister Mark Rutte, during her 18-month cooling-off period, the rule that limits former commissioners' work for companies. Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker had refused her request to work for Uber formally. The help came to light in the Uber Files, internal Uber documents leaked and published in July 2022. Kroes denies wrongdoing.
cite: The Guardian / ICIJ, 'The Uber Files', July 2022

n: Greensill Capital: founder inside Downing Street, civil servant on its side
rank: Chancellor of the Exchequer; Cabinet Office
d: Lex Greensill, founder of the supply-chain finance firm Greensill Capital, held an adviser role in the Cabinet Office (the department that supports the prime minister), which the Boardman review said gave him 'extraordinarily privileged' access to Downing Street. Bill Crothers, the government's former chief commercial officer, advised Greensill while still a civil servant. Former Prime Minister David Cameron, later paid by Greensill, texted Chancellor Rishi Sunak in 2020 asking for the firm to join a Covid lending scheme; Sunak declined. The firm collapsed in March 2021. The Treasury Committee (20 July 2021) and the Boardman review (21 July 2021) found Cameron broke no rules but called the rules too weak.
cite: House of Commons Treasury Committee report, 20 July 2021; Boardman review for the Cabinet Office, 21 July 2021

n: SNC-Lavalin: Trudeau pressed attorney general on company's behalf
d: SNC-Lavalin (now AtkinsRéalis), a Montreal engineering company facing bribery charges over Libya, got Canada's prime minister to act for it inside government. It lobbied for a law allowing deferred prosecution deals (agreements that let a company avoid trial), holding 51 meetings with officials and MPs over about 20 months. When prosecutors refused SNC such a deal, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau pressed Attorney General Jody Wilson-Raybould to overrule them. On 14 August 2019 Ethics Commissioner Mario Dion found Trudeau had broken section 9 of the Conflict of Interest Act, which bars officials from improperly furthering another person's interests. The company later pleaded guilty to fraud and was fined C$280 million (December 2019).
cite: Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner, 'Trudeau II Report', 14 Aug 2019

n: Qatargate: Qatar and Morocco allegedly paid MEPs via an NGO
rank: Vice-President of the European Parliament; MEPs
d: Prosecutors in Belgium allege that Qatar and Morocco paid members of the European Parliament to influence its work, passing money through Fight Impunity, a Brussels human-rights NGO led by former Italian MEP Antonio Panzeri. Belgian police raided homes and offices on 9 December 2022 and seized about €1.5 million in cash. Parliament Vice-President Eva Kaili was removed from that post and charged; MEPs Marc Tarabella and Andrea Cozzolino were arrested in February 2023, and ex-MEP Marie Arena was charged in 2025. Panzeri took a plea deal in January 2023. The others deny wrongdoing, and in February 2026 the Brussels Court of Appeal ruled the prosecution could go ahead.
cite: Belgian federal prosecutor; Brussels Court of Appeal ruling Feb 2026

n: Huawei lobbyist's associates allegedly paid MEPs to sign a 5G letter
d: Belgian prosecutors allege that associates of Valerio Ottati, a former lobbyist for the Chinese telecoms-equipment maker Huawei, paid members of the European Parliament to sign a 2021 letter opposing limits on foreign 5G network equipment: up to €15,000 for the author and €1,500 per co-signer. In March 2025 Belgian police searched Huawei's Brussels office and Parliament premises, and five people have been charged. MEPs have immunity from prosecution unless Parliament lifts it. On 16 June 2026 Parliament voted 344–234 to lift the immunity of Italian EPP MEP Fulvio Martusciello, who denies wrongdoing, while keeping immunity for three other MEPs.
cite: Belgian federal prosecutor; European Parliament plenary vote 16 June 2026 (Euronews)

n: Huawei Poland executive and ex-security official charged with spying
d: Polish prosecutors charge that Chinese intelligence worked through Wang Weijing, a senior Huawei employee in Poland, and Piotr Durbajło, a cybersecurity expert who had worked for state agencies including the Internal Security Agency (Poland's counter-intelligence service). Both were arrested in January 2019. Prosecutors say Wang sought contracts from 2011 to 2019 that would give Huawei insight into state and local government data systems. Both pleaded not guilty; the trial opened in Warsaw in June 2021 and was closed to the public.
cite: Polish prosecutors' indictment; Warsaw district court trial from June 2021 (AP via Courthouse News)

n: Odebrecht paid Peru's President Toledo for a highway contract
d: Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group, paid Peru's former president Alejandro Toledo about $35 million in return for the contract to build the Interoceanic Highway. In 2016 Odebrecht admitted to US authorities that it had paid $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries through a department set up for that purpose. Toledo was extradited from the United States on 23 April 2023, and on 21 October 2024 a Lima court sentenced him to 20 years in prison.
cite: Peru, National Superior Court of Specialized Criminal Justice, 21 Oct 2024

n: Odebrecht money in Peru's Humala campaigns; 15-year sentences
d: Peruvian prosecutors argued that Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group at the centre of Latin America's largest bribery case, and the Venezuelan government financed Ollanta Humala's 2006 and 2011 presidential campaigns. On 15 April 2025 a Lima court convicted Humala, president from 2011, and his wife Nadine Heredia of money laundering linked to Odebrecht and sentenced each to 15 years. Money laundering here means hiding the source of illegal funds. Heredia left for Brasília after Brazil granted her diplomatic asylum. Both deny the charges.
cite: Peru, National Superior Court of Specialized Criminal Justice, 15 Apr 2025

n: Odebrecht paid Ecuador's vice-president $13.5m in bribes
d: Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group that admitted paying bribes across Latin America, paid Ecuador's Vice-President Jorge Glas about $13.5 million. On 15 December 2017 Glas was sentenced to six years for taking the money, and the National Court of Justice upheld the sentence in October 2019. He received further sentences in 2020, 2021 and 2025. Police seized him inside Mexico's embassy in Quito, where he had sought refuge, on 5 April 2024, and he was moved to a maximum-security prison in November 2025.
cite: Ecuador, National Court of Justice, sentence 15 Dec 2017, upheld Oct 2019

n: Ex-Pemex chief accused of taking $10m from Odebrecht
d: Emilio Lozoya, who ran Mexico's state oil company Pemex from December 2012 to February 2016, is accused of taking about $10 million in bribes from the Brazilian construction group Odebrecht. Spanish police arrested him in Málaga in February 2020 and he was extradited to Mexico on 17 July 2020. He denies the charges. In February 2024 he was moved from prison to house arrest, and no verdict has been reported.
cite: Mexico, Fiscalía General de la República charges; extradition 17 July 2020

n: Car Wash: builders paid politicians for Petrobras contracts
d: A cartel of Brazilian construction firms, Odebrecht among them, paid politicians in return for contracts with the state oil company Petrobras. Operation Car Wash, the investigation that uncovered this from 2014 to 2021, charged 429 people. Former president Lula da Silva was convicted in July 2017 (over a beachfront apartment) and February 2019 (over a family country house) and jailed in April 2018. On 8 March 2021 Supreme Court justice Edson Fachin annulled both convictions because the Curitiba court of judge Sergio Moro lacked jurisdiction, restoring Lula's political rights. In 2023 Justice Dias Toffoli voided evidence from Odebrecht's leniency deal, its agreement to cooperate in exchange for lighter penalties.
cite: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil, Justice Edson Fachin ruling, 8 Mar 2021

n: Privinvest paid Mozambique's finance minister in 'tuna bonds' deal
d: Privinvest, an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilding group, paid Mozambique's finance minister Manuel Chang $7 million, prosecutors said, in a deal known as the 'tuna bonds'. About $2 billion in loans arranged by Credit Suisse and others went to three Mozambican state companies for fishing and maritime security, partly hidden from the IMF. A Brooklyn jury convicted Chang in August 2024 of wire-fraud and money-laundering conspiracy, and he was sentenced to eight and a half years on 17 January 2025. Credit Suisse paid about $475 million in 2021, and London's High Court let Mozambique recover over $825 million from the estate of Privinvest's owner.
cite: US District Court (E.D.N.Y.), verdict Aug 2024, sentence 17 Jan 2025; UK High Court judgment 2024

n: 1MDB: state fund money used to bribe officials; Najib convicted
d: Money arranged through Goldman Sachs bond deals for 1MDB, a Malaysian state investment fund, was diverted and used to bribe officials in Malaysia and the UAE, US authorities say. Goldman Sachs bankers Tim Leissner and Roger Ng arranged the deals with financier Jho Low. Goldman settled with Malaysia in July 2020 for about $3.9 billion; Leissner pleaded guilty and Ng was convicted in New York in 2022. On 26 December 2025 Malaysia's High Court found former prime minister Najib Razak guilty on all 25 counts tied to over $1 billion in his personal accounts and sentenced him to 15 years. He is appealing.
cite: High Court of Malaysia, 26 Dec 2025; US v. Roger Ng (E.D.N.Y.) 2022; Goldman–Malaysia settlement July 2020
who: Jho Low and Goldman Sachs bankers

n: Glencore bribed officials in Nigeria and four other African states
d: Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader that buys and sells oil and metals, paid bribes to government officials in several countries to win business. In May 2022 it pleaded guilty in the United States to bribery from 2007 to 2018 and agreed to pay over $1 billion. In June 2022 its UK subsidiary pleaded guilty to seven counts of bribery; the Serious Fraud Office, the UK agency that prosecutes major fraud and bribery, found more than $28 million in bribes paid in Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire and South Sudan between 2012 and 2016.
cite: US Department of Justice plea, May 2022; UK Serious Fraud Office, Southwark Crown Court plea, 21 June 2022

n: Glencore pays Congo $180m over bribery of officials
d: Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader that buys, sells and mines oil and metals, and one of the largest mining firms in the Democratic Republic of Congo, paid $27.5 million to third parties from 2007 to 2018 intending part of it to bribe Congolese officials, US authorities said. In December 2022 Glencore agreed to pay Congo $180 million to settle the claims.
cite: Glencore–DR Congo settlement, Dec 2022; US Department of Justice plea, May 2022

n: Gunvor bribed Ecuador's oil officials for oil-backed loan deals
d: Gunvor, a Geneva-based oil trader, paid bribes to officials at Ecuador's state oil company Petroecuador and its Ministry of Hydrocarbons. According to the US Justice Department, from 2012 to 2020 Gunvor paid more than $97 million to intermediaries, part of it for bribes, and in return officials helped it win oil-backed loan contracts and passed it confidential Petroecuador information. In March 2024 Gunvor resolved US and Swiss investigations, paying about $374 million in fines and $287 million in forfeiture, and the Swiss Attorney General convicted it of corruption in Ecuador. In 2019 Swiss authorities had already penalised it about $95 million for failing to prevent bribery of officials in Côte d'Ivoire and the Republic of Congo.
cite: US Department of Justice resolution and Swiss Office of the Attorney General summary penalty order, March 2024; US Department of Justice, EDNY press release 'Gunvor S.A. Pleads Guilty to Scheme to Bribe Ecuadorian Officials', 1 Mar 2024, https://www.justice.gov/usao-edny/pr/gunvor-sa-pleads-guilty-scheme-bribe-ecuadorian-officials-and-ordered-pay-over-600

n: Trafigura convicted in Switzerland for bribing an Angolan official
rank: official at a Sonangol (state oil) subsidiary
d: Trafigura, one of the world's largest oil and metals traders, paid €4.3 million in bribes in 2009–11 to an Angolan official linked to a subsidiary of Sonangol, Angola's state oil company. In January 2025 the Swiss Federal Criminal Court convicted Trafigura and its former chief operating officer Mike Wainwright.
