Trafigura was fined $3.3 million and ordered to pay $145.6 million; Wainwright got 32 months, 20 of them suspended. Trafigura has appealed, so the ruling is not yet final.
cite: Swiss Federal Criminal Court, Bellinzona, Jan 2025

n: Trafigura pleads guilty to bribing Petrobras officials
d: Trafigura, a commodity trader, bribed officials at Petrobras, Brazil's state oil company, from 2003 to 2014, paying up to 20 cents per barrel through shell companies (firms that exist only on paper). On 28 March 2024 it pleaded guilty in the United States to conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the US law against bribing foreign officials, and agreed to pay about $127 million.
cite: US Department of Justice plea agreement, 28 Mar 2024

n: Adani charged in New York over alleged bribes to Indian officials
d: US federal prosecutors in New York allege that Gautam Adani, founder of the Indian ports, power and airports conglomerate Adani Group, and his associates paid more than $250 million in bribes to Indian government officials to win solar power contracts. They charged Adani and associates with fraud on 20 November 2024. Adani denies the charges. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's civil case is ongoing; in January 2026 it asked an Indian court to serve summonses by email.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, indictment 20 Nov 2024; SEC civil complaint

n: FirstEnergy paid Ohio Speaker $60m network for a bailout law
rank: Speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives
d: FirstEnergy, an Ohio power company, funnelled about $60 million to a group around Ohio House Speaker Larry Householder in return for House Bill 6, a $1 billion-plus rescue of its nuclear plants. A jury convicted Householder of racketeering (running a corrupt organisation) on 9 March 2023, and he was sentenced to 20 years on 29 June 2023. FirstEnergy agreed in July 2021 to pay a $230 million penalty.
cite: US District Court (S.D. Ohio), verdict 9 Mar 2023, sentence 29 June 2023

n: ComEd gave jobs to Illinois Speaker Madigan's allies for its bills
rank: Speaker of the Illinois House of Representatives
d: Commonwealth Edison (ComEd), Chicago's electricity utility, gave jobs and contracts to associates of Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan to win his support for its bills, prosecutors showed. Madigan was the longest-serving legislative leader in US history. A federal jury convicted him on 12 February 2025 of 10 counts including bribery and conspiracy. He was sentenced to 7½ years and a $2.5 million fine and began serving in October 2025. The 7th Circuit appeals court upheld the conviction on 27 April 2026.
cite: US District Court (N.D. Ill.), verdict 12 Feb 2025; US Court of Appeals, 7th Circuit, 27 Apr 2026

n: Gates Foundation money steers WHO programmes
d: The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, a private US charity, funds the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN's health agency, in a way that lets it choose what the money is spent on. In 2020 it was the WHO's second-largest contributor; in the period cited it gave 45% of the WHO's funds from non-state bodies, about 12% of WHO operating spending. Most of this money is earmarked, meaning it can only be used for programmes the foundation picks. Academics and charities have warned that this can tilt WHO priorities toward the foundation's own.
cite: WHO contributor data as summarised by Wikipedia

n: IMF staffer made Pakistan's central bank chief during bailout talks
rank: Governor of the State Bank of Pakistan
d: Reza Baqir, a staff member of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), was appointed Governor of the State Bank of Pakistan on 4 May 2019 while Pakistan was negotiating an IMF bailout. The IMF lends to countries in crisis on condition that they change their policies, and a central bank governor sets interest rates and manages the currency, both points in such talks. Baqir had been the IMF's mission chief for Romania and Bulgaria. He was appointed a day after his predecessor was abruptly removed, Reuters reported. He served until 4 May 2022.
cite: Government of Pakistan appointment, 4 May 2019 (Reuters)

n: World Bank managing director became Nigeria's finance minister
rank: Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister for the Economy
d: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala moved from the World Bank, which lends to Nigeria, into the Nigerian ministry that deals with it. She had a 25-year career at the Bank and was a managing director from December 2007 to 2011. President Goodluck Jonathan appointed her finance minister and coordinating minister for the economy on 17 August 2011, a post she held until May 2015. She became Director-General of the World Trade Organization in March 2021 and was reappointed in November 2024.
cite: Nigerian presidential appointment, 17 Aug 2011; WTO General Council decisions 2021 and 2024

n: China-linked hackers inside UN aviation agency; evidence hidden
d: Hackers most likely from Emissary Panda, a group tied to the Chinese government, broke into the systems of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) in November 2016 and used them to infect visitors, CBC reported in February 2019 from internal documents. ICAO is the UN agency that sets world aviation standards. CBC said ICAO's IT staff and their supervisor tried to hide evidence, and sources said Secretary General Fang Liu, a Chinese national, shelved recommendations to investigate them. ICAO disputed the account. The US ambassador to ICAO later called the handling 'unacceptable'.
cite: CBC News investigation, Feb 2019

n: Chinese UN official says he had Uyghur leader removed for China
rank: UN Under-Secretary-General for Economic and Social Affairs
d: Wu Hongbo, a Chinese diplomat who headed the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs from 2012 to 2017, used that post to act for China's government. On China's state broadcaster CCTV in December 2018 he said that in 2017 he had UN security remove Dolkun Isa, president of the World Uyghur Congress, from the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, and that as a Chinese international civil servant he 'firmly defends the motherland's interests'. UN staff rules require officials not to take instructions from any government.
cite: CCTV programme 'Kaijiang La', Dec 2018 (transcript via China Digital Times)

n: China's vice-minister elected FAO head; accused of serving Beijing
rank: Director-General of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization
d: Qu Dongyu, China's vice-minister of agriculture (2015–19), won the top post at the FAO, the UN's food and farming agency in Rome, on 23 June 2019 with 108 of 191 votes, ahead of the EU-backed French candidate. Allegations of Chinese pressure and inducements on voting delegations featured in the election. A 2023 study by German public broadcasters found he had used the FAO for Beijing's interests. He remains Director-General.
cite: 41st FAO Conference vote, 23 June 2019; German public broadcasters' investigation 2023

n: Macau tycoon Ng Lap Seng bribed UN General Assembly president
rank: President of the UN General Assembly
d: Ng Lap Seng, a Macau property developer, paid about $500,000 in bribes to John Ashe, President of the UN General Assembly and Antigua's UN ambassador, and also paid Dominican Republic deputy ambassador Francis Lorenzo, to win UN backing for a conference centre he wanted to build in Macau. A Manhattan federal jury convicted him in July 2017, and he was sentenced to four years in May 2018.
cite: US District Court (S.D.N.Y.), verdict July 2017, sentence May 2018

n: FIFA president met Swiss attorney general in secret during FIFA probe
d: FIFA, world football's governing body, based in Zurich, got private access to the head of the Swiss prosecution service while that service was investigating corruption at FIFA. Its president, Gianni Infantino, held unrecorded meetings in 2016 and 2017 with Michael Lauber, Switzerland's attorney general. Lauber was found to have misled the body that oversees federal prosecutors about the meetings, in a 2020 ruling of the Swiss Federal Administrative Court, and he left office that year. A special prosecutor opened a criminal case against Infantino over the meetings; it was closed without charges on 26 October 2023.
cite: Swiss Federal Administrative Court ruling 2020; Swiss special prosecutor decision, 26 Oct 2023 (AP)

n: Tokyo 2020 sponsors paid an Olympic board member ¥198m
rank: board member, Tokyo 2020 Olympic organising committee
d: Companies sponsoring or licensed by the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, including Aoki Holdings and Kadokawa, paid about ¥198 million (about $1.4 million) to Haruyuki Takahashi, a board member of the organising committee, prosecutors charged. The committee ran the Games under the International Olympic Committee and counted as a public body under Japanese law, so its members could be charged with taking bribes. Takahashi, a former executive of the ad agency Dentsu, was arrested in 2022. About a dozen people on the paying side were convicted, all with suspended sentences. Takahashi pleaded not guilty and his trial opened in Tokyo District Court.
cite: Tokyo District Public Prosecutors indictment 2022; Tokyo District Court trial 2023–24 (AP)

n: La Línea: customs bribery ring reached Guatemala's president
d: 'La Línea', a bribery ring inside Guatemala's customs service, reached Vice-President Roxana Baldetti and President Otto Pérez Molina. It was exposed in 2015 by Guatemala's Public Ministry (the prosecution service) and CICIG, an international commission set up by a 2006 UN–Guatemala agreement to help prosecutors take apart criminal networks inside the state. Congress lifted Pérez Molina's immunity 132–0 and he resigned on 2 September 2015. On 7 December 2022 both were sentenced to 16 years; Pérez Molina was released on bond in January 2024.
cite: Guatemala, Sentencing Court, 7 Dec 2022; Congress vote 1 Sept 2015

n: Tony Blair Institute advisers placed inside Rwanda's government
rank: Office of the President / Prime Minister (strategy and delivery units)
d: The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a London-based non-profit founded by the former UK prime minister, places its advisers inside governments. In Rwanda it has supported a Strategy and Policy Unit and a Government Action Coordination Unit and worked on Imihigo, a system of performance contracts for officials; in Kenya it supported a Presidential Delivery Unit. It reports work with governments in more than 45 countries and had about 1,000 staff in 2026. Its largest donor is Larry Ellison's foundation, which gave over £52 million in 2023, The Guardian reported.
cite: Tony Blair Institute published programme descriptions; The Guardian, Apr 2025

n: Evangelical caucus holds 213 seats in Brazil's Chamber
rank: organised caucus in both houses of Congress
d: Protestant, mostly Pentecostal, churches in Brazil have built a voting bloc inside the National Congress, organised as the Frente Parlamentar Evangélica (Evangelical Parliamentary Front), a registered cross-party caucus of evangelical members. The bloc grew after the 2002 election brought in 60 deputies who declared themselves evangelical, and it was formally registered with the Chamber of Deputies in 2015. Its registered membership in the current legislature is 213 of 513 deputies and 26 of 81 senators. A few members sit on the left, such as Benedita da Silva and Marina Silva; most vote with the conservative bloc.
cite: Chamber of Deputies register 'Frentes e Grupos Parlamentares' (May 2023), via Wikipedia; Folha de S.Paulo, 5 Feb 2025

n: Universal Church pastors founded and run the Republicanos party
rank: party president and vice-president of the Chamber of Deputies
d: Pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (UCKG), a Brazilian neo-Pentecostal church founded by Bishop Edir Macedo in 1977, founded the party now called Republicanos in August 2005. The party's president since 2018, Marcos Pereira, is a UCKG bishop. He was Minister of Industry and Foreign Trade in 2016–18 and has been a vice-president of the Chamber of Deputies since 2019. Political scientist David Fleischer called Republicanos 'an evangelical party', though many of its members are Catholic.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Republicanos', citing Fleischer and party records

n: Universal Church bishop Crivella as senator, minister and Rio mayor
rank: federal minister, senator and mayor of Rio de Janeiro
d: Marcelo Crivella, a bishop of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (a Brazilian neo-Pentecostal church) and nephew of its founder Edir Macedo, held a run of public offices. He was a senator for Rio de Janeiro from 2003 to 2016, Minister of Fishing and Aquaculture under Dilma Rousseff in 2012–14, and mayor of Rio from 2017 to 2020. He was arrested on 22 December 2020, days before his term as mayor ended, in a corruption investigation.
cite: The Guardian, 22 Dec 2020; Wikipedia biography

n: Pastors without posts steered Brazil's education funds for bribes
d: Two pastors who held no government posts steered money from Brazil's National Education Development Fund (FNDE), which pays for school projects in towns, allegedly in exchange for bribes, according to a leaked audio published in March 2022. Education Minister Milton Ribeiro, a Presbyterian pastor from Santos whom Jair Bolsonaro appointed in July 2020, was linked to the scheme. Ribeiro left office on 28 March 2022, and the Federal Police arrested him on 22 June 2022 on a warrant citing passive corruption (an official accepting a bribe), malfeasance and influence peddling.
cite: G1, 10 Jul 2020; Federal Police arrest warrant, 22 Jun 2022, via Wikipedia

n: Evangelical pastor Damares Alves as minister, then senator
rank: Minister of Women, Families and Human Rights; senator
d: Damares Alves, an evangelical pastor who served in the Foursquare Gospel Church and the Lagoinha Baptist Church, was made Minister of Women, Families and Human Rights by President Jair Bolsonaro, serving from January 2019 to March 2022. She was then elected senator for the Federal District in 2022 for Republicanos, the party founded by pastors of the Universal Church, and took her seat in February 2023.
cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Brazilian press

n: Opus Dei numerary governed Kenya's central bank
rank: Governor of the Central Bank of Kenya
d: Patrick Njoroge, a numerary member of Opus Dei, governed the Central Bank of Kenya from June 2015 to June 2023. Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation whose celibate 'numerary' members live in its centres. Njoroge was nominated by President Uhuru Kenyatta and approved by Parliament in June 2015. As governor he also sat ex officio (by virtue of his post) on the IMF Board of Governors. His brother Anthony Muheria is Catholic archbishop of Nyeri.
cite: Parliament of Kenya approval, 18 Jun 2015; Wikipedia biography and 'List of members of Opus Dei'

n: US Fellowship network's Uganda chair floated death-penalty gay bill
rank: Minister of State for Trade, Industry and Cooperatives
d: David Bahati, a Ugandan politician who chairs Uganda's National Prayer Breakfast Fellowship, first floated his 2009 Anti-Homosexuality Bill, which proposed the death penalty, at the 2008 Uganda prayer breakfast, journalist Jeff Sharlet reported. The Fellowship (also called The Family) is a US Christian network that runs national prayer breakfasts for politicians; Fellowship member Bob Hunter confirmed Bahati's link to the network to NPR. Bahati has been a state minister since 2021 and was re-appointed in 2026.
cite: Jeff Sharlet reporting; NPR, Dec 2009; Wikipedia biography

n: Ghanaian minister confirms Freemason membership at his vetting
rank: Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment
d: Freemasonry, a fraternal society whose members meet in lodges, has members in Ghana's government and parliament. George Opare Addo confirmed he is a Freemason, naming his lodge as 'Amity', at his parliamentary vetting as a minister on 22 January 2025, and was then confirmed as a minister in President Mahama's government. The question came from Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin, who had himself said in February 2024: 'I am a Freemason and a Catholic.'
cite: Graphic Online (Ghana), Jan 2025

n: Ghana's security and transport ministers are serving Freemasons
rank: Majority Leader; National Security and Transport ministers
d: Freemasonry in Ghana counts serving ministers and the head of government business in parliament among its members. When the Grand Lodge of Ghana honoured the Asantehene (king of the Asante), Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, for 25 years in Freemasonry in May 2024, GhanaWeb reported that National Security Minister Albert Kan-Dapaah and Transport Minister Kweku Ofori Asiamah took part as members. It also reported that Majority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin had publicly said he is a Freemason. Former President John Kufuor has said he joined in 1967. The record shows membership and office; it does not show lodge direction of their decisions.
cite: GhanaWeb, 26 May and 1 Jun 2024

n: Mourides placed in Senegal's government; presidents court their caliph
d: Senegal's presidents have brought the Mourides, a Sufi Muslim brotherhood, close to government and court their caliph (spiritual leader). Abdoulaye Wade travelled to the Mouride holy city of Touba the day after his 2000 election and put Mourides in his government. Touba has run with wide autonomy from the state since 1928. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye visited Caliph Serigne Mountakha Mbacké on 7 August 2025 ahead of the Grand Magal pilgrimage, a pre-Magal visit that has become customary for heads of state.
cite: Seneweb, Aug 2025; Wikipedia 'Mouride' citing academic sources

n: Boutchichiya Sufi follower has run Morocco's religious ministry since 2002
rank: Minister of Habous and Islamic Affairs
d: Ahmed Toufiq, a follower of the Boutchichiya, Morocco's largest Sufi order, has been the king's Minister of Islamic Affairs, which oversees the country's mosques, since November 2002 under five prime ministers. Toufiq, a historian, has said a chance meeting with the order's sheikh, al-Abbas, set him on the Sufi path. In August 2025 a leaked letter from Toufiq warned the order about 'abuses' and 'appetites' during a dispute over its leadership.
cite: Religion Unplugged, 13 Mar 2020; TelQuel, 26 Aug 2025 (headline)

n: Nahdlatul Ulama's supreme leader became Indonesia's vice-president
d: Ma'ruf Amin, supreme leader (rais 'aam) of Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation, became the country's vice-president. NU is rooted in traditionalist and Sufi-influenced pesantren (Islamic boarding) schools. Amin was elected its supreme leader in 2015 and also chaired the Indonesian Ulema Council. President Joko Widodo picked him as running mate in August 2018; he resigned the NU post and served as vice-president from 2019 to 2024.
cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Indonesian press

n: Bodu Bala Sena monk Gnanasara made head of a legal-reform task force
rank: chair of the Presidential Task Force on 'One Country, One Law'
d: Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, the monk who leads Bodu Bala Sena (BBS), a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist movement, was appointed by President Gotabaya Rajapaksa on 26 October 2021 to chair a presidential task force on legal reform. In 2013 Gnanasara had told a rally that followers 'must become an unofficial civilian police force against Muslim extremism'. The Bar Association of Sri Lanka said the task force would usurp the roles of Parliament and the Justice Ministry.
cite: Government gazette, 26 Oct 2021, via Daily FT; The Morning (BASL statement)

n: NAR figure Paula White heads the White House Faith Office
rank: Senior Advisor, White House Faith Office
d: Paula White, a televangelist whom Wikipedia's account of the New Apostolic Reformation (NAR) lists among its figures, holds a post inside the White House. The NAR is a network of self-styled apostles and prophets that seeks Christian influence over the 'seven mountains' of society, including government. On 7 February 2025 Trump, whose long-time spiritual adviser she is, created a White House Faith Office led by White. She had been a special adviser on faith in his first term.
cite: White House announcement, Feb 2025; White House annual personnel report to Congress, 1 Jul 2025

n: Opus Dei member Guillermo Lasso as president of Ecuador
d: Guillermo Lasso, a banker reported by the newspaper El Universo since at least 2009 to be a supernumerary of Opus Dei, held Ecuador's presidency from May 2021 to November 2023. Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members; supernumeraries are its married lay members, who follow its spiritual discipline while working in ordinary jobs.
cite: El Universo, 2009; Wikipedia 'Guillermo Lasso' and 'List of members of Opus Dei'

n: Opus Dei member Przemysław Wipler in Poland's Sejm
d: Przemysław Wipler, reported by Gazeta Wyborcza as of 2023 to be a supernumerary (married lay member) of Opus Dei, the Catholic organisation of priests and lay members, holds a seat in Poland's parliament, the Sejm. He was elected for the Confederation party in October 2023 and in January 2024 became vice-chair of the parliamentary inquiry into the previous government's use of Pegasus spyware.
cite: Gazeta Wyborcza, 2023; Sejm records; via Wikipedia

n: Opus Dei numerary Luis Silva as Chile's under-secretary of justice
d: Luis Silva, a law professor and a numerary of Opus Dei, holds a senior post in Chile's justice ministry. Numeraries are celibate full members of Opus Dei, the Catholic organisation of priests and lay members, as La Tercera and El País reported when Silva topped the 2023 vote for Chile's Constitutional Council, the body elected to draft a new constitution, for the Republican Party. He took office as Undersecretary of Justice under President José Antonio Kast on 11 March 2026.
cite: La Tercera, 8 May 2023; El País Chile, 12 May 2023; Government of Chile appointment, Mar 2026

n: CIA and BND secretly owned Swiss cipher firm Crypto AG
d: The US CIA and West Germany's BND intelligence agency secretly bought Crypto AG, a Swiss firm that sold encryption machines to governments in more than 120 countries, in June 1970 for US$5.75 million. The BND co-owned it until about 1993 and the CIA alone until about 2018. Because they controlled the company, the two agencies could read the coded messages of the countries that bought its machines (Operation 'Thesaurus'/'Rubicon'). The Washington Post, ZDF and SRF revealed the ownership on 11 February 2020. A Swiss parliamentary inquiry reported in November 2020 that Swiss intelligence knew of the operation and benefited from it. The firm was liquidated in 2018 and its business passed to CyOne and Crypto International AG.
cite: Washington Post/ZDF/SRF investigation, 11 Feb 2020; Swiss parliamentary oversight inquiry report, Nov 2020

n: Saudi officials paid Twitter staff to look up critics' accounts
rank: media-partnerships manager with access to user data
d: Saudi officials paid Ahmad Abouammo, who managed Twitter's media partnerships in the Middle East, at least US$300,000 and gave him a luxury watch; in return he looked up private data on accounts critical of the Saudi government. A second Twitter employee, Ali Alzabarah, accessed data on about 6,000 accounts in 2015 and fled to Saudi Arabia when Twitter confronted him. A San Francisco jury convicted Abouammo in August 2022 of acting as an agent of Saudi Arabia, money laundering and falsifying records, and in December 2022 he was sentenced to three and a half years in prison. Alzabarah remains charged and is in Saudi Arabia.
cite: US District Court, N.D. California — jury verdict Aug 2022, sentence Dec 2022

n: Arizona 'laptop farm' put North Korean workers in 300+ US firms
rank: remote IT staff on company payrolls
d: North Korea places its own programmers in foreign companies as remote employees under stolen or false identities, and their wages go back to the state's weapons programmes. Christina Chapman, of Arizona, helped it get those workers inside US firms: she kept company laptops in her home (a 'laptop farm') so that North Korean workers abroad appeared to be working from the United States, and stole the identities of dozens of US citizens for them. Her scheme placed the workers in more than 300 US companies and some government agencies. A federal court in Washington, DC sentenced her in July 2025 to 102 months in prison.
cite: US District Court for the District of Columbia — sentence July 2025; NK News report 25 Jul 2025

n: New Jersey laptop farm placed North Koreans at 100+ US companies
rank: remote IT staff at Fortune 500 and other firms
d: Kejia Wang and Zhenxing Wang helped North Korea get its IT workers hired inside US companies. Their shell firms (Hopana Tech LLC, Tony WKJ LLC, Independent Lab LLC) hosted company laptops so the workers seemed to be in the United States. Prosecutors said the scheme stole the identities of more than 80 Americans and placed North Korean workers at more than 100 US companies, including several Fortune 500 firms, costing the companies over US$3 million to clean up. Both pleaded guilty after their June 2025 arrest, part of a US Justice Department sweep that found 29 laptop farms in 16 states. In April 2026 Kejia Wang was sentenced to 9 years and Zhenxing Wang to 7 years and 8 months.
cite: US Department of Justice — sentences announced April 2026

n: North Korean worker hired inside security firm KnowBe4
d: A North Korean worker got himself hired as a remote software engineer at KnowBe4, a US company that trains staff to spot security threats, using a stolen US identity and an AI-altered photo; he passed background checks and video interviews. North Korea uses such workers to earn money for the state and to reach company systems. On the day his work laptop arrived, KnowBe4's systems flagged him loading malware onto it, and the company cut his access. KnowBe4 disclosed the case publicly in July 2024 as a warning to other employers.
cite: KnowBe4 public disclosure by its CEO, July 2024

n: North Korean IT workers seek jobs inside European firms
rank: remote developers at tech and crypto firms
d: North Korea places programmers inside foreign companies as remote staff under false identities. Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported on 1 April 2025 that, under pressure from US enforcement, these workers were seeking jobs at European companies. It found worker personas applying in Germany and Portugal, several projects in the United Kingdom including blockchain and AI work, a UK-based facilitator, and a corporate laptop meant for New York in use in London. It also reported that since late 2024 workers who were fired had begun threatening to leak company source code unless paid.
cite: Google Threat Intelligence Group, 'DPRK IT Workers Expanding in Scope and Scale', 1 Apr 2025

n: Wirecard's COO Jan Marsalek worked with Russian intelligence
rank: chief operating officer of a DAX-listed payments firm
d: German investigators said Jan Marsalek, chief operating officer of the German payments company Wirecard from 2010 to 2020, had been working with Russian intelligence since at least 2010, which put a Russian intelligence contact in the top management of a company listed in the DAX index of Germany's largest firms. Wirecard collapsed in June 2020 after admitting that €1.9 billion did not exist. Marsalek fled and is wanted by German police; Handelsblatt, Der Spiegel, The Insider and Bellingcat reported that he lives in Russia under intelligence protection. The Bundestag set up an inquiry into the failure to stop the fraud in 2020, and British prosecutors later said Marsalek ran a Russian spy cell in the UK.
cite: Munich prosecutors; Bundestag Wirecard committee of inquiry (2020–21); Crown Prosecution Service, UK, 2025

n: Austrian intelligence officer spied for Russia via Marsalek
rank: former officer of Austria's domestic intelligence (BVT)
d: Russia, working through the fugitive ex-Wirecard executive Jan Marsalek, recruited Egisto Ott, an officer of Austria's former domestic intelligence agency. A Vienna court found on 20 May 2026 that Ott searched police databases for people Moscow wanted to locate, passed on journalist Christo Grozev's address, sold a secure SINA laptop for €20,000 and handed over three work phones from the interior minister's office. He was sentenced to four years and one month and plans to appeal.
cite: Vienna Regional Criminal Court — verdict 20 May 2026 (Reuters)

n: Thousand Talents member inside GE convicted of economic espionage
rank: engineer in GE Power's turbine-sealing unit
d: China's Thousand Talents Program, a state scheme that recruits scientists and engineers to bring expertise to China, had a member inside the US company GE Power, the FBI said: Xiaoqing Zheng, who worked as a turbine-sealing engineer at GE Power in Schenectady, New York, from 2008 to 2018. A jury convicted him on 31 March 2022 of conspiring to commit economic espionage by taking GE's turbine trade secrets to benefit China and China-based companies and universities. He was sentenced on 3 January 2023 to 24 months in prison.
cite: US District Court, N.D. New York — verdict 31 Mar 2022, sentence 3 Jan 2023

n: Chinese intelligence officer tried to recruit GE Aviation engineers
d: Xu Yanjun, a deputy division director in a provincial branch of China's Ministry of State Security (its main spy agency), tried to recruit engineers at GE Aviation and other aerospace firms as insiders to obtain jet-engine fan-blade technology. He was arrested in Belgium in 2018 and extradited to the United States, the first Chinese intelligence officer extradited for trial. A federal jury in Cincinnati convicted him in November 2021, and in November 2022 he was sentenced to 20 years in prison.
cite: US District Court, S.D. Ohio — verdict Nov 2021, sentence Nov 2022

n: Google engineer secretly worked for Chinese firms, took AI secrets
rank: software engineer on Google's AI supercomputing work
d: Linwei Ding, a Google software engineer, secretly worked with two China-based technology companies while employed at Google, founding and leading one of them as chief executive, and took more than two thousand pages of Google's confidential AI and supercomputer designs. In late 2023 he applied to a Shanghai government talent programme, a scheme that recruits experts to bring technology to China. A San Francisco jury convicted him on 29 January 2026 of seven counts of economic espionage and seven of theft of trade secrets. Sentencing is pending.
cite: US District Court, N.D. California — jury verdict 29 Jan 2026
who: China-based firms and a Shanghai talent programme

n: Russian trade envoy paid a SoftBank employee for network files
rank: employee with access to SoftBank servers
d: A Russian diplomat paid Yutaka Araki, a SoftBank Corp. employee, for company documents: in February 2019 Araki took manuals on mobile-phone base stations and other communication equipment from a company server and gave them to him, and admitted he was paid. Japanese police named Anton Kalnin, the second-ranking official of the Russian Trade Representation in Japan, as a suspect; he left for Russia when police asked to question him. Araki was arrested in January 2020 and indicted in February 2020 under the Unfair Competition Prevention Act, Japan's law on trade secrets.
cite: Tokyo District Public Prosecutors Office — indictment Feb 2020 (Japan Times)

n: Motor Sich managers charged with secretly supplying Russia's Rostec
rank: president of Ukraine's main aircraft-engine maker
d: Ukrainian prosecutors charge that the management of Motor Sich, a Zaporizhzhia maker of engines for military and civil helicopters and aircraft, ran hidden channels supplying engines and parts to Russia in collusion with Rostec, Russia's state technology corporation, and that in April 2022 former president Viacheslav Bohuslaiev blocked delivery of a helicopter to Ukraine's military intelligence. The SBU security service detained Bohuslaiev and the foreign-trade director in October 2022. Assets of about US$314 million were seized and he was sent to trial for treason, the crime of betraying one's country. The state had already taken over the company in 2021 after a sale to Chinese investors was blocked.
cite: Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and Prosecutor General — treason indictment

n: Communist Party places its cells inside China's private companies
rank: party organisation inside each firm, including foreign joint ventures
d: China's Company Law requires any company with three or more Communist Party members to set up a party organisation, giving the party its own body inside the firm. The party's Organization Department reported that 73.1% of private companies had one in 2018, up from 58.4% in 2013, and in 2017 all of the 100 largest state firms wrote the party's role into their charters. In 2017–18 Chinese state partners of some foreign joint ventures asked the foreign side to write party groups into the articles of association, the rules that govern a company. In September 2020 the party told its United Front departments, which manage relations with groups outside the party, to 'guide' the governance of private firms.
cite: PRC Company Law (party-organisation clause); CCP Organization Department statistics; CSIS analysis

n: Party committee and state board seat inside TikTok owner ByteDance
rank: party committee and state-held board seat in TikTok's parent
d: The Chinese Communist Party and state have their own presence inside ByteDance, the Beijing company that owns TikTok and Douyin: it has had an internal party committee since 2014, and in 2021 a state-owned fund bought 1% of its main Chinese subsidiary and took a board seat. In December 2022 ByteDance admitted that employees had used TikTok data to track journalists who reported on the company, and fired four staff. The US Congress passed a 2024 law forcing TikTok's sale on national-security grounds, which the Supreme Court upheld in January 2025.
cite: ByteDance admission Dec 2022; US Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act 2024; TikTok v. Garland (2025)
who: China (Chinese Communist Party and state fund)

n: Michael Calvey says a rival used FSB links to win a bank dispute
d: Michael Calvey, an American who founded the Baring Vostok investment fund, says a business rival used connections inside Russia's FSB security service to win a dispute over Vostochny Bank. When the FSB arrested Calvey and three colleagues on fraud charges on 14 February 2019, his fund held 52.5% of the bank and was suing a fellow shareholder, Artem Avetisyan, in London. Avetisyan is described as a friend of the son of former FSB director Nikolai Patrushev. A Moscow court gave Calvey a 5.5-year suspended sentence in August 2021; the conviction was vacated on 5 April 2024.
cite: Meshchansky District Court, Moscow — verdict Aug 2021, vacated 5 Apr 2024; London Court of International Arbitration ruling Mar 2019

n: Revolutionary Guards-linked foundations bought Iran's telecom monopoly
rank: controlling stake in the Telecommunication Company of Iran
d: Foundations linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards (the IRGC, Iran's ideological military force) gained control of the Telecommunication Company of Iran through an investor group. The company runs the country's fixed lines and owns the largest mobile operator, MCI. In 2009 the Mobin Trust Consortium, whose investors included those foundations, bought 50% plus one share for about US$7.8 billion in a privatisation, giving it control of the network the state uses to watch and filter communications. An IRGC unit announced in October 2018 that it had sold its share and left telecoms.
cite: Iranian privatisation tender 2009; IRGC announcement Oct 2018

n: Chinese state-linked owner Wingtech and Dutch chipmaker Nexperia
d: Through Wingtech, a Shanghai-listed firm in which almost 30% of shares trace back to the Chinese state, China gained a stake in the control of Nexperia, a Dutch chipmaker Wingtech bought in 2018 for US$3.6 billion. In October 2025 the Dutch economy ministry took control of Nexperia's governance under the Goods Availability Act, reportedly to stop chip know-how and production moving to China. China responded by banning exports of Nexperia chips packaged there, causing shortages for European carmakers. The Netherlands suspended its order in November 2025, and in February 2026 a Dutch court ordered an investigation into mismanagement at Nexperia.
cite: Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs order under the Goods Availability Act, Oct 2025; Dutch court order for a mismanagement inquiry, Feb 2026

n: Sinovel recruited an AMSC engineer to pass it turbine software
d: Sinovel, a Chinese wind-turbine maker that bought control software from the US company AMSC, recruited an engineer at AMSC's Austrian subsidiary to pass it the source code. With the code Sinovel could stop paying AMSC; AMSC said its losses exceeded US$800 million. A federal jury in Madison, Wisconsin convicted Sinovel of trade-secret theft on 24 January 2018, and AMSC announced a settlement in July 2018.
cite: US District Court, W.D. Wisconsin — jury verdict 24 Jan 2018

n: Tokyo Electron employee obtained TSMC's 2nm secrets from TSMC staff
d: Taiwanese prosecutors said a Tokyo Electron employee obtained secrets about TSMC's 2-nanometre chip process from TSMC staff, to help Tokyo Electron, a Japanese chip-equipment maker, win equipment orders from TSMC. TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker and the 2nm process is one of Taiwan's most guarded technologies. The former TSMC staff and the Tokyo Electron employee were indicted in August 2025 under the National Security Act. On 27 April 2026 a Taiwan court sentenced the main defendant to 10 years, three other ex-TSMC staff to two to six years, and fined Tokyo Electron's Taiwan unit; two of the sentences became final in July 2026.
cite: Taiwan district court judgment, 27 Apr 2026 (Al Jazeera/Reuters); final rulings for two defendants, Jul 2026

n: PCC crime group accused of controlling two São Paulo bus companies
rank: owners and directors of Transwolff and UpBus
d: São Paulo prosecutors charge that the PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), Brazil's largest criminal organisation, worked through the directors of the bus companies Transwolff (about 1,200 buses) and UpBus, who they say laundered PCC money from drug trafficking and robbery through city transport contracts. The charges came in Operação Fim da Linha on 9 April 2024, run by prosecutors, tax and police officials; courts froze up to R$600 million. The same day the mayor issued Decree 63.328 placing both companies under city control, and in 2025 the city moved to end their contracts and hand the lines to other operators.
cite: São Paulo Public Ministry (GAECO) — Operação Fim da Linha, 9 Apr 2024; Municipal Decree 63.328

n: Sicilian Mafia clan bribed Lidl Italia insiders to win contracts
rank: four regional management offices of Lidl Italia
d: The Laudani clan of Catania, part of the Sicilian Mafia (Cosa Nostra), used bribed insiders at the supermarket chain Lidl Italia to win work such as warehouse logistics and shop fitting for firms it controlled, Milan anti-mafia prosecutors said when they arrested 15 people in May 2017. A Milan court put four Lidl Italia management offices, overseeing about 200 shops, under judicial administration (court-appointed managers) for six months, as well as the company that guarded Milan's law courts. Lidl was not itself under investigation.
cite: Milan court — judicial administration order, May 2017

n: 'Ndrangheta clan took over firms in Emilia-Romagna
rank: construction and haulage companies of the region
d: The Grande Aracri clan of the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, ran and took over construction and other firms in Emilia-Romagna in northern Italy, including in rebuilding after the 2012 earthquake. The Aemilia maxi-trial, a single trial of many defendants, dealt with this branch. The first final convictions of five clan leaders came in October 2018. In May 2022 Italy's Court of Cassation, its highest appeal court, confirmed more than 70 convictions, and its reasoning described a self-standing 'Ndrangheta structure in Emilia rooted among local entrepreneurs who knowingly used the clan.
cite: Court of Cassation — Aemilia rulings Oct 2018 and May 2022

n: Russian offered a Tesla worker US$1m to plant malware
d: In 2020 Egor Kriuchkov, a Russian national, tried to recruit an employee at Tesla's Gigafactory near Reno as an insider for a criminal group, offering US$1 million to install malware on the plant's network so the group could steal data and demand ransom; he expected US$250,000 for the recruitment. The employee told the FBI, which recorded later meetings. Kriuchkov pleaded guilty on 18 March 2021, was sentenced in May 2021 to time served and was ordered deported.
cite: US District Court, District of Nevada — plea 18 Mar 2021, sentence May 2021

n: Opus Dei-linked bloc at the core of Banco Popular
rank: board and core shareholders of Banco Popular
d: Shareholder lawsuits showed that people and foundations tied to Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members, formed the core shareholder group of Banco Popular, Spain's sixth-largest bank. They included Opus Dei numerary (a celibate full member) and board secretary Francisco Aparicio Valls and the Fundación Universitaria de Navarra and Fomento de Fundaciones; Luis Valls Taberner, president from 1972 to 2004, was also a numerary. Journalist Gareth Gore's 2024 book 'Opus' says the bank channelled money to Opus Dei causes; Opus Dei and the Valls Taberner foundations call this false. The bank failed and was sold to Santander for €1 in June 2017.
cite: El Independiente, 10 Jun 2018 (shareholder lawsuits); Gareth Gore, 'Opus' (2024); Opus Dei statements 2024

n: Boeing staff did FAA safety checks and played down 737 MAX system
d: Under the Federal Aviation Administration's Organization Designation Authorization, Boeing employees carry out much of the work of certifying Boeing's own planes as safe on behalf of the FAA, the US agency responsible. After the Lion Air (2018) and Ethiopian Airlines (2019) 737 MAX crashes killed 346 people, a June 2020 Transportation Department Inspector General report found Boeing had played down the MCAS flight-control system during certification and the FAA had missed it. The House Transportation Committee's final report of September 2020 found Boeing withheld key information from the FAA and that the delegation system weakened the agency's oversight. The delegation programme is still in use.
cite: US House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, final 737 MAX report, September 2020; US DOT Office of Inspector General report, June 2020

n: Purdue helped the FDA reviewer draft his OxyContin approval
d: Purdue Pharma, owned by the Sackler family, helped write the US Food and Drug Administration's own review of its painkiller OxyContin. According to Purdue documents in a 2006 Justice Department review, Dr Curtis Wright IV, the FDA medical officer who approved OxyContin in 1995 for 'moderate to severe pain', met Purdue staff in a hotel room near FDA offices in Rockville from 31 January to 2 February 1995 and let the company help draft his review and approve label wording, including the claim that delayed absorption 'is believed to reduce the abuse liability'. Wright left the FDA about a year later and went to work for Purdue. That label sentence was quoted in Purdue's 2007 felony conviction for misbranding.
cite: US Justice Department review of Purdue documents (2006), as reported; Purdue 2007 misbranding conviction; Wikipedia 'Purdue Pharma'

n: Ex-DEA lawyer for drug industry wrote 2016 law weakening the DEA
rank: members of Congress; DEA enforcement powers
d: D. Linden Barber, a former senior lawyer at the Drug Enforcement Administration who had become an attorney for the drug industry, wrote the text of the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act of 2016, the Washington Post and CBS '60 Minutes' reported in October 2017, drawing on former DEA official Joe Rannazzisi. The law, pushed by the drug industry, changed the test for seizing suspicious narcotics shipments from an 'imminent' to an 'immediate' danger, making it harder for the DEA to act against distributors. Its House sponsor, Representative Tom Marino, withdrew as President Trump's nominee for drug czar on 17 October 2017.
cite: Washington Post / CBS 60 Minutes investigation, October 2017; WGBH/NPR, 17 October 2017

n: Monsanto email says EPA official offered to 'kill' a glyphosate review
d: Court papers unsealed in March 2017 in the US Roundup litigation include an email by a manager at Monsanto, maker of the weedkiller Roundup (glyphosate) and now owned by Bayer, saying that a senior EPA official offered to block another agency's safety review for the company. The official, Jess Rowland, chaired the EPA committee that found glyphosate unlikely to cause cancer; according to the email, he said in April 2015 'If I can kill this I should get a medal' about a planned glyphosate review by the ATSDR, a federal health agency. The ATSDR had promised its review for October 2015 and did not publish it then. Rowland had left the EPA in 2016. Monsanto said the emails showed a normal flow of information; plaintiffs' lawyers called the relationship 'highly suspicious'.
cite: In re: Roundup Products Liability Litigation, MDL 2741 (N.D. Cal.), unsealed documents; Insurance Journal (Bloomberg), 16 March 2017

n: Industry-written model bills copied into 10,000 US state bills
d: Outside groups, many funded by industry, wrote at least 10,000 bills introduced in US state legislatures from 2010 to 2018 that were almost entirely copied from their model legislation, a 2019 investigation by USA Today, the Arizona Republic and the Center for Public Integrity found after comparing nearly a million bills. More than 2,100 became law. More than 4,000 benefited industries, and over 80 limited people's ability to sue companies. Authors included the industry-funded American Legislative Exchange Council (an 'Asbestos Transparency Act' filed in at least 32 states and passed in 12), the Goldwater Institute and a for-profit cancer hospital chain, as well as the liberal State Innovation Exchange.
cite: USA Today / Arizona Republic / Center for Public Integrity, 'Copy, Paste, Legislate', 4 April 2019
org_note: alec used as the main author; the study covers several groups on both sides.

n: FPL's consultants tied to dark money for Florida 'ghost' candidates
d: Nonprofits partly overseen by the chief executive of Matrix LLC, a consulting firm then working for Florida Power & Light (FPL), the state's largest electric utility, channelled about $630,000 of the roughly $730,000 in dark money (political spending whose donors are hidden) that paid for 'ghost' candidates in the 2020 Florida Senate races. Republican operatives recruited these little-known candidates to split the vote and change who won seats; in District 37 the incumbent Democrat lost by under 40 votes. Several people were convicted or pleaded no contest and former senator Frank Artiles was charged; FPL was not charged, denies wrongdoing and says two outside law firms cleared it. Leaked Matrix records also showed surveillance of a journalist and payments to news outlets; FPL's chief executive retired in January 2023.
cite: Florida criminal cases (Miami-Dade and Seminole); Floodlight / Mother Jones, 18 September 2024

n: Musk led DOGE while agencies it cut regulated his companies
d: In 2025 Elon Musk, owner of Tesla, SpaceX and Neuralink, led the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which cut staff and contracts across federal agencies, including some that regulated his companies. An April 2025 memo by Democratic staff of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, under ranking member Richard Blumenthal, counted 65 active or potential federal enforcement actions against Musk's companies across 11 agencies and estimated that 40 of them carried $2.37 billion in potential liabilities that DOGE's influence could help them avoid. Musk denied conflicts and left DOGE in 2025.
cite: US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Minority Staff Memorandum, 27 April 2025; The Register, 28 April 2025

n: CDC director advised ex-Coca-Cola executive on lobbying the WHO
rank: director, CDC Division for Heart Disease and Stroke Prevention
d: Barbara Bowman, director of the Division for Heart Disease and Stroke Prevention at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), advised Alex Malaspina, a former Coca-Cola senior vice-president and founder of the industry-funded International Life Sciences Institute, on how to approach the World Health Organization, which he said did not want to work with industry. The emails, from 2011 to 2015, were obtained under Freedom of Information requests and analysed in a study in The Milbank Quarterly in February 2019. Coca-Cola said the emails pre-dated its 2015 pledge to disclose research funding.
cite: Hessari et al., The Milbank Quarterly 97(1), 2019; Mother Jones, 1 February 2019

n: Firms paid MP Owen Paterson, who lobbied regulators for them
rank: Food Standards Agency and Department for International Development
d: The diagnostics company Randox and the meat processor Lynn's Country Foods paid Owen Paterson, a sitting MP and former Environment and Northern Ireland Secretary, as a consultant, and he lobbied government bodies on their behalf. In October 2021 the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards found he had broken the paid-advocacy rule, which bars MPs from lobbying for those who pay them, by approaching the Food Standards Agency three times and the Department for International Development four times for Randox, and the Food Standards Agency seven times for Lynn's. A government attempt to overturn the recommended suspension collapsed, and Paterson resigned from Parliament on 5 November 2021.
cite: Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards and Committee on Standards report, October 2021

n: Peer Michelle Mone's hidden link to £200m PPE Medpro contracts
d: Conservative peer Michelle Mone, a member of the House of Lords, referred PPE Medpro into the UK government's 2020 'VIP lane', a fast track for pandemic protective equipment offers referred by ministers, MPs and officials, while denying any involvement with the firm. PPE Medpro won £200 million of contracts; its gowns were not shown to be sterile and went unused. Mone admitted her involvement in December 2023; leaked records showed £29 million of profits went to a trust she could benefit from. In October 2025 the High Court ruled PPE Medpro breached its contract and must repay about £122 million. Mone took leave from the House of Lords.
cite: High Court of England and Wales (Department of Health and Social Care v PPE Medpro), judgment October 2025; National Audit Office reports on PPE procurement
who: PPE Medpro (Michelle Mone and Doug Barrowman)
org_note: status 'convicted' used for a civil judgment against the company; not a criminal conviction.

n: Big-bank lobby hired EU banking regulator's chief
d: The Association for Financial Markets in Europe (AFME), the lobby group of Europe's largest banks, recruited the head of the European Banking Authority (EBA) while he still had access to the regulator's confidential information. The EBA writes and enforces common rules for EU banks. Adam Farkas, its executive director since 2011, left in February 2020 to run AFME. On 11 May 2020 European Ombudsman Emily O'Reilly found maladministration: the EBA should have forbidden the move, and should have cut off Farkas's access to confidential information as soon as he notified it of the new job. Moves like this, from regulator to the industry it regulates, are known as the 'revolving door'. The EBA then adopted a new revolving-door policy.
cite: European Ombudsman decision, 11 May 2020; EUobserver, 12 May 2020

n: Glyphosate makers' text copied into German safety review
rank: Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) assessors
d: Text written by the glyphosate makers, led by Monsanto, ended up in the official German safety review that the EU used to renew the weedkiller. Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) wrote the draft review behind the EU's 2017 renewal of glyphosate; the renewal request came from industry. A study for Members of the European Parliament published on 15 January 2019 by Stefan Weber and Helmut Burtscher-Schaden found that BfR had taken large passages from the industry application, with up to half of some chapters written by the applicants, and presented them as its own evaluation. BfR rejected the plagiarism charge. The EU renewed glyphosate again in 2023 for ten years.
cite: Weber and Burtscher-Schaden study for MEPs, 15 January 2019; Greens/EFA release
who: Monsanto (Bayer) and the Glyphosate Task Force

n: Novartis bribed Greek public hospital staff and doctors
rank: two former prime ministers and several health ministers (alleged)
d: Novartis, the Swiss drug company, paid bribes inside Greece's public health system to sell its medicines. In 2020 Novartis paid about $347 million to US authorities to settle charges that included bribing Greek hospital staff and doctors. Greek prosecutors had gone further in 2018, alleging that Novartis bribed officials from 2006 to 2015 and naming two former prime ministers and several former health ministers from the New Democracy and PASOK parties. Those politicians denied it, and the cases against them were dropped, so the established part of the case concerns hospital staff and doctors rather than ministers.
cite: Greek prosecutors' case file sent to Parliament, February 2018; US DOJ and SEC Novartis resolution, June 2020

n: Shell and Unilever lobbied for Dutch tax cut in coalition talks
rank: Prime Minister Mark Rutte's coalition talks
d: Shell and Unilever got a tax cut they wanted into the programme of a new Dutch government during closed-door coalition talks. In October 2017 Mark Rutte's new government announced it would abolish the 15% Dutch dividend withholding tax, a tax on payouts to shareholders, although no party had campaigned for it. Memos released in April 2018, after pressure in Parliament, showed the two companies had lobbied for it during the 2017 coalition talks, and an August 2017 memo called the tax 'decisive' for Unilever's choice of headquarters. Rutte survived a censure vote. In October 2018, after Unilever dropped its move to Rotterdam, the government abandoned the plan.
cite: Dutch government memos released to the House of Representatives, 24 April 2018; ESM Magazine (Reuters), 25 April 2018

n: Babiš kept control of Agrofert while serving as Czech PM
d: Andrej Babiš, Czech prime minister, kept control of his own company Agrofert, a farming, food and chemicals group that receives EU farm subsidies, according to a European Commission audit. A 2017 Czech conflict-of-interest law led Babiš to put Agrofert into two trust funds, but the Commission audit published in 2021 concluded he still controlled the company and was in a conflict of interest, meaning he could influence public decisions on money going to his own business. He became prime minister again in December 2025. He took back sole ownership in October 2025 and on 20 February 2026 moved the shares to a new trust, saying the conflict was resolved.
cite: European Commission audit, 2021; Radio Prague, 21 February 2026

n: Zelensky friend's network ran kickbacks at state nuclear firm
d: A group led by businessman Timur Mindich, a friend of President Zelensky and co-owner of the Kvartal 95 studio, took kickbacks from contractors of Energoatom, Ukraine's state nuclear power company, according to the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU). In November 2025 NABU said the scheme was worth $100 million. Mindich left Ukraine hours before NABU searched his home on 10 November 2025. Former deputy prime minister Oleksiy Chernyshov was charged with illegal enrichment. Zelensky asked justice minister German Galushchenko and energy minister Svitlana Hrynchuk to resign, and his chief of staff Andriy Yermak later became a suspect.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), Operation Midas, November 2025

n: Power station director's secret company linked to Malta's top aides
rank: Prime Minister's chief of staff and energy minister
d: Yorgen Fenech, a director of Electrogas, the company that built Malta's gas power station under a state contract, secretly owned 17 Black, a company registered in the UAE, as was revealed in November 2018. Leaked documents had listed 17 Black as a 'target client' expected to pay into secret Panama companies set up for Konrad Mizzi, the energy minister, and Keith Schembri, the prime minister's chief of staff. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating 17 Black when she was killed by a car bomb in 2017. Fenech is charged with complicity in her murder, a trial that began in mid-2026. Schembri resigned in November 2019. In February 2025 Fenech, Mizzi and Schembri were arraigned together on corruption charges over the Electrogas project.
cite: Maltese criminal proceedings, 2019–2026; Reuters / Times of Malta 17 Black investigation, November 2018; MaltaToday, 'Dubai company 17 Black was target client of Schembri's and Mizzi's Panama set-ups', April 2018

n: Bezeq owner allegedly bought favourable rulings from Netanyahu
d: Shaul Elovitch, controlling owner of Bezeq, Israel's largest telecoms company, is accused of obtaining regulatory decisions worth large sums from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was also communications minister and so regulated Bezeq. Prosecutors say that in return Elovitch's news site Walla! gave Netanyahu favourable coverage. Netanyahu is charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in what is called Case 4000; his trial began in May 2020 and his testimony ended in June 2026. He denies the charges and in November 2025 asked President Herzog for a pardon.
cite: Indictment filed by Israel's Attorney General, 2020; Jerusalem District Court trial, 2020–2026

n: Telia paid Uzbek president's daughter for mobile licences
rank: President Islam Karimov's daughter, Gulnara Karimova
d: Telia, the Swedish-Finnish telecoms group, got into Uzbekistan's mobile market by paying companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, daughter of then-President Islam Karimov, who in return secured licences and radio frequencies from the state. In September 2017 Telia agreed to pay about $965 million to US, Dutch and Swedish authorities to settle bribery charges. OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, reported in 2015 that Karimova took over $1 billion in bribes from Scandinavian and Russian telecom firms. She was later jailed in Uzbekistan.
cite: US DOJ and SEC resolution with Telia Company, September 2017; OCCRP, 2015

n: Airbus paid intermediaries to bribe officials for contracts
rank: airline and defence procurement officials in many countries
d: Airbus, the European aircraft maker, hired and paid intermediaries to bribe officials and win civil and military contracts in many countries. Investigators found the practice ran from 2012 onward, with suspect sales in countries including Saudi Arabia, Kazakhstan, the Philippines, Indonesia, Austria, China and Mauritius. In January 2020 Airbus agreed to pay about €3.6 billion to French, British and US prosecutors, the largest bribery settlement of its kind, under deferred prosecution agreements, deals in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms. The UK agreement covered bribes in Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan and Ghana.
cite: Deferred prosecution agreements with France's PNF, the UK Serious Fraud Office and the US DOJ, January 2020

n: BAE paid Saudi prince over Al-Yamamah arms deals
d: BAE Systems, Britain's largest arms maker, was reported in 2007 by BBC Panorama to have paid hundreds of millions of pounds to Prince Bandar bin Sultan, a senior Saudi royal and official, in connection with Al-Yamamah, a series of British arms sales to Saudi Arabia led by BAE since 1985. In December 2006 the Serious Fraud Office had dropped its investigation into alleged BAE slush funds, secret funds used for payments, after pressure from the Saudi and British governments; a new Typhoon fighter contract for 72 aircraft had been signed in 2006. In 2010 BAE pleaded guilty in the United States to false accounting and misleading statements and paid $400 million.
cite: UK Serious Fraud Office decision, 14 December 2006; US District Court for the District of Columbia plea, March 2010; BBC Panorama, June 2007

n: Rolls-Royce and Airbus bribes reached Garuda airline's chief
rank: president director of state airline Garuda Indonesia
d: Rolls-Royce and Airbus money reached the head of Garuda Indonesia, the state-owned national airline, while he was buying their aircraft and engines. In May 2020 the Jakarta Corruption Court sentenced former president director Emirsyah Satar to eight years in prison for taking Rp 49.3 billion (US$3.4 million) in bribes tied to those purchases, and for laundering Rp 87.5 billion. Prosecutors traced the money to the two companies through middleman Soetikno Soedarjo, who received six years. Both companies' bribery admissions to UK prosecutors covered Indonesia.
cite: Jakarta Corruption Court verdict, 8 May 2020; KPK; Jakarta Post, 9 May 2020

n: Monsanto paid Indonesian official reviewing its GM cotton
d: Monsanto, the US seed and chemicals company, paid a high-level official at Indonesia's environment ministry while that ministry was assessing Monsanto's genetically modified cotton. In 2002 a Monsanto senior manager had an Indonesian consulting firm pay the official a $50,000 bribe, disguised as consulting fees. The US Securities and Exchange Commission also found that Monsanto's Indonesian affiliates made illicit payments of at least $700,000 to at least 140 current or former officials and their families. Monsanto settled in 2005 under a deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms.
cite: US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement and SEC settlement, January 2005

n: Samsung heir bribed President Park's friend for state support
d: Lee Jae-yong, de facto head of Samsung, South Korea's largest business group, offered $38 million in bribes to entities controlled by Choi Soon-sil, a friend of President Park Geun-hye, to win government support for a merger that strengthened his control of Samsung. He was charged in 2017 and the scandal led to Park's impeachment. Lee was convicted in August 2017; after appeals he served a 2.5-year sentence from January 2021. President Yoon Suk Yeol pardoned him in August 2022, and he became Samsung chairman in October 2022.
cite: Seoul Central District Court, August 2017; Seoul High Court retrial, January 2021

n: TEPCO captured Japan's nuclear regulator before Fukushima
d: Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) and the nuclear industry had come to steer NISA, the Japanese agency meant to regulate them, according to the National Diet's independent inquiry into the Fukushima Daiichi meltdown of March 2011. The commission, chaired by Kiyoshi Kurokawa, reported in July 2012 that the relationship amounted to 'regulatory capture', meaning the regulator served the industry. It found regulators asked operators about their wishes before writing new rules, told them they need not plan for a station blackout, and allowed TEPCO to push earthquake checks due in 2009 to 2016. NISA was abolished and replaced by the Nuclear Regulation Authority in 2012.
cite: Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission (NAIIC), National Diet of Japan, report, 5 July 2012; Nuclear Engineering International
who: TEPCO and Japan's nuclear power industry

n: Coca-Cola-founded ILSI had its office inside China's CDC
rank: Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention
d: The International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI), an industry-funded science group, had its China branch housed inside the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the national public health agency. ILSI was founded in 1978 by Coca-Cola executive Alex Malaspina and is funded by food and chemical companies. Harvard anthropologist Susan Greenhalgh reported in the BMJ and the Journal of Public Health Policy in 2019 that ILSI-China shaped China's obesity policy toward exercise rather than diet and sugary drinks. Nutrition researcher Barry Popkin said ILSI had 'an extremely harmful influence' in China. Mars left ILSI in 2018 and Coca-Cola in 2021.
cite: Greenhalgh, BMJ, January 2019; Journal of Public Health Policy, 2019

n: AgustaWestland accused of bribes for Indian VIP helicopters
rank: Indian Air Force VVIP helicopter procurement
d: AgustaWestland, a helicopter maker owned by Italy's Finmeccanica (now Leonardo), was accused of paying bribes of about $60 million to win an Indian contract. India had agreed in February 2010 to buy 12 AgustaWestland AW101 helicopters to fly the president and prime minister. In February 2013 Finmeccanica chief executive Giuseppe Orsi was arrested in Italy over the alleged bribes, and India's Central Bureau of Investigation opened a case. India cancelled the $630 million deal in January 2014 and recovered its payments. Orsi was fully acquitted by Italian courts in 2019; Indian proceedings against middlemen continue.
cite: Italian courts (acquittal, 2019); Indian Ministry of Defence cancellation, January 2014; CBI case

n: UAE oil company's chief ran COP28 and prepared oil deal talks
rank: President of the UN climate summit (COP28)
d: Sultan Al Jaber, chief executive of the UAE state oil company ADNOC and chairman of the renewable firm Masdar, was named president of the COP28 UN climate talks, and his team prepared to use meetings in that role for company business. On 27 November 2023 the BBC, with the Centre for Climate Reporting, published leaked briefing papers for his meetings with foreign governments that included talking points on ADNOC and Masdar commercial interests for more than two dozen countries and plans to discuss oil and gas deals with 15. The COP28 team did not deny using meetings for business and said 'private meetings are private'; Al Jaber called the claims false.
cite: BBC / Centre for Climate Reporting leaked documents, 27 November 2023; CBS News, 27 November 2023

n: Azerbaijan's COP29 chief filmed discussing oil and gas deals
rank: chief executive of the UN climate summit (COP29)
d: Azerbaijan's oil and gas interests were inside the leadership of the COP29 UN climate talks it hosted in November 2024. The summit president, Mukhtar Babayev, had been vice-president for ecology at the state oil company SOCAR. The summit's chief executive, deputy energy minister Elnur Soltanov, was secretly filmed by Global Witness campaigners posing as investors, discussing possible oil and gas deals during the run-up to the talks. Critics said this broke the code of conduct for COP presidencies, which requires them to act impartially. Azerbaijan's economy rests on oil and gas.
cite: Global Witness undercover recording, November 2024; Wikipedia '2024 United Nations Climate Change Conference'
who: SOCAR and Azerbaijan's oil and gas sector

n: Philip Morris's secret campaign to get inside WHO tobacco treaty
rank: WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) meetings
d: Philip Morris International (PMI), the tobacco company, ran a secret campaign to get into and weaken the WHO tobacco treaty, Reuters reported on 13 July 2017 from thousands of leaked company documents. The treaty, the FCTC, in force since 2005, commits governments to tax tobacco, ban advertising and keep the industry out of health policy (Article 5.3). The documents showed PMI lobbying delegates, trying to get into treaty meetings and fighting tax, advertising and warning-label rules from the Americas to Africa and Asia. A 2014 company presentation said 'Roadblocks are as important as solutions'. PMI said it had a right to take part in policy debates.
cite: Reuters, 'Inside Philip Morris' campaign to subvert the global anti-smoking treaty', 13 July 2017

n: BAT arranged bribes to Comoros officials to block tobacco laws
d: British American Tobacco (BAT), the world's second-largest listed tobacco company, arranged bribes for officials in the Comoros Islands, Rwanda and Burundi, including payments aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws based on the WHO tobacco treaty. BBC Panorama reported this in November 2015 using documents from former BAT employee Paul Hopkins, putting the total at about $26,000. A 2021 University of Bath study of these and other leaked records counted 236 payments worth $601,502 from 2008 to 2013 in ten African countries. The UK Serious Fraud Office opened an investigation in 2017 and closed it in January 2021 without charges. BAT denied wrongdoing.
cite: BBC Panorama, 30 November 2015; University of Bath Tobacco Control Research Group, 2021; UK Serious Fraud Office closure, January 2021

n: BAT payments to Burundi officials to block tobacco laws
d: British American Tobacco (BAT) made payments to officials in Burundi, according to the leaked company records that BBC Panorama reported in 2015. The University of Bath's 2021 analysis says payments in Burundi, Comoros, Rwanda and Uganda were aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws modelled on the WHO Framework Convention, the global treaty that commits governments to cut smoking. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its investigation in 2021 without charges, and BAT denies the allegations.
cite: BBC Panorama, 30 November 2015; University of Bath Tobacco Control Research Group, 2021

n: Shipping industry sat inside national delegations at the UN's IMO
d: Shipping companies and their trade groups had people inside national delegations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the London-based UN agency that sets rules for global shipping, which emits close to 3% of greenhouse gases. An October 2017 InfluenceMap report found that at the IMO's latest environment committee meeting, 31% of member states had delegations that included direct business interests. It found that the International Chamber of Shipping, BIMCO and the World Shipping Council sought to delay climate rules and keep measures voluntary. The industry groups said they supported cutting emissions.
cite: InfluenceMap, 'Corporate Capture of the IMO', October 2017

n: ABB paid $37m to an Eskom executive for Kusile contracts
rank: senior official, state power utility Eskom
d: ABB, the Swiss-Swedish engineering group, paid more than $37 million in bribes between 2014 and 2017 to a high-ranking official at Eskom, South Africa's state-owned electricity company, to win work on the Kusile power station. ABB admitted this in December 2022 and paid $315 million to the US Justice Department, $75 million to the Securities and Exchange Commission and a Swiss fine. It also agreed to return $104 million to Eskom.
cite: US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement and SEC settlement with ABB, 2 December 2022

n: SAP bribed South African city, ministry and Eskom officials
rank: officials at Johannesburg, Tshwane, the water department and Eskom
d: SAP, the German business-software company, bribed officials at the City of Johannesburg, the City of Tshwane, the Department of Water and Sanitation and the state power company Eskom from 2013 to 2017 to win contracts, and bribed Indonesian officials from 2015 to 2018. In January 2024 SAP agreed to pay more than $220 million to US authorities and entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms. Up to $55.1 million was credited to a South African case. Earlier, SAP had been accused of paying a company linked to the Gupta family to win work at Transnet, the state freight company.
cite: US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement and SEC order, 10 January 2024; OCCRP, 12 January 2024

n: Bosasa paid South African officials while winning prison contracts
rank: Correctional Services officials; minister Nomvula Mokonyane
d: Bosasa (later African Global Operations), a company run by the late Gavin Watson, paid benefits to politicians while it won catering, security and other contracts from the Department of Correctional Services for years. Part 3 of the Zondo Commission's report on state capture, the takeover of state bodies by private interests (1 March 2022), found prima facie evidence of corruption by former minister Nomvula Mokonyane, for whom Bosasa paid a birthday party and Christmas groceries, and recommended she be investigated. It also called for corruption charges over Bosasa's payments to former ANC MP Vincent Smith. Mokonyane denies wrongdoing and has served as the ANC's first deputy secretary-general since December 2022.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo Commission), Report Part 3, 1 March 2022

n: Arms firm Thales accused of paying Zuma through his adviser
d: The French arms firm Thomson-CSF, now Thales, is accused of paying Jacob Zuma, then a senior South African politician, through his financial adviser Schabir Shaik in connection with a R30 billion arms package South Africa signed in 1999. Shaik was convicted of corruption in 2005 for payments to Zuma linked to the deal, including an arrangement with Thomson-CSF, and President Mbeki dismissed Zuma as deputy president. Charges against Zuma were dropped in 2009 and reinstated in 2018. On 22 January 2020 the Pietermaritzburg High Court ruled that both Zuma and Thales could stand trial; the trial has been delayed repeatedly. Both deny the charges.
cite: Durban High Court, Shaik conviction, 2005; Pietermaritzburg High Court ruling, 22 January 2020

n: P&ID bribed a Nigerian government lawyer during arbitration
rank: Ministry of Petroleum Resources legal adviser
d: Process & Industrial Developments (P&ID), a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, bribed Grace Taiwo, a lawyer working for Nigeria's government, while the two sides were in arbitration, a private legal process for settling contract disputes. P&ID had signed a 2010 gas-processing deal with Nigeria, did not build the plant, and won an arbitration award that grew to over $11 billion. In October 2023 Justice Robin Knowles in the London High Court set the award aside, finding P&ID obtained it by fraud: besides the bribe, it had used Nigeria's leaked privileged legal documents. Nigeria was later awarded costs.
cite: High Court of England and Wales (Commercial Court), Federal Republic of Nigeria v P&ID, judgment 23 October 2023
org_note: status 'convicted' used for a civil fraud finding; no criminal conviction of the company.

n: OPL 245 — $1.1bn oil block money went to ex-minister's firm
rank: former oil minister Dan Etete; government officials
d: Eni and Shell paid $1.1 billion in 2011 through a Nigerian government account for the offshore oil block OPL 245, and the money went on to Malabu Oil and Gas, a company controlled by former oil minister Dan Etete. Italian prosecutors charged both companies and their executives, including Eni chief executive Claudio Descalzi, with international corruption, alleging the payment was a route for bribes to Nigerian officials. On 17 March 2021 a Milan court acquitted all defendants, and in 2022 prosecutors dropped their appeal. Nigeria's government said it was disappointed.
cite: Milan Tribunal verdict, 17 March 2021; Guardian Nigeria / Reuters, 2022

n: Shell said it had placed its people in all Nigeria's key ministries
d: Shell, the oldest and largest foreign oil producer in Nigeria, said it had placed its own staff inside the Nigerian government ministries that dealt with oil. A US diplomatic cable of 20 October 2009, published by WikiLeaks and The Guardian in December 2010, records Ann Pickard, then Shell's executive vice-president for Africa, telling the US ambassador that the government had 'forgotten that Shell had seconded people to all the relevant ministries', meaning Shell had lent them staff, and that Shell therefore knew what was being done in them. Shell rejected the claim.
cite: US Embassy Abuja cable, 20 October 2009, published by WikiLeaks; The Guardian and Al Jazeera, December 2010

n: Steinmetz bribed Guinea president's wife for iron ore rights
d: BSG Resources, controlled by Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz, paid bribes to Mamadie Touré, a wife of Guinea's President Lansana Conté, to obtain mining rights at Simandou, one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits. In 2008 the government took blocks I and II from Rio Tinto and gave them to BSG Resources. On 22 January 2021 a Geneva court found Steinmetz guilty of corruption over the bribes, sentencing him to five years and a fine of 50 million Swiss francs. Swiss appeal courts upheld the conviction in 2022 and 2023. Steinmetz denies wrongdoing.
cite: Geneva Criminal Court, 22 January 2021; Swiss appeal rulings, 2022–2023

n: Dan Gertler used friendship with Kabila for Congo mining deals
rank: President Joseph Kabila; state miner Gécamines
d: Dan Gertler, an Israeli mining and oil investor, used his long friendship with Congolese president Joseph Kabila to obtain mining and oil deals from the state, according to the US Treasury. In December 2017 the Treasury sanctioned him under the Global Magnitsky Act, a US law for punishing corruption and abuses abroad, saying he amassed a fortune through hundreds of millions of dollars of opaque and corrupt mining and oil deals in the DRC using that friendship. Under a later settlement with the Congolese state his Ventora group handed back mining and oil licences and agreed to pay royalties to the state miner Gécamines. Gertler denies wrongdoing.
cite: US Treasury OFAC Global Magnitsky designation, 21 December 2017

n: Sanctioned state contractor Tagwirei made a Zimbabwe minister
rank: Minister of Economic Development and Investment Promotion; ZANU-PF Central Committee
d: Kudakwashe Tagwirei, a businessman whose company profited from state contracts, moved into Zimbabwe's ruling party and then its cabinet. His firm Sakunda Holdings grew through fuel trading with Trafigura and a $3 billion state 'Command Agriculture' contract from 2017 to 2019 paid with Treasury bills. In August 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned him, accusing him of misappropriating public funds and supporting senior officials; the UK followed in July 2021 and the US extended sanctions in March 2024. He was co-opted onto ZANU-PF's Central Committee in October 2025, and in October 2026 President Mnangagwa appointed him a cabinet minister. He denies the allegations.
cite: US Treasury designation, 5 August 2020 and March 2024; UK sanctions, July 2021

n: Ericsson paid Djibouti officials for a state telecom contract
d: Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, paid about €2.1 million to high-ranking officials in Djibouti to win a contract with the state-owned Djibouti Telecom. It admitted this in December 2019, when it agreed to pay more than $1 billion to settle US criminal and civil cases over corruption from 2000 to 2016 in China, Indonesia, Vietnam, Kuwait and Djibouti. In 2022 leaked internal Ericsson files, published by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), described corruption in at least ten countries; the company admitted 'serious breaches of compliance rules'.
cite: US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement and SEC settlement with Ericsson, 6 December 2019

n: SQM secretly funded Chilean politicians through fake invoices
rank: politicians and parties across Chile's spectrum
