d: SQM, a Chilean lithium and fertiliser miner whose main shareholder is Julio Ponce Lerou, former son-in-law of dictator Augusto Pinochet, secretly paid money to Chilean politicians' campaigns and parties. From 2015 Chilean prosecutors investigated how politicians, advisers and relatives issued fake invoices that SQM paid, passing money to campaigns in breach of finance laws. In 2017 SQM settled US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act charges under a deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms; the US Justice Department confirmed in 2020 that it had met the terms. In 2024 SQM agreed a long-term lithium partnership with the state copper company Codelco.
cite: Chilean Public Prosecutor's Office (Penta-SQM case); US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement, January 2017

n: Odebrecht says it paid $59m to Panamanian officials
d: Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, says it paid $59 million in bribes to Panamanian officials during Ricardo Martinelli's 2009–2014 government. Odebrecht admitted in 2016 paying $788 million in bribes in Latin America and Africa to win public contracts. Panama's main Odebrecht money-laundering trial opened on 12 January 2026 with more than 20 defendants; Martinelli, who received asylum in Colombia in 2025, took part by video and pleaded innocent. Two of his sons and former president Juan Carlos Varela, who has parliamentary immunity, are to be tried separately by the Supreme Court.
cite: Panama criminal court, Odebrecht trial opened 12 January 2026; Tico Times, 13 January 2026

n: Odebrecht money went into Santos's 2010 presidential campaign
d: Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, made illegal payments to Juan Manuel Santos's 2010 presidential campaign in Colombia. On 14 March 2017 Santos, then president, acknowledged the payments and said he had not known of them. Odebrecht's bribes in Colombia were tied to the Ruta del Sol highway contract, a state road-building contract; former senator Otto Bula was among those prosecuted.
cite: Statement of President Juan Manuel Santos, 14 March 2017; Colombian Attorney General's Odebrecht cases

n: Odebrecht executive says firm paid $35m to Maduro's campaign
d: Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, gave $35 million to Nicolás Maduro's 2013 presidential campaign in return for priority for its projects in Venezuela, according to Euzenando Prazeres de Azevedo, head of Odebrecht in Venezuela. He told Brazilian investigators in late 2017 that campaign manager Américo Mata had first asked for $50 million. Ousted Venezuelan attorney general Luisa Ortega Díaz released video of the testimony in October 2017. Maduro's government rejected the claim and no Venezuelan court has examined it. Transparency International Venezuela found Odebrecht finished 9 of its 33 contracted projects.
cite: Testimony to Brazilian prosecutors, leaked by Luisa Ortega Díaz; Washington Post, 12 October 2017

n: JBS owners accused of paying President Temer for state help
d: Joesley and Wesley Batista, the brothers who control JBS, the world's largest meat company, through J&F Investimentos, are accused of paying Brazil's President Michel Temer for government help. On 26 June 2017 Prosecutor-General Rodrigo Janot charged Temer with accepting bribes, alleging $5 million in return for help with JBS tax problems and a loan. In May 2017 O Globo had published a recording Joesley Batista secretly made of Temer discussing hush money, and police filmed a Temer aide carrying a suitcase of about $150,000 from JBS. The Chamber of Deputies voted in August 2017 not to let the case proceed while he was in office. The Batistas signed plea deals.
cite: Charges filed by Prosecutor-General Rodrigo Janot with the Supreme Federal Court, 26 June 2017

n: Notebooks case — contractors' cash to Kirchner-era officials
rank: President's office and Federal Planning Ministry (2003–2015)
d: Construction, energy and transport businessmen paid cash to officials under Presidents Néstor Kirchner and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, prosecutors in Argentina allege, in return for public works contracts. The evidence began with notebooks kept by a driver for a senior official of the Federal Planning Ministry, which surfaced in 2018 and recorded cash deliveries. Several executives testified as 'repentants', defendants who confess in exchange for leniency. The trial opened on 6 November 2025 with 87 defendants, including Fernández de Kirchner, former ministers and company executives. She denies the charges.
cite: Federal Oral Court, Cuadernos trial opened 6 November 2025; The Star (Reuters/AFP), 6 November 2025

n: Vitol bribed officials at Pemex, Petroecuador and Petrobras
rank: officials of state oil firms Pemex and Petroecuador
d: Vitol, the world's largest independent oil trader, paid bribes to officials at the state oil companies Petrobras (Brazil), Petroecuador (Ecuador) and Pemex (Mexico) to win business. In December 2020 it paid $135 million to US and Brazilian authorities over those bribes. In 2024 a US jury convicted former Vitol trader Javier Aguilar of paying more than $1 million in bribes to officials in Ecuador and Mexico.
cite: US DOJ resolution with Vitol Inc., 3 December 2020; US District Court, Eastern District of New York, Aguilar verdict, 2024

n: Agribusiness-funded institute drafts Brazil farm caucus agenda
d: Agribusiness and pesticide companies write the agenda of the farm caucus in Brazil's Congress, the Frente Parlamentar Agropecuária (FPA), through a think tank they fund, according to a July 2022 report by De Olho nos Ruralistas (Agribusiness Watch). The report found the agenda is drafted by the Instituto Pensar Agro, funded by 48 business associations whose members include Bayer, BASF, Syngenta, Cargill, Bunge, ADM, Louis Dreyfus, JBS, Marfrig, Nestlé and Danone. It also counted 278 meetings between agribusiness companies and Agriculture Ministry officials from January 2019 to June 2022, led by Syngenta (81), JBS (75) and Bayer (60).
cite: De Olho nos Ruralistas, 'Os Operadores da Boiada', July 2022
who: Agribusiness and pesticide companies (via Instituto Pensar Agro)

n: Fat Leonard bribed US Navy officers for ship schedules
rank: US Navy officers and Singapore contracting staff
d: Glenn Defense Marine Asia, a ship-supply contractor run by Leonard Francis ('Fat Leonard'), bribed US Navy officers with cash, travel and gifts in return for ship schedules and inside information, and overbilled the Navy for years while supplying its ships in Asian ports. A civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore quashed an early inquiry. US prosecutors charged 33 people; 22 pleaded guilty, including Francis and 17 Navy officials. Francis fled house arrest in 2022, was caught in Venezuela and was sentenced to 15 years in November 2024.
cite: US District Court, Southern District of California, prosecutions 2013–2024

n: Mafia groups got inside 402 Italian councils since 1991
rank: municipal councils and local health authorities
d: Italy's mafia groups, chiefly Cosa Nostra, the 'Ndrangheta, the Camorra and Puglia clans, have taken enough hold of town councils and health authorities for the national government to dissolve them 402 times. Under Law 164 of 1991, the Council of Ministers can dissolve a council after a prefect's inquiry finds it is conditioned by a mafia group; commissioners then run the town for 18 to 24 months. Il Sole 24 Ore counted 402 decrees between 2 August 1991 and 30 September 2025, covering 288 municipalities and 6 provincial health authorities; 83 bodies were dissolved more than once. Calabria, Campania and Sicily account for 360 decrees and Puglia for 26, but councils have also been dissolved in Lazio, Piedmont, Liguria, Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna and Valle d'Aosta. Courts annulled 24 decrees.
cite: Italian Interior Ministry dissolution decrees under Law 164/1991; Il Sole 24 Ore count, 2 December 2025
who: Cosa Nostra, 'Ndrangheta, Camorra and Puglia clans

n: Bari clans placed hires at city transport firm and bought votes
rank: city-owned transport company and a city councillor
d: Mafia clans in Bari, southern Italy, tried to place their people inside the city-owned transport company AMTAB and, prosecutors allege, paid to get a candidate onto the city council. In 2024 two prosecutions led to about 130 arrests. In one, three Parisi clan members working at AMTAB were charged with mafia association and extortion for pressing a manager to hire five clan-linked people; a court put AMTAB under judicial administration, later lifted after a reorganisation. In the other, Giacomo Olivieri is accused of paying the Parisi, Strisciuglio and Montani clans to get his wife Maria Carmen Lorusso elected in 2019; their trial began in July 2024. After an Interior Ministry inquiry from March 2024, the government decided on 7 February 2025 not to dissolve the council.
cite: Bari prosecutors; Bari court order on AMTAB; Council of Ministers decision of 7 February 2025, reported by Il Post

n: Sicily's President passed investigation secrets to Cosa Nostra
rank: President of the Region of Sicily
d: Salvatore Cuffaro, President of Sicily from 2001 to 2008, passed information about investigations to people linked to Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia. He was convicted of aggravated aiding of Cosa Nostra (article 416-bis of the criminal code), and the sentence of 7 years and a life ban from public office became final in January 2011. He served almost five years in Rebibbia prison and was released in December 2015. Since 2020 he has led a regional party, the Christian Democracy of Sicily.
cite: Italian Court of Cassation, January 2011

n: Senator Dell'Utri acted as go-between for Berlusconi and Cosa Nostra
rank: senator; aide to Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi
d: Marcello Dell'Utri, Silvio Berlusconi's long-time aide and a co-founder of the Forza Italia party, acted as mediator between Berlusconi and Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia, Italy's top court found. Dell'Utri sat in the Chamber of Deputies, the European Parliament and the Senate between 1996 and 2013. On 9 May 2014 the Court of Cassation upheld his conviction for external complicity in mafia association, meaning helping the mafia without being a member, and a 7-year sentence. In 1974 he had brought Vittorio Mangano, already charged with mafia crimes, to work at Berlusconi's villa in Arcore. A separate 12-year sentence in the State-Mafia negotiation trial was overturned on appeal in 2021.
cite: Italian Court of Cassation, 9 May 2014

n: Economy undersecretary Cosentino protected the Casalesi clan
rank: Undersecretary of State, Ministry of Economy and Finance
d: Nicola Cosentino, an Italian deputy and undersecretary at the Ministry of Economy and Finance, protected the interests of the Casalesi clan of the Camorra, the Naples-area mafia, including in the Caserta area's waste business. He was a Forza Italia and People of Freedom deputy from 1996 to 2013 and undersecretary from May 2008 until he resigned in July 2010. On 27 April 2023 the Court of Cassation made final a 10-year sentence for external complicity in mafia association, meaning helping the mafia without being a member.
cite: Italian Court of Cassation, 27 April 2023

n: Mafia Capitale — Carminati and Buzzi bribed Rome officials
rank: Rome city council president and city department heads
d: A network led by Massimo Carminati, a former far-right militant, and Salvatore Buzzi, head of social co-operatives, bribed Rome city officials to win contracts including migrant reception and park maintenance. Rome prosecutors arrested them in December 2014. Among those investigated were the president of Rome's city council and the head of the public-housing department; former mayor Gianni Alemanno was indicted in December 2015 for corruption and illicit financing over €125,000 from Buzzi. The Ostia district council was dissolved for mafia infiltration in 2015. The Court of Cassation ruled in 2019–20 that the network was not a mafia-type association, so convictions stand for corruption and ordinary criminal association.
cite: Rome prosecutors (Giuseppe Pignatone); Court of Cassation ruling on the 'Mondo di mezzo' case

n: Kuciak's last story — 'Ndrangheta-linked man's partner in PM's office
rank: chief state adviser in the Prime Minister's office
d: Mária Trošková, a former business partner of Antonino Vadala, an Italian businessman named in investigations into the 'Ndrangheta (the Calabrian mafia), had become an assistant to Slovakia's Prime Minister Robert Fico. Journalist Ján Kuciak was working on this when he and his fiancée Martina Kušnírová were shot dead in February 2018. His unfinished article, published by OCCRP partners on 28 February 2018, described Vadala's farm companies in eastern Slovakia. Trošková and Security Council secretary Viliam Jasaň stepped aside in March 2018, and Fico resigned that month after mass protests. No court has found that the Prime Minister's office acted for the 'Ndrangheta.
cite: OCCRP / Aktuality.sk, 'The Model, the Mafia, and the Murderers', 28 February 2018

n: Mafias secretly owned Malta-licensed online betting firms
rank: online gaming companies licensed by the Malta Gaming Authority
d: Italian mafia groups secretly owned or ran online betting companies licensed in Malta, using them to collect bets and launder money, Italian investigations from 2015 onward found. Francesco Martiradonna, said to be the hidden owner of Malta-licensed Centurionbet, was arrested in 2017 on mafia-association charges. In January 2018 Palermo's Operation 'Game Over' issued 26 arrest warrants over a Cosa Nostra-linked betting network, and the Malta Gaming Authority suspended licences including that of LB Group (Leaderbet). Some executives were later cleared: in a decade-long Calabrian case, Maltese-linked Betsolution executives were acquitted of mafia ties.
cite: OCCRP Daphne Project, 'How Maltese Online Gambling Became an ATM for the Italian Mafia', 10 May 2018; Malta Gaming Authority licence suspensions

n: Montenegro's top judge shielded her son's smuggling network
rank: President of the Supreme Court of Montenegro
d: Vesna Medenica, president of Montenegro's Supreme Court until 2020, used her position to protect a cigarette and narcotics smuggling network led by her son Miloš, the High Court in Podgorica found. On 28 January 2026 it sentenced her to 10 years for four counts of abuse of influence; Miloš received 10 years and 2 months. She was acquitted of creating a criminal organisation. The evidence included decrypted messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service used by criminals. Miloš Medenica fled while under house arrest, and prosecutors are appealing for longer sentences.
cite: High Court in Podgorica, verdict of 28 January 2026 (Special State Prosecutor's Office case)

n: Marty report: KLA-era 'Drenica Group' led by Kosovo's PM
d: A Council of Europe report said a criminal group of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commanders, the 'Drenica Group', was led by Kosovo's own Prime Minister, Hashim Thaçi. In December 2010 Swiss senator Dick Marty told the Council's Parliamentary Assembly that the group controlled criminal trades including heroin, and he found 'credible, convergent indications' of organ trafficking from captives after the 1999 war. The Assembly endorsed the report on 25 January 2011; Thaçi denied it. An EU task force later reported compelling indications of war crimes, which led to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, where Thaçi has been on trial for war crimes since 2023. The organised-crime claims have not been tested in court.
cite: Council of Europe PACE report by Dick Marty, December 2010, adopted 25 January 2011

n: 'The Notary' allegedly used compromising files to pressure judges
d: Martin Bozhanov, known as 'the Notary', is alleged to have collected compromising material on Bulgarian judges and prosecutors and used it to pressure them, giving him a hidden hold over decisions in the justice system. Bulgarian National Radio reported that he threatened prosecutors as well as judges, and former Prosecutor General Ivan Geshev was questioned in the case. The claims are under investigation and have not been tested in court.
cite: Bulgarian National Radio; BTA news agency reporting on the 'Notary' case

n: Plahotniuc — oligarch who controlled Moldova jailed for bank theft
rank: Democratic Party leader and first vice-president of Parliament
d: Vlad Plahotniuc, a businessman who led the Democratic Party and was widely described as controlling Moldova's government and parliamentary majority, was sentenced on 22 April 2026 to 19 years over the 2014 theft of about $1 billion, equal to 12% of Moldova's GDP, from three banks. The money was drained through loans that were paid off with new loans and moved through UK and Hong Kong shell companies. Plahotniuc fled in 2019, was arrested in Greece in July 2025 and extradited on 25 September 2025. During parliamentary hearings, the deputy head of the security service said President Nicolae Timofti had known of the theft since 2013.
cite: Chișinău court, sentence of 22 April 2026; Moldovan parliamentary hearings on the bank fraud
who: Plahotniuc network and the 'theft of the billion' group

n: Global Laundromat — Moldovan judges approved fake Russian debts
d: A Russian money-laundering network used Moldovan judges to move money out of Russia. Between 2010 and 2014 an estimated $20–80 billion left Russia this way: Russian companies 'guaranteed' fake debts, and Moldovan judges then ordered the debts paid into Moldindconbank, from where the money moved on through Latvian banks. The scheme was exposed by OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, and the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta; The Guardian reported about 500 people suspected. Moldovan prosecutors later charged judges who had validated the debts.
cite: OCCRP and Novaya Gazeta 'Global Laundromat' investigation (2014, 2017); Moldovan prosecutors

n: Kushchyovskaya — Tsapok gang ran for years under local protection
d: Sergei Tsapok's gang operated for years in the Krasnodar Krai village of Kushchyovskaya with protection from local authorities and police, Russian investigators found. This came out after 4 November 2010, when gang members murdered 12 people there, including four children. Tsapok was convicted and died in prison in 2014.
cite: Russian Investigative Committee and Krasnodar court

n: Swedish crime networks got inside agencies and welfare firms
d: Criminal networks in Sweden have got inside government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector and exploit social insurance, according to a research review by Carina Gunnarson of Uppsala University and the Swedish Defence Research Agency, published by the SNS think tank in November 2023. Incorrect welfare payments are estimated at SEK 13–16.3 billion a year. The review says municipalities are especially exposed because much public money is spent locally with weaker oversight. It cites Södertälje, where police saw warning signs in the late 1990s but decisive action came only after a double murder in 2010.
cite: SNS (Studieförbundet Näringsliv och Samhälle), 'The Vulnerable State', November 2023

n: Yakuza brokers placed workers in Fukushima's state-funded clean-up
rank: subcontractors on Environment Ministry decontamination contracts
d: Yakuza gangs, Japan's organised crime groups, placed workers inside the subcontracting chains of Japan's taxpayer-funded radiation clean-up after the 2011 nuclear disaster and took part of their pay. The programme, worth about $35 billion, is run through layers of subcontractors. Police arrested yakuza members at least three times in 2012 for illegally placing workers in subcontracting chains under the construction company Obayashi. In 2013 Yamagata police arrested a Sumiyoshi-kai member for sending men to decontamination work and taking about a third of their pay. A Reuters investigation in 2013 found gang-linked recruiters supplying homeless men from Sendai station.
cite: Japanese police arrests (Fukushima, Yamagata); Reuters special reports, October and December 2013

n: Bai crime family's head ran Myanmar's Kokang zone and sat as MP
rank: first head of the Kokang Self-Administered Zone; Shan State MP
d: Bai Suocheng, head of a family that ran scam and gambling centres in Laukkai, led the government of Myanmar's Kokang Self-Administered Zone as its first chief and sat as a Shan State MP for the army-backed USDP party. He was a former deputy commander of the Kokang armed group. Myanmar handed him to China in 2024. In November 2025 the Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court sentenced him, his son Bai Yingcang and three associates to death for telecom fraud and gambling run under armed guard, linked to the deaths of six Chinese citizens. Bai Suocheng died in custody; four Bai group members were executed on 2 February 2026, days after 11 members of the Ming family were executed.
cite: Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court (November 2025); Guangdong High Court (24 December 2025); Caixin and SCMP

n: Scam-city builders partnered with Myanmar army's Karen border force
rank: commander, Karen Border Guard Force under the Myanmar army
d: Chinese-run crime groups built scam centres in Myanmar in partnership with Colonel Saw Chit Thu, leader of the Karen Border Guard Force, a militia placed under the Myanmar army. In 2017 he partnered with She Zhijiang's Yatai group to build Shwe Kokko and also dealt with Wan Kuok-koi's Dongmei Group over Saixigang; Wan, a former leader of the 14K triad, was sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2020. Saw Chit Thu received the junta's Thiri Pyanchi honour in November 2022. The UK sanctioned him in December 2023 and the US later did the same, for links to forced labour in scam centres. She Zhijiang was extradited from Thailand to China on 10 November 2025.
cite: UK sanctions designation (December 2023); US Treasury designations; reporting collected by Wikipedia
who: Yatai (She Zhijiang) and Dongmei (Wan Kuok-koi) groups

n: Gangster Mukhtar Ansari held a UP assembly seat five times
rank: Member of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly (Mau)
d: Mukhtar Ansari, a gang leader, won the Mau seat in the Uttar Pradesh state assembly five times between 1996 and 2022, twice for the Bahujan Samaj Party, much of that time from prison, where he was held from 2005. He faced 65 criminal cases and had been convicted in eight, including a murder case in 2023 and a life sentence in March 2024 in a fake arms licence case. He died in custody on 28 March 2024. His son Abbas Ansari won the seat in 2022.
cite: Uttar Pradesh courts; The Indian Express, 29 March 2024

n: Iraq tax heist network had PM's office director and MP inside
rank: General Commission for Taxes and the Prime Minister's office
d: A network around businessman Nour Zuhair Jassim drew on officials inside Iraq's state, including the director of the Prime Minister's office, to take about $2.5 billion from a General Commission for Taxes account in 2021–22. The money left through 247 cheques paid to five front companies posing as oil firms owed tax refunds. In late 2024 a Baghdad court sentenced 10 people: Nour Zuhair in absentia to 10 years, former MP and finance-committee head Haitham al-Jubouri, Raed Juhi, former director of Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi's office, and a tax-commission director general and his deputy. Several former senior tax and Rafidain Bank officials have not been charged.
cite: Baghdad criminal court verdicts, November–December 2024, reported by The National

n: UN panel finds gang member on Haitian council and police aiding gangs
rank: former legislators, a municipal commissioner and police officers
d: Haiti's armed gangs have people inside the state: a 94-page report by the UN Security Council's panel of experts on Haiti, released in October 2026 and covering October 2025 to July 2026, says at least one member of a new Cité Soleil municipal commission is an active gang member and that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information. It accuses former Kenscoff legislator Alfredo Junior Antoine of arming groups and sponsoring a 2025 attack that killed more than 100 people, and former senator Nenel Cassy of controlling a criminal group in Miragoâne. It says the 'historic use of gangs' by former senator Youri Latortue and ex-lawmaker Prophane Victor fuels violence in the Artibonite ahead of elections. Antoine and Cassy deny the allegations.
cite: UN Security Council Panel of Experts on Haiti, report of October 2026, reported by AP
who: Viv Ansanm and other Haitian gangs

n: PCC crime group's money ran two São Paulo city bus firms
d: The PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), Brazil's largest criminal organisation, had its money in two São Paulo bus companies that held city contracts, state prosecutors allege. In April 2024 Operation Fim da Linha alleged that Transwolff (132 lines, about 583,000 passengers a day) and UPBus (158 buses) laundered PCC money from drug trafficking and robberies; the firms had received more than R$800 million in public funds the year before. The city took over both companies on 9 April 2024, the UPBus president was arrested in December 2024, and the city moved to end both concession contracts in December 2024–January 2025.
cite: São Paulo Public Prosecutor's Office (MPSP), Operation Fim da Linha; São Paulo city government decisions, reported by CNN Brasil

n: Rizzuto Mafia took a cut of Montreal public works contracts
d: The Rizzuto family, Montreal's Mafia, took a share of the city's public construction contracts through firms that also paid political parties, witnesses told Quebec's Charbonneau Commission. The commission (2011–2015) was a public inquiry into collusion and corruption in public construction contracts and organised-crime infiltration of the industry. During the inquiry Montreal mayor Gérald Tremblay resigned, and interim mayor Michael Applebaum and Laval mayor Gilles Vaillancourt were later convicted or pleaded guilty in related corruption cases. The commission reported on 24 November 2015.
cite: Commission of Inquiry on the Awarding and Management of Public Contracts in the Construction Industry (Charbonneau Commission), final report, November 2015
who: Rizzuto Mafia family and construction cartels

n: Mafia families controlled hiring on the New York docks
d: Mafia families controlled much of the hiring of dock workers at the port of New York and New Jersey, a state crime commission found before 1953. That year the two states created the Waterfront Commission of New York Harbor to fight criminal influence over that hiring, and it licensed and screened dock workers for 70 years. New Jersey moved to leave the agreement between the states in 2018, and after the US Supreme Court allowed it in 2023 the commission was dissolved on 17 July 2023. New Jersey State Police took over its role at New Jersey ports, and New York set up a new waterfront commission.
cite: Waterfront Commission Compact (1953); US Supreme Court, New York v. New Jersey (2023)
who: American Mafia families on the docks

n: Bikie gang members held roles in CFMEU construction union
d: Members of outlaw motorcycle gangs (bikies) and underworld figures held roles in the construction division of the CFMEU union on Victorian government building projects, media reports said in 2024. In August 2024 the federal government placed the division into administration under Mark Irving KC. An interim report by Geoffrey Watson SC in September 2024 found efforts to remove bikies inadequate and recommended further investigation of delegates' links to motorcycle gangs. In 2026 a further report's claims that Victorian ministers ignored warnings were referred to police, and Queensland held a commission of inquiry into the union.
cite: Federal administration of the CFMEU construction division (August 2024); Geoffrey Watson SC interim report (September 2024); Queensland Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU (2026)

n: South African police minister accused of colluding with syndicate
rank: Minister of Police and national police leadership
d: A criminal syndicate had senior South African police officials working with it, including Police Minister Senzo Mchunu, KwaZulu-Natal police commissioner Lt Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged on 6 July 2025. Mchunu was placed on leave and President Ramaphosa set up the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry. A R228 million police health-services contract had gone to businessman Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala's company in 2024; he faces corruption, fraud and money-laundering charges. By July 2026, 13 police officers faced criminal charges, including National Commissioner Fannie Masemola on a public-finance charge, and 15 faced discipline. Mchunu denies wrongdoing.
cite: Madlanga Commission of Inquiry; National Prosecuting Authority charges, reported by Daily Maverick, 5 July 2026

n: 'Construction mafia' bribes and threatens South African councillors
d: Extortion groups calling themselves 'business forums' try to capture ward councillors, the local elected officials, by bribery or threats, sometimes by joining local party branches, the Institute for Security Studies reported in October 2021. The forums demand a cut, often 30%, of public construction projects and shut down sites that refuse. The civil engineering contractors' body SAFCEC estimated that by March 2019 at least R25.5 billion of projects had been disrupted or halted. The ISS said three Tshwane councillors had been killed in under four years in killings linked to such syndicates. The National Prosecuting Authority agreed to prosecute violent extortion under the Prevention of Organised Crime Act.
cite: Institute for Security Studies, ISS Today, 25 October 2021; SAFCEC estimates

n: Black Axe-linked group paid to 'protect votes', given 80 state posts
rank: state government posts and election campaigns
d: The Neo Black Movement of Africa (NBM), which the BBC linked to the Black Axe confraternity, was given 80 government roles after it was paid to 'protect votes' in Nigeria's 2012 Edo governorship election, according to leaked documents in a BBC Africa Eye investigation of December 2021. The documents suggested 35 million naira went to the NBM. Black Axe is a Nigerian confraternity, a secretive student-born brotherhood, that police in several countries treat as an organised crime group. Former members told the BBC that members hold posts in state assemblies and executives and are hired by politicians for election violence. The NBM denies any link to Black Axe.
cite: BBC Africa Eye, 'Black Axe' investigation, December 2021

n: Fishrot — Samherji paid Namibian ministers' circle for quotas
rank: Minister of Fisheries and Minister of Justice
d: Samherji, an Icelandic fishing company, paid people close to Namibia's government to obtain quotas to catch horse mackerel, leaked files showed in November 2019. The files were published by WikiLeaks and investigated by Icelandic, Al Jazeera and Namibian journalists. Fisheries Minister Bernhardt Esau and Justice Minister Sacky Shanghala resigned and were arrested that month. They and other defendants are charged in Namibia with racketeering (running a criminal enterprise), corruption and money laundering under the Prevention of Organised Crime Act. Iceland also opened an investigation into Samherji.
cite: Namibian Anti-Corruption Commission and Prosecutor-General charges; Icelandic District Prosecutor investigation; Fishrot Files (WikiLeaks, November 2019)

n: 'Ndrangheta ties lead Italy to dissolve Reggio Calabria council
rank: mayor and city council of a provincial capital
d: 'Ndrangheta clans, the Calabrian mafia, had ties to councillors in Reggio Calabria, leading the Italian government on 9 October 2012 to dissolve the city council for mafia infiltration. Some councillors were suspected of links to clans during the centre-right administration of Giuseppe Scopelliti, mayor from 2002 to 2010. Mayor Demetrio Arena and all 30 councillors were removed and three commissioners ran the city. It was the first time the government of an Italian provincial capital had been dismissed over organised-crime links.
cite: Italian Council of Ministers dissolution decree, 9 October 2012 (Law 164/1991)

n: Chongqing gangs paid the city's deputy police chief for protection
rank: executive deputy head of the Public Security Bureau; head of the Judicial Bureau
d: Criminal gangs in Chongqing, a city of over 30 million in south-west China, paid bribes to Wen Qiang, who was executive deputy head of the city's Public Security Bureau (its police force) for 16 years and then head of its Judicial Bureau, to protect them. His case came out during a campaign against organised crime run from October 2009 to 2011 by the city's party chief Bo Xilai and police chief Wang Lijun, which arrested 4,781 suspects, including 19 alleged crime bosses, hundreds of triad members, six district police chiefs and other officials. Wen Qiang was convicted of taking bribes and protecting criminal gangs and was executed on 7 July 2010. Lawyers and scholars raised concerns about forced confessions and due process in the campaign's trials, and Bo Xilai was himself jailed for life in 2013.
cite: Chongqing courts (2010); reporting collected by Wikipedia

n: Georges Pompidou: Rothschild general manager to French prime minister
d: Georges Pompidou went from running Banque Rothschild, the French bank of the Rothschild banking family, to heading France's government. A literature teacher, he was hired in 1953 by Guy de Rothschild and was the bank's general manager from 1956 to 1962; Charles de Gaulle also hired him to run the Anne de Gaulle Foundation. De Gaulle made him Prime Minister in 1962, and he was elected President in 1969 and died in office in 1974. His move from the bank to the head of government is the best-known French case of a banker going straight to the top office. No court or inquiry has found that the bank directed his policies.
cite: Wikipedia 'Georges Pompidou'

n: Emmanuel Macron: Rothschild partner to Economy Minister and President
rank: Élysée deputy secretary-general; Economy Minister; President
d: Emmanuel Macron moved from the investment bank Rothschild & Cie Banque into the French posts that set economic and banking policy. He left the General Inspectorate of Finance, the state's financial audit body, in September 2008 for Rothschild, became a partner in 2010 and led Nestlé's €9 billion purchase of Pfizer's infant-nutrition unit; he reported earning about €2 million between December 2010 and May 2012. On 15 May 2012 he became deputy secretary-general of the Élysée (the president's office) under François Hollande, then Economy Minister (2014–16), and has been President since May 2017. Rival Benoît Hamon accused him of conflicts of interest from his Rothschild years, which Macron called 'demagogy'. No court or inquiry has found that the bank directs his policies.
cite: Le Monde, 16 May 2012 ('un banquier d'affaires nommé secrétaire général adjoint de l'Elysée'); Wikipedia 'Emmanuel Macron'

n: François Pérol: Rothschild banker oversaw a bank merger, then ran it
rank: Élysée deputy secretary-general; CEO of Groupe BPCE
d: François Pérol, a French Treasury official, moved from the bank Rothschild & Cie into the president's office, where he followed a bank merger he had advised on, and then took charge of the merged bank. As a Rothschild managing partner from 2005 to 2007 he advised Banque Populaire on creating Natixis. As deputy secretary-general of the Élysée under Nicolas Sarkozy he followed the 2008–09 merger of Banque Populaire and the Caisses d'Epargne, and in February 2009 he became head of the merged group, BPCE. He was prosecuted for illegal taking of interest (prise illégale d'intérêts), the offence of an official taking a stake in a business he supervised. The Paris criminal court acquitted him on 24 September 2015 and the Paris Court of Appeal confirmed the acquittal on 30 June 2017.
cite: Tribunal correctionnel de Paris, 24 Sept 2015; Cour d'appel de Paris, 30 June 2017 (Acteurs publics)

n: Pujo Committee: Morgan-linked men held 341 company directorships
d: Bankers linked to J. P. Morgan & Co. sat on the boards of 112 corporations at once, giving the bank's group a say inside companies it lent to. A 'directorship' is a seat on a company's board, which oversees its management. A House Banking subcommittee led by Arsène Pujo, with counsel Samuel Untermyer, investigated this 'money trust' in 1912–13 and questioned J. P. Morgan himself. Its 1913 report found that 180 individuals linked to the group held 341 directorships in those 112 corporations, which had $22.2 billion in resources, and that the 20 largest banks held 42.9% of US banking resources. It named bankers including Paul and Felix Warburg, Jacob Schiff, William Rockefeller and Benjamin Strong. Its findings fed the Federal Reserve Act and the 1914 Clayton Antitrust Act, whose limits on interlocking directorates (the same people sitting on rival boards) are still law.
cite: House Committee on Banking and Currency, Pujo Committee report (1913); Wikipedia 'Pujo Committee'
who: J. P. Morgan & Co. and allied banks

n: Bankers secretly drafted the Federal Reserve plan at Jekyll Island
d: Senior Wall Street bankers wrote the draft of the law that would set up a US central bank, in a meeting kept secret for two decades. In November 1910 Senator Nelson Aldrich, chairman of the National Monetary Commission, took Assistant Treasury Secretary A. Piatt Andrew, Henry Davison of J.P. Morgan & Co., Frank Vanderlip of National City Bank, Paul Warburg of Kuhn, Loeb & Co. and his secretary Arthur Shelton to the Jekyll Island Club in Georgia; other accounts also place Benjamin Strong of Bankers Trust there. Their plan was published in January 1911 as the Aldrich Plan, without saying where it came from, and participants did not admit the meeting until the 1930s. Congress never voted on the Aldrich Plan, but the Federal Reserve's own history says the plan written on Jekyll Island 'laid a foundation for what would eventually be the Federal Reserve System', created in 1913.
cite: Gary Richardson & Jessie Romero, 'The Meeting at Jekyll Island', Federal Reserve History (Federal Reserve Board); Wikipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.'
who: Morgan, National City and Kuhn, Loeb bankers

n: Paul Warburg: Kuhn, Loeb partner on the first Federal Reserve Board
rank: Member (1914–18) and vice chairman (1916–18), Federal Reserve Board
d: Paul Warburg, a partner of the New York investment bank Kuhn, Loeb & Co., helped design the US central bank and then sat on the board that runs it. German-born, from the Hamburg Warburg banking family, he was the leading public advocate of a US central bank, advised Senator Aldrich's National Monetary Commission and attended the secret 1910 Jekyll Island meeting that drafted the plan. President Woodrow Wilson appointed him to the first Federal Reserve Board in August 1914, and he was its vice chairman from 1916 to 1918, resigning his Wells Fargo directorship on appointment. He later presided over the Fed's Federal Advisory Council (1924–26) and sat on the founding board of the Council on Foreign Relations from 1921.
cite: Wikipedia 'Paul Warburg'

arch.t: Council on Foreign Relations — Submergence of US Sovereignty (Insider Testimony)

n: Thomas Lamont: Morgan partner on the US reparations team at Versailles
rank: US Treasury representative, Paris Peace Conference
d: Thomas W. Lamont, a partner of J.P. Morgan & Co., the bank that had been Britain's and France's main lender in the US during the First World War, was appointed with Norman Davis to represent the US Treasury at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, working on how much Germany should pay in reparations. Lamont later sat on the committees that drew up the Dawes Plan (1924) and Young Plan (1929), which reset those payments. Historian Carroll Quigley writes that Lamont gave £2,000 to fund the history of the Peace Conference commissioned in 1919 by the Hotel Majestic meeting of British and US experts, the project from which Chatham House grew, and lists him in the loose American Round Table group.
cite: Wikipedia 'Thomas W. Lamont'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, p. 183; Tragedy and Hope, p. 950

n: Quigley: Milner Group held half of Britain's Dawes Plan delegation
d: Historian Carroll Quigley writes that the Milner Group, a British network of officials and financiers also known through its Round Table journal, had 'half of the British delegation' on the 1924 Dawes committee, the panel of ten experts that reset Germany's war reparations. Britain's two experts were Sir Josiah Stamp and Sir Robert Kindersley, chairman of Lazard Brothers, who was the senior colleague at Lazard of Round Table leader Robert Brand. Quigley also writes that 'the chief influence was that of J. P. Morgan and Company'. The plan set a rising reparations schedule, put Germany's central bank, the Reichsbank, under a board of seven creditor-state and seven German members independent of the German government, and gave Germany an 800-million-mark loan, about half raised through Wall Street bond issues. German right-wing parties attacked its limits on German sovereignty. The attribution to the Milner Group is Quigley's.
cite: Wikipedia 'Dawes Plan'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 241–242

n: Quigley: Morgan bank's men held top US offices
rank: Secretary of State, Treasury and diplomatic posts held by Morgan associates
d: Men from the J.P. Morgan bank's circle held top US public offices, historian Carroll Quigley argued in Tragedy and Hope (1966), describing a 'system of influence which centered on the J. P. Morgan office at 23 Wall Street' and names men in it including Walter Burns, Clinton Dawkins, Edward Grenfell, Willard Straight, Thomas Lamont, Dwight Morrow, Nelson Perkins, Russell Leffingwell, Elihu Root, John W. Davis, John Foster Dulles and S. Parker Gilbert. Root was Secretary of War and of State, Davis Solicitor General and ambassador to London, Leffingwell Assistant Treasury Secretary, Gilbert Agent General for Reparations in Berlin, and Dulles Secretary of State. He says banking families such as Baring, Lazard, Warburg, Rothschild and Morgan were devoted to 'the secret use of financial influence in political life'; the description is his.
cite: Quigley, Tragedy and Hope (Macmillan, 1966), pp. 51–53

n: Quigley: Lazard's Robert Brand placed bank men in wartime Washington posts
rank: First Secretary and Counsellor, British Embassy; Combined Production and Resources Board
d: Historian Carroll Quigley writes that Robert Brand, a managing director of the London bank Lazard Brothers and a leader of the Round Table network (a group of British officials and financiers), moved men from the bank into Britain's wartime posts in Washington. Adam D. Marris, son of Sir William Marris of the network's founding circle, got his Lazard job through Brand in 1929, joined the British Embassy in Washington in 1940 as First Secretary and later Counsellor (to 1945), then ran the Emergency Economic Committee for Europe and returned to Lazard in February 1946, later succeeding Brand as managing director. Brand, still at Lazard until May 1944, put his nephew Thomas Henry Brand in his place at the bank and then brought him to Washington as chief executive on the British side of the Combined Production and Resources Board. Quigley says the network was 'monopolizing' the wartime embassy.
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 60, 80–81, 304; Tragedy and Hope, pp. 950–951

n: Max Warburg: Hamburg banker on the Reichsbank council and at Versailles
rank: German peace delegation expert; Reichsbank council
d: Max Warburg, head of the Hamburg bank M. M. Warburg & Co. from 1910 to 1938, moved between his bank and German state posts, including the governing council of the Reichsbank, Germany's central bank. He advised Kaiser Wilhelm II before the First World War. On 12 March 1919 Foreign Minister Count Brockdorff-Rantzau named him one of six chief delegates for the Versailles peace talks; he declined and served as an expert, and on his recommendation his partner Carl Melchior became principal delegate for economic and financial questions. He sat on the Reichsbank's general council from 1924 and on the supervisory board of IG Farben (1925–31). After the Nazis took power he had to leave the council because he was Jewish; the bank was 'Aryanised' in 1938 and he emigrated to the United States.
cite: German Wikipedia 'Max Warburg'; Wikipedia 'Max Warburg', 'M. M. Warburg & Co.'

n: Felix Rohatyn: Lazard partner ran New York City's rescue finances
d: Felix Rohatyn, a partner of the investment bank Lazard Frères, was put in charge of New York City's finances when the city ran out of money in April 1975. Governor Hugh Carey advanced state funds on condition that the city hand management of its finances to the state, and appointed Rohatyn to a panel that proposed the Municipal Assistance Corporation (MAC), a state body that borrowed on the city's behalf. As MAC chairman and chief negotiator with unions and creditors, Rohatyn insisted on a wage freeze, mass layoffs, a subway fare rise and tuition at the City University. A state law turned city sales and stock-transfer taxes into state taxes to secure MAC bonds, and an Emergency Financial Control Board oversaw the city budget. MAC sold almost $10 billion of bonds before winding up in 2008. Rohatyn was later US ambassador to France (1997–2000).
cite: Wikipedia 'Felix Rohatyn', 'Municipal Assistance Corporation'

n: Evelyn Baring ran Egypt's finances for its European creditors
d: Evelyn Baring, of the Barings banking family, became the British official controlling Egypt's finances while Barings Bank held a significant stake in Egyptian debt. After the Khedive Ismail, Egypt's ruler, went bankrupt in 1876, Britain and France imposed 'Dual Control', putting their own controllers over Egypt's finances; no conflict of interest was raised at the time. Baring pressed for Ismail's removal, which the powers obtained in 1879. After Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 he returned as agent and consul-general (1883–1907), the effective ruler of Egypt, and kept its revenues committed to paying its European creditors.
cite: Wikipedia 'Evelyn Baring, 1st Earl of Cromer'

n: Wallenberg bank hid German Bosch's ownership of American Bosch
d: Stockholms Enskilda Bank, the Wallenberg family's bank in neutral Sweden, held German-owned companies on paper so that the German firm Bosch kept control of them during the Second World War. In 1939–41 the bank bought Bosch subsidiaries, including the American Bosch Corporation, on condition that Bosch could buy them back after the war. The US government treated this as 'cloaking' enemy property (hiding the real owner behind a front), seized American Bosch in 1943 and in 1945 blacklisted the bank until 1947. At the same time the Swedish government used the bank's heads for its trade talks: Jacob Wallenberg dealt with Germany, and Marcus Wallenberg Jr. chaired the Swedish side of the Swedish–British commission (1939–43). Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau Jr. regarded Jacob Wallenberg as strongly pro-German.
cite: Wikipedia 'Stockholms Enskilda Bank', 'Marcus Wallenberg (1899–1982)', 'Wallenberg family' (citing G. Aalders, The Art of Cloaking Ownership, 1996)

n: Robert Rubin: Goldman co-chair to Treasury, then Citigroup
rank: National Economic Council director; Treasury Secretary
d: Robert Rubin moved from Goldman Sachs into the US posts that set financial policy, and then to Citigroup, a bank whose merger needed a change in the law he had argued for. After 26 years at Goldman, ending as co-chairman (1990–92), he ran Bill Clinton's National Economic Council (1993–95) and was Treasury Secretary (1995–99). He called the Glass–Steagall separation of commercial and investment banking obsolete; its repeal in 1999, pushed by Sanford Weill to legalise the Travelers–Citicorp merger, came at the end of his term. Rubin joined Citigroup in 1999 as chairman of its executive committee and was paid $126 million there to 2009. In 2001 he phoned a Treasury official seeking help for Citigroup client Enron, which a Senate staff inquiry found not illegal. Citigroup needed a federal rescue in 2008.
cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Rubin'

n: Henry Paulson: Goldman CEO to Treasury; AIG rescue paid Goldman $12.9bn
d: Henry Paulson went from chairman and chief executive of Goldman Sachs to US Treasury Secretary in July 2006, and in that post ran a rescue whose largest beneficiary was Goldman. On joining he sold about $600 million of Goldman stock under ethics rules, with capital-gains tax deferred. In September 2008 he and the Federal Reserve rescued the insurer AIG, whose trading partners were then paid in full; Goldman was the largest recipient of the public funds that passed through AIG, about $12.9 billion. The Special Inspector General for TARP, the rescue programme's watchdog, reviewed these payments in November 2009. The New York Times reported in August 2009 that Paulson spoke with Goldman chief Lloyd Blankfein some 24 times in the week of the AIG rescue, two of the calls before he obtained an ethics waiver.
cite: SIGTARP report on AIG counterparty payments (Nov 2009); NYT, Morgenson & Van Natta, 9 Aug 2009; Wikipedia 'Henry Paulson'

n: Gary Cohn: Goldman president to White House economic chief
d: Gary Cohn moved from the top of Goldman Sachs to run economic policy in the White House. He joined Goldman in 1990, ran its fixed income, currency and commodities division and was president and co-chief operating officer from 2006. On 20 January 2017 he became director of President Donald Trump's National Economic Council, which coordinates economic policy and does not require Senate confirmation. In that post he led the administration's work on the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, which cut the corporate tax rate. He left in 2018.
cite: Wikipedia 'Gary Cohn'

n: Mario Draghi: Goldman vice chairman to Bank of Italy, ECB and premier
rank: Governor, Bank of Italy; President, ECB; Prime Minister
d: Mario Draghi moved between Italy's Treasury, Goldman Sachs and the posts that regulate Europe's banks. As director-general of the Italian Treasury (1991–2001) he drafted the law still governing Italian financial markets and led the 1990s privatisations of state companies. He was then vice chairman and managing director of Goldman Sachs International (2002–05), leading its European business with governments and large companies. He became Governor of the Bank of Italy (2006), President of the European Central Bank (2011–19), which sets monetary policy for the euro and from 2014 supervised the euro area's largest banks, and Prime Minister of Italy (2021–22). Goldman's 2001 Greek currency swaps (separate record) were arranged before he joined the firm.
cite: Wikipedia 'Mario Draghi'

n: Mario Monti: Goldman adviser named senator for life and premier
d: Mario Monti, a former EU commissioner who had been an international adviser to Goldman Sachs and Coca-Cola, was appointed to head Italy's government without an election. He became president of the Trilateral Commission, a private forum of business and political leaders, in 2010 and was a leading member of the Bilderberg group, an annual private conference of the same kind. On 9 November 2011 President Giorgio Napolitano appointed him a senator for life and on 12 November, after Silvio Berlusconi resigned in the debt crisis, asked him to form a government. His unelected cabinet of technocrats (experts rather than party politicians) ran Italy until 2013 and passed austerity and pension measures.
cite: Wikipedia 'Mario Monti'

arch.t: Trilateral Commission — 19/20 Carter Senior Appointments Were Members

n: Mark Carney: Goldman banker to two central banks and Canada's premiership
rank: Governor, Bank of Canada and Bank of England; Prime Minister
d: Mark Carney moved from Goldman Sachs into the posts that regulate banks in Canada, Britain and worldwide, and then to head Canada's government. After 13 years at Goldman he joined the Bank of Canada as a deputy governor in 2003. He was Governor of the Bank of Canada (2008–13), Governor of the Bank of England (2013–20) and chair of the Financial Stability Board (2011–18), the international body that coordinates rules for banks and markets among the G20 economies. In March 2025 he became leader of the Liberal Party and Prime Minister of Canada, and won a seat in Parliament (Nepean) in April 2025.
cite: Wikipedia 'Mark Carney'

n: Jörg Kukies: Goldman Germany co-head to finance ministry and chancellery
rank: State Secretary for Finance; Chancellery State Secretary; Finance Minister
d: Jörg Kukies moved from Goldman Sachs into the German government post that oversees financial markets, and later became Finance Minister. He spent 17 years at Goldman, rising to co-head for Germany and Austria. Finance Minister Olaf Scholz made him state secretary for financial markets, the senior civil-service post in charge of banking and market policy, in 2018. From 2021 to 2024 he was state secretary in the Chancellery and Scholz's sherpa (personal negotiator) for G7 and G20 summits, and he was Finance Minister from November 2024 to May 2025.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jörg Kukies'

n: Ex-Goldman economist ran the New York Fed that supervised Goldman
rank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York supervision of Goldman
d: William Dudley, Goldman Sachs's chief US economist until 2007, was president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the regulator that supervises Goldman, from 2009 to 2018. Carmen Segarra, a New York Fed examiner placed at Goldman from October 2011, said she found Goldman had no firm-wide conflict-of-interest policy, was pressed by superiors to change her findings and was fired after seven months. In September 2014 she released recordings, broadcast by ProPublica and This American Life, of supervisors deferring to Goldman over a Santander deal they called 'legal but shady'. Her whistleblower suit was dismissed on legal grounds.
cite: Wikipedia 'Carmen Segarra', 'William C. Dudley'; ProPublica / This American Life, Sept 2014

n: BlackRock runs the Fed's 2020 bond-buying; its executive joins White House
rank: Federal Reserve emergency facilities; National Economic Council
d: BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, was hired by the US government to run public rescue programmes, and one of its executives moved into the White House post that coordinates economic policy. The Treasury retained BlackRock in 2009 for crisis work. In March 2020 the Federal Reserve chose it to manage its corporate bond-buying programmes, the $500 billion Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility and the Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility, plus purchases of commercial mortgage securities. In 2021 Brian Deese, BlackRock's former global head of sustainable investing, became director of President Biden's National Economic Council.
cite: Wikipedia 'BlackRock' (citing Pensions & Investments, 25 Mar 2020; Washington Post; CNBC, 20 Mar 2021)

n: Friedrich Merz: BlackRock Germany chairman to Chancellor
d: Friedrich Merz moved from chairing the German arm of BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, back into politics and became head of Germany's government. He left the Bundestag (Germany's parliament) in 2009 after losing a power struggle with Angela Merkel and worked as a corporate lawyer at Mayer Brown. From 2016 to 2020 he chaired the supervisory board of BlackRock's German arm, a hire the Wall Street Journal headlined 'BlackRock Hires Former Merkel Deputy'. He returned to parliament in 2021, became leader of the CDU party and was elected Chancellor in May 2025.
cite: Wikipedia 'Friedrich Merz' (citing Wall Street Journal, 17 Jan 2016)

n: JPMorgan hired Chinese officials' relatives to win business
rank: Chinese government officials and state-owned company executives
d: JPMorgan Chase, the US bank, hired around 100 relatives and friends of Chinese government officials and state-company executives so that those officials would steer business to it. The 'Sons and Daughters' programme was run by its Hong Kong subsidiary from 2006 to 2013 and bypassed the bank's normal hiring process. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said the bank won more than $100 million in business this way. In November 2016 JPMorgan agreed to pay $264 million to settle civil and criminal charges under the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which bans paying foreign officials, or giving them something of value, to win business.
cite: SEC and US Department of Justice settlements, 17 Nov 2016; OCCRP; Wikipedia 'JPMorgan Chase'

n: Citigroup executive's list mapped Obama's cabinet before the election
d: Michael Froman, a Citigroup executive, sent Barack Obama's team a list of names for the new cabinet a month before the 2008 election, and most of them got the jobs. On 6 October 2008 Froman, who had followed Robert Rubin from the Treasury to Citi, emailed John Podesta, co-chair of Obama's transition team, from his Citigroup address with candidate lists, including an outline of 31 cabinet-level posts. The email became public when WikiLeaks published Podesta's emails in 2016. The New Republic found the list 'almost entirely on the money': Eric Holder, Janet Napolitano, Robert Gates, Rahm Emanuel, Peter Orszag, Arne Duncan, Eric Shinseki and Kathleen Sebelius all got the posts listed, and for Treasury it named Rubin, Larry Summers or Timothy Geithner. Froman joined the White House in 2009 and became US Trade Representative in 2013.
cite: David Dayen, The New Republic, 14 Oct 2016 (WikiLeaks Podesta emails); Wikipedia 'Michael Froman'

n: Mozambique officials and Credit Suisse bankers bribed over hidden loans
rank: Finance ministry and state companies (hidden state guarantees)
d: Mozambican officials and Credit Suisse bankers took bribes and kickbacks to arrange $2.2 billion of state-guaranteed loans that were hidden from Mozambique's parliament and the IMF. In 2013–14 three Mozambican state companies borrowed $622 million from Credit Suisse and $535 million from Russia's VTB for tuna fishing and maritime security projects with the shipbuilder Privinvest. The US Justice Department said at least $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and officials; Credit Suisse banker Andrew Pearse received about $45 million. When the loans surfaced in 2016 the IMF and World Bank froze support, and one study estimated two million people were pushed into poverty. Mozambique's Constitutional Council declared the loans void (2019, 2020). In October 2021 Credit Suisse pleaded guilty to wire fraud in the US, was fined almost $500 million and forgave $200 million of Mozambique's debt.
cite: US DOJ plea agreement (Oct 2021); UK FCA; Mozambique Constitutional Council (2019, 2020); Wikipedia 'Tuna bonds'

n: Banco Rural cash paid Brazilian deputies for their votes
rank: Federal deputies of the governing coalition
d: In the 'mensalão' (big monthly payment) scandal of 2005, Lula's Workers' Party was accused of paying coalition deputies in Brazil's Congress monthly sums for their votes, with the cash drawn from Banco Rural. Documents from Brazil's financial intelligence unit (COAF) confirmed large cash withdrawals from Banco Rural branches in Brasília and Belo Horizonte, made through firms of publicist Marcos Valério, for deputies, their relatives or advisers. In 2012 the Supreme Federal Court found that public money and bank loans had been misused. It convicted Banco Rural's president Kátia Rabello of criminal association, fraudulent management, money laundering and currency evasion, sentencing her to 16 years and 8 months, along with Valério and party leaders including José Genoino.
cite: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil, Ação Penal 470 (2012); Portuguese Wikipedia 'Kátia Rabello'; Wikipedia 'Mensalão scandal'
who: Workers' Party via Banco Rural and Marcos Valério

n: Espírito Santo money linked to ex-PM Sócrates in corruption trial
d: Prosecutors in Portugal say money from the Espírito Santo banking group reached José Sócrates, prime minister from 2005 to 2011. Ricardo Salgado led Banco Espírito Santo (BES), of a banking family close to power since the Salazar dictatorship, and was nicknamed 'Dono Disto Tudo' ('owner of all this'); BES collapsed in 2014. In the case known as Operation Marquês, Sócrates was charged with receiving undue payments and Salgado with three counts of corruption and eight of money laundering. A judge threw out most charges in April 2021, but the Lisbon Court of Appeal reinstated them in January 2024 and the trial began on 3 July 2025; all defendants are presumed innocent. In a separate case from the same investigation, Salgado's sentence for breach of trust was raised to eight years on appeal in 2023.
cite: Lisbon Court of Appeal, 25 Jan 2024; Tribunal Central Criminal de Lisboa (trial from 3 July 2025); Portuguese Wikipedia 'Operação Marquês'
who: Banco Espírito Santo / Espírito Santo group (Ricardo Salgado)

n: Ex-JPMorgan and Deutsche bankers run Argentina's economy and central bank
rank: Minister of Economy; President of the Central Bank
d: Two former JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank executives were put in charge of Argentina's economy ministry and its central bank. Luis Caputo, who had been Mauricio Macri's finance minister (2017–18) and briefly central bank president in 2018, became Javier Milei's Minister of Economy on 10 December 2023. On Caputo's recommendation Milei named Santiago Bausili, who worked at JPMorgan from 1996 to 2007 and later ran debt business at Deutsche Bank, as President of the Central Bank of Argentina, which regulates the country's banks and manages its currency.
cite: Wikipedia 'Luis Caputo', 'Santiago Bausili' (citing Reuters, 3 Dec 2023; Buenos Aires Times)

n: CIA and BND secretly owned the cipher firm Crypto AG
rank: encrypted communications of ministries, armies and diplomats
d: The CIA and West Germany's intelligence service, the BND, secretly bought Crypto AG, a Swiss company that sold encryption machines to more than 120 governments, for $5.75m in 1970 (operation 'Thesaurus', later 'Rubikon'). The machines were rigged so the two services could read customer states' coded messages, including Iran's; Iran's arrest of salesman Hans Bühler in 1992 nearly exposed the operation. The BND left around 1993 and the CIA stayed sole owner until the firm was liquidated in 2018. The Washington Post, ZDF and SRF revealed the ownership in February 2020, and a Swiss parliamentary inquiry that year found Swiss authorities had known for years and benefited from the spying.
cite: Swiss parliamentary inquiry (2020); Washington Post / ZDF / SRF reporting Feb 2020; Wikipedia 'Crypto AG'

n: Cuba's spy Ana Montes was the DIA's top Cuba analyst
d: Cuba's intelligence service recruited Ana Belén Montes while she was a graduate student, and she went on to become the leading analyst on Cuba's military at the US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA), the Pentagon's intelligence arm, which she joined in 1985. From inside the agency she passed classified information to her Cuban handlers until her arrest on 21 September 2001. She pleaded guilty in 2002, was sentenced to 25 years and was released on 6 January 2023.
cite: US District Court, Washington DC, guilty plea Oct 2002; Wikipedia 'Ana Montes'

n: Mossad chief pressed ICC prosecutor; Israel spied on court staff
rank: chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court
d: Israel's intelligence services tried to steer the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the only permanent court that tries individuals for war crimes, by pressing and spying on its senior staff, according to a May 2024 investigation by the Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call. It reported that former Mossad director Yossi Cohen privately pressed prosecutor Fatou Bensouda before she opened an investigation into Palestine, telling her 'You should help us and let us take care of you.' It also reported that Israeli intelligence spied on, hacked and pressured senior ICC staff for nearly ten years, including intercepting communications of Bensouda and her successor Karim Khan. Israel's prime minister's office denied the claims.
cite: The Guardian / +972 Magazine / Local Call investigation, 28 May 2024
org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is mossad

n: 'Qatargate': Netanyahu aides suspected of being paid to promote Qatar
d: Israeli police suspect that two men close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took money to promote the image of Qatar, a Gulf state that mediates in the Gaza war and hosts Hamas's political office. In March–April 2025 police arrested Netanyahu adviser Jonatan Urich and former spokesman Eli Feldstein on suspicion of being paid through Third Circle, the firm of US lobbyist Jay Footlik, which was registered under the US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA). Channel 12 reported that Feldstein drew a salary from Footlik while working for Netanyahu. Netanyahu was questioned as a witness, not a suspect, and called it a political witch hunt. In May 2026 prosecutors announced a separate indictment of Urich over leaking a classified document.
cite: Israel Police and State Attorney investigation, 2025; Malay Mail/AFP explainer 3 Apr 2025; Arab News 28 May 2026
org_note: foreign_state = Qatar

n: Ex-US ambassador Richard Olson secretly helped Qatar lobby
rank: former ambassador and State Department special envoy
d: Richard Olson, a former US ambassador to the UAE (2008–2011) and Pakistan (2012–2015), pleaded guilty in 2022 to illegally helping the government of Qatar influence US officials soon after he left the State Department, where former senior officials are barred for a period from lobbying for foreign governments. He also admitted hiding gifts, such as first-class flights, from a Pakistani-American lobbyist tied to a Qatari official, who paid him $20,000 a month. In 2023 he was sentenced to three years' probation and a $93,350 fine.
cite: US District Court, Washington DC, plea 2022 and sentence 2023; Lawfare, 2 May 2022
org_note: foreign_state = Qatar

n: Saudi Arabia paid Twitter manager Ahmad Abouammo for users' data
d: Saudi officials paid Ahmad Abouammo, a Twitter employee, to take data from the company's systems that helped them identify and locate users they were interested in. Abouammo managed Twitter's relations with Middle East journalists and celebrities in 2013–2015 and received a $42,000 watch and two $100,000 wire transfers. A San Francisco federal jury convicted him in August 2022, and he was sentenced to three and a half years in December 2022. A second ex-employee, Ali Alzabarah, left the US before he could be charged.
cite: US District Court, Northern District of California, verdict Aug 2022 and sentence Dec 2022
org_note: foreign_state = Saudi Arabia

n: Saudi funding threat got coalition dropped from UN child-harm list
d: Saudi Arabia and its allies used their funding of UN programmes to get the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen taken off a UN blacklist. The UN Secretary-General's annual 'children and armed conflict' report lists parties to wars that kill and maim children. On 9 June 2016 Ban Ki-moon said he had temporarily removed the coalition from the list because of 'undue pressure' from its supporters, who threatened to stop funding many UN programmes. Saudi Arabia's UN ambassador denied making threats.
cite: UN Secretary-General press remarks, 9 June 2016 (AP)
org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is Saudi Arabia (foreign_state)

n: McLaren report: Russia's FSB inside the Moscow anti-doping lab
rank: WADA-accredited Moscow laboratory and Sochi 2014 testing
d: Russia's FSB security service and Ministry of Sport worked through the Moscow laboratory accredited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), the body that sets drug-testing rules for world sport, to hide doped athletes. Richard McLaren's reports for WADA in July and December 2016 found a 'state-directed failsafe system' involving the ministry, the national team centre, the FSB and the laboratory. FSB-linked staff opened supposedly tamper-proof sample bottles at the 2014 Sochi Olympics to swap urine. More than 1,000 Russian competitors in over 30 sports benefited between 2011 and 2015, and the 'disappearing positive' method hid at least 643 positive samples.
cite: McLaren Independent Investigation Reports to WADA, 18 July and 9 Dec 2016
org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is fsb

n: FIFA voters allegedly paid to back Russia for the 2018 World Cup
d: People seeking Russia's 2018 World Cup allegedly paid members of FIFA's executive committee, the 22-member board that chose World Cup hosts, to vote for Russia. FIFA is the world governing body for football, based in Switzerland. The committee chose Russia (2018) and Qatar (2022) in December 2010. A US indictment unsealed in April 2020 alleges that Jack Warner of Trinidad and Tobago received about $5m and Guatemala's Rafael Salguero about $1m to vote for Russia. The 2020 charges were brought against media executives; the voters named were already charged or dead, so these bribes have not been tried. Russia called the claims baseless.
cite: US District Court, Eastern District of New York, superseding indictment unsealed 6 April 2020

n: FIFA voters allegedly paid to back Qatar for the 2022 World Cup
d: People seeking Qatar's 2022 World Cup allegedly bribed members of FIFA's executive committee, the board of football's world governing body that chose World Cup hosts in December 2010. The April 2020 US indictment alleges that Brazil's Ricardo Teixeira, Paraguay's Nicolás Leoz and an unnamed co-conspirator received bribes in return for their votes for Qatar. Separately, Qatari FIFA executive Mohamed bin Hammam was banned for life in 2012, and leaked emails published by the Sunday Times in 2014 showed him making payments of $10,000 to $200,000 to football officials before the 2010 vote. Qatar denies wrongdoing.
cite: US District Court, E.D. New York, superseding indictment April 2020; FIFA Ethics Committee bans 2011–12; Sunday Times 'FIFA Files' June 2014

n: Tokyo 2020 bid paid firm tied to IOC voter's son
rank: IOC member and Japanese Olympic Committee president
d: Tokyo's 2020 Olympic bid committee paid about $2m in 2013 to Black Tidings, a Singapore company tied to Papa Massata Diack, son of IOC member Lamine Diack, at the time African votes in the International Olympic Committee were being sought. The IOC picks Olympic host cities by a vote of its members. French financial prosecutors opened a corruption investigation of Tsunekazu Takeda, president of the Japanese Olympic Committee (JOC), in December 2018. A JOC panel concluded the payments were not bribes but could not interview key people. Takeda denied wrongdoing and stepped down from the JOC and IOC in 2019.
cite: French Parquet National Financier investigation, 2018–19

n: Indian Chronicles: pro-India network used UN-accredited NGOs in Geneva
rank: UN Human Rights Council and European Parliament
d: A network linked to India's Srivastava Group used UN-accredited NGOs, some with direct ties to the group, to get speakers into sessions of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, where they promoted Indian interests and criticised Pakistan. NGOs with UN accreditation may speak at Council sessions. EU DisinfoLab, a Brussels research group, reported this in 2019 and in December 2020 ('Indian Chronicles'). The network revived dead NGOs, impersonated dead rights activists and ran hundreds of fake local news sites (750 across 116 countries by 2020, by later counts). It also worked on the European Parliament, mainly to 'discredit Pakistan'. EU DisinfoLab did not show that the Indian government directed it.
cite: EU DisinfoLab, 'Indian Chronicles' (Dec 2020); BBC; swissinfo.ch, 'Report reveals targeted operation to serve Indian interests at the UN', Dec 2020

n: Hungarian spies at Hungary's EU mission tried to recruit Commission staff
d: Hungarian intelligence officers posing as diplomats at Hungary's Permanent Representation in Brussels, its embassy to the EU, tried to recruit Hungarians working at the European Commission, the EU's executive body. Der Spiegel, Direkt36, De Tijd and others reported this in October 2025. A Commission letter leaked in July 2026 confirms that the mission ran such a network from 2012 to 2018, though no serious breaches were found. Olivér Várhelyi, Hungary's EU ambassador from 2015 to 2019 and now a Commissioner, denies knowing; the Commission's May 2026 findings largely cleared him.
cite: European Commission internal investigation, findings May 2026 and letter to MEPs; Euronews 2 July 2026
org_note: foreign_state = Hungary; target body eu

n: Egyptian intelligence's man in the German government press office
rank: employee of the Federal Government Press Office
d: Egypt's General Intelligence Service had a man inside Germany's Federal Press Office, which runs the German chancellor's communications. The man, named as Amin A., an Egypt-born German citizen, worked in its visitor service from 1999. Federal prosecutors charged him in November 2020 with helping the Egyptian service from at least 2010 by compiling reports on German media coverage and, in 2014–2015, helping an attempt to recruit a source, in exchange for favours for his family. Germany's interior minister said he had no access to sensitive data.
cite: German Federal Prosecutor General, indictment Nov 2020; BfV annual report 2019

n: Slovak ministry plane used in Vietnam's abduction of Trinh Xuan Thanh
d: Vietnamese intelligence got help from inside Slovakia's government to move a man it had kidnapped. Trinh Xuan Thanh, a former Vietnamese state-company executive seeking asylum, was seized in Berlin on 23 July 2017; Germany blamed Vietnamese intelligence, expelled an intelligence officer, and a Berlin court in 2018 jailed one accomplice. In 2019 a Slovak journalist found a €17,000 invoice from Slovakia's interior ministry to Vietnam's for a 26 July 2017 flight to Moscow, and ex-president Andrej Kiska wrote that then-interior minister Robert Kaliňák was behind lending the plane. Thanh was later given life in Hanoi.
cite: Kammergericht Berlin verdict July 2018 (upheld 2019); Slovak interior ministry invoice reported 2019
org_note: foreign_state = Vietnam

n: Sue Mi Terry charged as South Korean intelligence agent in Washington
rank: former CIA analyst and policy adviser to US officials
d: US prosecutors charged that South Korea's National Intelligence Service (NIS) recruited Sue Mi Terry, a former CIA analyst and Council on Foreign Relations fellow, to work for it inside Washington's policy world from 2013. The Council on Foreign Relations is a leading US foreign-policy think tank. She was indicted in July 2024 as an unregistered foreign agent. Prosecutors said she passed notes from a 2022 private meeting with Secretary of State Antony Blinken and wrote op-eds at the NIS's request, in exchange for designer goods and over $37,000 for her programmes. In October 2026 the Justice Department agreed to drop the charges after one year if she stays out of trouble; she signed a statement acknowledging contacts with and some sponsorship by South Korean officials but no wrongdoing.
cite: US District Court, Southern District of New York, indictment July 2024; deferred prosecution Oct 2026

arch.t: Council on Foreign Relations — Submergence of US Sovereignty (Insider Testimony)

n: Indian RAW officers cultivated Australian politicians and an insider
rank: politicians, a state police service, cleared officials
d: Officers of India's foreign intelligence service, RAW, cultivated Australian politicians and a state police service and recruited an Australian security-clearance holder with access to defence technology. ASIO, Australia's domestic security agency, disrupted the group, and two RAW officers were expelled in 2020 after seeking secrets on defence projects, airport security and trade. In a March 2021 speech ASIO chief Mike Burgess described a foreign 'nest of spies' that had also cultivated a foreign embassy and monitored a diaspora community, without naming the country. In April 2024 Australian media and the Washington Post reported it was India.
cite: ASIO Director-General annual threat assessment, March 2021; ABC, The Australian, Washington Post, April 2024

n: Pakistan's ISI paid Ghulam Nabi Fai to lobby the US Congress on Kashmir
rank: members of Congress (campaign donations and lobbying)
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, paid Ghulam Nabi Fai at least $3.5m to lobby US officials on Kashmir, according to US prosecutors. Fai ran the Kashmiri American Council in Washington, which prosecutors called a front for the ISI. He also gave political donations, including to Representatives Dan Burton and Joe Pitts, who said they did not know the source. The FBI arrested him in July 2011. He pleaded guilty in December 2011 and was sentenced in March 2012 to two years.
cite: US District Court, Eastern District of Virginia, plea Dec 2011, sentence Mar 2012

n: Haqqani network, called an arm of Pakistan's ISI, runs Taliban security
d: The Haqqani network, which the US military's top officer called an arm of Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), now holds senior posts in Afghanistan's Taliban government. The network is a militant group within the Taliban, designated a terrorist organisation by the US in 2012. In September 2011 Admiral Mike Mullen told the US Senate it 'acts as a veritable arm' of the ISI. After the Taliban took Kabul in 2021 the network was given control of Kabul's security, and its leader Sirajuddin Haqqani became the Taliban government's interior minister. Pakistan denies ties.
cite: US Senate Armed Services Committee testimony of Adm. Mike Mullen, 22 Sept 2011; US FTO designation 7 Sept 2012

n: Iran Experts Initiative: Tehran cultivated scholars at Western think tanks
rank: Pentagon official and US policy circles
d: Iran's Foreign Ministry ran a project, the Iran Experts Initiative, to cultivate Iranian-heritage academics at Western think tanks so they would promote Tehran's positions, according to leaked ministry emails reported by Semafor and Iran International in September 2023. It began in 2014 on a proposal by diplomat Saeed Khatibzadeh. Think tanks are research groups that advise governments. Pentagon official Ariane Tabatabai was linked to it, prompting House Armed Services chairman Mike Rogers to object. The Pentagon reviewed her case and in October 2023 said she had been properly vetted and kept her security clearance.
cite: Semafor and Iran International, Sept 2023 (leaked Iranian ministry emails); Pentagon statement Oct 2023

n: North Korean IT workers placed inside 300+ US companies via laptop farm
rank: remote IT staff positions in US companies
d: North Korea got its IT workers hired, under false identities, inside more than 300 American companies. It places such workers in remote jobs abroad to earn money for the state. Arizona resident Christina Chapman ran a 'laptop farm' for three years: she kept company laptops at her home so the North Korean workers appeared to be working from the US. The scheme generated more than $17m for the North Korean government. She was sentenced to eight years in federal prison in 2025.
cite: US federal court, sentence July 2025

n: UN experts: Rwanda commands M23 and placed Rwandans over eastern Congo
rank: provincial governments of North and South Kivu
d: Rwanda's army commands the M23 armed group and has placed Rwandans in charge of state functions in the parts of eastern Congo it holds, according to the UN Group of Experts, which monitors sanctions on Congo for the Security Council. M23, whose political arm is the AFC, took Goma in January 2025 and Bukavu after.
