The experts reported in June 2025 that Rwandan army reinforcements backed the capture of Goma and that officials said President Kagame decided to take both cities. They described a 'systematic effort to dismantle existing State authority': new governors appointed, Rwandans placed over mining, tax, banking and border control, and 18 customary chiefs removed. Rwanda denies directing M23.
cite: UN Security Council Group of Experts on the DRC, final report June 2025
org_note: foreign_state = Rwanda

n: Cuba took over restructuring of Venezuela's military counterintelligence
d: Under secret agreements, Cuba oversaw the rebuilding of Venezuela's military intelligence service and placed Cuban officers to inspect its units. Documents seen by Reuters show that on 26 May 2008 Venezuela's defence minister and Cuba's deputy defence minister signed two agreements: Cuba would oversee the restructuring and train Venezuelan officers in Havana, and an eight-member Cuban team (GRUCE) would inspect units. The service, renamed DGCIM in 2011, shifted to watching Venezuela's own soldiers and grew to at least 1,500 agents. Reuters published this in August 2019. After US forces seized Maduro in January 2026, Reuters reported Cuban advisers being removed from DGCIM posts and withdrawing.
cite: Reuters special report 'How Cuba taught Venezuela to quash military dissent', 22 Aug 2019; Reuters reporting Feb 2026

n: Samherji allegedly paid Namibian ministers for fishing quotas ('Fishrot')
d: Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, paid Namibian officials to obtain horse-mackerel fishing quota, according to documents released by WikiLeaks on 12 November 2019 and its former Namibia manager Jóhannes Stefánsson. A quota is a government licence to catch a set amount of fish. Fisheries Minister Bernhardt Esau and Justice Minister Sacky Shanghala resigned the next day, and in December 2019 they and four associates (the 'Fishrot Six') were arrested on corruption, fraud and money-laundering charges. Samherji denies paying bribes and blames Stefánsson; the criminal case in Namibia is still before the courts.
cite: Fishrot Files (WikiLeaks, Kveikur/Al Jazeera, Stundin), Nov 2019; Namibian Anti-Corruption Commission arrests and charges, Dec 2019–Feb 2020

n: Bashar Kiwan ran Comoros's passport sales; ex-president jailed for life
d: Syrian-French businessman Bashar Kiwan helped run the Comoros government's passport-sale programme, under which much of the money never reached the state treasury. Under the 2008 'economic citizenship' law, Comoros sold passports in bulk to stateless people (bidoon) living in the Gulf, with Gulf money paying for them. Prosecutors said the programme brought in about 200 million dollars. On 28 November 2022 a court in Moroni, the capital, sentenced former president Ahmed Abdallah Sambi to life in prison for high treason and related charges; Kiwan was tried with him.
cite: Comoros State Security Court verdict, 28 Nov 2022 (as summarised on Wikipedia)
who: Bashar Kiwan and Gulf-funded passport buyers

n: Zuneth Sattar's firms won Malawi police and army contracts via officials
rank: vice president, police inspector general, ministers
d: Companies linked to Zuneth Sattar, a UK-based businessman, won 16 contracts worth over 150 million dollars from Malawi's police and the Malawi Defence Force between 2017 and 2021, and Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau said he paid officials to secure them. The bureau reported in June 2022; President Lazarus Chakwera said 84 people were named and withdrew all delegated powers from Vice President Saulos Chilima. Former police chief George Kainja and lands minister Kezzie Msukwa were arrested. In November 2022 the bureau arrested Chilima, alleging he received $280,000 and other items between March and October 2021 for helping two Sattar-linked firms win contracts. Chilima denied wrongdoing; he died in a plane crash in June 2024.
cite: Malawi Anti-Corruption Bureau report to the President, June 2022; President Chakwera's address, 21 June 2022; Al Jazeera, 'Malawi vice president arrested by anti-corruption bureau', 25 Nov 2022

n: Dutch cocaine fugitive 'Bolle Jos' protected inside Sierra Leone's elite
d: Jos Leijdekkers ('Bolle Jos'), on the Dutch and EU most-wanted lists for cocaine trafficking, has 'high-level protection' in Sierra Leone and two sources said he is married to President Julius Maada Bio's daughter Agnes, Reuters reported on 25 January 2025, citing three sources and video. The footage shows him two rows behind the president at a New Year's Day mass. Sierra Leone said it was investigating and the head of immigration was dismissed; the government denies knowing his whereabouts.
cite: Reuters exclusive, 25 Jan 2025; Dutch Public Prosecution Service statements

n: Guinea-Bissau's navy and army chiefs charged in US cocaine cases
rank: former navy chief; army chief of staff
d: US prosecutors charged the heads of Guinea-Bissau's navy and army with offering their positions to help cocaine traffickers. Guinea-Bissau, in West Africa, has served since the mid-2000s as a transit point for South American cocaine headed to Europe. On 2 April 2013 the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) arrested former navy chief José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto at sea in a sting; he pleaded guilty to drug conspiracy in New York. An indictment unsealed on 18 April 2013 charged army chief Antonio Indjai with offering to store cocaine for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla group, and sell it weapons; he stayed in Bissau and was not arrested. In February 2022 President Umaro Sissoco Embaló blamed Na Tchuto, by then back home, for a failed attack on the government palace.
cite: US Attorney SDNY indictments, April 2013; Na Tchuto guilty plea; Al Jazeera, 11 Feb 2022

n: Hezbollah financiers got Gambian state monopolies under Jammeh
d: Businessmen the US designates as financiers of Hezbollah got control of state monopolies in Gambia through President Yahya Jammeh. Hezbollah is the Lebanese Shia party and armed group; 'designated' means placed on a US sanctions list. OCCRP, a journalist network, reported on 27 March 2019 ('Great Gambia Heist') that Lebanese businessman Mohamed Bazzi was one of Jammeh's closest associates and received monopolies including the fuel supply. Ali Charara, also designated, paid 35 million dollars for half of the state telecoms firms Gamtel and Gamcel, and OCCRP estimated over 100 million dollars from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah. Jammeh left office in 2017.
cite: OCCRP, 'Jammeh's Taiwanese Alliance and the Hezbollah Laundromat', 27 Mar 2019; US Treasury designations of Bazzi and Charara

n: Benjamin Bol Mel: Kiir's state contractor moved into the vice presidency
d: Benjamin Bol Mel, a businessman whose company held South Sudan government contracts, moved into the country's top offices. He is president of ABMC Thai-South Sudan Construction, which received government road contracts worth tens of millions of dollars without competitive bidding, and he served as President Salva Kiir's principal financial adviser and private secretary. The US sanctioned him under the Global Magnitsky corruption order on 21 December 2017. He was named one of South Sudan's vice presidents on 10 February 2025 and deputy secretary general of the ruling SPLM, before a decree removed him from both posts on 12 November 2025.
cite: US Executive Order 13818 designations, 21 Dec 2017; presidential decrees of Feb and Nov 2025; Radio Tamazuj, 'U.S. sanctions Benjamin Bol Mel over corruption', Dec 2017
who: Benjamin Bol Mel and his companies

n: Burmeister & Wain debarred for paying Mauritian officials in power tenders
d: Burmeister & Wain Scandinavian Contractor, a Danish power-plant builder, paid members of the Mauritian administration through intermediaries during tenders for the Saint-Louis power station of the Central Electricity Board, Mauritius's state power company. The African Development Bank, which lends for such projects, reached that finding 'on the balance of probabilities' in June 2020 and debarred the firm for 21 months, meaning it could not bid on bank-funded projects.
cite: African Development Bank sanctions decision, June 2020

n: Al-Qaeda-affiliated leaders in the Taliban government, UN monitors say
d: At least three key leaders in Afghanistan's Taliban government are affiliated with al-Qaeda, the UN Security Council's sanctions Monitoring Team assessed in June 2023. The team reports each year on al-Qaeda and the Taliban. Its sixteenth report (December 2025) says al-Qaeda keeps close ties with the Taliban and a presence in several provinces, and that the Pakistani Taliban (TTP), with about 6,000 fighters, has strong support from elements within the Taliban; one member state said TTP chief Noor Wali Mehsud's family receives a monthly payment from the Taliban. The Taliban reject the reports.
cite: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team, reports of June 2023 and Dec 2025 (16th report), as reported by Dawn and the Washington Examiner

n: Telecom firms paid Karimova over a billion for Uzbek licences
d: Three foreign telecom companies paid entities controlled by Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of the late Uzbek president Islam Karimov, to get into the Uzbek mobile market. VimpelCom (2016, 795 million dollars), Telia (2017, 965 million dollars) and MTS (2019, 850 million dollars) settled US foreign-bribery cases over those payments; the figures are what each paid to settle. Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at 869.3 million dollars. She was convicted in Uzbekistan in 2017 and 2020 and remains in prison; Switzerland dropped its own trial in 2026.
cite: US DOJ/SEC FCPA resolutions with VimpelCom (2016), Telia (2017) and MTS (2019); Uzbek court verdicts 2017, 2020

n: Businesspeople bribed Marshall Islands lawmakers for a 'special region' law
d: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, China-born businesspeople who had bought Marshallese passports, paid tens of thousands of dollars from about 2016 to 2020 to Marshall Islands officials, including legislators, to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region'. Both pleaded guilty in New York; Zhou was sentenced in February 2023 and Yan to 42 months in May 2023. In December 2023 the US State Department barred former president Kessai Note and MP Mike Halferty from entering the US for taking those bribes; Note denies it.
cite: US DOJ sentencing release, 16 May 2023; US State Department 7031(c) designation, Dec 2023; OCCRP investigation

n: Micronesian president accuses China of 'political warfare'
d: Micronesia's outgoing president, David Panuelo, accused China of bribing and threatening officials in the Federated States of Micronesia to keep the Pacific country aligned with Beijing, or neutral, in any war over Taiwan. He made the accusation in a 13-page letter in March 2023 and called it 'political warfare'. He wrote that he had considered switching diplomatic recognition to Taiwan. China rejected the claims.
cite: Letter of President David Panuelo, 9 Mar 2023, as reported by Reuters and CNN

n: Getax charged with bribing Nauru politicians for phosphate
d: Getax Australia, a Gold Coast phosphate trader, is charged by Australian federal prosecutors with conspiring to bribe politicians in Nauru, a Pacific island state whose main export is phosphate, between 2007 and 2012 to win phosphate deals. The case has been repeatedly delayed. In a related case Sydney businessman Mozammil Bhojani pleaded guilty to paying over 120,000 dollars to a Nauruan MP and a minister and was jailed in 2018.
cite: Australian Federal Police investigation; NSW District Court sentence of Bhojani, 2018

n: Australian detention subcontracts paid firms tied to Nauru's leaders
d: Firms tied to Nauru's leaders received subcontracts worth millions under Australia's offshore asylum centre on Nauru, which Australia pays contractors to run. A 2023 investigation by Nick McKenzie and colleagues for the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age found banking records showing over 120,000 dollars in suspect payments to justice minister David Adeang, and about 2.6 million dollars to a company of Lionel Aingimea, later president. It said Australia's Home Affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations since 2010. The reporters stressed they were not claiming the payments were bribes; Adeang denies it.
cite: Sydney Morning Herald / The Age investigation, July 2023

n: Paladin's Manus contract: 'visa' payments alleged as bribes
d: Paladin, a company paid 530 million Australian dollars from 2017 to 2019 to run Australia's asylum centre on Manus Island in Papua New Guinea, sent money to a businessman close to senior PNG officials, according to its former director Ian Stewart. He told the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age in 2023 that over 3 million dollars went to a Singapore account of that businessman, and that a 1.5 million dollar invoice marked 'Visas' was a bribe. Paladin's former chief executive denies any improper payment.
cite: Sydney Morning Herald / The Age investigation, July 2023

n: Albanian interior minister Tahiri and his cousin's cannabis group
d: Saimir Tahiri, Albania's interior minister until 2017 and so in charge of its police, was tied to his cousin Moisi Habilaj's cannabis-trafficking group. Italian police arrested Habilaj in October 2017 in a probe into an Albanian-Italian group moving over 3.5 tonnes of cannabis, and wiretaps mentioned Tahiri. On 19 September 2019 Albania's Serious Crime Court convicted him of abuse of office and sentenced him to 3 years and 4 months, but dropped the drug-trafficking and organised-crime charges.
cite: Albanian Serious Crime Court verdict, 19 Sep 2019; Italian Guardia di Finanza operation, Oct 2017

n: Croatian PM Sanader convicted of taking €10m from MOL for control of INA
d: Hungary's oil company MOL paid Croatian Prime Minister Ivo Sanader a 10 million euro bribe to give it management control of Croatia's national oil company INA, Croatian courts found. MOL is a Hungarian company in which the state has influence. The courts found the payment came from MOL chief executive Zsolt Hernádi. A 2012 verdict was quashed in 2015, but Sanader was convicted again in 2020 and the Supreme Court confirmed it in 2021. Hungary has not handed Hernádi to Croatia and MOL denies the bribe.
cite: Zagreb County Court verdict 2020, upheld by the Croatian Supreme Court 2021

n: Lithuanian president impeached over Russian donor Borisov
d: Yuri Borisov, a Russian businessman who ran the helicopter firm Avia Baltika, reportedly gave about 400,000 dollars to Rolandas Paksas's 2002 presidential campaign and then received Lithuanian citizenship by Paksas's decree. On 31 March 2004 the Constitutional Court found Paksas had broken the constitution and his oath, and on 6 April 2004 the Seimas, Lithuania's parliament, removed him, the first European head of state impeached. The European Court of Human Rights later found his lifetime ban from parliament disproportionate.
cite: Constitutional Court of Lithuania ruling, 31 Mar 2004; Seimas impeachment vote, 6 Apr 2004

n: Yorgen Fenech's 17 Black and Malta's prime minister's office
rank: PM's chief of staff and energy minister
d: Yorgen Fenech, a Maltese businessman, owned 17 Black, a Dubai company that leaked papers showed was expected to pay Panama companies held by the prime minister's chief of staff Keith Schembri and minister Konrad Mizzi. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia had exposed the companies; she was murdered in 2017. Fenech was arrested in November 2019 and indicted in 2021 for commissioning her murder; Schembri and Mizzi resigned. A 2021 public inquiry found the state created an 'atmosphere of impunity', and a magisterial inquiry led to charges over 17 Black against Fenech, Schembri and Mizzi.
cite: Public inquiry into the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia, report July 2021; Maltese indictments

n: 'Monacogate': Rybolovlev graft case over courting officials closed
d: Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including former public prosecutor Jean-Pierre Dreno, to get favourable treatment. The suspicion rested on messages from the phone of his lawyer Tetiana Bersheda. In November 2018 he was made a formal suspect in a corruption and influence-peddling probe. The case against Dreno and Rybolovlev was dismissed in 2023, and in February 2025 Monaco's courts closed it, ruling the phone data unlawfully obtained after a European Court of Human Rights finding.
cite: Monaco investigating judges 2018–2023; European Court of Human Rights judgment, June 2024; Monaco court ruling, Feb 2025

n: 'Conto Mazzini': businessmen paid San Marino politicians for licences
rank: former state secretaries and party leaders
d: Construction and banking entrepreneurs paid San Marino politicians to obtain building permits and banking licences, prosecutors said, with cash drawn from an account in the name of 'Giuseppe Mazzini' at Banca Commerciale Sammarinese. Twenty-one former political figures, including former state secretaries (ministers) Fiorenzo Stolfi and Claudio Podeschi, went on trial in 2015 for criminal association to launder bribes; about 200 million euros were seized. Several were convicted in 2017, and an appeal court upheld most convictions in March 2022 with lower sentences.
cite: San Marino criminal court, 2017; appeal ruling, March 2022; Freedom House 'Freedom in the World' 2023

n: Slovak PM's chief adviser co-founded firm with 'Ndrangheta-linked man
rank: chief state adviser to the prime minister
d: Mária Trošková, chief state adviser to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, had co-founded a company in 2011 with Antonino Vadalà, an Italian businessman with suspected links to the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia. Journalist Ján Kuciak, murdered on 21 February 2018, had been finishing an article showing this and on other Italian businessmen in eastern Slovakia with suspected 'Ndrangheta links. It was published on 28 February 2018. Trošková and security council secretary Viliam Jasaň stepped down that day, saying their names were being misused; Fico resigned in March after mass protests.
cite: Aktuality.sk, Kuciak's posthumous article, 28 Feb 2018; Slovak Spectator

n: Patria armoured-vehicle bribery case against Janez Janša
d: Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, paid bribes partly aimed at Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša to win a 278 million euro deal for 135 armoured vehicles signed in 2006, Finnish broadcaster YLE alleged in 2008. A Ljubljana court sentenced Janša to two years in 2013, but the Constitutional Court annulled the verdict and the case lapsed in 2016. In Finland the defendants were acquitted on appeal; Austria convicted one middleman.
cite: Ljubljana District Court, 5 June 2013; Constitutional Court of Slovenia, 2015; Finnish and Austrian proceedings

n: Stanford paid Antigua's bank regulator to look away, US charges
rank: head of the Financial Services Regulatory Commission
d: R. Allen Stanford paid Leroy King, head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, the body that supervised Stanford's bank, more than 100,000 dollars in bribes to ignore the bank's real assets and help obstruct an SEC investigation, according to a June 2009 US indictment. Stanford ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was convicted in the US of a 7 billion dollar fraud. The SEC is the US securities regulator. Antigua extradited King to Houston on 12 November 2019.
cite: US DOJ indictment (S.D. Texas, June 2009); DOJ release on extradition, 12 Nov 2019

n: Iranian donor got Dominica diplomatic post, Al Jazeera reports
d: Iranian businessman Alireza Monfared gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Dominican Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's 2014 campaign in return for an ambassadorship and a diplomatic passport, Al Jazeera reported in November 2019; a witness said Skerrit handed it over in Kuala Lumpur. Dominica, a Caribbean island state, sells citizenship; OCCRP found about 7,700 buyers by 2023, including Afghanistan's former spy chief and sanctioned Russians. Monfared was later jailed in Iran for oil-revenue theft. Skerrit denies any trade.
cite: Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, 27 Nov 2019; OCCRP/Government Accountability Project, 11 Oct 2023

n: Odebrecht paid 92 million dollars in Dominican bribes for public works
d: Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction company, paid 92 million dollars in bribes in the Dominican Republic to win public works, it admitted to the US in 2016. In October 2021 a Dominican court convicted businessman Ángel Rondón, named as the channel for the bribes, and former public works minister Víctor Díaz Rúa; four other defendants were acquitted. An appeal court upheld both convictions on 19 May 2023.
cite: US DOJ plea agreement with Odebrecht, Dec 2016; Dominican court verdict Oct 2021, upheld 19 May 2023

n: Investor says he paid Grenada's PM; diplomatic posts for kickbacks alleged
d: Investor Eric Resteiner claimed he paid about half a million dollars to Grenada's Prime Minister Keith Mitchell, Al Jazeera reported in November 2019; Mitchell said he received only 15,000 dollars for travel costs. Grenada sells citizenship and has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen. US businessman Leo Ford said a partner was offered a diplomatic post for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies.
cite: Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, 27 Nov 2019

n: Mohamed gold family bribed Guyanese officials, US says
d: Guyanese gold traders Nazar Mohamed, his son Azruddin and their firm Mohamed's Enterprise bribed customs officials, paid officials for favourable treatment in court matters and bribed to win state contracts, the US Treasury said on 11 June 2024 when it sanctioned them. It said they left over 10,000 kg of gold off customs declarations in 2019–2023 and evaded more than 50 million dollars in duty. It also sanctioned Mae Thomas, permanent secretary (the top civil servant) of the home affairs ministry from 2020 to 2023, for taking cash and gifts in return for contract, gun-permit and passport favours. The Mohameds deny wrongdoing.
cite: US Treasury OFAC press release JY2401, 11 June 2024

n: Honduran president Hernández took trafficker bribes to protect cocaine
d: Drug traffickers paid Juan Orlando Hernández, president of Honduras from 2014 to 2022, millions of dollars in bribes to protect US-bound cocaine shipments, a New York jury found. Several convicted traffickers testified that they had paid him. He was convicted in the Southern District of New York of conspiracy to import cocaine and related weapons counts, and sentenced to 45 years in June 2024. His brother, a former congressman, was convicted in the same district in 2018. He was granted a full US presidential pardon on 1 December 2025 and released the same day; Honduras then asked Interpol, the international police network, to execute a 2023 domestic arrest order written to take effect if US authorities freed him.
cite: US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y., verdict March 2024, sentence June 2024; presidential pardon 1 December 2025; Honduran Ministerio Publico arrest order, December 2025; Al Jazeera, 'Honduras ex-president sentenced to 45 years for helping drug traffickers', 26 June 2024
undone: Pardoned by the US president in December 2025; released the same day.

n: Sinaloa Cartel paid Mexico's security chief García Luna
d: The Sinaloa Cartel paid Genaro García Luna, Mexico's Secretary of Public Security from 2006 to 2012 and the cabinet minister who ran the federal police, in exchange for protection from arrest, safe passage for its shipments and warnings of coming operations. He held the post during the militarised phase of the drug war. A US federal court in the Eastern District of New York convicted him in February 2023 on all five counts, including continuing criminal enterprise (running a large drug operation), and sentenced him in 2024. In May 2025 a US court ordered him and his wife to pay Mexico more than $2.4 billion in a civil suit over public contracts, the largest financial judgment attached to any official on this map.
cite: US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., verdict February 2023, sentence 2024; US civil judgment for the Government of Mexico, May 2025

n: Medellín Cartel paid Panama's ruler Noriega for protection
d: Manuel Noriega, Panama's military ruler and head of state from 1983 to 1989, took money from the Medellín Cartel as protection money, bribes or shares of profits, and a 1988 US indictment said he turned Panama into a shipping platform for South American cocaine bound for the US. After the US invasion removed him, a Miami federal court convicted him in 1992 on eight of ten counts of drug trafficking, racketeering (running a criminal enterprise) and money laundering. On 10 July 1992 he was sentenced to 40 years. It was the earliest case in which a sitting head of state's control of the security apparatus was prosecuted as a trafficking enterprise.
cite: US v. Noriega, S.D. Fla., 1992; Wikipedia, 'Manuel Noriega' (conviction on eight of ten counts; sentence 10 July 1992)

n: Guinea-Bissau's navy chief Na Tchuto offered his post to traffickers
d: José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto, chief of staff of Guinea-Bissau's navy, offered to use his position to help move cocaine into the United States. He was taken in a sting by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) in international waters and pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine. The country's air force chief was indicted in the same operation. Guinea-Bissau, in West Africa, has been a transit point for South American cocaine headed for Europe.
cite: US v. Na Tchuto, S.D.N.Y., plea 2014

n: Parapolítica: AUC paramilitaries' collusion with Colombia's Congress
d: Colombia's AUC paramilitaries, armed groups that were themselves among the country's largest cocaine traffickers, colluded with members of Congress, and roughly 30% of the Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over it. The scandal is known as 'parapolítica' and was prosecuted by the Supreme Court of Justice from 2006. By April 2012, 139 members of Congress were under investigation; five governors and 32 legislators had been convicted. A later review by the Inspector General's office counted more than 500 elected officials investigated over a decade.
cite: Supreme Court of Justice proceedings from 2006; Human Rights Watch; Procuraduria General

n: Bolivia's anti-drug police chief sold protection for cocaine loads
d: René Sanabria, former commander of Bolivia's national anti-narcotics force (FELCN) and from 2009 head of an elite drug intelligence unit inside the Interior Ministry, sold protection to cocaine shippers. He was taken in a sting by the US Drug Enforcement Administration: his group agreed to protect Miami-bound cocaine loads for a 50,000 payment, and one container shipment was seized on arrival. He pleaded guilty in Miami and was sentenced on 23 September 2011 to 14 years; his co-defendant got nine.
cite: US v. Sanabria-Oropeza and Foronda-Azero, S.D. Fla., pleas June 2011, sentences 23 September 2011

n: H-2 cartel used Nayarit's attorney general Veytia
d: The H-2 cartel used Edgar Veytia, attorney general (chief prosecutor) of the Mexican state of Nayarit, to serve it from 2013 to 2017, US prosecutors established. He directed officers to wiretap and arrest rival traffickers, released the cartel's members from custody and assisted acts of violence. He had campaigned on the claim that there was no room for organised crime in Nayarit. He pleaded guilty in Brooklyn to a conspiracy to import heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and marijuana, and on 26 September 2019 was sentenced to 20 years with $1 million in forfeiture. Two months earlier the US Treasury had sanctioned his governor, Roberto Sandoval.
cite: US v. Veytia Cambero, E.D.N.Y., guilty plea 2019, sentence 26 September 2019 before Judge Carol Bagley Amon

n: Tamaulipas governor Yarrington took $3.5m in bribes for state business
d: Tomás Yarrington, governor of the Mexican state of Tamaulipas from 1999 to 2005 and a presidential candidate, admitted taking more than $3.5 million in bribes; US prosecutors said they came from individuals and private companies in Mexico in exchange for deals with the state government. He fled Mexico in 2012, was arrested in Italy in 2017 and extradited to the US the following year. He pleaded guilty in 2021 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and was sentenced in March 2023 to nine years. Charges of conspiracy to import cocaine and marijuana and of bank fraud were dismissed under the plea. He was released in November 2024 after a sentence adjustment for time served and returned to Mexico in April 2025 to face a second laundering case.
cite: US v. Yarrington Ruvalcaba, S.D. Tex., plea 25 March 2021, sentence 15 March 2023; Bureau of Prisons release records, 2024; Fiscalia General de la Republica proceedings, 2025; US Attorney's Office, S.D. Texas, 'Former Mexican governor and presidential candidate sentenced for money laundering', March 2023

n: 'Metastasis': traffickers paid Ecuador's judges, prosecutors and police
d: Drug traffickers paid judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials in Ecuador to fix cases and protect them, a case known as 'Metastasis'. It came to light from the decrypted phone of a trafficker. After 28 days of hearings the National Court sentenced 20 of 21 defendants on 25 November 2024 to between three and ten years, with public service treated as an aggravating factor. The former president of the Judiciary Council, which oversees Ecuador's judges, drew nine years and four months for delaying a habeas corpus in favour of a trafficker's brother for money; another judge was convicted over a release order priced at $200,000. Two fugitives, a former legislator and a businessman, are subject to extradition requests to Venezuela and the United States.
cite: Fiscalia General del Estado, Caso Metastasis, from December 2023; Corte Nacional de Justicia verdicts, 25 November 2024; extradition requests, 2026

n: Albanian interior minister Tahiri convicted over cannabis-network links
d: Saimir Tahiri, Albania's former interior minister, the minister in charge of its police, was prosecuted over links to a cannabis-trafficking network run by his cousin's group. Albanian courts convicted him in 2019 of abuse of office, and the conviction was upheld on appeal; the trafficking counts did not result in conviction. Albania is a candidate to join the EU, which makes ministerial ties to crime groups a test of its institutions.
cite: Tirana courts, conviction 2019, upheld on appeal

n: 'Ndrangheta inside Calabria's local councils and professions
d: The 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, has got its people and influence into local government in Calabria, southern Italy. Dozens of Calabrian municipal councils have been dissolved for mafia infiltration under Italian law, which lets the national government remove a council found to be under mafia control. The Rinascita-Scott proceedings, with verdicts from 2021, convicted officials, lawyers and elected representatives alongside clan members. European law enforcement assesses that the 'Ndrangheta controls a large share of the cocaine entering Europe.
cite: Tribunale di Vibo Valentia / Catanzaro, Rinascita-Scott verdicts from 2021

n: Cocaine networks recruited Antwerp port workers, police and customs
d: Cocaine trafficking networks have recruited port workers, police officers and customs staff at the Port of Antwerp in Belgium to pull containers out and pass on information, and successive prosecutions from 2018 to 2024 have convicted such insiders. Antwerp is the port through which the largest volumes of cocaine in Europe move. In 2022 the Belgian justice minister was placed under protection after a kidnap plot.
cite: Antwerp criminal court proceedings, multiple, 2018–2024

n: Mexican cartels took over whole municipal police forces
d: Mexican drug cartels have taken control of entire municipal police forces, so that local officers worked for trafficking groups. Whole forces in Michoacán, Guerrero, Tamaulipas and elsewhere have been disarmed, disbanded or handed to federal control after being assessed as working for those groups, by federal and state government orders. Because the remedy is administrative, almost none of it produces a criminal conviction record.
cite: Mexican federal and state government disbandment orders, various

n: El Chapo paid Honduran president's brother Tony Hernández
d: Cocaine traffickers, including Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán of the Sinaloa Cartel, paid Juan Antonio 'Tony' Hernández, a member of Honduras's Congress and brother of President Juan Orlando Hernández. At his 2019 trial in Manhattan a former mayor and trafficker, Amílcar Alexander Ardón, testified that Guzmán personally gave Hernández $1 million in 2013 to be able to move cocaine through Honduras. Evidence also included cocaine packages stamped 'TH' and testimony that the proceeds funded the National Party's campaigns. He was convicted in October 2019 of importing cocaine, weapons offences and false statements, and sentenced in March 2021 to life plus 30 years.
cite: US v. Juan Antonio Hernandez Alvarado, S.D.N.Y., verdict October 2019, sentence March 2021; AP via KSL, 'Witness: El Chapo gave $1M to Honduran president's brother', 7 Oct 2019

n: Honduran police chief 'El Tigre' Bonilla protected cocaine loads for pay
d: Traffickers paid Juan Carlos 'El Tigre' Bonilla, Honduras's national police chief in 2012–2013, to provide armed police protection for cocaine loads crossing the country, US prosecutors said. He was extradited to New York in 2022, pleaded guilty in February 2024 to a cocaine trafficking conspiracy and was sentenced in August 2024 to 19 years. Through his family he maintains that the plea was tactical.
cite: US v. Bonilla Valladares, S.D.N.Y., plea February 2024, sentence August 2024

n: Cachiros cartel laundered money through the Rosenthals' Grupo Continental
d: The Cachiros, a Honduran drug-trafficking group, moved their money through Grupo Continental, a business group owned by the Rosenthal family, one of Honduras's most powerful political families. In October 2015 the US Treasury sanctioned a former vice-president, his son (a congressman and later presidential candidate) and a nephew as launderers for the Cachiros, under a US law targeting drug kingpins. Honduran regulators liquidated the family's bank within weeks. Yani Rosenthal pleaded guilty in New York in 2017 and served three years.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, October 2015; US v. Yankel Rosenthal, S.D.N.Y., plea 2017

n: Juárez Cartel used Quintana Roo under Governor Villanueva
d: The Juárez Cartel used the coast and airstrips of the Mexican state of Quintana Roo with the protection of its governor, Mario Villanueva Madrid, who governed from 1993 to 1999. Quintana Roo, on the Caribbean, includes Cancún. He was convicted in Mexico, then extradited to the US, where he pleaded guilty in Manhattan in 2010 to laundering the cartel's proceeds and was sentenced in 2011. He served his US and Mexican sentences one after the other across two decades.
cite: US v. Villanueva Madrid, S.D.N.Y., plea 2010, sentence 2011

n: Cartel paid commander of Mexico's US-vetted police unit for secrets
d: The El Seguimiento 39 cartel paid Iván Reyes Arzate, commander of the Mexican Federal Police's Sensitive Investigative Unit, $290,000 in 2016 to tell it what a joint investigation knew. The unit was vetted by US agencies so they could share intelligence with it. He pleaded guilty in Brooklyn in October 2021 and was sentenced in February 2022 to ten years.
cite: US v. Reyes Arzate, E.D.N.Y., plea October 2021, sentence February 2022

n: Mexico's defence minister accused of protecting the H-2 cartel
d: US prosecutors charged that Salvador Cienfuegos, Mexico's Secretary of National Defence from 2012 to 2018 and head of its army, took payments from the H-2 cartel to shield its members, including warning them about US investigations. He was arrested in Los Angeles in October 2020 on trafficking and money-laundering charges from a 2019 indictment. A month later the US Department of Justice dropped the case at the request of the State Department, after Mexico threatened to cut its security cooperation. Mexico's own inquiry closed in 2021 without charges, so the allegations were never tested in court.
cite: US v. Cienfuegos Zepeda, E.D.N.Y., indictment 2019, dismissal November 2020; FGR statement January 2021; NBC News, 'Former Mexican defense minister accused of smuggling drugs to U.S.', October 2020 (H-2 cartel, payments for protection)
undone: Charges dismissed by the Department of Justice at the State Department’s request after Mexico threatened security cooperation.

n: Traffickers had Guatemala's anti-drug police chief working for them
d: Adan Castillo, director of SAIA, Guatemala's lead anti-narcotics police agency, and his deputy operations chief were themselves working to move cocaine for traffickers into the United States. Both were arrested in Virginia while on a US-funded training visit, and in September 2006 they pleaded guilty in Washington to conspiring to distribute cocaine bound for the United States. The officers in charge of stopping cocaine in Guatemala were helping it through.
cite: US v. Castillo Aguilar and Aguilar Garcia, D.D.C., pleas September 2006

n: Guatemala's Vice-President and Interior Minister charged over cocaine
d: US prosecutors charged that drug traffickers bought protection from Guatemala's Vice-President, Roxana Baldetti, and its Interior Minister, Mauricio Lopez Bonilla, who ran the police. A US extradition request says Baldetti took money from traffickers during her 2011 campaign in return for a promise to limit law enforcement against them. Both were indicted in Washington in 2016 on one count of conspiring to distribute cocaine for import to the United States, over conduct between 2010 and 2015. She denies it. The drug charge has never been tried: Guatemala approved extradition only after her domestic cases end. She was convicted there instead of corruption: 15 and a half years in 2018 over a lake-cleaning contract whose chemical was water, salt and chlorine, and 16 years in 2022 for customs fraud.
cite: US District Court for the District of Columbia, indictment 2016; Guatemalan convictions October 2018 and 2022; extradition approved subject to prior resolution of domestic cases; InSight Crime, 'US Extradition Request Depicts Deep Ties Between Guatemala Ex-VP, Zetas', 2017

n: Santa Lucia mayor used his office to move a cartel's cocaine
d: A trafficking organisation used Romeo Ramos Cruz, mayor of the town of Santa Lucia in Escuintla, Guatemala, as its fixer inside local government. From 2022 to 2024 he used the mayor's office to organise its logistics. In one case he agreed to disguise a cocaine shipment from Venezuela as a delivery of cement and prepared a letter on official town-hall letterhead to help it get past inspection. He was extradited to the United States in August 2025 and pleaded guilty to conspiring to import cocaine. He faces a maximum of life in prison.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Columbia, extradition August 2025, guilty plea July 2026

n: Huistas trafficking leader sat in the Central American Parliament
d: US prosecutors say Freddy Salazar Flores, a sitting member of PARLACEN, the Central American Parliament (a regional assembly of Central American states), is a leader of the Huistas, a drug-trafficking organisation on Guatemala's border with Mexico, together with his father-in-law. That would mean the organisation had one of its own leaders holding a seat in a regional parliament. Both men appeared in a Washington court in May 2025 on a 2017 indictment for importing cocaine. Neither has been tried.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Columbia, indictment 2017, initial appearances May 2025

n: El Salvador officials secretly bargained with MS-13 and Barrio 18
d: According to the US Treasury, two Salvadoran officials, the director of prisons and the head of the Social Fabric Reconstruction Unit (a government programme for violence-hit neighbourhoods), secretly negotiated with the leaders of the MS-13 and Barrio 18 gangs. The gangs got privileges and money inside the prisons; in return they were to keep homicide numbers down and give the government electoral support. El Faro, a Salvadoran news site, reported the talks from 2020, and Treasury imposed sanctions in December 2021. The government denies it, and no case has been tried.
cite: OFAC designations, December 2021; El Faro reporting from 2020

n: AUC paramilitaries had the Colombian president's security chief
d: The AUC, a Colombian right-wing paramilitary army that was then among the country's largest cocaine exporters, had help from General Mauricio Santoyo, the national police general who ran security for President Alvaro Uribe. Santoyo pleaded guilty in Virginia in August 2012 to providing material support to the AUC, which the US listed as a terrorist group, and was sentenced to 13 years. The case showed that the paramilitaries had reached the officer closest to the president's own protection.
cite: US v. Santoyo Velasco, E.D. Va., plea August 2012

n: Venezuela's military intelligence chief worked for drug traffickers
d: Hugo Carvajal, head of Venezuela's military intelligence, used his post to help move cocaine and to aid the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army. US prosecutors describe him as a leader of the Cartel de los Soles, a name they use for trafficking that they say runs through Venezuela's officer corps itself. He was extradited from Spain in 2023 and in June 2025 pleaded guilty in New York to cocaine importation, narco-terrorism for the benefit of the FARC, and weapons charges.
cite: US v. Carvajal Barrios, S.D.N.Y., plea June 2025

n: Bolivia's anti-drug chief guarded traffickers' cocaine
d: Traffickers had Maximiliano Davila, head of the FELCN, Bolivia's anti-narcotics police force, working for them until 2019. At his trial in Manhattan, prosecutors showed he steered investigations away from traffickers allied with him and assigned armed FELCN officers under his command to guard their cocaine loads. He was convicted in October 2025 and sentenced to 25 years.
cite: US v. Davila Perez, S.D.N.Y., verdict October 2025, sentence March 2026

n: A Ultranza Py: a cocaine network inside Paraguay's police and Congress
d: A cocaine and money-laundering network in Paraguay had police officers, prosecutors and a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies on its side. The investigation, called A Ultranza Py, opened in February 2022, brought charges against them and led to the seizure of hundreds of properties. The man prosecutors named as the network's central figure fled before he could be arrested, and the proceedings continue.
cite: Ministerio Publico del Paraguay, Operativo A Ultranza Py, from February 2022

n: Suriname's counter-terrorism chief trafficked cocaine
rank: security unit chief and presidential family
d: Dino Bouterse, son of Suriname's President and head of the country's counter-terrorism unit, used his position to traffic cocaine and offered Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed group, a base in Suriname. US agents lured him to Panama and arrested him. He pleaded guilty in New York in August 2014 to cocaine importation, weapons offences and the Hezbollah offer, and was sentenced to 16 years in March 2015.
cite: US v. Dino Bouterse, S.D.N.Y., plea August 2014, sentence March 2015

n: Haitian police commander took drug traffickers' bribes
d: Drug traffickers paid Guy Philippe, then a senior commander in the Haitian National Police, to protect their cocaine shipments into Haiti. In his guilty plea he admitted taking $1.5 million to $3.5 million in bribes between 1999 and 2003 and sharing some with other police and security staff to keep their support. He was arrested in Port-au-Prince days after winning a Senate seat, pleaded guilty in Miami in April 2017 to conspiring to launder drug money, and was sentenced to nine years. He was deported to Haiti in 2023 and went back into politics.
cite: US v. Guy Philippe, S.D. Fla., plea April 2017; deportation November 2023; US Department of Justice press release, 'Haitian National Pleads Guilty to Conspiring to Launder Money Derived from Drug Trafficking', April 2017

n: Jamaica's government shielded the Shower Posse leader from extradition
rank: head of government and security forces
d: Christopher Coke led the Shower Posse, a gang based in Tivoli Gardens, a Kingston neighbourhood in the constituency of Prime Minister Bruce Golding. When the United States asked for Coke's extradition, the Jamaican government resisted for nine months and hired a Washington law firm to lobby against it. The police and army operation to arrest him in 2010 killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York in 2011. Golding had already resigned over the affair, and a 2016 commission of enquiry found the operation unjustified in how it was carried out.
cite: US v. Christopher Coke, S.D.N.Y., plea August 2011; West Kingston Commission of Enquiry report, 2016; Wikipedia, 'Bruce Golding' (MP for West Kingston)

n: Cuban officers moved cocaine for the Medellin cartel
rank: army general and interior ministry officers
d: Colombia's Medellin cartel had senior Cuban officials helping it move cocaine to Florida. General Arnaldo Ochoa, a decorated army commander, and a Ministry of the Interior colonel who ran the state's hard-currency businesses were court-martialled in 1989 for letting the cartel's cocaine pass through Cuban waters and airspace. Both were executed by firing squad in July 1989. The interior minister was dismissed and jailed in the same purge.
cite: Cuban special military tribunal, Causa No. 1, June–July 1989; TIME, 'Cuba: Reading the Coca Leaves', July 1989 (Medellin cartel)

n: Rosario traffickers had the Santa Fe police chief
d: A drug-trafficking network around Rosario, Argentina's third-largest city, was protected by Hugo Tognoli, who had headed Santa Fe province's drug unit and then took command of the whole provincial police. A federal court in Rosario convicted him in 2016 of protecting the network and sentenced him to six years. Rosario's murder rate has since run several times the national figure.
cite: Tribunal Oral Federal de Rosario, conviction 2016

n: Operation Guard Shack: Puerto Rico police guarded cocaine deals
d: Cocaine traffickers in Puerto Rico paid serving police officers to guard their deals. In an FBI undercover operation, officers were paid $500 to $4,500 per deal to provide armed protection in 125 transactions. In October 2010 89 law enforcement officers and 44 others were charged. Around 750 FBI personnel were flown in for the arrests, and the FBI called it the largest police corruption case in its history.
cite: US v. Rivera Guzman et al. and 25 related indictments, D.P.R., October 2010

n: Zemun clan merged with Serbia's special police unit
d: The Zemun clan, a Belgrade crime group with a share of the Balkan heroin trade, had merged with the JSO, the special operations unit of Serbia's interior ministry. In March 2003 a serving JSO commander shot dead Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic. A special court for organised crime in Belgrade convicted twelve people in May 2007, and the unit was disbanded.
cite: Special Court for Organised Crime, Belgrade, verdicts May 2007

n: Kavac clan protected by Montenegro's top prosecutor and police
d: The Kavac clan, a Montenegrin crime group trading cocaine, had protection from inside the state, prosecutors say. Messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service that police cracked, were passed by Europol (the EU's police agency) to Montenegro. They led to charges against the former chief special prosecutor, a former assistant police director and his son, a state security officer. Separate indictments name a former president of the Supreme Court, two former police directors and the mayor of Budva.
cite: Special State Prosecutor's Office of Montenegro, indictments 2023–2024

n: Susurluk crash exposed Turkish security ties to heroin traffickers
d: Heroin traffickers were working with Turkey's police and security services, as a car crash near Susurluk in November 1996 revealed. The crash killed a deputy police chief and a wanted trafficker and hitman who carried a diplomatic passport, and injured a member of parliament travelling with them. Interior minister Mehmet Agar, who ran the police, resigned on 8 November 1996. The parliamentary commission that followed in 1997 documented the working relationship between the security services and heroin trafficking, but almost no one was convicted.
cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk commission report, 1997

n: Crime groups paid UK police and prison officers
d: UK organised crime groups paid serving police and prison officers to pass them information and to move contraband. This came out through Operation Venetic, the National Crime Agency's use of EncroChat, an encrypted phone network that European police hacked in 2020. Reading the criminals' own messages led to thousands of UK prosecutions, among them those officers. The corruption was found through the traffickers' messages, not by internal checks.
cite: National Crime Agency Operation Venetic reporting, from 2020

n: Boshe meth labs were shielded by the village party secretary
d: Methamphetamine producers in Boshe village, Lufeng, in China's Guangdong province, had the village's Communist Party secretary, Cai Dongjia, shielding the labs and warning suspects. Three thousand police raided the village in December 2013 and seized three tonnes of meth. Officials said a fifth of its households were in the trade and that Boshe had supplied a third of China's meth. Cai was sentenced to death in 2016 and executed in 2019; a Lufeng drug squad captain was detained in the same investigation.
cite: Guangdong Higher People's Court, sentence 2016; Xinhua, execution January 2019

n: Yaba trafficker list named a sitting MP for Cox's Bazar
d: Bangladesh's own government list of yaba traffickers (yaba is a methamphetamine pill) named Abdur Rahman Bodi, the member of parliament for Cox's Bazar, the district through which almost all yaba enters the country. That placed the trade's alleged patron in parliament. He was convicted in February 2018 of concealing wealth and jailed for three years, but the trafficking allegations were never tried. In 2019 102 dealers, several of them his relatives, surrendered in a staged ceremony.
cite: Dhaka Special Judge's Court, Anti-Corruption Commission case, conviction February 2018

n: Ahmed Wali Karzai: opium trade and CIA payroll alleged
rank: provincial council chairman and presidential family
d: Ahmed Wali Karzai, half-brother of Afghanistan's President and chair of the Kandahar provincial council, was described by US officials as taking part in the opium trade, and was reported to be on the payroll of the CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency. Both allegations put outside interests, drug traders and a foreign spy service, inside the most powerful office in southern Afghanistan. He denied the drug claims and was never charged in any court. He was shot dead by his own security chief in 2011.
cite: US State Department and military reporting, 2009–2010; SIGAR and UNODC assessments

n: Kyrgyz customs deputy chief ran a smuggling scheme from inside
d: Raiymbek Matraimov, deputy head of Kyrgyzstan's customs service, used the post to run a customs scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country. Reporting by OCCRP (a journalists' network on organised crime) and the Kyrgyz outlet Kloop in 2019–2020 tied the scheme to a smuggling business run by a secretive Uighur family. In December 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned him under the Magnitsky Act, a law for punishing corrupt officials abroad. Journalists who documented the network were prosecuted or forced out. He settled a domestic corruption case by repayment and served no prison term at the time.
cite: OFAC Global Magnitsky designation, December 2020; OCCRP and Kloop investigations 2019–2020; OCCRP, 'U.S. Sanctions Matraimov Under Magnitsky Act', December 2020

n: Akasha brothers paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police
d: The Akasha brothers, who ran a heroin organisation in Mombasa, Kenya, paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police officers over two years to block their extradition to the United States. They admitted this as part of an obstruction count when they pleaded guilty in New York in October 2018, and were sentenced in 2019. None of the Kenyan officials who took the money has been named or charged in Kenya.
cite: US v. Baktash Akasha Abdalla et al., S.D.N.Y., pleas October 2018, sentences 2019

n: Guinea-Bissau's air force chief charged with moving cocaine
d: US prosecutors charged that Ibraima Papa Camara, chief of staff of Guinea-Bissau's air force, conspired with traffickers to store and move cocaine through the country, alongside the navy chief. Guinea-Bissau is a transit point for South American cocaine heading to Europe. The US Treasury had already named him a drug trafficker in 2010 under the Kingpin Act, which lets it freeze traffickers' assets. He was indicted in New York in 2013 but stayed in Bissau and was never handed over.
cite: US v. Na Tchuto and Camara, S.D.N.Y., indictment 2013; OFAC Kingpin designation 2010

n: Ghana police operations chief taped with MV Benjamin cocaine suspects
d: Cocaine traffickers in Ghana were taped meeting a senior police commander after their load vanished. In 2006 seventy-seven parcels of cocaine were landed from the vessel MV Benjamin and then disappeared. A secret recording surfaced of ACP Kofi Boakye, Director of Operations at police headquarters, meeting suspects including Kwabena 'Tagor' Amaning and Alhaji Issah Abass at his home, where they discussed the missing drugs. A committee of enquiry led by Supreme Court judge Georgina Wood found the police account unsatisfactory, said Boakye's conduct damaged the integrity of the police, and recommended his prosecution; he was sent on leave. Around 2009 President John Atta Mills recalled him to duty, and he later headed the police education department.
cite: Georgina Wood Committee report, Government of Ghana, 2006; GhanaWeb, 'The 2006 MV Benjamin cocaine saga that nearly cut short COP Kofi Boakye's career' (https://mobile.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/NewsArchive/The-2006-MV-Benjamin-cocaine-saga-that-nearly-cut-short-COP-Kofi-Boakye-rsquo-s-career-1746635)

n: Air Cocaine: Mali officials alleged to protect a traffickers' flight
d: Cocaine traffickers flying a Boeing 727 from Venezuela had protection from local officials and armed groups in northern Mali, UN and Malian investigations indicated. In 2009 the plane unloaded cocaine at a desert airstrip at Tarkint and was then burned. Arrests were made in the capital, Bamako, but they led to no senior conviction, and the owners of the aircraft were never established. The case was examined in UNODC and UN Panel of Experts reporting from 2010 and in Malian judicial proceedings.
cite: UNODC and UN Panel of Experts reporting from 2010; Malian judicial proceedings

n: Tabasco's security secretary accused of leading a CJNG-linked gang
d: Prosecutors accuse Hernan Bermudez Requena, Tabasco state's Secretary of Security and top police official from 2018 to 2024, of running La Barredora, a criminal group tied to the CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel), from inside his office. He fled Mexico in early 2025, was arrested in Paraguay in September and sent back within days. He is held at the Altiplano federal prison on charges of criminal association, extortion and kidnapping.
cite: Fiscalia General del Estado de Tabasco warrant, February 2025; Paraguayan SENAD arrest and expulsion, September 2025

n: Los Zetas ran parts of Piedras Negras state prison
d: Los Zetas, a Mexican cartel, used the state prison in Piedras Negras, Coahuila, as a base, a workshop and a site for disposing of bodies, after the prison administration handed it control of parts of the facility. Testimony in Texas trials of Zetas leaders and a Coahuila state investigation in 2016–2017 established the arrangement. Prosecutions reached prison staff but not the officials who authorised it.
cite: Coahuila state attorney general investigation, 2016–2017; testimony in US v. Trevino Morales, W.D. Tex.

n: Guatemalan congressman passed information and cash for a trafficker
d: Jose Armando Ubico Aguilar, a member of Guatemala's Congress from 2016 to 2024, worked for a drug trafficker while in office. He admitted passing drug-related information and cash to another Guatemalan official on the trafficker's behalf. He was indicted in Texas in March 2021 while still sitting in Congress, and pleaded guilty in May 2024 to an international trafficking conspiracy.
cite: US v. Ubico Aguilar, E.D. Tex., indictment March 2021, plea May 2024

n: Venezuelan general armed the FARC
d: The FARC, Colombia's guerrilla army, had a retired Venezuelan army major general, Cliver Alcala Cordones, supplying it with firearms, he admitted in a US court. Alcala was charged in the same 2020 US indictment as President Nicolas Maduro, which alleges that senior Venezuelan officers worked with the FARC to move cocaine; prosecutors use the name Cartel de los Soles for that network. Alcala surrendered to the US Drug Enforcement Administration in Colombia, pleaded guilty to providing material support, including firearms, to the FARC, and was sentenced to 260 months in April 2024. He was the first defendant in that indictment to be sentenced.
cite: US v. Alcala Cordones, S.D.N.Y., plea 2023, sentence April 2024

n: Cocaine rings used police officers in the Campo de Gibraltar
d: Cocaine smugglers in the Campo de Gibraltar, the Spanish area around the port of Algeciras, used police officers to protect their loads. In April 2024 a municipal officer and two national police officers were sentenced to more than seven years each for guarding a 367-kilogram shipment. A separate 2022 operation arrested five municipal officers at the port with an officer stationed in Ceuta, a customs official and a former police official over 6.2 tonnes moved through the Strait of Gibraltar.
cite: Audiencia Provincial de Cadiz, sentence April 2024; Policia Nacional operation, Algeciras, 2022

n: Antwerp cocaine networks had serving police officers
d: Cocaine networks working through the port of Antwerp, Belgium, had serving police officers among their members. In January 2024 22 people, three of them police officers, were arrested. In October 2024 a Brussels court sentenced dozens in Belgium's largest trafficking trial, built almost entirely on decrypted messages from the Sky ECC and EncroChat encrypted phone networks. Customs seized 116 tonnes of cocaine at the port in 2023 alone.
cite: Belgian federal police operation, January 2024; Brussels correctional court verdicts, October 2024

n: Vietnamese drug officers shielded a Laos–Vietnam network
d: A drug network moving narcotics from Laos into Vietnam had protection from police drug investigators. In 2024 two former officers of a Hanoi district drug team were indicted for shielding the network, which moved 137 kilograms. In 2025 a senior officer in Viet Tri, Phu Tho province, was sentenced to life for financing the purchase of 12,000 tablets that he planned to turn into a staged arrest. Vietnam imposes the death penalty for trafficking quantities like these.
cite: Supreme People's Procuracy indictments, 2024; Hanoi People's Court verdict, 2025

n: Venezuela's Vice-President named as protector of traffickers
d: The US Treasury found that Tareck El Aissami, appointed Venezuela's Executive Vice-President in 2017, helped cocaine shipments leave Venezuela and protected traffickers operating inside it. In February 2017, weeks after his appointment, Treasury sanctioned him under the Kingpin Act, which freezes traffickers' US assets, together with a front man and a network of petroleum, engineering and holding companies. This is a government finding, not a court verdict, and it has never been tested at trial.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, February 2017

n: CJNG and Los Cuinis paid a Mexican federal judge for rulings
d: The US Treasury found that Isidro Avelar Gutierrez, a sitting Mexican federal magistrate judge, took payments from the CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel) and its allied group Los Cuinis in return for rulings favouring their senior members. Treasury sanctioned him under the Kingpin Act in May 2019. The case came as a US sanctions listing rather than a Mexican prosecution.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, May 2019

n: Nayarit governor took bribes from the CJNG and Beltran Leyva
d: The US Treasury found that Roberto Sandoval Castaneda, Governor of Nayarit state from 2011 to 2017, took bribes from the CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel), and earlier from the Beltran Leyva organisation, in return for information and protection, and misappropriated state assets. Treasury sanctioned him in May 2019 under the Global Magnitsky order on corruption. His state attorney general, Edgar Veytia, had pleaded guilty to drug charges in Brooklyn two months earlier.
cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 13818, May 2019

n: Los Pochos trafficking group led by a Guatemalan mayor
d: Erik Suniga Rodriguez led a Guatemalan drug-trafficking organisation, Los Pochos, while serving as a town mayor, according to the US Treasury. In December 2019 Treasury sanctioned him under the Kingpin Act together with the organisation, four associates and five Guatemalan companies. It sanctioned the group again in February 2024, noting a change of leadership and that its members were still involved in local politics.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, December 2019; redesignation under E.O. 14059, February 2024

n: Haiti's former president accused of using office for traffickers
d: The US Treasury found that Michel Martelly, President of Haiti from 2011 to 2016, abused his influence to help traffic cocaine to the United States, worked with Haitian drug traffickers and sponsored and financed gangs. Treasury sanctioned him in August 2024; Canada had sanctioned him in November 2022 over financing gangs. In Haiti the gangs and the cocaine transit route have become closely tied. He denies the allegations, and no court has heard them.
cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, August 2024; Global Affairs Canada sanctions, November 2022; Al Jazeera, 'US sanctions former Haitian president over alleged drug trafficking', 20 August 2024

n: Captagon producer held a seat in Syria's parliament
d: Amer Khiti, a sitting member of Syria's parliament, was sanctioned by the UK in March 2023 and the EU in April 2023 over companies used to produce, package and move captagon, an amphetamine-type pill smuggled across the Middle East. The captagon trade thereby had one of its own operators holding a seat in the national legislature.
cite: UK FCDO designation, March 2023; Council of the EU designation, April 2023

n: PCC gang allegedly paid Sao Paulo police for protection
d: Prosecutors allege that the PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), Brazil's largest criminal faction, arranged around 30 million reais in payments to a police chief, an officer and three investigators of the Sao Paulo civil police to shield its members from investigation, and that one produced a false document for the faction. The arrests came in December 2024 under Operation Tacitus. The judge who authorised them wrote that no faction reaches the PCC's size without officials in the security services. The defence says the facts were investigated and shelved before.
cite: Ministerio Publico de Sao Paulo, Operacao Tacitus, arrests December 2024

n: Gulf Cartel paid Mexico's deputy attorney general
d: Mario Ruiz Massieu, Mexico's Deputy Attorney General from 1993 to 1994, ran the country's drug prosecutions while taking traffickers' money. He moved about $9 million in cash into Houston bank accounts, carried by an aide on some twenty-five commercial flights. In 1997 a Houston civil jury, in a case to seize the money, found that it had been paid by traffickers, mainly the Gulf Cartel, for protection. He fought extradition under house arrest for four years and killed himself in New Jersey in 1999 before any criminal trial.
cite: US civil forfeiture proceedings, S.D. Tex., jury finding 1997; extradition litigation 1995–1999

n: Cali Cartel funded Colombia's 1994 presidential campaign
rank: head of state and campaign officials
d: The Cali Cartel put money into Ernesto Samper's 1994 presidential campaign, prosecutors established in the Proceso 8000 investigation that began in 1995. The campaign treasurer, the defence minister and the comptroller were convicted. In June 1996 a congressional commission cleared Samper himself, in a vote his opponents called a whitewash. The United States revoked his visa.
cite: Fiscalia General de la Nacion, Proceso 8000, from 1995; Camara de Representantes vote, June 1996

n: Guinea-Bissau's army chief charged with cocaine and arming the FARC
d: US prosecutors charged that General Antonio Indjai, chief of staff of Guinea-Bissau's armed forces and leader of the 2012 coup, conspired with traffickers to move cocaine through the country and to arm the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army, including a proposal to supply surface-to-air missiles in return. He was indicted in New York in 2013 and never handed over. The navy and air force chiefs were charged in the same period.
cite: US v. Indjai, S.D.N.Y., indictment 2013

n: Lungi airport staff helped land a cocaine flight in Sierra Leone
d: Cocaine traffickers had airport and security staff at Lungi, Sierra Leone's international airport, working for them. With that help, in July 2008 a twin-engine aircraft painted with Red Cross markings landed there carrying around 700 kilograms of cocaine. The prosecutions that followed in Sierra Leone's High Court convicted airport and security personnel along with the foreign crew. In June 2009 testimony to the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee called the convictions historic for the region, since neighbouring Guinea-Bissau had tried no drug case since 2005.
cite: Sierra Leone High Court convictions, 2009; US Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing, June 2009

n: Operation Black Tie: Bosnian officials worked for the Nizic network
d: The Nizic network, a Balkan cocaine organisation whose kingpin was already sentenced in the Netherlands, had corrupt Bosnian officials working as its facilitators, according to Europol, the EU police agency. Twenty-three people were arrested in Sarajevo in April 2024 for trafficking and laundering for the kingpin's inner circle. Europol said those detained included corrupt officials as well as accomplices.
cite: Europol and Bosnian security agencies, Operation Black Tie, April 2024

n: Thai senator charged over a Myanmar-linked drug network
d: Prosecutors charged that a drug network linked to Myanmar reached into Thailand's upper house through Senator Upakit Pachariyangkun. He was indicted in 2023 on narcotics trafficking and money-laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman arrested in Bangkok in 2022, whom the United States had sanctioned for supporting Myanmar's military government. The senator's Thai-American son-in-law was among those arrested, and Thailand's Narcotics Control Board seized property worth over 400 million baht from his homes. The drugs came from Shan State, a production area in Myanmar.
cite: Thai Office of the Attorney General indictment, 2023; Narcotics Control Board seizures; OFAC designations of the associated network

n: Cosa Nostra and Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti
d: Palermo prosecutors charged that Giulio Andreotti, seven times Prime Minister of Italy, put the influence of his office at the disposal of Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia, in return for electoral support, and that the Mafia expected him to fix the Maxi Trial, which had convicted 475 of its members over a heroin trade running through New York. He was acquitted in October 1999 and again on appeal in 2003. The appeal judges found he had ties to mobsters before 1980 but held that the time limit for prosecuting them had expired. The Court of Cassation, Italy's highest court, closed the case in 2004.
cite: Tribunale di Palermo, acquittal October 1999; Corte d'Appello 2003; Corte di Cassazione 2004

n: Traffickers bought federal judges in Oran and Salta, Argentina
d: A drug trafficker in northern Argentina's Salta province bought rulings from federal judges. In March 2019 the former federal judge of Oran, Reynoso, was sentenced to 13 years as head of a group that took money and property in return for rulings that favoured traffickers. The same trafficker had bought a different federal judge in 2007, who was removed and convicted; that judge killed himself in 2020 as his arrest approached. A federal judge in Mendoza was separately charged over links to trafficking groups.
cite: Tribunal Oral Federal de Salta, conviction of ex-judge Reynoso, March 2019; earlier conviction of judge Sola Torino, 2007

n: Caso Purga: a former legislator steered Guayas courts
d: Ecuadorian prosecutors say a former legislator was the power behind the courts of Guayas province, the area around the port city of Guayaquil, and arranged payments to judges to get people released. The Caso Purga file, opened in 2024, charged judges alongside him. Testimony described payments for releases, including a failed attempt to free a former vice-president. The usual method was sentence reductions granted by prison-guarantee judges (judges who oversee sentences and prison conditions), who had no power to grant them.
cite: Ecuadorian Fiscalia General del Estado, Caso Purga, from 2024

n: Brazilian judge signed rulings for a cocaine trafficking route
d: A cocaine trafficking route from Bolivia through Paraguay into Minas Gerais and on to Rio and north-east Brazil had a judge working in its favour. Federal police arrested Amaury de Lima e Souza, judge of the criminal enforcement court (which oversees sentences) in Juiz de Fora, in June 2014 during an operation against the route. Investigators found a series of rulings he had signed for traffickers, including one granting house arrest to a defendant prosecutors had charged. In October 2022 he was sentenced to 24 years and four months.
cite: Tribunal de Justica de Minas Gerais, 5th criminal chamber, sentence October 2022; Policia Federal operation, June 2014

n: Cartel de la Toga: politicians bought Colombia's Supreme Court
rank: supreme court presidents and anti-corruption prosecutor
d: Members of Congress under investigation for ties to the AUC, a right-wing paramilitary army, paid judges of Colombia's Supreme Court, which tries sitting legislators, to shelve or steer their cases. This bribery network, known as the Cartel de la Toga (the Robes Cartel), included two former presidents of the Supreme Court, a sitting magistrate and the national anti-corruption prosecutor, all convicted. One former court president was sentenced to 16 years; another was sentenced to 10 in February 2026 and is subject to an Interpol red notice. The prosecutor was convicted in Colombia and separately in Miami.
cite: Corte Suprema de Justicia de Colombia, Sala Especial, convictions 2021–2026; US v. Moreno Rivera, S.D. Fla., 2019

n: Colombian prosecutor held property for the Gulf Clan
d: A serving Colombian prosecutor was charged in July 2023 with lending her name to hide property belonging to a front man for the Gulf Clan, Colombia's largest cocaine trafficking organisation. Putting assets in her name placed the Gulf Clan's property under the protection of someone inside the prosecution service. She was placed under house arrest.
cite: Fiscalia General de la Nacion charge and house arrest order, July 2023

n: Michoacanazo: officials accused of La Familia ties, all freed
d: La Familia Michoacana, a cartel based in the Mexican state of Michoacan, was accused of having more than 30 state and municipal officials, including ten mayors, working for it. Mexican federal police arrested them in May 2009 in an operation that became known as the 'Michoacanazo'. Within two years every one of them had been released after federal judges found the prosecution's evidence insufficient. The case pitted the federal government against the state government and against its own courts, and ended without a single conviction.
cite: Procuraduria General de la Republica prosecutions, May 2009; federal judicial releases 2009-2011; Mexican Law Review study of the case

n: Kenyan MP and ports minister named a drug kingpin
d: Harun Mwau was designated by the US as a drug kingpin in June 2011 while a sitting member of Kenya's parliament. He had earlier headed the national anti-corruption agency, funded a presidential campaign, and been appointed assistant transport minister with responsibility for container arrangements and the Ports Authority, which gave him a say over the port through which drugs would pass. He resigned after being named in parliament and has always denied the allegations. A police investigation cleared him, in what researchers described as controversial circumstances.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, June 2011; Kenyan parliamentary naming and subsequent police inquiry

n: Trafficker paid South Africa's police chief and Interpol head
d: Glenn Agliotti, a drug trafficker, paid Jackie Selebi while Selebi was national commissioner of the South African Police Service and at the same time president of Interpol, the international police cooperation organisation. Selebi was convicted of corruption in July 2010 and sentenced to 15 years; the Supreme Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in 2011. In a separate case in 2011 Sheryl Cwele, wife of the state security minister, was convicted of conspiring to traffic drugs.
cite: South Gauteng High Court, conviction July 2010, sentence August 2010; Supreme Court of Appeal 2011; separate conviction of Sheryl Cwele, 2011

n: Ruling party figures and heroin traffickers in Mozambique
d: Heroin traffickers in Mozambique worked for three decades in what researchers call 'a tight integration' with figures in the ruling party. The 2018 research for the Global Initiative and ENACT, by Haysom, Gastrow and Shaw, pointed to near-zero heroin seizures in Mozambique as evidence that state protection kept the trade moving. It named a principal figure who was designated as a trafficker abroad while remaining a prominent businessman at home. Members of his family were arrested in Portugal and Eswatini, and one was shot dead in Maputo in 2012. None was charged in Mozambique.
cite: Global Initiative and ENACT research by Haysom, Gastrow and Shaw, 2018; LSE International Development working paper 18-190

n: Liberian police and airport security charged over a cocaine route
d: After Liberia's largest recorded seizure, close to four tonnes of cocaine bound for Europe, the police inspector general said senior government officials were involved in trafficking. The national police charged the head of its own Major Crimes Unit and another official, and named a deputy commander responsible for security at Roberts International Airport, the main airport, as an active participant. Twelve suspects were charged in the seizure case in 2026, and a former vice-president was separately indicted on trafficking charges.
cite: Liberia National Police charges and Inspector General statements, 2026; indictment of the former vice-president, 2026

n: Sierra Leone's aviation minister cleared a cocaine flight
d: Proceedings in the 2008 Lungi cocaine case indicated that Sierra Leone's minister of transport and aviation had given landing clearance for the aircraft carrying around 700 kilograms of cocaine, giving the traffickers help from inside the cabinet. He was dismissed, but only by administrative decision; the allegation was never tried in court.
cite: Sierra Leone government dismissal, 2008–2009; Africa Center for Strategic Studies review of the case

n: Costa Rican security official and judge worked for cocaine traffickers
rank: vice-minister of public security, later judge
d: The US Treasury found that Gamboa Sanchez, a former Vice Minister of Public Security in Costa Rica who later sat as a judge, helped move tens of millions of dollars' worth of cocaine from Colombia through Costa Rica to the United States and Europe, and used his contacts inside the government to obtain information on ongoing counter-narcotics investigations. He was arrested on 23 June 2025 on a US extradition request, weeks after Costa Rica changed its constitution in May 2025 to allow extradition of its own citizens for drug trafficking and terrorism. Treasury sanctioned him on 15 August 2025.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0227 and OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, 15 August 2025; Costa Rican arrest, 23 June 2025; constitutional reform on extradition signed May 2025

n: Caso Colorado: traffickers recruited Costa Rican police as lookouts
d: A drug-trafficking group that controlled the Caribbean lowland corridor of Costa Rica recruited police officers stationed at Guapiles and Cariari de Pococi to warn it of raids, checkpoints and investigators' movements, so drugs could be moved or hidden in time. Investigators of the OIJ, Costa Rica's judicial police, found regular telephone contact between the group and the officers. In 2026 five officers were charged before the specialised organised crime court.
cite: Organismo de Investigacion Judicial, case file 21-000115-0622-PE; Fiscalia Adjunta contra el Narcotrafico charges, 2026

n: Dominican drug agency and navy officers worked for traffickers
d: Traffickers in the Dominican Republic had officers of the National Drug Control Agency (DNCD) and the navy working for them. Three senior DNCD officials were arrested while providing security to traffickers waiting for a shipment bound for Puerto Rico. A navy officer in charge of port security was accused of moving 800 kilograms to Spain, and in 2008 nearly twenty officials, mostly navy, were accused of killing seven Colombian traffickers to take 1.3 tonnes. Since 2009 more than 700 DNCD staff have been removed, around 200 of them suspected of trafficking, and the national police expelled about 1,400 officers from 2010.
cite: DNCD arrests and dismissal statistics reported 2012-2013; Dominican prosecutions of navy and police personnel

n: Escobar of the Sahara network included Moroccan MPs
d: The Escobar of the Sahara network, a cannabis and cocaine trafficking organisation named after a jailed Malian trafficker, had Moroccan politicians among its members. In June 2026 a Casablanca court sentenced 29 people after a two-year trial, among them a construction figure and former head of a regional council, who got 12 years, and two former members of parliament from the governing party, who got 10 each. The case began when the Malian said his Moroccan political associates had seized his assets after his 2019 arrest. Charges covered drug and gold trafficking, corruption and laundering. One defendant was acquitted and appeals are open.
cite: Casablanca Court of Appeal, verdicts 26 June 2026

n: Guyanese police officer arranged safe passage for traffickers
d: The US Treasury found that a serving Guyanese law enforcement officer arranged safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers moving cocaine through Guyana. Treasury sanctioned him on 5 June 2025, along with a former officer wanted over the 2024 abduction of a policeman. Neither has been tried.
