Treasury noted that Guyana is a close US partner, but that the State Department treats corruption there as a significant obstacle to counter-narcotics work.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0156 and OFAC designations under E.O. 14059, 5 June 2025; ICE HSI New York investigation

n: Kings Romans network controls part of a Lao economic zone
d: The Kings Romans network, headed by Zhao Wei, gained control of part of Laos through a state concession. In 2007 Laos granted the Chinese company Kings Romans a concession over the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone, on the Lao side of the area where Laos, Thailand and Myanmar meet. In January 2018 the US Treasury sanctioned Zhao Wei and his wife over heroin and methamphetamine trafficking and laundering. The US State Department reported in 2024 that the zone is controlled and administered in part by transnational criminal organisations, and that no complicit official has been investigated or prosecuted. Laos arrested more than 20,000 people for drug offences between 2015 and 2019.
cite: OFAC Transnational Criminal Organizations designation, January 2018; US State Department Trafficking in Persons Report 2024

n: Papua New Guinea police accused of enabling cocaine flights
d: Australian-based organisers flew cocaine through Papua New Guinea, and police officers there were alleged to have helped the night flights. In 2020 a Cessna loaded with 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed on a makeshift runway outside Port Moresby. The police commissioner then said publicly that there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary and promised to remove them. The organisers were convicted in Victoria, Australia, and the pilot was jailed for 18 years in PNG, but the officers were not charged. Fiji's drug intelligence chief has raised the same concern about infiltration of law enforcement there.
cite: Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary statements, 2020; Victoria County Court sentences, July 2026; Lowy Institute analysis of Pacific trafficking

n: Chapitos accused of installing Sinaloa's governor
d: US prosecutors allege that the Chapitos, the faction of the Sinaloa Cartel led by sons of Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzman, helped Ruben Rocha Moya win the 2021 election for Governor of Sinaloa and then gained control of state and local police. They say he met the faction before the election and promised to install friendly officials, and that cartel members stole ballot boxes and intimidated rivals. He and nine other current and former officials, including a senator and the mayor of Culiacan, were indicted in Manhattan in April 2026. He rejects the accusations and resigned on 1 May 2026. Mexico said the extradition request lacked evidence and opened its own inquiry; none of the ten is in custody.
cite: US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026; Fiscalia General de la Republica statement, 2026; resignations reported 1-2 May 2026; widely reported background on the Chapitos as the faction led by Joaquin Guzman's sons

n: Sinaloa Cartel protection network in Culiacan's government and police
rank: mayor, police commanders and a senator
d: US prosecutors allege that the Sinaloa Cartel had a protection network across Sinaloa state's government and police. Nine officials were charged alongside Governor Ruben Rocha Moya in an indictment unsealed in Manhattan on 29 April 2026: the mayor of Culiacan, the state capital, a sitting senator, the state deputy attorney general, a former public security secretary and several police commanders. One is also charged over the kidnapping of a source for the US Drug Enforcement Administration and a relative, both of whom died.
cite: US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026

n: Guatemalan anti-drug police official worked for traffickers
d: Cocaine traffickers had the leadership of Guatemala's anti-drug police working for them. The force's chief, Adan Castillo, his deputy and a third official, Rubilio Orlando Palacios, were arrested when the three travelled to the United States in November 2005, after a four-month investigation by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and Guatemalan authorities. A three-count Washington indictment charged them with helping traffickers ship cocaine, and they pleaded guilty in 2006. The DEA administrator called them Trojan horses for the addiction they were meant to prevent.
cite: US District Court for the District of Columbia, indictment November 2005; pleas 2006

n: Tramadol network included Chad's own security and intelligence officials
d: A transnational network trafficking tramadol, a prescription painkiller sold illegally across the Sahel, counted high-ranking Chadian security and intelligence officials among its members. A court in N'Djamena, Chad's capital, sentenced ten people on 24 July 2020, those officials among them. Analysts at the Institute for Security Studies and ENACT who read the court documents described a network with strong Chadian connections and large sums circulating among its members, some of which was used in attempts to corrupt judges and the security services. Because senior army and intelligence figures were inside the network, the institutions expected to enforce the law against it were the same ones it had reached.
cite: Court judgment, N'Djamena, 24 July 2020; Institute for Security Studies and ENACT analysis of the court documents, 2020; UNODC Sahel tramadol reporting, 2017

n: Maduro charged with using Venezuela's state to move FARC cocaine
d: US prosecutors allege that Nicolas Maduro, as Venezuela's head of state, worked with the FARC, a Colombian guerrilla group, to traffic cocaine to the United States, using Venezuelan military and intelligence resources to protect shipments. The indictment, filed in the Southern District of New York in March 2020, charges him with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation and weapons counts alongside serving and former officials. The State Department reward for his arrest was raised twice, reaching $50 million in 2025. US forces captured Maduro in Caracas on 3 January 2026; he pleaded not guilty in New York on 5 January, and a trial is set for June 2027. No trial has yet taken place and the evidence is untested; the indictment is an accusation.
cite: US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment March 2020; US Department of State Narcotics Rewards Program notices; Wikipedia, 'Prosecution of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores' (capture 3 January 2026, not-guilty plea 5 January 2026, trial date 1 June 2027 set 22 July 2026)

n: Cabello accused of leading a trafficking structure from high office
d: US authorities accuse Diosdado Cabello, one of the most powerful figures in Venezuela's ruling party, of helping lead the 'Cartel de los Soles', the name US prosecutors give to Venezuelan officials who allegedly protected and profited from cocaine trafficking. The US Treasury's sanctions office, OFAC, designated him under the Kingpin Act (a law that freezes the assets of alleged drug traffickers) in May 2018, and the 2020 New York indictment against Nicolas Maduro names him as a leader of the same structure. Cabello has held the presidency of the National Assembly, the vice-presidency of the ruling party and, from 2024, the interior ministry, which runs the police. Both US actions are executive and prosecutorial steps, not findings by a court.
cite: US Treasury OFAC Kingpin Act designation, May 2018; US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., 2020

n: Honduran ex-president Lobo named as taker of traffickers' money
d: Honduran drug traffickers are alleged to have paid Porfirio Lobo Sosa, President of Honduras from 2010 to 2014. US prosecutors named him as a recipient of trafficking proceeds during the New York cases against his son, Fabio Lobo, and against his successor, Juan Orlando Hernandez. In July 2021 the State Department put him on its Engel list, a public list of officials in Central America it considers corrupt or undemocratic. He has never been charged. The allegations come from cooperating witnesses (defendants testifying in return for lighter sentences) in other people's trials, the weakest category of evidence on this map.
cite: US Department of State section 353 corrupt and undemocratic actors list, July 2021; trial testimony in US v. Fabio Lobo and US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y.

n: US trial witnesses said cartels bribed a serving Mexican president
d: Witnesses in two US trials testified that Mexican cartels paid bribes to a serving president of Mexico. The testimony came in the 2019 trial of Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzman, leader of the Sinaloa Cartel, and the 2023 trial of Genaro Garcia Luna, Mexico's former federal security chief, both in Brooklyn federal court. The witnesses were cooperating with prosecutors and negotiating their own sentences, no documents corroborated the claim, and no charge has been brought. It is recorded because it was said under oath in a US federal court, not because it is established.
cite: Trial testimony, US v. Guzman Loera, E.D.N.Y., 2019, and US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., 2023

n: Venezuela's anti-drug chief charged with tipping off traffickers
d: US prosecutors allege that Nestor Reverol, while head of Venezuela's national anti-drug office, worked for drug traffickers by warning them of raids and blocking seizures. He was indicted in the Eastern District of New York in 2015, with the charges made public in August 2016. Instead of being removed, he was promoted to Interior Minister the following year, putting him in charge of the police, and later moved to the electricity ministry. Venezuela does not extradite its officials, and the indictment has never been acted on.
cite: US v. Reverol Torres and Ordonez, E.D.N.Y., indictment 2015, unsealed August 2016

n: Oran cocaine case reached officials; Algeria's police chief removed
d: A cocaine-importing network around the businessman Kamel Chikhi reached Algerian judges and officials, and its exposure brought down the head of the national police. In May 2018 Algerian authorities seized 701 kilograms of cocaine at the port of Oran, hidden in a shipment of frozen meat Chikhi had imported. Press reports said investigators found video of Chikhi meeting judges and other officials, and the case was linked to judges, prosecutors, mayors and the children of senior politicians. Abdelghani Hamel, Director-General of National Security (head of the national police), was removed after the seizure. Military and civilian courts later convicted Hamel and several generals of corruption and illicit enrichment, rather than narcotics offences; Algeria published little about the trafficking case itself.
cite: Algerian Blida military tribunal and Tipaza court judgments, 2019-2020; Algerian Ministry of Justice statements; Fanack, 'Cocaine Seizure Stirs Algerian Politics', 2018 (frozen-meat shipment, Kamel Chikhi, reported video with judges and officials)

n: Zawiya smuggling networks ran a Libyan coast guard unit
d: Smuggling networks in Zawiya, a port town in western Libya, had their own man commanding the local coast guard unit, the force meant to stop them. Abd al-Rahman Milad, known as 'Bija', was serving as the Zawiya coast guard commander when the UN Security Council sanctioned him in June 2018 for fuel smuggling, migrant trafficking and violence at sea. He was detained in Libya in 2020 and released without conviction in 2021, and was shot dead west of Tripoli in September 2024. The same coastal networks move hashish and medicines; the UN designation covers the smuggling economy rather than narcotics specifically.
cite: UN Security Council Committee on Libya sanctions listing, June 2018; UN Panel of Experts on Libya reports; The National, 'Notorious Libyan coastguard commander killed', 2 September 2024

n: Captagon smugglers recruited Jordanian soldiers at the Syrian border
d: Smugglers moving captagon, an amphetamine-type pill produced in Syria, recruited serving and former Jordanian soldiers to carry the pills and weapons across the border. Jordan's State Security Court, which hears security and drug cases, has convicted soldiers in cases running from 2022 onward. The Jordanian army also carried out airstrikes inside Syria against production and storage sites. The convictions show the smugglers' protection reached into the force responsible for stopping them.
cite: Jordanian State Security Court judgments, 2022-2024; Jordanian Armed Forces statements

n: Scam-compound owners protected by Cambodian politics, one a senator
d: The owners of Cambodian fraud compounds, sites where trafficked workers are forced to run online scams, have had political protection, and one of them sat in Cambodia's Senate. US Treasury designations (sanctions that freeze assets and bar dealings) in December 2019, September 2024 and October 2025, and matching UK designations, named Cambodian tycoons and companies and repeatedly gave political protection as the reason the compounds operate openly. One designated figure was a serving senator. The designations are executive findings; Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of them.
cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, December 2019, September 2024 and October 2025; UK sanctions designations

n: Smuggling networks protected by Bulgarian customs and border officials
d: Smuggling networks in Bulgaria had protection from officials inside the customs and border services, according to the US Treasury. In June 2021 it named Bulgarian officials and business figures, several of them in customs and border roles, under the Global Magnitsky Act, a US law that sanctions foreign officials for corruption. It was the largest single Magnitsky action ever taken against one country. Bulgarian prosecutions largely did not follow. The customs checkpoints on the Balkan route, the main land route for drugs into the EU, are run by the same institutions.
cite: US Treasury OFAC Global Magnitsky designations, June 2021; European Commission Rule of Law reports on Bulgaria

n: Belivuk crime group carried Serbian state security identification
d: Members of the Belivuk-Miljkovic group, a Belgrade criminal gang, held identification from Serbia's state security service and had access to protected facilities, according to evidence in their prosecution. Serbia's Special Prosecutor's Office for Organised Crime brought charges from 2021, and a former head of the security service was later charged in connection with the group. The case is still running, and the specific attributions remain contested in Serbian politics.
cite: Serbian Special Prosecutor's Office for Organised Crime indictments, 2021-2024; Belgrade Higher Court proceedings

n: 'Ndrangheta reached a senator, police and officials in Calabria
d: The 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, had people working for it inside Italian politics, policing and public offices, according to the Rinascita-Scott trial. With over 300 defendants it was Italy's largest organised crime trial since the Palermo maxi-trial of the 1980s, and in November 2023 the court in Vibo Valentia convicted 207 at first instance. Those convicted included a former senator and lawyer who had acted for 'Ndrangheta figures, along with police officers, officials and a former regional politician. Appeals are running.
cite: Tribunale di Vibo Valentia, Rinascita-Scott judgment, November 2023; Italian Direzione Nazionale Antimafia reporting

n: Cocaine network A Ultranza Py had a prosecutor and court staff
d: A Ultranza Py, a cocaine network shipping product along the Hidrovia (the Paraguay-Parana river route to the Atlantic), had a serving prosecutor, court officials and figures connected to Paraguay's legislature working with it. The 2022 investigation by Paraguay's public prosecutor's office charged them alongside the traffickers. One of the case's own prosecutors was later removed, and several principals fled before arrest.
cite: Paraguayan Ministerio Publico, Operacion A Ultranza Py case file, 2022-2024; Paraguayan Jurado de Enjuiciamiento de Magistrados

n: Guerreros Unidos ran Iguala's mayor and municipal police
d: Guerreros Unidos, a drug-trafficking gang in Guerrero state, had the mayor of Iguala, Jose Luis Abarca, and the town's municipal police acting for it. In September 2014 municipal police took forty-three students from the Ayotzinapa teacher-training college, who disappeared. Abarca was convicted of organised crime and kidnapping. The Interdisciplinary Group of Independent Experts, appointed by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, documented federal and state forces monitoring the events in real time. It is the best-evidenced case on this map of a town government operating as an arm of a trafficking organisation.
cite: Mexican federal court judgments, 2019 and 2022; GIEI Ayotzinapa reports; Mexican Comision para la Verdad y Acceso a la Justicia, 2022

n: Rio militias' allies held seats in Congress and the police
d: Rio de Janeiro's militias, groups that began as off-duty police running protection rackets and now control neighbourhoods, had allies holding elected and police office. In March 2024 Brazil's Federal Police arrested federal deputy Chiquinho Brazao, his brother Domingos Brazao, a former state accounts councillor, and Rivaldo Barbosa, a former head of the civil police intelligence bureau, over the 2018 killing of city councillor Marielle Franco. The Brazao brothers are alleged to have ties to militias, and Barbosa is accused of steering the investigation away from those who ordered the killing. All deny it. The case is at indictment stage.
cite: Brazilian Policia Federal and Procuradoria-Geral da Republica filings, March 2024; Supremo Tribunal Federal proceedings; Boston Globe, 'Three Rio officials arrested in connection with Marielle Franco killing', 24 March 2024

n: Crime boss alleged a Turkish minister protected trafficking
d: Turkish trafficking networks had protection from a former interior minister, according to Sedat Peker, a convicted Turkish organised crime figure. Turkey's interior minister commands the police. In a long series of videos posted from abroad in 2021, Peker made the claim in detail, including about a specific cocaine shipment. Opposition members raised it in parliament, but no charge followed and the allegations have never been tested. They are recorded because they were made publicly and in detail, and because the Susurluk scandal already on this map, a 1996 car crash that exposed links between police, politicians and gangsters, established the pattern they describe.
cite: Public statements by Sedat Peker, 2021; Turkish parliamentary opposition motions; no prosecution filed

n: Mexican cartels pay US border officers to wave loads through
d: Mexican cartels pay officers of US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the agency that inspects people and goods at the border, to let drug loads pass through ports of entry. CBP is the largest federal law enforcement agency in the United States, and its officers have produced more than 200 corruption convictions across a decade. In 2016 the agency's Integrity Advisory Panel found its internal affairs office too small for the caseload and said so publicly.
cite: CBP Integrity Advisory Panel final report, 2016; CBP Office of Professional Responsibility annual statistics; DOJ prosecution records
who: Mexican cartels at ports of entry

n: London crime families had officers inside the Metropolitan Police
d: London organised crime families were able to place or recruit officers inside the Metropolitan Police at will, according to Operation Tiberius, an internal Met report written in 2002 that named officers connected to specific families. The report was never published; it was leaked in 2014 and the Home Affairs Select Committee of MPs questioned police about it. No prosecutions followed and its findings have not been tested in any forum. It is the most senior internal assessment of its kind in a Western police service.
cite: Metropolitan Police Operation Tiberius report, 2002 (leaked 2014); UK Home Affairs Select Committee questioning, 2014

n: Hashish importer worked with Oslo's police narcotics chief
d: A hashish importer had the head of the Oslo police narcotics unit, Eirik Jensen, working with him. Jensen ran Oslo's narcotics section for years and was convicted of aggravated corruption and of complicity in importing around fourteen tonnes of hashish with an informant he had handled. The Borgarting Court of Appeal sentenced him to twenty-one years in 2020, and Norway's Supreme Court refused his appeal in 2021. It is the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia.
cite: Oslo District Court 2017 and Borgarting Court of Appeal 2020 judgments; Norwegian Supreme Court refusal, 2021

n: Swedish crime networks get police register data from insiders
rank: police employees and a security service officer
d: Swedish criminal networks obtain information from police databases through employees inside the police. Swedish courts have convicted police staff of passing data from law enforcement registers to networks, and separately convicted an officer of Sakerhetspolisen, the Security Service, of unauthorised disclosure. Police reporting describes insider access to registers as a systematic weakness rather than an isolated failure.
cite: Swedish district court judgments, 2021-2024; Polismyndigheten and Sakerhetspolisen public reporting

n: Cocaine importers recruit customs and terminal staff at German ports
d: Cocaine importers recruit customs officers and terminal employees at Hamburg and Bremerhaven, Germany's main container ports, to clear containers and pass on scanner information. Courts in Hamburg and Bremen have convicted such insiders in cases from 2020 to 2024. Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office treats port-side insider access as the decisive weakness in the northern European cocaine flow, as Belgian and Dutch assessments do for Antwerp and Rotterdam.
cite: Hamburg and Bremen Landgericht judgments, 2020-2024; Bundeskriminalamt Rauschgiftkriminalitat Bundeslagebild

n: Israeli crime families received case files from serving officers
d: Israeli crime organisations have obtained investigative material, such as details of cases being built against them, from serving police officers. Israeli district courts have convicted officers of passing it on, in cases brought between 2019 and 2024 by Mahash, the justice ministry department that investigates police. The organisations receiving the material are the same crime families shown on this map's group layer.
cite: Israeli Department for Investigation of Police Officers (Mahash) case records; district court judgments, 2019-2024

n: Chilean drug distributors protected by Carabineros officers
d: Drug distributors in Chile have had protection from officers of the Carabineros, Chile's national police. Chilean prosecutors have charged officers with reselling seized narcotics and protecting distribution in Santiago and the northern border region, in cases from 2020 to 2024 that ran alongside the force's wider crisis after the 2019 protests. In the same period Chile shifted from a consumer market to a transit route.
cite: Chilean Fiscalia Nacional and Fiscalia de Alta Complejidad case records, 2020-2024

n: Traffickers on the Golden Triangle route paid Malaysian drug police
d: Traffickers on the Golden Triangle export route have got Malaysian narcotics officers to work for them. The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission has prosecuted officers for releasing suspects and reselling seized drugs, in cases from 2018 to 2024 concentrated in Johor and the Klang Valley around Kuala Lumpur. The Golden Triangle, where Myanmar, Laos and Thailand meet, is Asia's main source of methamphetamine, and Malaysia hosts the region's busiest transhipment port.
cite: Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission prosecution records, 2018-2024; Malaysian sessions court judgments

n: Drug importers recruited Australian border and police officers
d: Drug importers have recruited Australian Border Force and state police officers to help bring drugs through Sydney and Melbourne. Courts in New South Wales and Victoria have convicted such officers in cases from 2016 to 2024, after referrals from the Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity, the body that investigates corruption in federal law enforcement. Australia pays the highest wholesale drug prices of any market on this map, which is the sum against which an insider is paid.
cite: Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity annual reports and referrals; NSW and Victorian court judgments, 2016-2024

n: Smugglers paid Canadian border officers to wave vehicles through
d: Drug smugglers have got Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers to wave their vehicles through at the Windsor-Detroit and Pacific Highway crossings. Ontario and British Columbia courts convicted officers in cases from 2014 to 2023. The CBSA had no independent civilian oversight body until legislation was brought forward in the 2020s, which is unusual among comparable agencies.
cite: Ontario and British Columbia court judgments, 2014-2023; CBSA internal affairs reporting; Public Safety Canada oversight legislation

n: Online gambling network allegedly protected by Thai deputy police chief
d: An online gambling network is alleged to have had protection from Thailand's deputy national police chief. He was removed and investigated in 2023, in a case that split the police leadership publicly, with disciplinary proceedings and filings by the Office of the Attorney-General running into 2024. The charges concern gambling proceeds rather than narcotics, but the protection arrangement and the laundering routes are the same ones the drug trade uses.
cite: Royal Thai Police disciplinary proceedings and Thai Office of the Attorney-General filings, 2023-2024

n: Smuggling channels run through customs officers at Ukraine's western border
d: Smuggling networks moving contraband into the European Union work through customs and border service officers at the crossings in Zakarpattia, Ukraine's westernmost region. Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau and State Bureau of Investigation charged officers there with running those channels in cases from 2022 to 2024. The charges concern smuggling generally rather than narcotics; the crossings are the same ones used by the eastern corridor on this map's route layer.
cite: Ukrainian National Anti-Corruption Bureau and State Bureau of Investigation case records, 2022-2024

n: Laundering networks bribed TD Bank staff to move $670 million
d: Money-laundering networks bribed employees of TD Bank, the US arm of Canada's Toronto-Dominion Bank, to move more than $670 million through its accounts over six years. Those bribed included a store manager; one employee took $11,000 in retail gift cards. The bank had left $18.3 trillion of activity unmonitored. In October 2024 TD Bank became the first bank in US history to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering. Penalties totalled about $3.09 billion, and regulators capped the size of its US units.
cite: US v. TD Bank NA, D.N.J., guilty plea October 2024
rank: Retail bank — branch staff and compliance (banks & money transmission)

n: Bulgarian cocaine group had a Credit Suisse banker handling its money
d: A Bulgarian cocaine-trafficking organisation led by Evelin Banev, a former wrestler, had a Credit Suisse relationship manager (the banker who handles a client's accounts) moving its money. Elena Pampoulova-Bergomi, a former Bulgarian tennis player, built the relationship with Banev. In June 2022 the Swiss Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona convicted her of money laundering and convicted Credit Suisse of failing to prevent it, the first criminal conviction of a major Swiss bank. The bank was fined 2 million Swiss francs and ordered to pay about 18.6 million euros; both said they would appeal.
cite: Bundesstrafgericht / Tribunal pénal fédéral, Bellinzona, June 2022; Irish Times, 'Credit Suisse found guilty over Bulgarian drug money failings', 27 June 2022
rank: Private bank — relationship management (banks & money transmission)

n: Launderers for crime groups worked through Banca Privada d'Andorra's managers
d: Professional launderers acting for transnational criminal organisations had senior managers at Banca Privada d'Andorra (BPA), a private bank in Andorra, knowingly processing their transactions. The US Treasury's financial-crime unit, FinCEN, found in March 2015 that hundreds of millions had moved through four US correspondent banks. Andorra took over BPA the next day and wound it up within the week, splitting it into a continuing bank and a bad bank; clients had to prove their funds legitimate to recover them. In July 2025 a court sentenced eighteen executives, the former chief executive to seven years and a 30 million euro fine. The defendants are appealing; shareholders argue the bank was closed on an administrative finding.
cite: FinCEN Section 311 notice of finding, 10 March 2015; Andorran intervention and liquidation, March 2015; Andorran court sentences, July 2025
rank: Private bank — third-party laundering (banks & money transmission)

n: Cocaine smugglers recruited the crew of MSC Gayane
d: Cocaine smugglers recruited officers and crew of the MSC Gayane, a container ship of the Mediterranean Shipping Company, to take drugs aboard at night at sea. In 2019 about 20 tonnes were seized from the ship in Philadelphia, the largest such seizure in US history at the time. Eight seafarers pleaded guilty, among them the chief mate and second mate, and received about 50 years in prison between them. The ship was released after the operator posted security. Because the cargo bypassed the export terminal, the weakness lay in who was on the crew list, not in the container manifest. The operator called itself a victim and said it was spending over $100 million on security.
cite: US v. Vasquez Reyes, Penda, Ilic, Kavaja and others, E.D. Pa., pleas and sentences 2019-2022
rank: Container vessel — chief mate, second mate and crew (shipping, freight & ports)

n: Cocaine networks recruit staff with access at Antwerp's terminals
d: Cocaine networks recruit employees of Antwerp's terminal operators, the companies that run the container docks, to get container reference codes, gate access and scanning records. Antwerp handles the largest cocaine volumes in Europe; seizures reached 116 tonnes in 2023. The port authority and operators have since restricted access and changed codes more often. A 2025 joint report by the EU drugs agency (EUDA) and the World Customs Organization found the weakness lies in staff access rather than screening technology.
cite: Antwerp port authority and terminal operator measures, 2022-2024; EUDA and World Customs Organization joint report, 2025
rank: Container terminals — hiring, gate systems and scan records (shipping, freight & ports)

n: Rotterdam extraction crews got container PIN codes from terminal staff
d: Crews that extract cocaine from containers at Rotterdam, known in Dutch as 'uithalers', have obtained PIN codes from terminal employees with access to the port's own container release system. The PIN releases a container for collection, so a stolen code lets the crew drive the box out. Rotterdam District Court has heard multiple prosecutions of such cases from 2019 to 2024. The weakness is administrative access rather than physical security.
cite: Rotterdam District Court proceedings, multiple, 2019–2024
rank: Terminal access and IT systems (shipping, freight & ports)

n: Ecuadorian cocaine exporters recruited Guayaquil port and customs staff
d: Ecuadorian cocaine exporters hide drugs in legitimate banana shipments leaving Guayaquil and have recruited port staff and customs officials to get them through. Prosecutions by Ecuador's attorney-general's office have reached exporters, port workers and customs officers, and national seizure volumes rose alongside export growth. Ecuador's criminality score on the Global Organized Crime Index rose to 7.48 in 2025.
cite: Fiscalia General del Estado prosecutions; UNODC seizure reporting
rank: Export logistics and cold chain (shipping, freight & ports)

n: 'Ndrangheta controls hiring at Gioia Tauro port
d: The 'Ndrangheta, the mafia organisation based in Calabria in southern Italy, has gained control over hiring and container handling at Gioia Tauro, Italy's largest transhipment port (a port where cargo is moved between ships rather than unloaded for the country). The port sits in the province of Reggio Calabria, where the 'Ndrangheta's hold is most complete. Deciding who works on the docks lets a crime group decide who handles which containers. This control has been documented by the Direzione Investigativa Antimafia, the Italian police directorate that investigates mafia groups, in its twice-yearly reports, and in proceedings brought by the anti-mafia prosecutors of Reggio Calabria. The drug seizures published each year at the port record only part of what passes through it.
cite: Direzione Investigativa Antimafia semi-annual reports; Reggio Calabria DDA proceedings
rank: Transhipment terminal — labour and clearance (shipping, freight & ports)

n: Drug networks recruited police and customs at Algeciras port
d: Hashish and cocaine trafficking networks around the Port of Algeciras, Spain's largest container port, have recruited members of the municipal police, the customs service and the port workforce to let their shipments through. Algeciras lies on the Strait of Gibraltar, eight miles from Morocco, the main source of hashish entering Europe. Successive operations by Spain's two national police forces, the Policia Nacional and the Guardia Civil, between 2018 and 2024 have arrested serving officers, not only dock workers, and the cases have gone before the provincial court in Cadiz. The arrests show the networks reached the officials whose job is to inspect the cargo.
cite: Spanish Policia Nacional and Guardia Civil operations, 2018–2024; Audiencia Provincial de Cadiz proceedings
rank: Container port and strait crossing — access control (shipping, freight & ports)

n: EU review finds cocaine networks have got inside EU ports
d: Cocaine smuggling networks have significantly penetrated EU ports, including the likely corruption of some port staff, a 2025 joint review by the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA) and the World Customs Organization (WCO), which coordinates customs services worldwide, concluded. Its evidence was the size of the seizures: more than 1,826 tonnes of drugs were seized in or bound for EU ports between January 2019 and June 2024, 1,244 tonnes of it at the ports themselves and 82 percent of it cocaine, mostly at Antwerp and Rotterdam. The average consignment was too large to move without help from inside, and the review placed the weak point in staff access rather than in screening technology. Belgian customs reported a record 116 tonnes seized at Antwerp in 2023.
cite: European Union Drugs Agency and World Customs Organization joint report, 2025; Belgian customs figures, January 2024
rank: Container terminals across the EU (shipping, freight & ports)

n: Drug networks recruited drivers in Ontario's trucking sector
d: Drug trafficking networks set up a broker-style operation inside Ontario's licensed cross-border trucking sector and recruited drivers to carry drug loads within legitimate supply chains. In trucking, a broker arranges which carrier and driver move a given load. Project Bay, a 2025–2026 investigation by Windsor Police, the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) and the Ontario Provincial Police, found drivers knowingly moving these loads. Twenty-one people were charged with 104 offences and about 1.7 tonnes of drugs were seized. Unlike a port, road freight has no single fixed checkpoint to corrupt, so the networks did their recruiting at the brokerage stage, where loads are assigned to drivers.
cite: Windsor Police, CBSA and Ontario Provincial Police, Project Bay, 2025–2026
rank: Commercial road freight — brokers and drivers (shipping, freight & ports)

n: PCC gang money placed in Sao Paulo funds, fintechs and fuel firms
d: The Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), a gang that began in Sao Paulo's prisons and now runs much of Brazil's drug trade, placed its money inside investment funds and fintechs (online financial-technology firms) in Faria Lima, Sao Paulo's financial district. Through more than 40 funds it held a port terminal, ethanol plants, a truck fleet and over a thousand petrol stations, and ran a fuel scheme built on illegal methanol imports. Operation Carbono Oculto, launched on 28 August 2025 by Brazil's federal tax authority (Receita Federal) and the Sao Paulo prosecutors' organised-crime unit (GAECO), put the sum laundered over four years at some 26 billion reais. Fintechs were not then regulated as financial institutions, which made the transactions hard to follow. Named firms deny wrongdoing and describe themselves as used rather than complicit.
cite: Operacao Carbono Oculto, Receita Federal and Sao Paulo GAECO, from 28 August 2025
rank: Investment funds and payment fintechs (banks & money transmission)

n: Gacanin drug organisation allegedly paid Bosnian officials
d: Bosnian prosecutors allege that the drug trafficking organisation of Bosnian trafficker Gacanin paid politicians in Bosnia and Herzegovina and worked with the head of the country's state security service, the agency responsible for intelligence and protecting the state. Gacanin has been designated, meaning placed on a sanctions list that freezes assets and bars dealings, by the US in action coordinated with Europol partners the Netherlands, France and Belgium. Leaked corporate records analysed by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) in August 2024 showed he used British Virgin Islands and Dubai free zone companies to employ men prosecutors describe as his cartel's operatives. UAE law then required a local sponsor, who was named on the filings; the sponsor's representative said she had no knowledge of narcotics or laundering.
cite: ICIJ analysis of leaked corporate records, August 2024; OFAC and Europol-coordinated designations with the Netherlands, France and Belgium
rank: Free zone company formation and local sponsorship (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)

n: CJNG hid its money inside tequila firms and petrol stations
d: Mexico's Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), a major drug-trafficking group, secretly owned or controlled ordinary businesses in Jalisco, Nayarit, Michoacán and Zacatecas: tequila distilleries and agave producers, beverage crop companies, gas stations, a private security firm, wholesale clothing and a children's footwear store. On 23 July 2026 the US Treasury named more than fifty individuals and entities in its largest single action against CJNG, sixteen of the companies listed under both its drug and terrorism sanction programmes. Designation freezes their US assets and bars dealings with them. The action was coordinated with Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit, followed nearly thirty earlier actions covering more than 250 targets since 2015, and also named the cartel's new leader, who took over after his stepfather was killed in a Mexican government operation in February 2026.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0573 and OFAC recent actions, 23 July 2026, under E.O. 14059 and E.O. 13224 as amended; coordinated with Mexico's Unidad de Inteligencia Financiera
rank: Agave and beverage crop production, fuel retail (gold, commodities & agribusiness)

n: CJNG used a Puerto Vallarta resort to feed its timeshare fraud
d: Mexico's Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) controlled Kovay Gardens, a resort near Puerto Vallarta that had run for more than two decades as an ordinary tourist business. The resort sold genuine timeshares, then passed its customer list to cartel-run call centres that sold the same owners fake resale and re-rental services. Between 2019 and 2023 the schemes cost roughly 6,000 American victims about $300 million. On 19 February 2026 the US Treasury designated (sanctioned) the resort with five individuals and seventeen companies in timeshare, real estate, tourism, travel, automotive services, accounting and financial services. It was Treasury's sixth action against CJNG timeshare fraud, bringing the total past 90 individuals and entities, and a 30-day licence was issued for others to wind down dealings with the resort.
cite: OFAC designations and Treasury statement, 19 February 2026, with General License authorising wind-down; prior CJNG timeshare designations from March 2023 and August 2025; investigation by FBI, DEA, IRS and CBP coordinated with Mexico's Unidad de Inteligencia Financiera
rank: Resort, call centres and 17 associated companies (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)

n: PCC hid its money in forty investment funds and a port terminal
d: Brazil's First Capital Command (PCC), a prison-born crime group from São Paulo, secretly owned businesses through about forty investment funds holding roughly 30 billion reais, some $5.5 billion: four ethanol plants, a port terminal, around 1,600 trucks and more than a thousand petrol stations across ten states. Federal Police and tax investigators uncovered the structure in Operation Carbono Oculto; the August 2025 raids ran 14 search and arrest warrants with roughly 350 searches in eight states and blocked about 1.2 billion reais. A follow-up operation found six fintechs operating as unlicensed parallel banks that had moved some 26 billion reais. Authorities named no individuals or companies, citing sealed proceedings. In May 2026 the United States designated the PCC as a terrorist organisation, exposing the holding structure to sanctions before any Brazilian trial.
cite: Operação Carbono Oculto, Brazilian Federal Police and Receita Federal, 28 August 2025; São Paulo state prosecutors; follow-up operation on fintech platforms, 2026; US Department of State designations, 28 May 2026
rank: Investment funds, ethanol plants, a port terminal, a truck fleet (banks & money transmission)

n: PCC controlled more than a thousand Brazilian petrol stations
d: Prosecutors in São Paulo allege that Brazil's First Capital Command (PCC), a prison-born crime group, controlled more than a thousand petrol stations generating some 52 billion reais in retail sales, along with fuel distributors, four ethanol plants and a transport fleet. The businesses were held through investment funds uncovered in Operation Carbono Oculto in August 2025. Owning the fuel chain let the PCC both clean drug money and earn from selling adulterated fuel to ordinary motorists, so the harm reached people with no link to the drug trade. Fuel also appears as a primary revenue source in US designations against Mexican groups. The US Department of State designated the PCC on 28 May 2026.
cite: Operação Carbono Oculto, August 2025, and São Paulo prosecutors; US Department of State designation statement, 28 May 2026
rank: Fuel retail, distribution and ethanol production (gold, commodities & agribusiness)

n: Clan del Golfo trafficker funded mayoral campaigns on its orders
d: A Colombian trafficker working for the Clan del Golfo, Colombia's largest armed drug-trafficking group, provided campaign support and funding to mayoral candidates in several Colombian municipalities on the orders of a Clan del Golfo member. The US Treasury revealed this when it designated (sanctioned) him under the Kingpin Act on 1 December 2020, together with three relatives and associates and four companies — an engineering firm, a homes business, a distributor and a general operations company — that laundered the profits with the relatives installed as figureheads and managers. Treasury assessed that he moved about 4,500 kilograms of cocaine during the autumn of 2018. The case links a crime group's front companies to its attempt to place friendly officials in local government.
cite: US Treasury press release sm1197, OFAC Kingpin Act designations, 1 December 2020, coordinated with US Southern Command; State Department statement, 1 December 2020; Clan del Golfo identified under the Kingpin Act, 31 May 2013
rank: Four companies held through relatives as figureheads (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)

n: Guyana police officer arranged safe passage for traffickers
d: A serving Guyanese police officer was accused by the US Treasury of arranging safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan drug traffickers, putting trafficking groups' interests inside the police force. He was one of four Guyanese and two Colombian nationals designated (sanctioned) on 5 June 2025 after an ICE Homeland Security Investigations inquiry; the others included two men Treasury says run the largest trafficking organisations in the country, two Colombians managing clandestine airstrips, and a former officer wanted over the abduction of a policeman in 2024. The networks use semi-submersibles from Guyanese and Surinamese ports and bury cocaine at airstrips, often in Barima-Waini. In March 2025 a vessel out of Guyana was stopped off Trinidad with about 182 kilograms stamped with a Sinaloa Cartel logo. Treasury called corruption in Guyana a significant obstacle.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0156 and OFAC designations, 5 June 2025; ICE HSI New York investigation; State Department International Narcotics Control Strategy Report, 2025
rank: Semi-submersible vessels and clandestine airfields (shipping, freight & ports)

n: Scam-compound boss advised two Cambodian prime ministers
d: Chen Zhi, founder of Cambodia's Prince Group, served as an adviser to two Cambodian prime ministers while, according to a US indictment in Brooklyn, his group ran scam compounds where trafficked workers held under debt bondage carried out investment fraud. The United States and United Kingdom designated (sanctioned) the Prince Group in October 2025 with 146 individuals and entities, adding nine people and 26 entities on 23 June 2026. A sitting Cambodian senator, Kok An, and his network were designated over the same scam-compound economy in April 2026. Chen Zhi was stripped of his Cambodian citizenship and sent to China in January 2026. Treasury cited at least $10 billion lost by Americans to Southeast Asian scam operations in 2024.
cite: OFAC designations under E.O. 13581 as amended, 23 June 2026 (Treasury release sb0538) and 14 October 2025; designation of Senator Kok An and network, 23 April 2026; US v. Chen Zhi, E.D.N.Y. indictment unsealed October 2025
rank: Senator's companies and a scam-compound network (casinos & junkets)

n: Cocaine gangs recruited IT staff inside Dutch and Belgian terminals
d: Cocaine-importing gangs recruited IT contractors and terminal planners working at the container ports of Rotterdam and Antwerp. Dutch and Belgian courts have convicted these insiders of handing over PIN codes, which release containers from the terminal, and of changing where containers were stacked, so that the gangs' extraction crews could find a specific box among millions and remove the drugs before customs checks. The cases came to light through prosecutions between 2021 and 2024. Because the insiders' access to the systems is legitimate, this kind of corruption is hard to screen for in advance.
cite: Rotterdam and Antwerp court judgments, 2021-2024; Dutch Openbaar Ministerie reporting
rank: Container terminal software and planning staff (shipping, freight & ports)

n: Traffickers recruited airport ground staff to move drugs
d: Drug-trafficking groups have recruited people already working inside airports — ground handlers, who load and unload baggage and cargo, along with cleaners and catering staff — to carry drugs past the security checkpoint for them. Prosecutors in Spain, France and Belgium, and in West African countries including Nigeria, have charged such staff between 2020 and 2024. The method works because these employees hold valid passes to secure areas, so the trafficking group does not need to beat the security check, only to pay someone who is allowed through it.
cite: Spanish, French and Belgian prosecution records, 2020-2024; Europol airport security reporting
rank: Ramp, catering and baggage staff (shipping, freight & ports)

n: Philippine mayor linked to scam hub found to be a foreign national
d: Offshore gambling and scam operators in the Philippines had a town mayor on their side who was later found to be a foreign national. Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) were companies licensed to run online gambling for customers abroad, and the sector employed tens of thousands. Alice Guo, mayor of Bamban in Tarlac province, was linked to a licensed operation in her town that was found to host fraud compounds and laundering, and she was later found unable to lawfully hold office. Senate hearings in 2024 exposed the abuses. The Philippine Ombudsman dismissed her in August 2024, and a Manila court later ruled she had never been qualified to serve. The president ordered the sector shut by the end of 2024, which displaced the operations rather than ending them.
cite: Philippine Presidential directive, July 2024; PAGCOR licence revocations; Philippine Senate committee hearings, 2024; Philippine Ombudsman dismissal order, August 2024 (Philstar, Inquirer, GMA News); Manila Regional Trial Court ruling on Guo's disqualification, June 2025 (Manila Bulletin)

n: Crime groups bought or funded football clubs to launder money
d: Organised crime figures in Spain, Italy and Belgium have bought or funded lower-division football clubs and then used them to move drug money, according to charges brought by prosecutors between 2018 and 2024. Once in control of a club, they pass proceeds through transfer fees (the price one club pays another for a player) and sponsorship deals. Transfer values are subjective, cross-border and agreed privately between clubs, so an inflated fee is hard to prove false. The cases describe the same structure in all three countries, with the club's owners or backers serving the crime group rather than the sport.
cite: Spanish Fiscalia Anticorrupcion and Belgian federal prosecution filings, 2018-2024; Europol financial crime reporting
rank: Sports clubs and player transfers (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)

n: Glencore bribed officials who allocated oil business
d: Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trading company, paid bribes to officials in other countries who decided who got oil cargoes and contracts, so that the business went to Glencore; it also manipulated markets. The bribery came to light through US, UK and Swiss prosecutions. Glencore pleaded guilty in the United States and the United Kingdom in 2022 and paid penalties totalling around $1.5 billion; the UK case concerned bribery in Africa. A Swiss court convicted it again in 2024.
cite: US Department of Justice and CFTC resolutions, May 2022; UK Serious Fraud Office conviction and sentencing, 2022-2023; Swiss Office of the Attorney General conviction, 2024; OCCRP, Glencore pleads guilty in the UK to bribery in Africa, 2022

n: Trafigura bribed an Angolan state oil official
d: Trafigura, a Swiss-based commodity trading company, paid bribes to an official at Sonangol, Angola's state oil company, to win oil business there. It was tried in Switzerland's Federal Criminal Court in December 2024, and in January 2025 the court convicted the company and a former executive, the second major trader convicted in a Swiss court. The Sonangol official was convicted alongside them. Trafigura also settled separately with Brazilian and US authorities over bribery. Physical commodity trading moves value across borders in a form that financial regulators do not see.
cite: Swiss Federal Criminal Court judgment, 2024; US Department of Justice resolution, 2024; Brazilian leniency agreement; Reuters, Trafigura and former executive found guilty of bribing Angolan official, January 2025; Ver Angola, Swiss company and former Sonangol executive convicted of corruption, January 2025; AP, Trafigura goes on Swiss trial, December 2024

n: Fuel smugglers had naval and customs officers inside Mexico's ports
d: A fuel-smuggling scheme in Mexico, known as 'huachicol fiscal' (tax-dodging fuel theft), had serving and former naval officers and customs officials working for it inside the ports that the Mexican Navy controls. Fuel was imported declared as lubricant additive to avoid import duty. In 2025 Mexican authorities arrested naval officers, customs officials and business figures over the scheme. It is the largest documented case of an armed force's own customs role being used for a private business, and the same terminals handle container traffic on known drug routes.
cite: Mexican Fiscalia General de la Republica and Secretaria de Marina statements, 2025; Mexican federal court filings
rank: Fuel importation and customs (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
